Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Explain the components of the skeletal system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 1 — Basic concepts of the MSK system: skeletal system

★ Memory hook — Skeleton = 206: Support · Protection · Movement · Haemopoiesis · Mineral store — axial 80, appendicular 126.

1Introduction

The skeletal system is the body's living framework: 206 bones in the adult, plus the cartilage, ligaments and joints that bind them. Mechanism first — bone is metabolically active tissue that constantly remodels itself in response to the loads it feels. Five functions you must name: support (rigid levers for posture), protection (skull for brain, rib cage for heart and lungs), movement (levers for muscle pull), haemopoiesis (red marrow makes blood cells), and mineral storage (about 99% of body calcium and most phosphorus, with yellow marrow storing fat).

2Physiology

By shape: long (femur), short (carpals), flat (ilium), irregular (vertebra), sesamoid (patella — the largest, embedded in quadriceps tendon to improve its leverage and shield the knee). By structure: compact bone (dense outer shell, resists bending) and cancellous bone (spongy inner mesh with trabeculae aligned along stress lines, resists compression). Developmentally, bones form by intramembranous or endochondral ossification.

3Pathophysiology

Bone is dynamic: Wolff's law states that bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress — thickening where loaded, resorbing where unloaded. So prolonged immobilisation causes disuse osteoporosis, while graduated weight bearing rebuilds stock. Indian context: with widespread vitamin D deficiency and postmenopausal osteoporosis, axial bone loss presents as thoracic kyphosis and fragility fractures — early weight-bearing exercise and DEXA screening are our preventive tools.

Examiner's tip: most students stop at a bone list. The 2 clinical marks sit in Wolff's law plus one Indian-context line (vitamin D deficiency, osteoporotic kyphosis) — write those and you separate yourself from the pack.

4Answer

The axial skeleton forms the upright axis of the body: the skull (22 bones plus 6 ear ossicles and the hyoid), the vertebral column (26 bones — 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx), and the thoracic cage (24 ribs and the sternum). Mechanism: this column transmits the entire superimposed body weight downwards and protects the spinal cord — which is why axial loading injuries (a fall from a scaffold, so common at Indian construction sites) damage it most at the thoracolumbar junction.

Pectoral girdles (clavicle and scapula, 4 bones) anchor the upper limbs (60 bones), and the pelvic girdles (2 hip bones) anchor the lower limbs (60 bones). Mechanism: the pectoral girdle sacrifices stability for mobility (shallow glenoid), while the pelvic girdle sacrifices mobility for stability (deep socket, strong ligaments) to bear weight in standing and gait — a comparison examiners reward.

Articular hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces (low friction, no blood supply — heals poorly), fibrocartilage forms menisci and discs (resists compression), ligaments passively limit joint range, and joints are classified as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial. The synovial joint — with its capsule, synovial membrane, cartilage and reinforcing ligaments — is the functional unit we treat every day.

Fig 1 — the two-division tree with bone counts, plus the five shapes. Reproduce both rows and the numbers: counts are where the easy marks hide.

5Recent advances

  • Watson et al. (2018) — the LIFTMOR randomised trial showed that 8 months of supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training improved lumbar-spine and femoral-neck bone mineral density and physical function in postmenopausal women with osteopenia/osteoporosis, with no fractures, challenging the belief that high-intensity loading is unsafe.
  • Kistler-Fischbacher et al. (2020) — a meta-analysis of exercise intensity and bone found that bone-targeted loading (progressive resistance and impact exercise) produces small but significant gains in lumbar-spine and hip bone mineral density in postmenopausal women, supporting supervised exercise as a core anti-osteoporosis therapy.
  • Osteocyte mechanosensing research (Bone Research, 2020; Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology, 2022) — osteocytes are the master mechanosensors of bone: mechanical loading suppresses sclerostin and disinhibits the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway, driving new bone formation — the molecular basis of Wolff's law and of therapeutic exercise for bone.
  • Regenerative-rehabilitation research (npj Regenerative Medicine, 2021) — exercise is now framed as 'regenerative rehabilitation': a single bout of cyclic stretch activates osteocyte signalling linked to bone regeneration, tying physiotherapy loading dose directly to bone mechanobiology.

6References

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — skeletal tissue structure.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — axial and appendicular divisions.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — bone remodelling and calcium homeostasis.
  4. Bonewald LF, et al. Molecular mechanosensors in osteocytes. Bone Research 2020;8:23.
  5. Robling AG, Bonewald LF, et al. The central role of osteocytes in the four adaptive pathways of bone's mechanostat. Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews 2020.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Enumerate the tools for measurement of body fat analysis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 2 — Anthropometry: body composition measurement

★ Memory hook — Fat tools ladder: Tape · BMI · Skinfold · BIA · Bod Pod · DEXA — cheap to criterion.

1Introduction

Body composition divides body mass into fat mass and fat-free mass (water, protein, bone mineral). Total body weight alone hides the difference between a muscular athlete and a sarcopenic obese patient — both can share a BMI of 28. Fat measurement quantifies obesity, tracks rehabilitation progress, and stratifies cardiometabolic risk. Arrange your answer as a ladder: from cheap field tools to criterion laboratory methods.

2Physiology

A painless, portable current (50 kHz) is passed through the body; fat-free mass, being water- and electrolyte-rich, conducts better, and fat resists the current — impedance predicts total body water and hence fat-free mass. Mechanism worth stating: it assumes constant tissue hydration, so dehydration or post-exercise readings distort it.

Hydrostatic (underwater) weighing: the patient is submerged and fully exhales; body density is computed from underwater weight by Archimedes' principle, then the two-compartment Siri equation converts density to fat percentage. Accurate but laborious and unpleasant. Air-displacement plethysmography (Bod Pod) replaces water with air displacement in a sealed chamber — same principle, far better tolerated.

3Pathophysiology

Measuring tape: waist circumference and waist–hip ratio estimate central (visceral) fat — for Asian Indians the cutoffs are 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women, lower than the western 102/88, because Indians develop diabetes at lower BMI. BMI (weight in kg divided by height in metres squared) is an obesity screen; the Asian-Indian action point is 23 kg/m², not 25. The skinfold caliper pinches subcutaneous fat at standard sites — the Durnin–Womersley four sites (biceps, triceps, subscapular, suprailiac) or Jackson–Pollock three or seven sites — and estimates total body fat from regression equations.

4Answer

DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) is today's practical gold standard — it splits the body into fat, lean soft tissue and bone mineral with a low radiation dose and regional (trunk vs limb) output. Isotope dilution (deuterated water) measures total body water. Others to name for the enumeration mark: near-infrared interactance, ultrasound of subcutaneous fat, and, for research, CT and MRI volumetry. Add potassium-40 whole-body counting if you remember it.

Fig 2 — the accuracy ladder, left to right, with the Indian cutoffs boxed below. Draw the ladder and name the tool on every rung: that alone is half the enumeration marks.

Match the tool to the purpose: tape and BMI for every clinic screening; calipers where you need percentage fat on a budget; DEXA when you need regional fat and bone together (obesity plus osteoporosis in the postmenopausal patient); isotope and CT methods stay research tools. One comparison line earns the last 1.5: field tools are cheap and repeatable but population-specific; criterion methods are accurate but costly and immobile.

Examiner's tip: the question says "enumerate" — the marks are for the complete list, not deep detail on any one tool. Seven-plus tools, one mechanism line each (how it actually estimates fat), and the Indian cutoffs as your finishing flourish.

5Recent advances

  • Campa et al. (2023) — new bioelectrical impedance vector analysis (BIVA) tolerance ellipses and phase-angle centile curves updated the 30-year-old adult reference values; phase angle is a portable, physiotherapy-relevant index of cell integrity and muscle quality.
  • Yi et al. (2022) — high-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis (2-3 MHz, e.g. InBody 970) shows good agreement with DEXA for fat-free mass and percentage body fat, extending BIA beyond single-frequency devices in clinical assessment.
  • Li et al. (2024) — a diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis found BIA agrees well with DEXA for muscle mass (pooled sensitivity 79%, specificity 95%), supporting BIA as a practical, radiation-free body-composition tool where DEXA is unavailable.
  • Csiernik et al. (2022) — a systematic review showed BIA is affordable and easy to use but heterogeneous and not consistently sensitive for detecting low muscle mass (sarcopenia), so device- and population-specific validation remains essential.

6References

  1. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — body composition assessment.
  2. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — anthropometry in clinical practice.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — body fluid compartments underlying BIA.
  4. Kim M, et al. A comparative study of high-frequency bioelectrical impedance analysis and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry for estimating body composition. Life 2022;12:994.
  5. Ward LC, et al. Individualized body geometry correction factor (KB) for bioimpedance spectroscopy. Physiological Measurement 2022.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the applications of Newton's second law in the human body.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 3 — Biomechanics: force, kinetics and kinematics

★ Memory hook — F = ma and torque = I x angular acceleration — force builds, force breaks.

1Introduction

Newton's second law: the net force acting on a body equals its mass times its acceleration (net force = mass × acceleration), and acceleration is in the direction of the net force. Angular form: net torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration. Mechanism first — the law is the bridge between muscle (which creates force) and motion (which is acceleration); almost every therapeutic exercise we prescribe is an application of it.

2Physiology

In walking, the ground reaction force is roughly 1.1 to 1.5 times body weight at loading response, rising to 2 to 3 times body weight in running — every step is your mass being decelerated and re-accelerated. In a vertical jump the athlete must generate force well above body weight to leave the ground. In sit-to-stand, quadriceps force must exceed body weight enough to produce upward acceleration of the trunk — which is exactly why elderly patients rock forward first, building acceleration over a longer path. Indian context: head-load carriers and porters walk with shorter, smoother steps — minimising the acceleration component lowers peak force on the spine.

Muscles create torque about joints; the segment's angular acceleration depends on its moment of inertia, which depends on how mass is distributed about the axis. A figure skater pulling the arms in reduces moment of inertia and spins faster with unchanged angular momentum. A cricket bowler or a badminton-smash player sequences proximal-to-distal so each segment accelerates off the previous one — the kinetic chain. A long lever arm (outstretched arm holding a dumbbell) multiplies the torque demand on the shoulder compared with the elbow-bent position.

3Pathophysiology

Injury occurs when net force produces an acceleration the tissue cannot survive. A fall on the outstretched hand dissipates the body's momentum through the wrist in milliseconds — large deceleration, large force, hence Colles' fracture. Whiplash: the head accelerates forward on a fixed trunk, loading cervical soft tissue beyond its tolerance. Non-contact ACL rupture: a strong quadriceps contraction decelerates an extending tibia rapidly — the same force that protects also tears. Helmets and crash helmets work by extending the deceleration time, which by the impulse relationship lowers the peak force.

Fig 3 — left: mass and acceleration feeding net force; right: the joint as an axis with torque spinning a segment. One line of algebra plus one limb sketch carries both forms of the law.

4Answer

Progressive resistance training works because strength adapts to the force demand. In osteoarthritis we teach slow, controlled movement — small accelerations mean small peak joint forces. In plyometrics we deliberately train rate of force development. The same principle guides assistive devices: a walker with a heavy patient requires a controlled, gradual rise from a chair rather than a quick push, because force needed falls when acceleration falls. This closes the loop: understand force, and you can both break and rebuild the body.

Examiner's tip: write the linear equation AND the angular (torque) equation — students who give only force = mass times acceleration cap themselves at 4 of the 10. Then give one named example per domain: gait, throwing, fall injury, and one treatment application.

5Recent advances

  • Wearable IMU gait-analysis studies (Sensors, 2021) — wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) now allow laboratory-grade joint kinetics and gait analysis outside the lab, with root-mean-square joint-angle differences of about 1.7-9.2 degrees versus optical capture.
  • Real-time OpenSim frameworks (Sensors, 2021) — real-time, OpenSim-based musculoskeletal frameworks compute joint moments, muscle forces and reaction loads live, enabling gait retraining that targets joint load as it happens.
  • Kanko et al. (2021) — markerless motion capture (Theia3D) shows good agreement with marker-based systems for spatiotemporal gait parameters and lower-limb kinematics, making quantitative clinical gait analysis feasible with simple video cameras.
  • Wang et al. (2021) — a finite-element musculoskeletal model driven solely by IMU sensors predicts knee contact mechanics and muscle forces (e.g. peak medial knee contact pressure about 11.3 MPa at loading response), linking Newtonian force analysis to clinical joint-load estimation.

6References

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — kinetics chapters.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — torque and levers.
  3. Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — determinants of gait and force in locomotion.
  4. Al Borno M, et al. OpenSense / IMU-driven biomechanical modelling of gait. Sensors 2021;21:7690.
  5. Mundt M, et al. Estimation of gait mechanics based on simulated and measured IMU data using an artificial neural network. Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology 2020;8:41.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Write basic concepts of exercise metabolism during core muscle strengthening.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 5 — Physiological basis of movement: exercise metabolism

★ Memory hook — Core holds run aerobic: low load, long hold, type I fibres, mitochondria.

1Introduction

The core is a cylinder: local stabilisers — transversus abdominis, multifidus, diaphragm and the pelvic floor — working at low intensity, continuously, anticipating limb movement; and global movers — rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, erector spinae — producing force and trunk motion. Mechanism first: the deep system provides segmental stiffness (spinal stability at low energetic cost), the superficial system produces torque. Their metabolic demands differ, and the examiner wants you to see why.

2Physiology

Three systems supply ATP: the phosphagen system (immediate, about 10 seconds of all-out work), anaerobic glycolysis (up to roughly 2 minutes, lactate-forming), and aerobic metabolism (unlimited in duration at low intensity, yielding about 36 ATP per glucose molecule in the mitochondria). Core strengthening is classically low-load, high-duration — sustained submaximal isometric holds of 10 to 30 seconds, repeated many times — so it runs predominantly on the aerobic system, with anaerobic glycolysis contributing as hold time and fatigue build up.

Neural adaptations come first (better anticipatory activation timing of transversus abdominis and multifidus), then peripheral ones: increased mitochondrial density and capillarisation of the deep stabilisers, higher oxidative enzyme activity, and greater fatigue resistance. This is why stabiliser training emphasizes endurance — more repetitions, longer holds, brief rests — rather than heavy loading, which would merely recruit the global movers.

Fig 4 — the three-system continuum over hold time, with the aerobic block oversized because that is what core work mainly uses. Label the time boundaries: they carry the metabolic marks.

3Pathophysiology

Recruitment follows the size principle: small, fatigue-resistant type I motor units fire first; type II units join only as force demand rises. A sustained isometric hold above about 15 to 20% of maximal voluntary contraction compresses intramuscular vessels, occluding local blood flow — oxygen delivery falls while the muscle keeps consuming ATP, so stored phosphocreatine depletes, glycolysis accelerates, and hydrogen ions and inorganic phosphate accumulate. That accumulation — not lactate itself — is what the student feels as burning, trembling and the breath-holding urge. Release of the hold restores reperfusion and clears metabolites.

4Answer

Prescription follows the metabolism: begin with 5 to 10 second holds with rest, progress to 20 to 30 seconds, because brief rests allow reperfusion and metabolite clearance. Teach diaphragmatic breathing during holds — a core exercise is also a breathing exercise, and breath-holding (a Valsalva manoeuvre) spikes blood pressure, which matters in the many hypertensive Indian patients in our OPDs. In type 2 diabetes, regular aerobic-dominant core and endurance work improves glucose uptake. If a patient trembles or burns early, that is metabolic fatigue telling you the load — not the willpower — is wrong.

Examiner's tip: the question asks for metabolism, not a list of core exercises. Anchor every paragraph to ATP: which system, why, and how the isometric hold changes it. Then one line on Valsalva avoidance shows you can translate theory into safe practice.

5Recent advances

  • BFR dose-response meta-analysis (Frontiers in Physiology, 2022) — a meta-analysis found blood-flow-restriction (BFR) training improves lower-limb extensor strength, with optimal parameters of a load of 30% or less of 1RM, more than 4 weeks, at least 3 sessions a week and cuff pressure of 200 mmHg or less.
  • Low-load isometric BFR studies (BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation, 2021) — low-load isometric exercise with BFR augments muscle activation, metabolic stress and cell swelling — effects similar to dynamic exercise — and is valuable where large joint movement is contraindicated.
  • Centner et al. (2019) — a meta-analysis showed low-load BFR training and BFR-walking increase muscle strength and mass in older adults, offering a low-mechanical-stress way to build muscle when high-load exercise is not tolerated.
  • Wang et al. (2012) — a meta-analysis found core stability exercise was more effective than general exercise for short-term pain and back-specific function in chronic low back pain, supporting progressive core-stabilisation training in rehabilitation.

6References

  1. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — energy systems and muscle metabolism.
  2. ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — metabolic responses to resistance training.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — core stabilisation progression.
  4. Centner C, Lauber B. A systematic review and meta-analysis on neural adaptations following blood flow restriction training. Frontiers in Physiology 2020;11:887.
  5. Dose-response relationship of blood flow restriction training on isometric and maximum muscle strength: a meta-analysis. Frontiers in Physiology 2022.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Explain mechanics and pathomechanics of the knee joint.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6 — Mechanics and pathomechanics: knee joint

★ Memory hook — Knee: screw-home locks, meniscus hoops, Q angle pulls — popliteus unlocks.

1Introduction

The knee moves mainly in the sagittal plane: flexion about 0 to 135 or 150 degrees, extension to 0, with hyperextension up to about 5 to 10 degrees in some. Rotation is only possible when the knee is unlocked — about 45 degrees total when flexed, and it is coupled: as the knee approaches terminal extension the tibia rotates laterally about 10 to 15 degrees, the screw-home mechanism, which locks the knee into a close-packed, energy-efficient standing position (the femur rotates medially on the tibia if you describe it from the femur's side — state your reference). Popliteus unlocks it by laterally rotating the femur.

2Physiology

Arthrokinematically the femoral condyles both roll and glide posteriorly on the tibia during flexion, and the menisci travel with the femur — moving posteriorly in flexion, anteriorly in extension. The menisci are fibrocartilage (mostly circumferentially arranged type I collagen) carrying roughly half the joint load; their wedge shape converts vertical compression into hoop stress along their circumference, spreading load onto the tibial rim. After total meniscectomy, contact stress in that compartment rises several-fold — which is why degenerative changes follow, and why we now preserve, repair or transplant menisci.

The patella acts as a pulley, increasing the quadriceps extensor moment arm by roughly 30% in early flexion. The Q angle — anterior superior iliac spine to patella centre to tibial tuberosity, about 13 to 18 degrees — directs the quadriceps pull laterally on the patella, resisted by the vastus medialis obliquus and the medial retinaculum. Patellofemoral joint reaction force rises with knee flexion — near 3 times body weight climbing stairs, up to about 7 times body weight in a deep squat. That single number explains anterior knee pain in deep-squatting activities.

3Pathophysiology

Coronal malalignment: genu varum (bow legs — not uncommon in India from nutritional rickets) shifts load medially and accelerates medial compartment osteoarthritis; genu valgum shifts it laterally. Ligament failure: anterior cruciate ligament insufficiency removes the check to anterior tibial translation and rotational laxity — the pivot-shift give-way on pivoting; posterior cruciate injury reverses the translation, worse on downhill steps. Extensor mechanism: excessive Q angle, weak vastus medialis obliquus or tight lateral retinaculum cause lateral patellar tracking, retropatellar compression and eventual chondromalacia. Meniscal derangement: the locked bucket-handle tear blocks terminal extension — a knee that will not fully straighten is a mechanical sign, not pain behaviour.

Fig 5 — left: the Q angle from ASIS through patella to tibial tuberosity; right: the screw-home rotation of the tibia in terminal extension. Draw the two together and both the patellofemoral and tibiofemoral stories are told in one figure.

4Answer

Assessment: varus and valgus stress tests for the collateral ligaments, Lachman (most sensitive) and the anterior drawer for the ACL, posterior sag and drawer for the PCL, McMurray for meniscal tears, and patellar apprehension for instability. Treatment follows mechanism: strengthen quadriceps (especially vastus medialis) and hamstrings, correct dynamic valgus in landing and squatting, restore full extension after a locked knee, and respect the deep squat and cross-legged sitting so central to Indian daily life — after meniscal repair or arthroplasty, graded return to floor sitting is a realistic, culturally relevant goal.

Examiner's tip: "mechanics and pathomechanics" means normal first, abnormal second — keep the symmetry. Score the easy anchors: screw-home (with popliteus unlocking), meniscal hoop stress, Q angle with the 3×–7× body weight patellofemoral reaction, and one named malalignment with its compartment consequence.

5Recent advances

  • Willy et al. (2019) — the APTA clinical practice guideline for patellofemoral pain recommends exercise therapy combining hip- and knee-targeted exercises as the critical component, and advises against using manual therapy or electrophysical agents in isolation.
  • Crossley et al. (2016) — the international patellofemoral pain consensus statement recommends combining hip and knee exercises in preference to knee exercises alone, and supports short-term foot orthoses, informing evidence-based knee rehabilitation.
  • Screw-home measurement in knee OA (cross-sectional study, 2020) — screw-home movement is reduced and total tibial rotation altered in knee osteoarthritis; it can be measured with an inertial sensor, and restoring normal articular motion is a rehabilitation target.
  • Six-DOF patellofemoral simulation studies (Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine, 2020) — six-degrees-of-freedom patellofemoral simulation shows that patella alta, trochlear groove depth, TT-TG distance and femoral anteversion interact to change patellar tilt, translation and contact force, informing assessment and loading modification.

6References

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — knee arthrokinematics.
  2. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — joint forces and meniscal load sharing.
  3. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — knee special tests.
  4. Alteration of screw-home movement in patients with knee osteoarthritis: a cross-sectional study. 2020.
  5. Patellofemoral mechanics: a review of pathomechanics. Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine 2020.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain postural abnormalities seen in the thoracic region.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 7 — Posture: normal and abnormal, deformities

★ Memory hook — Flexible vs rigid: prone extension corrects postural kyphosis, not Scheuermann's.

1Introduction

Thoracic posture is the sagittal shape of the upper spine — the normal kyphosis and its deviations. Because the thoracic curve must absorb load and shield the heart and lungs, abnormalities here are common, often postural and sometimes structural, and they present daily in physiotherapy practice — from the adolescent slouch to the osteoporotic dowager's hump.

2Physiology

The thoracic spine is a primary (kyphotic) curve, present from birth, measuring roughly 20 to 45 degrees of forward convexity. Mechanism first: the curve is a shock absorber — it increases column flexibility and raises load-bearing capacity, and the attached rib cage converts the thorax into a stiff protective cylinder for heart and lungs. Normal posture is assessed against a plumb line through the ear, shoulder and greater trochanter; the small, compensatory interplay of cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis keeps the head over the pelvis at minimal energy cost.

3Pathophysiology

Increased round-back from sustained slouched sitting, weak thoracic extensors and tight anterior structures. The defining test: the deformity corrects on voluntary extension or on lying prone over a bolster. It causes fatigue-type ache across the mid-scapular region, and typically responds to postural re-education, thoracic extension strengthening and ergonomic correction — in young students, heavy backpacks carried on one shoulder make this a daily OPD presentation.

Scheuermann's disease is a structural adolescent kyphosis: at least three adjacent vertebrae each wedged 5 degrees or more, with irregular vertebral end-plates and Schmorl's nodes, classically in the thoracic or thoracolumbar spine of teenage boys. It is rigid — it does not correct on extension or prone hyperextension over a bolster. Pain is variable; cardiopulmonary compromise appears only in severe curves. Differentiating rigid from flexible is the diagnostic hinge of the whole answer.

Thoracic flat back is loss of the normal kyphosis — a straight, stiff thoracic spine that transmits axial load more like a column, reducing shock absorption and often associated with a flat scapular posture and posterior ligamentous strain. Thoracic scoliosis is a lateral curvature with vertebral rotation — most often adolescent idiopathic, with asymmetric shoulder height, a prominent scapula, and a rib hump on forward bending. Osteoporotic compression fractures in the elderly form a third, increasingly common structural kyphosis — multiple wedge fractures in the postmenopausal Indian woman present as the dowager's hump, with loss of height and a compensatory cervical extension posture to keep the eyes level.

Fig 6 — left: the normal S with the plumb line; right: the exaggerated rigid kyphosis and the rib hump of scoliosis seen on forward bending. Mark the 20–45 degree normal range and the "three vertebrae, five degrees" rule.

4Answer

Inspect from the side and behind with the patient standing: plumb line alignment, shoulder and scapular symmetry, depth of the cervical and lumbar curves. The prone extension test distinguishes flexible from rigid kyphosis. The Adam's forward bend test with a scoliometer quantifies the rib hump; radiographic Cobb angle grades scoliosis (10 degrees defines it; bracing is usually considered above 25 to 40 degrees in a growing child). Always screen the whole spine — a primary lumbar curve produces a compensatory thoracic one.

Flexible kyphosis: postural re-education, thoracic extensor and scapular retractor strengthening, anterior chest stretching, ergonomic advice. Structural kyphosis: extension exercises over a roll or bolster, and for progressive Scheuermann's in the growing child, a brace plus a structured exercise programme. Scoliosis: observation for small curves, bracing for moderate progressive curves in the immature, physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises as an adjunct, and surgery for severe ones. The osteoporotic spine additionally needs medical bone protection, safe weight-bearing and balance training to prevent the next fracture.

Examiner's tip: the structure of this answer is the marks. Normal parameters, then each abnormality with its one discriminating feature — flexible versus rigid, rib hump versus plumb line — and always end with assessment. Students who write four kyphosis paragraphs and forget flat back and scoliosis lose 2 easy marks.

5Recent advances

  • Fernández et al. (2025) — a systematic review found therapeutic exercise significantly improves thoracic kyphosis angle in adolescents and young adults, with Schroth-based three-dimensional and corrective programmes among the most effective.
  • Ponzano et al. (2021) — exercise reduces kyphosis angle in adults aged 45 and over, with improvements in back-extensor strength, endurance, quality of life and pain.
  • Gheitasi et al. (2023) — combining corrective exercise with bracing produced a 15.5-degree reduction in Cobb angle versus 8.8 degrees for bracing alone in adolescents with thoracic hyperkyphosis.
  • Bezalel et al. (2019) — Schroth three-dimensional exercise produced significantly greater improvement in thoracic kyphosis angle than anti-gravity exercises in adolescents with Scheuermann's kyphosis, supporting curve-specific physiotherapy.
  • Taslimipour et al. (2020) — virtual-reality dance training improved kyphosis angle and respiratory parameters (forced vital capacity and FEV1) in young women with postural hyperkyphosis.

6References

  1. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — spinal curves and posture.
  2. McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine — postural syndrome and sagittal alignment.
  3. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — scoliosis and kyphosis examination.
  4. Ponzano M, et al. Exercise for improving age-related hyperkyphosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis with GRADE assessment. Osteoporosis International 2021.
  5. Therapeutic exercise on the management of hyperkyphosis in adolescence and young adulthood: a systematic review. 2025.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Write the biomechanical analysis of gait in ankle instability.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 8 — Gait and function: gait analysis, gait deviations

★ Memory hook — Unstable ankle: inversion at loading, early heel rise, weak push-off, hip hike.

1Introduction

Gait is the window into lower-limb function, and the ankle is where it most often fails. Chronic ankle instability — the residual giving-way and recurrent sprain after an inversion injury — leaves a characteristic biomechanical fingerprint across the gait cycle. This analysis keeps the normal ankle trace as its reference, then reads every stance and swing deviation against it.

2Physiology

At initial contact the ankle is neutral; through loading response it plantarflexes, then dorsiflexes progressively to about 10 degrees by terminal stance as the tibia advances over the foot, and finally plantarflexes sharply to about 20 degrees at push-off. The subtalar joint pronates at loading response (mobile adapter, shock absorption), then supinates into a rigid lever through push-off. The ankle plantarflexors deliver the burst for push-off, and the triceps surae works eccentrically through mid-stance to control tibial advancement. Keep this trace in mind: every deviation below is a corruption of it.

3Pathophysiology

Chronic instability follows the typical inversion sprain; define both halves. Mechanical instability is ligament laxity (anterior talofibular ligament, calcaneofibular ligament) on stress testing. Functional ankle instability is recurrent giving way without measurable laxity — a sensorimotor failure. Mechanism: damaged mechanoreceptors in the torn ligaments and capsule feed inaccurate proprioception to the central nervous system, so reflex correction of sudden inversion arrives late. During stance the patient shows excessive or prolonged pronation or sudden inversion episodes at loading response, early heel rise from a shortened, guarded push-off, reduced single-limb support time on the affected limb, decreased stride and step length, slower comfortable speed, and a wider base of support. The ground reaction force vector passes lateral to the ankle precisely when the peroneals are least ready.

The unstable foot is carried in slight plantarflexion and inversion to protect the lateral structures, so toe clearance suffers. Compensations appear from the next joint up: increased hip and knee flexion (an exaggerated steppage-like strategy), hip hiking of the swing-side pelvis, and sometimes circumduction. The result is an energy-costly swing with poor foot placement accuracy at the next initial contact — and the cycle of self-distrust continues.

Laboratory gait analysis shows reduced peak plantarflexion moment and power burst at push-off (a weak push), altered vertical ground reaction force shape with a flattened second peak, and increased ankle inversion moments in some patients. Electromyography reveals delayed peroneal reaction time, reduced peroneus longus strength, and co-contraction of the pretibial group with the triceps surae to splint the joint. Dynamic balance tests such as the Star Excursion Balance Anterior reach (anterior reach deficit greater than about 4 cm between limbs predicts future sprain) and single-leg hop tests objectify it in the clinic.

Fig 7 — one gait cycle bar with the four key deviations flagged along it. Anchoring each deviation to its phase converts a memorised list into a biomechanical analysis.

4Answer

Because the mechanism is sensorimotor, rehabilitation is more than strengthening: proprioceptive and balance training (single-leg stance progressions, wobble board, eyes closed), peroneal strength and reaction training, perturbation and hopping/landing control, agility before return to sport, and taping or bracing during the vulnerable early weeks. Barefoot balance work on uneven surfaces is practical in the Indian setting where much daily life occurs unshod — a culturally native form of proprioceptive training.

Examiner's tip: "biomechanical analysis" demands phase-by-phase structure — normal first, then stance, then swing, then the measurable kinetics. Spend the first paragraph on the normal trace; deviations only earn marks when the reader can see what they deviate from.

5Recent advances

  • Tajdini et al. (2022) — individuals with chronic ankle instability (CAI) show greater inter-limb asymmetry in the first peak of vertical ground reaction force, loading rate, and peroneus longus and gluteus medius activity during walking.
  • Ortega et al. (2024) — a systematic review and meta-analysis showed gait-training interventions improve lower-extremity biomechanics in CAI, medialising plantar pressure and increasing fibularis longus activity, so targeted gait training should be considered in rehabilitation.
  • Mollà-Casanova et al. (2021) — a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found balance training significantly improves function, ankle instability and dynamic balance in CAI, supporting balance training as a core rehabilitation component.
  • Martin et al. (2021) — the International Ankle Consortium clinical practice guideline recommends proprioceptive and neuromuscular exercise to improve dynamic postural stability and patient-perceived stability in CAI.
  • CAI proximal-joint systematic review (Frontiers in Physiology, 2022) — CAI alters proximal joints too: altered hip and knee movement strategies during side-cutting, stop-jump and landing may raise anterior cruciate ligament injury risk, guiding proximal-focused rehabilitation.

6References

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — ankle complex mechanics.
  2. Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — determinants of gait framework.
  3. Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — ankle rehabilitation.
  4. Inter-limb asymmetry of kinetic and electromyographic during walking in patients with chronic ankle instability. Scientific Reports 2022;12:4025.
  5. Lower limb biomechanics in individuals with chronic ankle instability during gait: a case-control study. 2021.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Explain the theories and models of pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 9 — Pain theories, specific pain states and syndromes

★ Memory hook — Specificity to Pattern to Gate (1965) to Neuromatrix (1999) to Biopsychosocial.

1Introduction

Pain is the commonest reason a patient reaches a physiotherapist, yet it correlates poorly with tissue damage — phantom limb pain hurts in a limb that no longer exists; imaging-identical disc bulges incapacitate one patient and not another. Each theory in this answer is an attempt to close that gap, and the examiner wants to see the progression, not four unrelated paragraphs: each model fixes the failure of the one before it.

2Physiology

The landmark gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, published in Science in 1965) placed modulation in the dorsal horn: large-diameter A-beta (touch) fibres and small-diameter A-delta and C (nociceptive) fibres both end on transmission cells in the substantia gelatinosa. Large-fibre activity closes the gate (inhibits transmission); small-fibre activity opens it. Descending fibres from the brain can set the gate too — the first theory to put the brain inside the pain loop. It explains, in one stroke, why rubbing an injury helps, why TENS at high frequency relieves pain, and why distraction and mood matter. Limitation to name for balance: it stops at the spinal cord, so it still cannot explain chronic pain or phantom phenomena fully.

3Pathophysiology

Melzack's neuromatrix (Pain, 1999) answers that limitation: pain is the output of a widely distributed neural network — the body-self neuromatrix — integrating somatosensory, limbic, thalamic and cortical inputs with genetic and experiential determinants. Pain is a multidimensional percept produced by the brain's "neurosignature" of the body, not a direct readout of tissue signals. It explains phantom limb pain (the neurosignature persists after the input is gone), chronic pain without ongoing damage, and why stress, sleep and beliefs modulate pain — the conceptual foundation of modern pain neuroscience education.

Fig 8 — the classic gate diagram: large fibres in, small fibres in, the substantia gelatinosa gate, T cells, and descending control from the brain. Label all five boxes; this figure is the highest-yield drawing in the pain unit.

4Answer

Specificity theory (Descartes' pathway concept, refined by von Frey): pain is a dedicated modality with its own receptors, dedicated A-delta and C afferents, and a specific line to a pain centre in the brain. Strong point: it predicted nociceptors, which were later found. Weak point: it cannot explain why gentle touch relieves pain or why pain persists after healing. Pattern (intensity) theory (Goldscheider): there are no dedicated pain fibres; pain results from intense stimulation producing a specific spatio-temporal pattern of firing. Strong point: it recognised central summation. Weak point: intense stimuli do not always cause pain. Keep each theory to a strong-point, weak-point pair — that is the analytical style that scores.

The current working model treats pain as the product of interacting biological (tissue state, sensitisation), psychological (fear, catastrophising, expectations) and social (family, work, culture) factors — the neuromatrix applied to a whole person. Physiotherapy translates the models directly: TENS, massage, thermal agents and movement all act by closing the gate with large-fibre input; graded exposure and pain education target fear-avoidance; exercise remodels the neurosignature. In the Indian clinic, pain beliefs shaped by family opinion and the cultural meaning of rest versus activity are genuinely part of the biology you are treating — address them or your exercise programme fails.

Examiner's tip: name, date, journal — Melzack and Wall, Science, 1965; Melzack, Pain, 1999. Then one clinical application per theory (rubbing and TENS for the gate; phantom limb for the neuromatrix; yellow flags for biopsychosocial). Theories with no application read like history; applications are what a physiotherapy examiner pays for.

5Recent advances

  • Central sensitisation as a third pain mechanism (Lancet Rheumatology, 2021) — central sensitisation is now recognised as a third core pain mechanism (alongside nociceptive and neuropathic pain), documented across fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and spinal pain — the basis for targeted pain education and graded activity.
  • Louw et al. (2016) — a systematic review of 13 RCTs found pain neuroscience education reduces pain, improves function, lowers disability and reduces psychosocial factors in chronic musculoskeletal pain.
  • Siddall et al. (2021) — a meta-analysis showed combining pain neuroscience education with exercise produces greater short-term improvements in pain, disability and kinesiophobia than exercise alone.
  • Wood & Hendrick (2019) — a meta-analysis found adding pain neuroscience education to usual physiotherapy improves short-term pain and disability in chronic low back pain, supporting its routine use alongside exercise.
  • The 'distributed nociceptive system' framework (Trends in Neurosciences, 2020) — pain is reframed as population-coded and highly distributed across the neuraxis, supporting cognitive and physical therapies as system-level treatments.

6References

  1. Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965;150:971–979.
  2. Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999;Suppl 6:S121–S126.
  3. Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System — pain physiology and clinical translation.
  4. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — pain management principles.
  5. Curatolo M. Central sensitization and pain: pathophysiologic and clinical insights. 2022.
  6. Central sensitisation in chronic pain conditions: latest discoveries and their potential for precision medicine. Lancet Rheumatology 2021.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe soft tissue repair and healing in meniscal injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6 — Mechanics and pathomechanics: skeletal and soft tissue, meniscus

★ Memory hook — Red-red heals, white-white does not — the blood supply decides.

1Introduction

The menisci are C-shaped fibrocartilaginous wedges built of densely packed type I collagen, predominantly circumferential with a few radial tie fibres — the architecture that converts compressive load into hoop tension. Their cells are fibrochondrocytes, hybrids that behave part-fibroblast, part-chondrocyte, sitting sparse and avascular in the deep matrix. The peripheral third receives blood from the genicular arterial network; the inner two-thirds are nourished only by diffusion from synovial fluid. Hence the surgical zones: red-red (outer, vascular), red-white (middle, transitional), and white-white (inner, avascular). Every prediction about healing follows from this one anatomical fact — build the answer on it.

2Physiology

1. Inflammatory (bleeding) phase, roughly days 0 to 7: only a red-zone tear forms a fibrin clot scaffold, releasing platelet-derived growth factor and attracting inflammatory cells. A white-zone tear does not even bleed — the healing cascade never starts. 2. Proliferative (fibroblastic) phase, roughly 2 to 6 weeks: fibrochondrocytes and invading vascular buds migrate into the clot and lay down disorganised type I and III collagen; a fibrovascular scar bridges the tear, weakest at about 1 to 2 weeks. 3. Remodelling phase, months: scar collagen reorients to withstand shear and compression, cellularity falls, and the tissue approaches — but never equals — native organisation and strength.

3Pathophysiology

(1) The avascular inner two-thirds cannot mount the inflammatory first phase without a clot; (2) fibrochondrocyte density is low and their proliferative capacity is modest; (3) constant loading and motion in synovial fluid dilutes and washes out the fibrin scaffold and growth factors; (4) the complex load environment — hoop tension plus shear — repeatedly tests the immature scar. This is why a peripheral vertical tear can heal while a complex degenerative white-zone tear cannot.

Fig 9 — top: the three-zone cross-section, blood fading centripetally; bottom: the three healing phases. The two drawings together ARE the answer — zones predict healing, phases describe it.

4Answer

Zone (red-red heals, white-white does not), tear pattern (peripheral vertical-longitudinal heals best; complex, horizontal and degenerative tears poorly), rim width from the synovial attachment (tears within about 3 mm heal best), patient age and vascularity, knee stability (an unstable ACL-deficient knee repeatedly displaces the meniscus and impairs healing), and the quality of rehabilitation — protected weight bearing and controlled motion stimulate, premature deep flexion under load disrupts.

Repairable red-zone tears in the young — peripheral vertical tears — are sutured (inside-out, all-inside techniques) because they can heal; irreparable white-zone degenerative tears in the older patient undergo partial meniscectomy, sacrificing the least tissue possible (remember the contact-stress arithmetic from the knee mechanics answer). Rehabilitation honours the biology: a phased progression of range and weight bearing over about 4 to 6 weeks, avoiding deep loaded flexion in the early scar phase — then a graded return to the squats and cross-legged sitting of daily Indian life, and back to sport with the landing-control training of the ankle answer.

Examiner's tip: this is two answers braided into one — soft tissue healing phases AND meniscal specifics. The braiding sentence is "the blood supply decides whether the general healing script even begins." Zones, phases, four reasons for poor healing, then treatment: that skeleton, filled in, is a full 10.

5Recent advances

  • Kise et al. (2016) — in a randomised trial (BMJ), 12 weeks of supervised exercise therapy alone gave knee-function outcomes comparable to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy at 2 years for degenerative meniscal tears, with greater thigh-muscle strength, supporting exercise-first management.
  • van de Graaf et al. (2018) — the ESCAPE randomised trial found exercise-based physical therapy noninferior to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for patient-reported knee function at 24 months in nonobstructive degenerative meniscal tears.
  • van de Graaf et al. (2022) — the 5-year follow-up of the ESCAPE trial showed exercise-based physical therapy remained noninferior to surgery for knee function, with comparable radiographic osteoarthritis progression, reinforcing physiotherapy as preferred first-line care.
  • Skou et al. (2022) — the DREAM randomised trial (NEJM Evidence) found that in young, active adults with meniscal tears, early surgery was not superior to 12 weeks of supervised exercise and education, with three of four avoiding surgery at 1 year.

6References

  1. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — meniscal structure and load sharing.
  2. Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — meniscal injury management.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — soft tissue healing and rehabilitation timelines.
  4. Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — meniscal testing and surgical decision context.
  5. Keller RE, et al. Biological augmentation of meniscal repair: a systematic review. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy 2022;30:1915-1926.
  6. Meniscal repair: the current state and recent advances in augmentation. 2021.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe mechanics and pathomechanics of the hip joint.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper II Unit 6 — Mechanics and pathomechanics: hip joint

★ Memory hook — Hip: abductor arm short, body-weight arm long, 3x BW — cane in the opposite hand.

1Introduction

The hip is a synovial ball-and-socket joint: the femoral head (about two-thirds of a sphere) seated in the deep acetabulum, deepened by the fibrocartilaginous labrum and secured by the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments — the strongest ligament in the body among them. Three degrees of freedom: flexion about 0 to 120 degrees (more with knee flexion), extension 0 to 10 or 15 degrees, abduction 0 to 45, adduction 0 to 30, and medial and lateral rotation about 0 to 45 each. Mechanism first: the socket trades the shoulder's mobility for near-dislocation-proof stability, because this joint must transmit the largest loads in the body — which brings us to the lever arms.

2Physiology

In single-leg stance, body weight acts through a vertical line roughly two-thirds of the way between the hip and the midline, at a moment arm about twice that of the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus). Equilibrium therefore demands abductor force of roughly two times body weight, and the femoral head compresses under a joint reaction force of about two to three times body weight in single-leg stance — rising toward about four times body weight in fast walking or stairs (Levangie & Norkin, 6th ed.). Add 10 kg of shopping and the arithmetic punishes the head. This lever model is the master key to the pathomechanics below.

3Pathophysiology

Osteoarthritis: cartilage loss and superolateral femoral head migration shorten the abductor moment arm, raise the required abductor force, and increase joint stress — pain, effusion, capsular contracture produce the classic pattern of flexion, abduction and lateral rotation deformity, with apparent (not true) shortening. Abductor failure: weakness of gluteus medius or superior gluteal nerve palsy produces a positive Trendelenburg sign — the pelvis drops on the unsupported side. Femoroacetabular impingement: a cam deformity (aspherical head) or pincer over-coverage jams the head against the labrum in deep flexion and adduction — the sitting-induced anterior groin pain of the younger patient. Childhood hip: developmental dysplasia (shallow socket, unstable head) and Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the capital epiphysis) deform the growing head and cause secondary osteoarthritis decades later — Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres at birth matter in Indian screening programmes.

In gluteus medius weakness, an uncompensated Trendelenburg gait shows lateral trunk lurch toward the weak side during its stance phase; most patients compensate by leaning over the stance hip to shorten the body-weight moment arm and reduce the required abductor force. Hip flexion contracture produces an anterior pelvic tilt and compensatory lumbar hyperlordosis in stance, and a shorter step on the affected side; hip OA shows antalgic shortening of stance phase, and a coxalgic limp with the trunk lurching toward the painful side to reduce joint reaction force.

Fig 10 — the first-class lever of single-leg stance: body weight on the long arm, abductors on the short arm, hip as fulcrum, and the 3× body weight compression beneath. Reproduce this and paragraph (b) draws itself.

4Answer

Strengthen gluteus medius (side-lying abduction, supported single-leg stance), stretch the hip flexors and adductors that contracture shortens, and teach trunk-lean economy when weakness is fixed. A cane held in the hand opposite the affected hip is pure biomechanics: it lengthens the body-weight moment arm's counter-lever and reduces the joint reaction force by up to half or so — say it exactly that way and the examiner knows you understand, not memorised. Post-arthroplasty, the same lever logic underlies gait re-education and abductor protection; in floor-sitting Indian habits, a graded return to cross-legged posture after arthroplasty is a culturally real functional goal.

Examiner's tip: the lever arm diagram is the highest-yielding single drawing of this paper. Numbers that must appear: 3× body weight joint reaction in single-leg stance, the roughly 2:1 moment arm ratio, and cane in the opposite hand. Then one line each on OA, Trendelenburg, impingement and childhood hip — breadth plus one mechanism drawn deep.

5Recent advances

  • Bannuru et al. (2019) — the OARSI guidelines make structured land-based exercise plus arthritis education the core treatments for hip and polyarticular osteoarthritis, establishing exercise as first-line physiotherapy for hip OA.
  • Skou & Roos (2017) — the GLA:D programme of patient education and supervised neuromuscular exercise, delivered by physiotherapists, improved pain, physical function and quality of life in people with hip and knee osteoarthritis at national scale.
  • Tateuchi et al. (2020) — larger cumulative hip adduction moment impulse is associated with hip OA progression; excessive hip adduction and pelvic tilt toward the swing limb increase it, while trunk lean toward the stance limb reduces it, a gait-retraining target.
  • Unilateral hip OA biomechanics (Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology, 2021) — unilateral hip OA unloads the affected hip and overloads the contralateral knee, raising the contralateral knee adduction moment and the risk of knee OA progression.
  • Wearable-sensor gait analysis in hip OA (Sensors, 2021; Journal of Orthopaedic Research, 2021) — wearable-sensor gait analysis identifies hip-specific kinematic deviations in hip osteoarthritis (reduced hip flexion and extension range) that correlate with patient-reported outcome scores.

6References

  1. Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — hip joint forces and lever arms.
  2. Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — hip mechanics and Trendelenburg analysis.
  3. Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — hip joint structure and pathomechanics.
  4. Hislop, Avers & Brown, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — gluteus medius testing.
  5. Gait kinematics of the hip, pelvis, and trunk associated with external hip adduction moment in patients with secondary hip osteoarthritis. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 2020;21:19.
  6. Assessing site specificity of osteoarthritic gait kinematics with wearable sensors. Sensors 2021;21:5363.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper II

QP 8130 · 21-May-2025 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Skeletal system

  • 206 bones = axial 80 + appendicular 126 · skull 22, ear bones 6, hyoid 1, vertebrae 26, ribs 24, sternum 1.
  • Five functions: support, protection, movement, haemopoiesis, mineral storage.
  • Wolff's law: bone follows stress — immobilise and it dissolves.

2Body fat tools

  • Ladder: tape/BMI → skinfold caliper (4 Durnin–Womersley sites) → BIA → tank/Bod Pod → DEXA (criterion).
  • Asian-Indian cutoffs: BMI 23, waist 90 (men) / 80 (women) cm.

3Newton's second law

  • Net force = mass × acceleration · angular: torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration.
  • GRF: 1.1–1.5× BW walking, 2–3× BW running · helmets work by stretching deceleration time.

4Core metabolism

  • Local stabilisers (TrA, multifidus, diaphragm, pelvic floor) vs global movers.
  • Low-load long holds = aerobic (~36 ATP/glucose) · isometric hold over 15–20% MVC occludes blood flow → metabolite burn · progress 5 s to 30 s holds · no Valsalva in hypertensives.

5Knee

  • Screw-home: tibia laterally rotates in terminal extension; popliteus unlocks.
  • Menisci carry ~50% load via hoop stress · PF reaction force: ~3× BW stairs, ~7× BW deep squat · Q angle 13–18°.
  • Varus → medial OA; ACL loss → pivot shift; locked knee = bucket-handle.

6Thoracic posture

  • Normal kyphosis 20–45° · flexible corrects on extension; Scheuermann's is rigid: 3 vertebrae × 5° wedging + Schmorl's nodes.
  • Adam's test + scoliometer for rib hump · Cobb 10° defines scoliosis.

7Gait in ankle instability

  • Mechanical = laxity (ATFL); functional = give-way without laxity, proprioceptive delay.
  • Stance: excess inversion/pronation, early heel rise, less single support, wider base · Swing: hip hiking + extra knee flexion · SEBT anterior reach deficit over 4 cm predicts sprain.

8Pain theories

  • Specificity (dedicated fibres) → pattern (intensity coding) → gate control (Melzack & Wall, Science 1965: big fibre closes, small fibre opens, descending control) → neuromatrix (Melzack 1999: pain is brain output; phantom limb) → biopsychosocial.
  • TENS and rubbing = closing the gate.

9Meniscal healing

  • Zones: red-red (vascular, heals) / red-white / white-white (avascular, no clot, no healing).
  • Phases: inflammation 0–7 d → proliferation 2–6 wk (weakest scar) → remodelling months.
  • Poor healing: no blood inner two-thirds, few fibrochondrocytes, synovial washout, constant load.

10Hip

  • 3° freedom ball-and-socket · single-leg stance: abductors ~2× BW, joint reaction ~3× BW, body-weight arm ≈ 2× abductor arm.
  • Trendelenburg: pelvis drops on unsupported side, weakness same side · cane in OPPOSITE hand · FAI = flexion-adduction groin pinch.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall — 206 = 80 + 126 · F = ma · screw-home + popliteus · gate 1965 / neuromatrix 1999 · red-red heals, white-white does not · hip = 3× BW and cane opposite.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Enumerate basic assessment methods for joint play movements.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 1a — Introduction to assessment: basic assessment methods

★ Memory hook — Roll, Spin, Glide, Traction — four circles and two rules (convex–concave); then the nine-item enumeration: PAIVM, PPIVM, spring, end-feel.

1Introduction

Joint play assessment examines the accessory, involuntary component of joint movement that a patient cannot perform voluntarily. It is the bridge between diagnosis and manual therapy: the examiner's hands test the accessory layer that voluntary range and imaging cannot show.

2Physiology

Every joint moves in two layers. The layer the patient controls is osteokinematics — flexion, abduction, rotation. Beneath it runs the layer the patient cannot command: joint play, the accessory roll, spin and glide of the surfaces plus traction and compression between them. A knee that bends to 120 degrees can still be restricted by a stiff posterior glide, and a shoulder that abducts fully may hide a hypomobile inferior glide. So the examiner's first principle is: if the voluntary range looks normal but the joint hurts or feels tight, the answer often sits in the accessory layer.

The second principle is the convex-concave rule — a convex surface moving on a fixed concave one glides opposite to its roll, while a concave surface moving on a fixed convex one glides in the same direction as the movement. This rule tells you the direction in which your glide must be tested and treated.

Fig 1 — Two-layer picture with the four accessory components. Drawing the circles for roll, spin, glide and traction is the fastest way to show the examiner you know what "enumerate" means.

3Pathophysiology

When the accessory layer is lost the joint becomes either hypomobile — a firm or hard end-feel with reduced glide, as in capsular tightness or osteoarthritis — or hypermobile — a soft, spongy end-feel with excessive travel, as in ligamentous laxity. A restriction that reproduces the patient's symptom at grade I points to an irritable, pain-dominant joint; reproduction only near the limit points to a stiffness-dominant joint.

4Answer

1. Passive accessory intervertebral and peripheral joint movements (PAIVMs) — central and unilateral glides for the spine, translatoric glides for peripheral joints. 2. Passive physiological movements (PPIVMs) — the therapist moves the joint through its voluntary arc and grades the feel. 3. Assessment of roll, spin and glide in the loose-packed position. 4. Long-axis traction and distraction. 5. Compression and joint-springing to reproduce the patient's symptom. 6. End-feel assessment at the physiological limit — bony, capsular, soft-tissue approximation. 7. Maitland's grading of the oscillation — grades I to IV small-to-large amplitude within or up to the limit. 8. Ligamentous stress tests for stability of the accessory restraint system. 9. Hypermobility screening on the other side of the spectrum — Beighton score.

Position the joint close to its loose-packed position so the capsule is slack. Stabilise the proximal segment with one hand; apply the glide with the other, taking up the slack before grading the oscillation. Compare with the contralateral side — the patient is their own control. Ask two questions of every glide: how far does it travel, and does it reproduce the familiar pain?

A firm or hard end-feel with reduced glide indicates hypomobility — this joint wants mobilisation. A soft, spongy end-feel with excessive travel indicates hypermobility — this joint wants control, not stretching. Note whether the symptom is reproduced at grade I (pain-dominant, irritable) or only near the limit (stiffness-dominant).

In Indian OPDs, the classic example is knee osteoarthritis that lacks the last 15 degrees of extension: the missing movement is a restricted anterior tibial glide, and graded anterior glides become the treatment. Assessment of joint play is therefore not an extra skill — it is the bridge between diagnosis and manual therapy.

"Enumerate" means a numbered list. Nine one-line items score better than three well-written paragraphs. Learn the numbers, write the list, then add only one sentence of interpretation.
"Enumerate" means a numbered list. Nine one-line items score better than three well-written paragraphs. Learn the numbers, write the list, then add only one sentence of interpretation.

5Recent advances

  • O'Donohue & Wise (2021) — the Mobil-Aider device gave objective, reliable measurement of accessory glide (intra-rater ICC 0.771 for glenohumeral posterior glide and 0.904 for radiocarpal volar glide), allowing joint-play deficits to be quantified rather than judged by feel alone.
  • Gorgos et al. (2014) — a systematic review found strong evidence that intra-clinician reliability of joint mobilisation force application is good but inter-clinician reliability is only poor to moderate, so standardising applied force (for example with feedback devices) matters when testing accessory motion.
  • Pfluegler et al. (2020) — a systematic review found passive joint mobilisation immediately alters local muscle function, decreasing superficial muscle activity and improving motor patterns in symptomatic individuals.
  • Staes et al. (2009) — intra- and inter-rater reliability of accessory motion testing at the carpal joints was acceptable, with end-feel agreement very good, supporting accessory-motion testing as a usable clinical joint-play assessment.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — principles chapter and regional chapters.
  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function — arthrokinematics chapters.
  3. Maitland GD. Peripheral Manipulation — grades of movement.
  4. Evaluation of lumbar segmental motion using ultrasound imaging following common joint mobilization techniques. J Man Manip Ther. 2025;33(4):343-355.
  5. Gulick DT. Measurement of accessory motion of the glenohumeral and radiocarpal joints: intra-rater reliability of the Mobil-Aider device. 2020.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Explain screening the head and neck in upper cross syndrome.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2a — Screening regions: head, neck and back

★ Memory hook — Tight, Weak, Forward, Rounded — pair every tight muscle you name with its weak opponent.

1Introduction

Upper cross syndrome is Janda's classical muscle-imbalance pattern of the head, neck and shoulder girdle, and screening it means reading a crossed pattern of tightness and weakness from posture and a small set of endurance and length tests. This answer sets out that screen in the order it is performed: pattern, observation, tests, interpretation.

2Physiology

The head, neck and shoulder girdle work as a balanced system. The deep cervical flexors (longus colli and capitis) and the scapular stabilisers (lower and middle trapezius, serratus anterior) hold the head and scapulae against gravity, while the upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals and pectorals provide movement and postural set. In balance the ear sits over the acromion and the cervico-thoracic angle is preserved.

3Pathophysiology

Upper cross syndrome is Janda's classical muscle-imbalance pattern of the head, neck and shoulder girdle. Two lines drawn on the trunk cross like an X. The upper line runs through the tight muscles: upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals and pectoralis major and minor. The lower line runs through the inhibited ones: deep neck flexors, lower and middle trapezius, and serratus anterior. The postural result is a forward head, loss of the cervico-thoracic angle, rounded shoulders with protracted and elevated scapulae, and a chin that pokes forward. Mechanically, for the eyes to stay level the upper cervical spine extends, the lower cervical spine flexes, and the suboccipitals shorten while the deep flexors are held long and weak.

Fig 2 — The crossed X with tight on top and weak below. This two-minute sketch carries the whole pattern and is what examiners scan for first.

4Answer

Stand the patient in profile. Check the plumb line: the ear should sit over the acromion; in the syndrome it falls forward. Look at the cervico-thoracic angle, the prominence of the spinous process of C7, scapular position (protracted, elevated, winged), and pectoral prominence. Palpate upper trapezius and levator scapulae for tone and tenderness, then take the cervical spine through active range with overpressure to clear the joints themselves.

The craniocervical flexion test with a pressure biofeedback unit is the heart of the answer: the supine patient nods the head on the neck in five graded stages of 2 mmHg from a 20 mmHg baseline while the examiner watches for superficial flexor substitution. The deep neck flexor endurance test complements it: the patient tucks the chin, lifts the head about two to three centimetres off the couch and holds it while the quality of the position is timed. Then screen the tight side — pectoralis minor length in supine lying (distance of the acromion from the couch), pectoralis major and suboccipital length, and upper trapezius and levator length in side-lying. Finally, Janda's shoulder abduction test: observe the patient abduct the arms slowly — immediate scapular hitching before 60 degrees of humeral elevation confirms that upper trapezius and levator dominate over the weak lower stabilisers.

Positive findings cluster together: the chin juts and the sternocleidomastoid visibly tightens during craniocervical flexion, endurance holds fall far short of the expected duration, pectoralis minor measures more than the normal few centimetres from the couch, and the scapula hikes early in abduction. That cluster — not any single test — is the screen.

The screen feeds directly into treatment: deep neck flexor retraining with the biofeedback cuff, lengthening of the pectorals and suboccipitals, lower trapezius and serratus strengthening, and ergonomic correction of the desk and the mobile-phone posture that drives the pattern. In the Indian clinic this presentation is everywhere — students with heavy shoulder bags, young IT professionals, and long hours of floor-level sitting with the neck flexed.

The four words that score: tight, weak, forward, rounded. Pair every tight muscle you name with its weak opponent — examiners look for the pairing, not the shopping list.
The four words that score: tight, weak, forward, rounded. Pair every tight muscle you name with its weak opponent — examiners look for the pairing, not the shopping list.

5Recent advances

  • Seidi et al. (2020) — an 8-week comprehensive corrective exercise programme improved alignment, muscle activation and scapular movement in men with upper crossed syndrome, and the gains were maintained after four weeks of detraining.
  • Aneis et al. (2022) — a multimodal programme (muscle energy technique plus cervical and scapulothoracic stabilisation and postural correction with ergonomic advice) outperformed muscle energy technique alone for craniovertebral angle, sagittal shoulder angle, pain and disability.
  • Chaudhuri et al. (2023) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found physiotherapy significantly improves craniovertebral angle, kyphotic angle and rounded shoulder versus no treatment.
  • Yaghoubitajani et al. (2022) — a randomised trial in office workers with upper crossed syndrome found online-supervised corrective exercise improved neck-shoulder pain, postural angles, workability and upper-trapezius activity, supporting telerehabilitation for screening and correction.
  • Nitayarak & Charntaraviroj (2021) — a randomised controlled trial showed scapular stabilisation exercises improved posture and muscle imbalance in women with upper crossed syndrome.

6References

  1. Janda V. Evaluation of muscular imbalance, in Liebenson C. Rehabilitation of the Spine.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — cervical spine chapter.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — posture chapters.
  4. Bayattork M, Seidi F, Minoonejad H, Andersen LL, Page P. The effectiveness of a comprehensive corrective exercise program on alignment, muscle activation and movement pattern in men with upper crossed syndrome: RCT. Sci Rep. 2020.
  5. Physiotherapeutic interventions for upper cross syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis. 2023.

On the evaluation form — Q2: Upper cross syndrome / forward head posture

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: young to middle-aged adult, typically a desk/IT worker or student. Chief complaints: insidious-onset neck and suboccipital ache, often bilateral, present for months; frequently reported suboccipital headache, fatigue on reading, and sometimes tingling over the upper limb with sustained postures. Past medical/personal history: prolonged screen exposure, ergonomically poor workstation, stress. Symptom analysis: site — suboccipital region, cervical spine, interscapular area; onset — insidious; duration — months; type — dull ache with occasional "tight band" feeling; severity 4-6/10 on NPRS; aggravating factors — prolonged computer or smartphone use, sustained forward head postures, driving; relieving factors — posture change, rest, mild activity, heat. Pain evaluation: NPRS 4-6/10 with the mechanical, posture-related behaviour described above. Red-flag screen: trauma, night pain, fever and neurological deficit screened for. Vital signs: usually within normal limits.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Forward head posture with protracted chin; increased cervicothoracic angle; elevated and protracted scapulae with rounded shoulders (pectoralis tightness); increased thoracic kyphosis; visible upper trapezius hypertrophy; attitude of head held in slight flexion.

On palpation. Tenderness and trigger points in upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals, sternocleidomastoid and pectoralis minor; increased deep tissue tension over the cervical extensors; reduced mobility (hypomobility) of the upper cervical segments on palpation.

1. Motor assessment

AROM/PROM of the cervical spine — reduced extension and rotation; flexion is full, giving a flexion-dominated movement pattern; end-feel typically of muscular tightness. MMT: deep neck flexors (longus colli/capitis) weak (3/5 or less on cranio-cervical flexion); lower and middle trapezius weak; scapular retractors inhibited. Resisted isometrics: cervical rotation/flexion painful at end range in the tight structures. Postural photograph with goniometry/inclinometry for the craniovertebral angle.

2. Sensory assessment

Dermatomes C4-T2 screened if radicular symptoms are reported; myotomes C5-T1 tested. In classic postural syndrome the screen is normal — abnormal findings suggest concurrent cervical radiculopathy and alter management.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: ability to sustain sitting posture over 30 minutes (desk simulation), functional reach, and posture during gait; condition-relevant tests — timed reading/computer tolerance and sit-to-stand with head position noted. Outcome measures: Neck Disability Index (NDI, 0-50; higher scores indicate greater disability), NPRS (0-10), craniovertebral angle by photogrammetry, cervical ROM by goniometer/inclinometer.

4. Gait analysis

Posture during gait observed as part of the functional assessment; no gait deviation specific to this postural syndrome is expected.

5. Balance

Static and dynamic balance are not typically affected in this postural syndrome; balance is observed informally during gait and desk-task simulation.

6. Hand function

Reaching, grasping and releasing are not affected in this condition, though tingling over the upper limb may be reported with sustained postures; no assistive devices are required for hand tasks.

7. Coordination

Coordination is not impaired in upper cross syndrome; upper limb coordination is screened within the neurological examination, and abnormal coordination would suggest a different diagnosis.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the expected pattern for this condition; each test is recorded individually as positive or negative for the patient on testing — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
Cranio-cervical flexion test (CCFT, Jull)Supine; inflatable pressure sensor under cervical spine inflated to 20 mmHg; patient performs gentle head-nod to five incremental levelsUnable to hold 10 s at lower pressure levels; substitution with superficial neck flexorsDeep neck flexor motor-control impairment
Deep neck flexor endurance testSupine chin-tuck with head lifted 2–3 cm off plinth, heldTremor, neck extension, or hold time below expectedWeakness/low endurance of deep neck flexors
Pectoralis minor length testSupine; distance from posterior shoulder to plinth, or pectoralis minor indexPosterior shoulder rests well off the tableAdaptive pectoralis minor shortening
Pectoralis major wall testStanding facing wall with shoulder abducted 90° and elbow flexed 90°, forearm to wallInability to keep forearm in contact with the wall without compensatory lumbar extensionAdaptive pectoral tightness
Cervical flexion-rotation testSupine, maximal cervical flexion, then passive rotationRotation restricted by >10° from the contralateral sideC1-C2 (suboccipital) joint dysfunction
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Forward head posture with deep neck flexor and scapular stabilizer weakness
  • Pectoral and suboccipital tightness
  • Upper cervical hypomobility
  • Trigger points

Functional limitations:

  • Inability to sustain upright sitting/reading tasks
  • Reduced tolerance for computer work
  • Headache

Disabilities:

  • Reduced work productivity
11. Functional diagnosis

Reduced tolerance for sustained sitting, reading and computer work due to forward head posture with deep neck flexor and scapular stabilizer weakness, pectoral and suboccipital tightness, upper cervical hypomobility and trigger points.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): reduce pain from 5/10 to 2/10 on NPRS; achieve independent self-correction of head position in sitting; begin deep neck flexor training at a tolerated level.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): normal deep neck flexor endurance on CCFT; symmetrical scapular control during overhead and desk tasks; measurable improvement in craniovertebral angle; NDI reduction by at least 5 points; return to full-time desk work with ergonomic modifications.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: education on posture and workstation ergonomics; trigger-point release and stretching for upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals and pectorals. Stage 2: cranio-cervical flexion training with progression; scapular retraction and lower/middle trapezius strengthening; thoracic extension mobilization. Stage 3: postural endurance training and functional integration with task-specific practice.

14. Home programme

Chin tucks; doorway pectoral stretch; wall angels; micro-breaks every 30 minutes.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Illustrate primary care of intervertebral disc prolapse.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 3a — Direct access, primary care and autonomous practice

★ Memory hook — Red flags first, then McKenzie: Centralise = treat, Peripheralise = refer.

1Introduction
