Intervertebral disc prolapse is one of the commonest reasons a patient reaches a physiotherapist in direct-access primary care. This answer presents primary care as a clinical pathway — triage first, treat second, refer third — rather than a list of modalities.

2Physiology

The intervertebral disc is a fibrocartilaginous cushion: a gel-like nucleus pulposus enclosed by the concentric lamellae of the annulus fibrosus, anchored in front and behind by the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments. It distributes compressive load, permits controlled segmental motion and acts as the shock absorber of the lumbar spine.

3Pathophysiology

The nucleus pulposus sits contained within the annulus fibrosus. The posterior longitudinal ligament is strong in the midline but weak at its lateral edges, so under repeated flexion-and-load the disc fails posterolaterally — most often at L4-L5 and L5-S1, irritating the L5 and S1 roots and producing dermatomal sciatica. The physiotherapist in primary care is often the first clinician to see this patient, so the answer must read like a clinical pathway, not a list of modalities.

4Answer

Red flags come before any treatment line. Cauda equina features — saddle anaesthesia, retention or incontinence of bladder or bowel, bilateral or rapidly progressive leg weakness — are an emergency requiring immediate referral. Also screen for fever with spinal pain, night pain unrelated to position, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, recent significant trauma, and progressive neurological deficit. Then run the neurological screen: myotomes (ankle dorsiflexion, big-toe extension, plantarflexion), dermatomes, ankle reflexes, and the straight leg raise. Document all of it — in direct-access practice the red-flag screen is what protects both the patient and you.

Fig 3 — The primary-care flow. The two diamonds of the pathway — red flags present? and does the pain centralise? — decide everything downstream; drawing this earns the "illustrate" marks.

Educate first: the disc heals, most radicular pain settles within six to twelve weeks, and strict bed rest is harmful. Then apply McKenzie mechanical diagnosis and therapy — repeated movements in the direction of preference. The key phenomenon is centralisation: distal leg pain retreating toward the low back with the correct repeated movement predicts a good response to that exercise programme. Around this core, add graded activity, neural mobilisation once the acuity settles, trunk (core) stabilisation, ergonomic advice for sitting and lifting, and a short course of traction only where it clearly centralises symptoms. Analgesia advice sits with the referring physician; the physiotherapist's prescription is movement.

Routine imaging is not needed in the first four to six weeks if red flags are absent. Refer urgently for cauda equina features or progressive motor weakness; refer for surgical opinion when disabling radicular pain persists despite a competent six-to-twelve-week conservative programme, or when the neurological deficit fails to improve. Physical therapists in primary care escalate — they do not wait and watch a worsening limb.

Direct access means the patient with three days of sciatica reaches you before any specialist. Two habits matter: document the red-flag screen on day one, and actively discourage the family's default advice of two weeks flat on a hard cot. Early, guided movement is the treatment; the cot is not.

Ten-mark structure for any "primary care" question: triage first, treat second, refer third. If your answer starts with a modality instead of red flags, you have already lost the first two marks.
Ten-mark structure for any "primary care" question: triage first, treat second, refer third. If your answer starts with a modality instead of red flags, you have already lost the first two marks.

5Recent advances

  • Finucane et al. (2020) — the IFOMPT International Framework for Red Flags provides a clinical-reasoning pathway for serious spinal pathology and reframes red flags as a level-of-concern judgement rather than a checklist.
  • Hill et al. (2011) — the STarT Back trial showed prognostic screening with matched treatment pathways (including psychologically informed physiotherapy for high-risk patients) improved disability and was cost-effective compared with usual primary care for low back pain.
  • WHO (2023) — the WHO guideline for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in primary and community care recommends education, exercise and self-management as first-line care, placing physiotherapy at the centre of primary care for disc-related back pain.
  • Fischer et al. (2026) — a systematic review of direct-access physiotherapy found 10-30% fewer GP consultations and reduced imaging and medication use, with clinical outcomes non-inferior to GP-referred pathways.
  • Edwards et al. (2019) — an observational study of video-recorded UK consultations found safety-netting advice is often non-specific and left undocumented (recorded for only 45% of problems), so the red-flag explanation must be documented and given in writing.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — spinal chapters.
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — lumbar spine.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — lumbar spine chapter.
  4. McKenzie R, May S. The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy.
  5. IFOMPT. International Framework for Red Flags for Potential Serious Spinal Pathologies. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2020;50(7):350-372.
  6. Systematic review of direct access physiotherapy for musculoskeletal conditions in primary care. 2026.

On the evaluation form — Q3: Acute lumbar disc prolapse with sciatica — primary care pathway

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: adult 25-50 years, often with a lifting or twisting mechanism. Chief complaints: acute low back pain radiating below the knee, usually unilaterally along L5 or S1. Past medical/personal history: previous episodes; occupation involving driving/heavy loads. Symptom analysis: site — lumbar spine with radiation to posterior/lateral leg; onset — sudden or gradual over days; type — sharp shooting leg pain with deep backache; severity 6-8/10 on NPRS; aggravating factors — sitting, bending, coughing, sneezing (Valsalva); relieving factors — standing, walking, lying with pillow under knees. Pain evaluation: NPRS 6-8/10 with the behaviour described above. Red-flag screen essential: fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, cancer history; ask specifically about bladder/bowel dysfunction and saddle anaesthesia (cauda equina syndrome — emergency referral). Vital signs recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Antalgic list to one side; reduced lumbar lordosis; guarded walking; difficulty sitting; attitude of slight hip/knee flexion on the painful side.

On palpation. Paraspinal muscle spasm and tenderness at the affected level (commonly L4-L5/L5-S1); increased tissue tension; no visible swelling; step-off and spinal alignment palpated.

1. Motor assessment

AROM limited by pain — flexion typically reproduces leg pain; extension may centralize symptoms (McKenzie directional preference assessment). Myotome testing: L4 (ankle dorsiflexion), L5 (great toe extension), S1 (ankle plantarflexion; heel walk/toe walk). Resisted isometrics and reflexes: diminished ankle jerk (S1) or knee jerk (L4). Straight leg raise limited on the involved side.

2. Sensory assessment

Dermatome testing over medial foot (L4), dorsum/first web space (L5), lateral foot (S1); light touch and pinprick. Combined with myotomes and reflexes to grade the severity and level of radiculopathy.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: difficulty with sit-to-stand and bed mobility; ability to don shoes/socks; tolerated sitting time; 50-foot walk time. Outcome measures: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI, 0-100%), NPRS (0-10), Quebec Back Pain Disability Scale, and the Orebro Musculoskeletal Pain Questionnaire (identifies psychosocial risk of chronicity).

4. Gait analysis

Antalgic gait pattern with limited stride on the affected side and guarded walking; difficulty with sit-to-stand and bed mobility.

5. Balance

Balance screen performed if severe guarding is present; static and dynamic balance are otherwise not directly limited by this condition.

6. Hand function

Hand function (reaching, grasping, releasing) is not directly affected in lumbar disc prolapse; the shoe/sock donning task serves as the relevant reaching assessment. No assistive devices for hand tasks.

7. Coordination

Lower limb coordination is screened within the neurological examination (myotomes, reflexes); it is not primarily affected in this condition.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the diagnostic pattern for this condition; each test is recorded individually as positive or negative for the patient on testing — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
Straight leg raise (SLR)Supine; slow passive hip flexion with knee extendedReproduction of radicular pain, typically below 60°; sensitized by ankle dorsiflexionDural/lower lumbar nerve root tension (L5-S1)
Crossed SLRSLR performed on the unaffected legPain reproduced in the affected legStrongly suggests disc prolapse with nerve root compression
Slump testSeated slump (thoracic/lumbar flexion, neck flexion), then knee extension with ankle dorsiflexionReproduction of sciatic symptomsNeurodynamic mechanosensitivity of the sciatic tract
Femoral nerve tension testSide-lying; extension of hip with knee flexionAnterior thigh/groin pain reproducedUpper lumbar root involvement (L2-L4), e.g. higher prolapse
Prone instability testProne; palpation of painful segment during passive SLR with and without muscle activationPain disappears when posterior elements are loadedClinical instability component; responds to stabilization
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Radicular pain
  • Dural tension
  • Paraspinal spasm
  • Reduced lumbar ROM
  • Possible myotomal weakness

Functional limitations:

  • Cannot sit >10 minutes
  • Difficulty bending and lifting

Disabilities:

  • Work absenteeism
11. Functional diagnosis

Acute lumbar disc prolapse with L5/S1 nerve root irritation causing radicular pain, dural tension, paraspinal spasm and reduced lumbar ROM, limiting sitting, bending, lifting and work attendance.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): centralize radicular pain to the low back; reduce NPRS by 2 points; SLR improve by 20°; independent in positions of comfort and safe bed mobility.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): full resolution of radicular symptoms; full pain-free lumbar ROM; ODI below 20%; return to work and lifting with correct technique.

13. Treatment plan

Primary care pathway: rule out red flags (refer cauda equina immediately); reassure and educate — avoid bed rest beyond 1-2 days; advise positions of comfort and stay active within tolerance. Stage 1: McKenzie directional preference exercises (usually extension), gentle neural mobilization, cryotherapy/heat for pain and spasm, analgesia as per physician. Stage 2: graded lumbar stabilization and core strengthening; aerobic walking programme. Stage 3: lifting mechanics, work conditioning, prevention education.

14. Home programme

Prone press-ups (as directed); walking 20 minutes daily; posture and micro-break advice; warning signs for immediate re-attendance.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe physiotherapy diagnosis in lower cross syndrome.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4a — Physical therapy diagnosis

★ Memory hook — A physiotherapy diagnosis describes the movement dysfunction, not the pathology — then name the cluster.

1Introduction

A physiotherapy diagnosis is a syndrome-level statement about the movement system, distinct from the medical label of ‘mechanical low back pain’. Lower cross syndrome is the pelvic mirror of Janda's upper cross, and this answer shows how its findings are assembled into a diagnosis that converts clause-by-clause into treatment.

2Physiology

Normal lumbopelvic control depends on balance between the hip flexors and thoracolumbar extensors and their opponents — the gluteals and deep abdominals. With balanced length and recruitment the pelvis stays in neutral and the lumbar lordosis is physiological; the hip extends through the gluteals rather than through compensatory lumbar extension.

3Pathophysiology

Lower cross syndrome is the pelvic mirror of the upper cross. The tight line runs through the iliopsoas and rectus femoris (and often the tensor fasciae latae and adductors) and the thoracolumbar erector spinae. The weak line runs through the gluteus maximus, gluteus medius and the deep abdominals. The mechanical result is an anterior pelvic tilt with lumbar hyperlordosis: the tight hip flexors pull the pelvis forward into anterior tilt, the erectors reinforce the lordosis, the gluteals are held long and inhibited, and the protruding, splayed abdomen gives the classic clinical silhouette. Facet-joint compression and repeated ligamentous strain in the lordotic segment explain why these backs ache.

Fig 4 — One figure, both crosses drawn as an X over the pelvis: tight hip flexors and erectors above, weak gluteals and deep abdominals below, with the anterior-tilt arrow.

4Answer

Observe standing: pelvic tilt from the ASIS-PSIS relationship, depth of the lumbar curve, gluteal bulk, splayed lower abdomen, and genu recurvatum that often accompanies the pattern. Watch gait: a lurching trunk lean toward the stance leg suggests gluteus medius weakness, and the hip often extends poorly with compensatory lumbar extension. Ask the patient to stand on one leg (Trendelenburg test) and to squat — the lumbar spine is recruited for hip extension when the gluteals fail.

The modified Thomas test in supine with the patient holding one knee to the chest: the test leg demonstrates hip flexor tightness if the thigh lifts off the plinth, rectus femoris involvement if the knee extends, and TFL tightness if the thigh drifts into abduction. The prone hip extension test exposes the sequencing — a strong patient extends the hip with the gluteus maximus first; the crossed patient fires the hamstrings and erector spinae with an anterior pelvic tilt. The leg-lowering test and the double straight-leg raise grade the deep abdominals, which fail to control the pelvis long before the legs reach low angles. Each test should be linked to the muscle it confirms — that linkage is what makes this a physiotherapy diagnosis rather than a collection of positive signs.

A physiotherapy diagnosis is a syndrome-level, movement-system statement, distinct from the medical label of "mechanical low back pain". Write it as a cluster: "Anterior pelvic tilt with lumbar hyperlordosis, shortened hip flexors (positive modified Thomas), gluteal weakness with substitution in prone hip extension, and poor deep abdominal control on leg lowering — consistent with lower crossed syndrome." Framed in ICF terms: the impairment is muscle imbalance and restricted hip extension; the activity limitation is pain-limited standing, walking and lifting; participation follows from there.

Treatment inverts the findings — lengthen the iliopsoas, rectus femoris and TFL; recruit and strengthen the gluteals and the deep abdominals; retrain the hip-hinge pattern; and address the sitting and floor-sitting postures that maintain the syndrome. The diagnosis is only useful because every clause of it converts into one treatment clause.

The marks hide in one sentence: "a physiotherapy diagnosis describes the movement dysfunction, not the pathology." Then give the cluster of positive findings and name it. That structure separates a 10 from a 6.
The marks hide in one sentence: "a physiotherapy diagnosis describes the movement dysfunction, not the pathology." Then give the cluster of positive findings and name it. That structure separates a 10 from a 6.

5Recent advances

  • Ghaffari et al. (2026) — an 8-week NASM-based corrective exercise programme reduced lumbar lordosis and increased gluteus maximus electrical activity (EMG) in women with lower cross syndrome.
  • Hassani & Hosseinimehr (2026) — a comparative trial found core-stability and NASM exercise programmes both reduced lumbar lordosis and pelvic tilt; the NASM protocol was superior for lateral trunk flexor endurance.
  • Kale et al. (2020) — Janda's stretching-and-strengthening approach improved abdominal and gluteal strength and reduced hip flexor tightness in school children screened for lower crossed syndrome.
  • Baik et al. (2021) — a systematic review of gluteus medius weakness confirms 'synergistic dominance' of the tensor fasciae latae and quadratus lumborum, so gluteal strengthening must be prescribed with substitution in mind.
  • Alyarnezhad & Shams Majalan (2021) — a controlled study found that performing stretching and strengthening exercises intermittently reduced lumbar curvature more than delivering them simultaneously in students with lower crossed syndrome.

6References

  1. Janda V. Evaluation of muscular imbalance, in Liebenson C. Rehabilitation of the Spine.
  2. Sahrmann S. Diagnosis and Treatment of Movement System Impairment Syndromes.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — hip and posture chapters.
  4. World Health Organization. ICF framework.
  5. The effect of NASM-based corrective exercises on lumbar lordosis angle and selected muscle activity in women with lower cross syndrome: a randomized clinical trial. PLoS One. 2025.
  6. Which exercise protocol is optimal for improving lower crossed syndrome in athletes? Core stability or NASM. 2026.

On the evaluation form — Q4: Lower cross syndrome / anterior pelvic tilt

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: adult, often sedentary or with a prolonged standing occupation. Chief complaints: chronic dull low back ache; insidious onset over months. Past medical/personal history: prolonged sitting, pregnancy (postpartum laxity), deconditioning, previous low back episodes. Symptom analysis: site — lumbar spine and buttock; onset — insidious over months; type — dull ache with morning stiffness; severity 3-5/10 on NPRS; aggravating factors — prolonged standing, walking downhill, sleeping prone; relieving factors — position change, stretching. Pain evaluation: NPRS 3-5/10 with the mechanical behaviour described above. Vital signs normal; red-flag screen performed.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Anterior pelvic tilt; increased lumbar lordosis; abdominal protrusion with flanks relaxed; flat/inhibitable gluteals; compensatory thoracic kyphosis and forward head (associated upper cross features).

On palpation. Hypertonic and tender lumbar erector spinae, tensor fasciae latae, iliopsoas and rectus femoris; palpable tightness over the hip flexor group; iliac crests assessed for pelvic obliquity.

1. Motor assessment

AROM/PROM of lumbar spine and hip; hip flexor extensibility via Thomas test. MMT: gluteus maximus and gluteus medius weak (3/5 range); abdominals (especially lower) weak; hip flexors strong but tight. Trunk muscle endurance tests: prone/side planks, timed. Reflexes normal; limb length measured to exclude true shortening driving the tilt.

2. Sensory assessment

Dermatomes and myotomes of the lower limb screened — expected normal in a pure postural syndrome; abnormal findings suggest concurrent lumbar pathology.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: standing tolerance, sit-to-stand quality. Outcome measures: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI, 0-100%) if pain-related disability is present, NPRS (0-10), pelvic tilt angle via palpation (ASIS/PSIS) or inclinometer, photo-documentation of posture. FIM scoring if inpatient.

4. Gait analysis

Gait analysis for hip extension and pelvic control; gait may show reduced hip extension; single-leg squat quality assessed.

5. Balance

Balance tested by single-leg stance time.

6. Hand function

Hand function (reaching, grasping, releasing) is not affected in this lumbo-pelvic postural syndrome; no assistive devices.

7. Coordination

Coordination is screened within the neurological examination; it is not primarily affected in this condition.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the expected pattern for this condition; each test is recorded individually as positive or negative for the patient on testing — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
Thomas testSupine at table edge; one hip and knee held flexed, other hip allowed to extendExtended thigh lifts off the table or knee extendsIliopsoas / rectus femoris tightness
Modified Thomas testSide-lying or seated edge position isolating one hip; observe knee extension and thigh positionKnee remains extended >15° or thigh rests above horizontalRectus femoris vs iliopsoas shortening distinguished
Trendelenburg testStanding on one leg, pelvis observed from behindPelvis drops on the unsupported side, or trunk leans to stance sideGluteus medius weakness / poor pelvic stabilization
Prone hip extension testProne; active hip extension observedLumbar hyperextension and hamstring substitution precede gluteal firingGluteus maximus weakness with faulty recruitment
Active straight leg raise (ASLR)Supine; patient lifts leg 5 cm and rates effort/abilityHeavy/weak sensation or inability to lift; improves with pelvic compressionImpaired lumbopelvic load transfer
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Anterior pelvic tilt with hip flexor and lumbar extensor tightness
  • Gluteal and abdominal weakness
  • Poor lumbopelvic control

Functional limitations:

  • Poor tolerance of standing/walking
  • Faulty lifting pattern

Disabilities:

  • Reduced occupational endurance
11. Functional diagnosis

Anterior pelvic tilt with hip flexor and lumbar extensor tightness and gluteal/abdominal weakness causing poor lumbopelvic control, limiting standing, walking, lifting and occupational endurance.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): reduce pain by 2 points on NPRS; independent in corrected neutral spine posture; begin gluteal activation in isolation.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): negative Thomas test (hip extension to neutral); gluteal MMT improved to 4/5 or 5/5; hold neutral pelvis during single-leg tasks and gait; measurable increase in plank endurance; pain-free prolonged standing.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: education on pelvic neutral and posture; release/stretch tight iliopsoas, rectus femoris, TFL and erector spinae; heat and soft-tissue techniques. Stage 2: gluteus maximus/medius strengthening (bridging progressions, clam shells, mini-squats); abdominal and core stabilization (dead bug, bird dog, planks). Stage 3: functional integration — lunges, squats, gait re-education, lifting mechanics, aerobic conditioning.

14. Home programme

Daily hip flexor and quadriceps stretches; gluteal sets with bridges; bird dog progression; postural micro-breaks at work.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Write exercise testing in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4b — Exercise testing in musculoskeletal disorders

★ Memory hook — 90-90-90: 90% limb symmetry, four hop tests, nine-to-twelve months.

1Introduction

After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, return to pivoting sport must be criteria-based, not calendar-based. Exercise testing is what converts ‘the knee feels fine’ into measurable, defensible criteria — and this answer sets out that battery and how it is interpreted.

After reconstruction — patellar tendon bone-tendon-bone or hamstring autograft — the graft passes through biological maturation and is weakest to re-injury in the middle months. Return to pivoting sport is therefore criteria-based, not calendar-based: earliest at six months, safer at nine to twelve, and only if the test battery is passed. Exercise testing is what converts "the knee feels fine" into measurable, defensible criteria.

2Physiology

The anterior cruciate ligament resists anterior tibial translation and controls rotational stability of the knee. After reconstruction the graft is avascular and passes through revascularisation and ligamentisation; it is mechanically weakest in the early-to-middle months and regains strength over nine to twelve months.

3Pathophysiology

Rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament causes anterolateral rotatory instability, giving-way and, if untreated, meniscal and chondral damage. After reconstruction the greatest risk is a second injury: the graft is weakest in the middle months and re-injury rates are highest in athletes under 25 returning to pivoting sport.

4Answer

Isokinetic dynamometry at 60 and 180 degrees per second gives quadriceps and hamstring peak torque of the operated limb against the uninvolved limb. The key index is the limb symmetry index — the ratio expressed as a percentage — with 90 per cent or better in both quadriceps and hamstrings as the accepted threshold. Also report the hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, because a strong hamstring set protects the graft. Where no isokinetic machine exists — the honest situation in many Indian setups — a handheld dynamometer with a fixed belt and the same symmetry calculation is an acceptable substitute; naming that adaptation earns marks for clinical realism. Baseline laxity testing with the Lachman test or an arthrometer completes the objective record of the graft.

Fig 5 — A limb-symmetry bar chart. This single figure shows the examiner that you know the criterion (90 per cent), the tests, and how a failing bar keeps the athlete in rehab.

Four single-leg hop tests make up the standard battery: the single hop for distance, the triple hop for distance, the crossover hop and the six-metre timed hop. Each is scored as a limb symmetry index, again 90 per cent or better. Add the side-hop endurance test and a drop-jump landing screen — watch for the valgus collapse and stiff-knee strategy that preceded the original injury. The hop battery matters because strength measured lying down does not guarantee control under landing forces.

Single-leg stance errors on firm and foam surfaces, the Star Excursion or Y-balance test (again compared between limbs), and agility drills in the final phase complete the physical picture. Then document the psychosocial domain — readiness scales such as the ACL-RSI and fear measures — and a patient-reported outcome such as the IKDC. Young athletes who pass every physical test but still distrust the knee re-injure at higher rates; the mind is part of the battery.

The decision is all-or-nothing per criterion: symmetrical strength, all hop indices at or above 90 per cent, clean landing mechanics, restored balance, and psychological readiness. Failing even one index means continuing rehabilitation. Athletes under 25 returning to pivoting sport carry the highest re-injury risk, and it is the exercise test results — not the surgical scar — that decide.

Three numbers open the answer and three numbers close it: 90 per cent symmetry, four hop tests, nine to twelve months. Any examiner marking this question is looking for those digits within the first five lines.
Three numbers open the answer and three numbers close it: 90 per cent symmetry, four hop tests, nine to twelve months. Any examiner marking this question is looking for those digits within the first five lines.

5Recent advances

  • Grindem et al. (2016) — the Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort showed that returning to level I sport at least 9 months after reconstruction, and only after passing strength and hop tests, reduced knee re-injury risk by 84%.
  • Kyritsis et al. (2016) — in 158 professional athletes, failing to meet all six discharge criteria (including quadriceps and hamstring strength and hop tests) before return to sport was associated with a four-fold greater risk of ACL graft rupture.
  • Liang et al. (2024) — the APKASS 2024 consensus reached unanimous agreement that single-leg hop tests are required before return to play, with limb symmetry index (LSI) and standardised functional testing as key benchmarks, and warned against purely time-based decisions.
  • Figueroa et al. (2022) — the ISAKOS consensus recommends isokinetic strength testing plus hop tests with an LSI of 90-100% before returning to pivoting sport.
  • Meredith et al. (2020) — the Panther Symposium consensus reported that for every 1% increase in quadriceps limb symmetry index there is a 3% reduction in subsequent knee injury risk.

6References

  1. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient — knee chapters.
  2. Daniels L, Worthingham C. Muscle Testing — techniques of manual muscle testing.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — knee chapter.
  4. Noyes FR, Barber-Westin SD. Return-to-sport and functional testing criteria (primary literature).
  5. APKASS 2024 consensus statement on anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, part III: return to play. 2024.
  6. Meredith SJ, Rauer T, Chmielewski TL, et al. Return to sport after anterior cruciate ligament injury: Panther Symposium ACL Injury Return to Sport Consensus Group. J ISAKOS. 2021;6:138-146.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Post-ACLR return-to-sport testing battery

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: athlete at 6-9 months (or later) after ACL reconstruction. Chief concern: readiness to return to pivoting sport. Past medical/surgical history: graft type (hamstring/bone-patellar tendon-bone/quadriceps) and any complications noted from records; rehab milestones achieved (full extension, strength phases); episodes of giving way or swelling; kinesiophobia and confidence; pre-injury level of sport. Symptom analysis: site — anterior knee; current pain 0-2/10 on NPRS; aggravating factors — cutting, jumping, stairs; relieving factors — rest. Vital signs and general condition as per records.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Quadriceps wasting of the operated thigh compared with the contralateral limb; surgical scar condition; resting knee position; any effusion on contour comparison.

On palpation. Scar mobility; anterior knee/tibial tuberosity tenderness; effusion assessed by ballottement and sweep test; tissue temperature.

1. Motor assessment

AROM/PROM of knee — full pain-free extension (including hyperextension equal to the other side) and flexion required; end-feel assessed. Strength: quadriceps and hamstrings by handheld dynamometry (widely used in Indian setups where isokinetic systems are scarce) or isokinetic testing; limb symmetry index (LSI) calculated for each muscle group. Reflexes screened; muscle girth: thigh circumference measured 5, 10 and 15 cm above the patella to quantify atrophy.

2. Sensory assessment

Sensation over the anterior knee and leg (donor-site numbness with hamstring or BPTB graft is common and documented); myotomes L3-S1 strength screen to exclude concomitant nerve involvement.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: hop-and-stop tasks and agility drills (dynamic function); ability classification against sport demands. Outcome measures: IKDC Subjective Knee Form (knee symptoms, function and sport participation), KOOS (knee-related quality of life, sport and symptoms), ACL-RSI scale (psychological readiness to return to sport), NPRS (0-10), thigh girth and LSI percentages.

4. Gait analysis

Gait and running analysis (video) for dynamic valgus, landing and cutting quality; single-leg squat depth and control.

5. Balance

Balance assessed by the Y-balance test and single-leg stance with perturbation.

6. Hand function

Hand function (reaching, grasping, releasing) is not relevant to this lower-limb condition; no assistive devices.

7. Coordination

Neuromuscular coordination is assessed through the landing, cutting and hop-and-stop tasks of the testing battery.

8. Investigations

Graft type and operative details from the surgical records; post-operative imaging as per the operating surgeon's records — none reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the diagnostic pattern; each test is recorded individually as positive or negative for the patient on testing — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
Lachman testSupine, knee 20-30° flexed; anterior tibial translation with femur stabilizedIncreased translation or soft end-feel vs the opposite limbResidual anterolateral rotatory laxity
Pivot shift testSupine; valgus and internal rotation applied while moving knee from extension to flexionVisible/clunking subluxation-reductionRotatory instability — poor prognosis for pivoting sport
Single-leg hop test battery (single, triple, crossover, 6-m timed hop)Single-leg hops for distance/time compared with the uninvolved limbLSI < 90% on any hop testInsufficient functional strength/power for RTS
Y-balance (lower quarter) testSingle-leg stance reaching in anterior, posteromedial, posterolateral directionsMarked asymmetry between limbs on composite reachDynamic balance and neuromuscular control deficit
Isokinetic/handheld dynamometer strength testMaximal concentric quadriceps and hamstring testing at 60°/s and 180°/s (or HHD break test)Quadriceps or hamstring LSI < 90%Residual strength deficit — contraindicates RTS clearance
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Quadriceps weakness with thigh atrophy
  • Possible effusion
  • Dynamic valgus on loading
  • Psychological hesitation

Functional limitations:

  • Unable to hop/cut/land symmetrically

Disabilities:

  • Not cleared for competitive pivoting sport
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-ACLR residual quadriceps weakness with thigh atrophy, possible effusion, dynamic valgus on loading and asymmetrical hop performance, leaving the athlete below the criteria for return to pivoting sport.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): pain-free full ROM; quadriceps LSI improved toward 70-80%; no effusion after loading sessions.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): quadriceps and hamstring LSI ≥ 90% (ideally approaching 100% for pivoting sport); all four hop tests LSI ≥ 90%; symmetrical Y-balance; complete sport-specific drills; decision-based RTS clearance with confidence on the ACL-RSI.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: effusion control; quadriceps activation and strengthening (progressive resistance, single-leg press, Bulgarian split squat); hamstring strengthening. Stage 2: plyometric progression (bilateral to unilateral, landing mechanics emphasizing knee-over-toe control); perturbation and agility training. Stage 3: sport-specific chaotic drills with decision-making; monitored return to team practice; criteria-based clearance involving surgeon, physiotherapist and coach.

14. Home programme

Single-leg calf raises; step-downs with mirror feedback; Nordic hamstring curls; jump-landing drills; continued gym programme three times weekly.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain pre-operative and post-operative assessment of fracture neck of femur.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5a — Assessment of fractures: pre-operative and post-operative

★ Memory hook — Garden I–II fix, III–IV replace — the operation decides your whole post-operative plan.

1Introduction

Fracture of the neck of the femur is the classic fragility fracture of the elderly, and its rehabilitation depends entirely on which operation was performed. This answer covers the mechanism and classification first, then the pre-operative and post-operative assessment.

2Physiology

The proximal femur transmits body weight from the pelvis to the shaft through a trabecular arch. The femoral head receives its blood supply mainly from the retinacular (medial circumflex femoral) vessels that run along the neck; this supply is the reason an intracapsular fracture threatens the viability of the head.

3Pathophysiology

The typical patient is elderly with osteoporotic bone: a trivial fall, pain in the groin, inability to stand, and the classic picture of a shortened and externally rotated limb. Because the fracture lies within the capsule, the retinacular blood supply to the head is at risk, making avascular necrosis and non-union the defining complications of displaced fractures. The Garden classification grades the injury in four stages and, more importantly for rehabilitation, predicts the operation: stages I and II are treated by internal fixation, while stages III and IV are treated by arthroplasty — hemiarthroplasty in the low-demand elderly, total replacement in the fit and active. Every post-operative assessment must begin by establishing which of these was done, because precautions, weight-bearing and progression all differ.

Fig 6 — Garden I to IV across the page, fixation under I-II, arthroplasty under III-IV. The examiner wants to see that the classification is not trivia — it chooses the operation and therefore your entire post-operative plan.

4Answer

History: mechanism of injury, comorbidities (cardiac disease, diabetes, osteoporosis, anticoagulant use), and the pre-injury mobility level — the single best predictor of outcome. Physical: pain, deformity, limb shortening and external rotation, skin integrity over the trochanter, and a full neurovascular examination of the limb; an abbreviated general screen of chest, heart and hydration status because this population deconditions on day one of bed rest. Review the radiograph and the Garden stage with the team. Then the physiotherapy pre-operative work: teach ankle pumps, static quadriceps, breathing exercises and effective coughing, practise the bed-to-chair transfer and gait pattern with a frame on the unaffected side, and counsel the family on stairs and toilet arrangements at home — in Indian homes, the Indian-style toilet and staircase access decide the discharge plan as much as the fracture does.

Structure it day by day and procedure by procedure. Early: vital state, wound and drain, pain, oedema, and quadriceps sets. Fixation cases carry the surgeon's weight-bearing orders and need protection of the construct; hemiarthroplasty by a lateral approach allows freer flexion but still needs gluteal retraining; total hip replacement through a posterior approach needs the standard dislocation precautions — no adduction, internal rotation beyond neutral, or flexion past 90 degrees in the first six weeks. Assess hip range of motion, manual muscle testing of the abductors and quadriceps, sitting and standing balance, then gait — frame to crutches to stick — and progress stair training. Measure limb length and gait deviations each visit.

Deep vein thrombosis (calf swelling, tenderness), pulmonary infection in the bed-bound patient, wound infection, dislocation (sudden shortening and pain with rotation), and in fixation cases the late failures of non-union and avascular necrosis presenting as persistent groin pain. Any of these is a referral, not a treatment modification.

Record objective outcomes — Harris Hip Score, Timed Up and Go, walking distance achieved, and independence in transfers and toileting. Plan discharge around the home: floor-level versus western toilet, stair access, and a family member trained in safe assistance. Follow up at six weeks and three months for progression of aids and resistance.

Say "assessment depends on the operation performed" in your first paragraph. Half the marks in this question are for distinguishing fixation from arthroplasty management — a single answer that ignores this reads as a generic hip protocol.
Say "assessment depends on the operation performed" in your first paragraph. Half the marks in this question are for distinguishing fixation from arthroplasty management — a single answer that ignores this reads as a generic hip protocol.

5Recent advances

  • Mazarello Paes et al. (2025) — a systematic review of 317,173 patients found early mobilisation within 48 hours of hip fracture surgery was associated with better patient-reported outcomes, reduced length of stay, fewer complications and lower mortality.
  • Sheehan et al. (2021) — analysis of the UK National Hip Fracture Database showed mobilisation within 36 hours of surgery was associated with a 2-fold increase in the adjusted odds of hospital discharge by 30 days.
  • Kronborg et al. (2017) — a randomised controlled trial found acute in-hospital physiotherapy with knee-extension strength training was feasible and reduced quadriceps strength deficits soon after hip fracture surgery.
  • Sylliaas et al. (2011) — a randomised controlled trial showed a 12-week progressive strength-training programme after hip fracture improved lower-limb strength, balance and mobility in older patients.
  • Siminiuc et al. (2024) — a cohort study found each additional physiotherapy session per day was associated with 2.2 fewer acute hospital days, and earlier walking improved the odds of returning to private residence.

6References

  1. Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures — femoral neck.
  2. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient — hip chapters.
  3. McKinnis LN. Musculoskeletal Imaging — hip and pelvis.
  4. Greenspan A, Beltran J. Orthopaedic Imaging — fractures of the hip.
  5. Mazarello Paes V, Ting A, Masters J, et al. Time to mobilization following hip fracture surgery and patient outcomes: a systematic review. Bone Jt Open. 2025.
  6. Sheehan KJ, Goubar A, Almilaji O, et al. Discharge after hip fracture surgery by mobilisation timing: secondary analysis of the UK National Hip Fracture Database. Age Ageing. 2021;50(2):415-422.

On the evaluation form — Q6: Fracture neck of femur — pre- and post-operative assessment

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: elderly patient with a classic history of trivial fall. Chief complaints: groin and thigh pain; unable to stand or bear weight after the fall. Past medical/personal/socioeconomic history: osteoporosis; previous falls; vision deficit; comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension, cardiac status for anaesthetic fitness); medications (anticoagulants); living circumstances and pre-fracture mobility. Symptom analysis: site — groin/hip; type — sharp; severity 7-9/10 at rest and on movement. Vital signs recorded; consent and counselling for surgery documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Pre-operative: limb shortening with external rotation deformity (typically 45-60°), abduction attitude variable; patient unable to roll or lift the limb. Post-operative: surgical scar/dressing; limb alignment; pillow position; drains if any.

On palpation. Pre-operative: gentle assessment only; palpation not performed beyond this. Post-operative: wound tenderness, temperature and effusion signs in the hip region.

1. Motor assessment

Pre-operative: myotomal screening deferred; documented inability to actively raise the straight limb. Post-operative (per surgeon's protocol): AROM of hip (avoiding ranges restricted by approach/fixation); MMT of hip abductors, flexors, extensors and quadriceps (gluteus medius weakness central after surgery); knee AROM; reflexes; muscle girth of thigh to track quadriceps atrophy; true and apparent limb length measured.

2. Sensory assessment

Sensation over the thigh and leg to exclude sciatic/femoral nerve injury (rare but documented post-operatively); sensorium and cognition screening (delirium risk) in the elderly.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: post-operative bed mobility, transfers and stair negotiation; Parker Mobility Score documents pre- and post-operative mobility. Outcome measures: Harris Hip Score (0-100), Oxford Hip Score (0-48), TUG, Berg Balance Scale (0-56), Visual Analogue Scale/NPRS (0-10) for pain.

4. Gait analysis

Post-operative gait with walker/frame starting on day 1-2 per protocol; weight-bearing status per fixation (often touch-down after fixation, weight-bearing as tolerated after cemented arthroplasty).

5. Balance

Balance assessed by the Berg Balance Scale (0-56) for falls risk.

6. Hand function

Grip, reaching and release relevant to safe use of the walking frame during gait and transfer training; assistive-device use documented with the gait prescription.

7. Coordination

Coordination is screened within the neurological examination; in this elderly group, sensorium and cognition screening (delirium risk) is the more relevant safety assessment.

8. Investigations

Radiographs of the hip, correlated with all examination findings — Garden classification (I-II undisplaced; III-IV displaced) determines management: internal fixation for undisplaced fractures, hemi- or total arthroplasty for displaced fractures in the elderly.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the diagnostic pattern; each test is recorded individually as positive or negative for the patient on testing — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
Axial compression / heel percussion testGentle percussion on the heel of the extended limbSharp groin painIntracapsular femoral neck fracture
Log roll testGentle passive internal/external rotation of hip with knee extendedPain and guardingFracture neck of femur (screening)
Trendelenburg testStanding on one leg, pelvis observedPelvis drops on unsupported sideAbductor insufficiency post-surgery
Thomas testSupine; lumbar flattened by flexing one hip, other hip extendedExtended thigh lifts off plinthPost-operative hip flexion contracture
Timed up and go (TUG)Rise from chair, walk 3 m, return, sitTime increased vs age norm / assists neededFunctional mobility and falls risk post-op
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Post-surgical pain
  • Abductor and quadriceps weakness
  • Reduced hip/knee ROM
  • Gait deviation

Functional limitations:

  • Dependent transfers and gait

Disabilities:

  • Loss of independent ambulation and community participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-operative fracture neck of femur with pain, abductor and quadriceps weakness, reduced hip/knee ROM and gait deviation, causing dependence in transfers and ambulation and loss of community participation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): independent bed mobility and transfers; ambulate 30 m with frame within weight-bearing orders; pain 3/10 or less; prevent chest infection/DVT (breathing exercises, ankle pumps).

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): independent gait with stick and then unaided as able; hip abductor strength 4/5; Berg above 45; independent stairs and activities of daily living; falls-prevention plan in place.

13. Treatment plan

Pre-operative: chest physiotherapy, breathing exercises, DVT prophylaxis exercises, positioning for comfort, patient education. Post-operative Stage 1: pain and oedema management, ankle pumps, quadriceps and gluteal isometrics, bed mobility and transfer training, progressive ambulation within weight-bearing orders. Stage 2: progressive abductor and quadriceps strengthening, hip/knee ROM, gait re-education progressing from walker to stick, stair training. Stage 3: long-term bone-health and osteoporosis follow-up with the physician.

14. Home programme

Standing abductor exercises; sit-to-stand repetitions; walking progression; home-hazard modification and balance/falls-prevention training.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe assessment methods in poliomyelitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5b — Pediatric orthopedics and residual paralysis

★ Memory hook — Sensation is intact — and any muscle below grade 3 must be tested gravity-eliminated.

1Introduction

Poliomyelitis destroys anterior horn cells and leaves a patchy, asymmetrical, flaccid paralysis with intact sensation. Assessment in the residual stage is muscle-by-muscle, because every orthotic and surgical decision depends on the strength chart — this answer sets out those methods.

2Physiology

The anterior horn cell is the lower motor neuron that forms the final common pathway from the spinal cord to skeletal muscle. A muscle graded on the MRC scale from 0 (no contraction) to 5 (normal power) reflects the number and function of surviving motor units innervating it; grade 3 marks the landmark of movement against gravity.

3Pathophysiology

The poliovirus destroys anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, producing lower motor neuron flaccid paralysis that is characteristically asymmetrical and patchy — a whole limb is rarely equally weak. Sensation is intact, which separates it from every compressive radiculopathy and from leprosy neuropathy, a distinction you may be the first to make in an Indian OPD. The disease runs through stages — acute febrile stage, recovery phase over months as oedema settles and surviving neurons reinnervate, and the long residual stage with atrophy, imbalance and deformity where most physiotherapy assessment happens.

4Answer

Manual muscle testing of every major muscle group of the limbs and trunk using Daniels and Worthingham's standard positions, graded on MRC grading from 0 to 5. Two habits make the assessment polio-specific: test in the gravity-eliminated plane first for muscles below grade 3, and chart a detailed segmental map rather than a summary grade per limb, because orthotic and surgical decisions are made muscle by muscle. Grade each muscle at its strongest joint position, watch for trick movements, and note fatigue — a muscle that holds grade 4 for the first five repetitions may collapse by the tenth.

Fig 7 — The MRC line with grade 3 circled. In polio, the whole orthotic and tendon-transfer plan hangs on whether a muscle is above or below that circle.

Limb circumference measured at fixed bony landmarks (10, 15, 20 centimetres from the joint line) and compared between sides quantifies disuse and denervation atrophy. Joint range of motion charting picks up the contractures of the residual stage — hip flexion-abduction, knee flexion, and equinus at the ankle. Record leg-length discrepancy from ASIS to medial malleolus, and check for joint laxity in the flail limb.

Watch gait and read the weakness from it: gluteus medius lurch, a hand-on-thigh or hand-on-knee push-off for quadriceps weakness, high stepping if the dorsiflexors are gone, and calcaneal gait if triceps surae is lost. Assess transfers, floor sitting and rising — a daily necessity in Indian households — and independence in activities of daily living. Examine the spine in forward bending for paralytic scoliosis and measure the rib hump. In severe involvement, record respiratory muscle function (vital capacity, breath-hold, accessory muscle use) and screen for the late picture of post-polio syndrome: new weakness, fatigue and pain decades after the original illness, diagnosed by those features in a confirmed polio survivor.

The muscle map converts directly into a plan: grade 3 quadriceps with weak hip flexors points to a knee-ankle-foot orthosis with a knee lock; unbalanced feet progress toward tendon-transfer referral; progressive scoliosis is referred for bracing or surgery. That is the purpose of the entire assessment — each grade on the chart should be traceable to one recommendation.

Write "sensation is intact" early and underline it mentally. Examiners use polio to test whether you can distinguish lower motor neuron disease from peripheral nerve lesions, and that single phrase settles it.
Write "sensation is intact" early and underline it mentally. Examiners use polio to test whether you can distinguish lower motor neuron disease from peripheral nerve lesions, and that single phrase settles it.

5Recent advances

  • Kumru et al. (2013) — quantitative sensory testing revealed mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in polio survivors, suggesting a more generalised sensory component to the pain.
  • Silva et al. (2020) — interactive videogame (Wii Sports) upper-limb training was safe and feasible in post-polio syndrome and improved dexterity compared with conventional active exercises.
  • Chan et al. (2003) — a randomised controlled trial found moderate-intensity progressive resistance training of the thumb muscles was safe and increased strength in post-polio patients without harming motor-unit survival.
  • Koopman et al. (2015) — a Cochrane review of treatments for post-polio syndrome found muscle strengthening is safe and may improve strength, but evidence for most interventions is limited, guiding cautious, individualised exercise prescription.
  • Cup et al. (2007) — a systematic review of exercise therapy and other physical therapy for neuromuscular diseases found supervised strengthening and aerobic training can improve function in polio survivors without adverse effects.

6References

  1. Daniels L, Worthingham C. Muscle Testing: Techniques of Manual Examination.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — neurological and orthotic chapters.
  3. Chui K, Jorge M, Yen SC, Lusardi MM. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  4. Li Hi Shing S, Chipika RH, Finegan E, Murray D, Hardiman O, Bede P. Post-polio syndrome: more than just a lower motor neuron disease. Front Neurol. 2019;10:773.
  5. Neuwirth C, Nandedkar S, Stalberg E, Weber M. Motor Unit Number Index (MUNIX) as a biomarker of motor unit loss in post-polio syndrome versus needle EMG. J Electromyogr Kinesiol. 2019.

On the evaluation form — Q7: Residual poliomyelitis — assessment methods

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: patient with a history of febrile illness in childhood followed by acute flaccid asymmetric limb weakness that stabilized after the paralytic stage; education, occupation and home environment enquired. Chief complaints: residual weakness with or without deformity, shortening and caliper use; fatigue with activity; joint pain from overuse of compensatory muscles. Past medical/personal history: distribution and progression of weakness (new weakness or pain screens for post-polio syndrome if new progression appears decades later); orthosis/assistive device use; vaccination history. Symptom analysis: weakness — constant, non-progressive; fatigue — with activity; joint pain — from overuse of compensatory muscles. Vital signs normal; respiratory symptoms if bulbar/spinal involvement history.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Asymmetric muscle wasting; limb shortening; attitude/deformities — equinovarus foot, genu recurvatum, knee flexion contracture, scoliosis, pelvic obliquity, talipes; trophic changes absent. Type of gait: high-stepping, hand-to-knee, Trendelenburg or circumduction gait depending on the affected muscles.

On palpation. Diminished bulk with flaccid tone; no spasticity; joint mobility assessed for contracture; limb girth reduced on the affected side.

1. Motor assessment

The core of the assessment: MMT graded on the MRC 0-5 scale, charted muscle-by-muscle (both limbs charted for comparison and to detect compensatory overuse); AROM/PROM with end-feel (flaccid, soft end-feel); resisted isometrics to grade strength; reflexes diminished or absent in affected myotomes with no upper motor neuron signs; circumferential girth measurement at fixed landmarks; true and apparent limb length; joint laxity/contracture measurement. The grading guides method selection: grade-specific exercises, gravity-eliminated or anti-gravity positions, hydrotherapy for very weak muscles.

2. Sensory assessment

Critical and characteristic: sensation is intact in polio (anterior horn cell disease) — this differentiates it from other lower motor neuron lesions; document normal dermatomes, intact bowel/bladder and normal cognition.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: functional ambulation distance; wheelchair skills where relevant; transfers; stairs. Outcome measures: MRC manual muscle grading, FIM (18-126) for overall independence in Indian inpatient rehabilitation settings, Berg Balance Scale (0-56) where applicable, Six-Minute Walk Test (functional walking endurance), girth and limb length measurements.

4. Gait analysis

Gait analysis with and without orthosis; the pattern (high-stepping, hand-to-knee, Trendelenburg, circumduction) depends on the muscles affected, as noted on observation.

5. Balance

Balance assessed by the Berg Balance Scale (0-56) where applicable.

6. Hand function

Hand function (reaching, grasping, releasing) is assessed where the upper limbs are affected; caliper and assistive-device use is documented as part of the assessment.

7. Coordination

Coordination is characteristically preserved in poliomyelitis (anterior horn cell disease); it is screened within the neurological examination, and marked incoordination would suggest an alternative diagnosis.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the assessment pattern for this condition; each test is recorded individually with the patient's actual value — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
Manual muscle testing (MRC scale)Muscle tested in graded positions (gravity-eliminated, anti-gravity, against resistance)Grades 0-3 typical in affected musclesDenotes strength level; guides exercise and orthotic prescription
Circumferential girth measurementTape at fixed bony-anchored landmarks (thigh, calf)Reduced girth vs the sound limbQuantifies wasting and tracks progress
True vs apparent limb lengthTape ASIS to medial malleolus; umbilicus to malleolusTrue shortening from growth arrestLeg-length discrepancy — heel raise/orthosis planning
Spirometry / single-breath countFVC and peak flow measuredReduced vital capacityRespiratory muscle involvement
Gowers'/proximal weakness screenObserve rising from floor and stair climbingHand-to-thigh push-off or hand-to-knee gaitQuadriceps/gluteal weakness pattern
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Flaccid weakness and wasting of specific muscle groups
  • Joint contractures/deformities
  • Limb shortening
  • Fatigue

Functional limitations:

  • Altered gait
  • Reduced mobility and transfers

Disabilities:

  • Impaired community participation
  • Schooling/employment barriers
11. Functional diagnosis

Residual poliomyelitis with flaccid weakness, wasting, joint contractures/deformities, limb shortening and fatigue, causing altered gait, reduced mobility and transfers, and impaired community participation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): measurable strength gain of one grade in targeted muscles; 10° improvement in a treatable contracture; independent home exercise programme with correct orthosis donning.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): improved gait independence with orthosis; FIM gain in locomotion items; reduced energy cost of walking; independence in self-care and, where appropriate, vocational/functional return.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: grade-specific strengthening (gravity-eliminated for grades 1-2, anti-gravity and resisted work for grade 3 and above; hydrotherapy where pool access exists); passive stretching and serial casting/splints for contractures. Stage 2: orthotic prescription and training (calipers, knee-ankle-foot orthoses, heel raises for shortening), gait re-education, balance training. Stage 3: functional and vocational rehabilitation, endurance within fatigue limits (energy conservation for post-polio fatigue), family education, surgical referral options (tendon transfers) where indicated.

14. Home programme

Daily graded exercises for weak muscle groups; stretches for contractures; gait practice with orthosis; periodic reassessment of the strength chart.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Enumerate ergonomic risk assessment in musculoskeletal disorders.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6a — Ergonomic risk assessment

★ Memory hook — RULA seated, REBA whole-body, NIOSH lifting, Strain Index wrist — pair each tool with its task.

1Introduction

Ergonomic risk assessment quantifies the mismatch between job demands and worker capacity so that work-related musculoskeletal disorders can be predicted and prevented. This answer enumerates the risk factors, the stepwise process, and the validated tools with their territories.

2Physiology

The musculoskeletal system tolerates load within the limits set by tissue strength, posture and recovery time. Force, repetition, posture, vibration and recovery interact; a task is safe when the imposed demand stays within the worker's structural and physiological capacity and adequate recovery is allowed.

3Pathophysiology

Ergonomic risk assessment quantifies the mismatch between job demands and worker capacity. The risk factors to enumerate are: forceful exertion; repetition and pace; awkward and static postures; whole-body and hand-arm vibration; contact stress; prolonged sitting or standing; cold environment and poor lighting; and psychosocial factors such as low control over work. Together these drive the work-related musculoskeletal disorders seen in clinics — low back pain, neck and shoulder complaints of computer users, and hand-wrist conditions of repetitive workers.

4Answer

Assessment follows a fixed sequence: 1. Job analysis — observe the actual task, tools, cycle times and workstation layout; 2. Hazard identification — match observed exposure to the risk-factor list; 3. Risk quantification with a validated instrument; 4. Interpretation of scores against action levels; 5. Intervention by the hierarchy of controls — engineering change before administrative change before worker training; 6. Re-assessment after the change. Writing the sequence earns the process marks even before any tool is named.

Fig 8 — The REBA scoring route. Knowing that one tool's internal logic to this depth demonstrates you can use it, not just spell it — which is the difference between enumeration and understanding.

For lifting tasks, the NIOSH lifting equation computes a recommended weight limit from load, horizontal distance, vertical height, travel distance, asymmetry and frequency, and expresses the actual load as a lifting index, where values above 1 indicate increased risk. For whole-body postural load, RULA scores the upper limb (used at computer and assembly workstations) and REBA scores the entire body including force and activity, giving action levels 0 to 4 from negligible to immediate change. For repetitive upper-limb work, OCRA counts technical actions against a recommended frequency, and the Strain Index rates distal upper-limb exposure for conditions such as carpal tunnel syndrome in hand-intensive trades. The Quick Exposure Check allows the worker to co-rate exposure — fast, participative, useful on a live shop floor. OWAS classifies whole-body postures from observation and video. Alongside the instruments sit job-demand analysis and worker symptom surveys, which complete the picture with the worker's own report.

Each tool ends in an action level, and the level dictates the response — engineering redesign (raise the workbench, add a hoist), administrative limits (rotate jobs, micro-breaks), and worker training. The Indian application is wide: garment and electronics assembly lines for RULA and OCRA, hospital patient handling and agricultural lifting for REBA and NIOSH, and the small workshop with no formal safety officer where the physiotherapist's assessment is the only one the worker will ever get.

Marks live in the pairing of tool with task: "RULA for seated assembly work, REBA for whole-body, NIOSH for lifting, Strain Index for the wrist." Ten marks for four correct pairings and one worked score.
Marks live in the pairing of tool with task: "RULA for seated assembly work, REBA for whole-body, NIOSH for lifting, Strain Index for the wrist." Ten marks for four correct pairings and one worked score.

5Recent advances

  • Takala et al. (2010) — a landmark systematic evaluation of observational methods for assessing biomechanical exposures at work compared the reliability, validity and usability of tools such as RULA, REBA and OWAS, guiding clinicians in choosing an appropriate ergonomic risk assessment.
  • David (2005) — a review of ergonomic methods for assessing exposure to work-related musculoskeletal disorder risk factors clarified which observation-based tools are valid and practical for workplace assessment.
  • Huang et al. (2020) — wearable inertial-sensor systems now automate RULA and REBA scoring from joint angles, achieving high agreement with expert raters (ICC ≥ 0.83, classification accuracy > 88%).
  • Baklouti et al. (2024) — a novel IMU-based system benchmarked against RULA, REBA, Strain Index and Rodgers Muscle Fatigue Analysis reduced assessment time from about 70 minutes to about 2 minutes.
  • Battini et al. (2022) — the WEM-Platform provides real-time full-body ergonomic assessment (RULA, REBA, OWAS and PERA) with visual feedback to workers using an inertial suit and activity tracker.

6References

  1. Kroemer KHE, Grandjean E. Fitting the Task to the Human — ergonomics text.
  2. Waters TR, Putz-Anderson V, Garg A. NIOSH Revised Lifting Equation (primary).
  3. Hignett S, McAtamney L. REBA (primary paper); McAtamney L, Corlett EN. RULA (primary paper).
  4. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice — occupational context.
  5. A novel IMU-based system for work-related musculoskeletal disorders risk assessment. Sensors. 2024;24(11):3419.
  6. Development and validation of a wearable inertial-sensors-based automated system for WMSD risk assessment. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2020;17(17):6050.

On the evaluation form — Q8: Ergonomic risk assessment in work-related musculoskeletal disorders

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: worker — job title, task description and daily routine (shifts, overtime, targets), tools and machinery, duration of repetitive or static exposures. Chief complaints: region-wise symptoms. Symptom analysis per region: site; onset (related to job change); type; severity on NPRS (0-10); aggravating factors — specific tasks, sustained postures, forceful or repetitive exertion, vibration; relieving factors — rest, leave, task change. Pain evaluation: pattern suggesting occupational causation — symptoms improve on weekends/leave and recur on resumption. Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire administered region-wise. Vital signs and general health recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation (at the actual workstation). Working posture — neck/trunk flexion, shoulder abduction/elevation, wrist deviation; repetitive cycle time; force exertion; contact stress; static loading; workstation dimensions (chair, monitor, desk heights); hand-arm or whole-body vibration exposure; video recording for later analysis where permitted.

On palpation. Tenderness, muscle tension or trigger points in the symptomatic region (e.g., forearm extensors, trapezius, low back), correlating symptoms with the observed exposure.

1. Motor assessment

AROM/PROM, MMT and resisted isometrics of the involved region to document impairment; functional capacity such as grip strength, overhead reach, lifting ability compared with the job's physical demands; postural endurance in the required task position.

2. Sensory assessment

Screen relevant to exposure: carpal tunnel (median nerve) symptoms with repetitive wrist work — Phalen/monofilament or two-point discrimination if indicated; radiculopathy screen for neck/back postures; otherwise normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: task simulation of the actual job cycle; tolerated repetition counts; task duration before symptom onset; functional positional tolerance (sitting, standing, overhead work); walking/lifting demands matched to the worker's capacity. Outcome measures: Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (region-wise symptom mapping), NPRS (0-10), symptom diary against shifts, RULA/REBA scores repeated after redesign as objective outcome, days of sickness absence.

4. Gait analysis

Walking demands of the job matched to the worker's capacity as part of the task analysis; no gait deviation is expected from the disorder itself unless the lower limb is the involved region.

5. Balance

Balance is not a routine component of this ergonomic risk assessment; it is considered only where the job involves balance-critical tasks.

6. Hand function

Reaching, grasping, releasing and tool handling are observed during task simulation; wrist deviation and repetitive hand tasks are key exposure variables, and tool modification/assistive devices are considered under ergonomic redesign.

7. Coordination

Coordination is observed within the task simulation and posture analysis rather than tested separately.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the scoring pattern of each assessment tool; the worker's own scores are recorded on testing — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
RULA (Rapid Upper Limb Assessment)Observe/photograph working posture of neck, trunk, upper limb with force/load scoresFinal score 1-7 mapped to action levels 1-4; levels 3-4 = prompt or immediate changeUpper limb postural risk requiring intervention priority
REBA (Rapid Entire Body Assessment)Score postures of trunk, neck, legs, arms with coupling and loadFinal score 1-15 mapped to action levels 0-4Whole-body postural risk, especially dynamic tasks
OWAS (Ovako Working Posture Analysis)Sample working postures by observation; classify trunk/arms/legs with loadAction categories 1-4 (category 4 = immediate corrective action)Urgency of posture correction in industry
NIOSH lifting equationCompute recommended weight limit from horizontal, vertical, distance, frequency, asymmetry and coupling multipliersLifting index > 1 (load exceeds recommended limit)Lifting task exceeds safe capacity; redesign needed
Quick Exposure Check (QEC)Combine observer posture scores with worker's perceived exertion and discomfortHigh exposure scores for back, shoulder, wrist, neckPrioritizes ergonomic intervention with worker participation
Strain IndexRate repetitive hand tasks on intensity, duration, frequency, hand posture, speed, shift lengthScore above threshold indicates elevated risk of distal upper limb disorderRepetitive hand-intensive work risk (e.g., assembly, packing)
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Localized muscle tension
  • Tenderness
  • Reduced ROM or strength
  • Exposure risks driving the disorder: sustained awkward posture, high repetition, excessive force, vibration, inadequate recovery

Functional limitations:

  • Reduced task tolerance

Disabilities:

  • Sickness absence
  • Reduced productivity
11. Functional diagnosis

Work-related musculoskeletal disorder with localized muscle tension, tenderness and reduced ROM or strength, driven by sustained awkward postures, high repetition, excessive force and vibration, causing reduced task tolerance, sickness absence and reduced productivity.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): symptom reduction by 2 points on NPRS; workstation micro-adjustments implemented; micro-break and stretch routine established.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): RULA/REBA action level reduced to an acceptable level; full-duty task tolerance without symptom recurrence; zero sickness absence attributable to the disorder; worker trained in self-management.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: symptom management (education, stretches, soft-tissue work for the involved region). Stage 2: ergonomic redesign of the workstation — chair and monitor height, tool modification, job rotation, mechanical aids, reduced repetition/force, vibration damping; administrative controls (breaks, task variety) — feasible and low-cost in Indian small-industry and IT settings. Stage 3: worker-specific conditioning for the task, workplace stretch programme, training and re-audit of scores, periodic surveillance with the Nordic questionnaire.

14. Home programme

Daily regional stretches; strengthening; general fitness; advice on posture during commute and domestic work.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Explain evaluation of work capacity and return to work.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6b — Functional and work capacity evaluation

★ Memory hook — Match capacity to the job, not the diagnosis.

1Introduction

Work capacity evaluation measures what a person can actually sustain in a real task and judges it against the demands of the job. This answer sets out the concepts, the functional capacity evaluation, job demand analysis, and the return-to-work plan.

Three words that students blur: impairment is what the body has lost (a weak back after disc surgery); work capacity is what the person can actually sustain in a real task; and disability is the gap between capacity and the job's demands. Work capacity evaluation measures the middle term and judges it against the third. Frame it in ICF language — impairment, activity, participation — and add the psychosocial flags that predict slower return: yellow flags (fear-avoidance and catastrophising in the worker), blue flags (worker's perception of the workplace) and black flags (actual system barriers — no light duty available, pending compensation). Capacity is behavioural as much as physical.

2Physiology

Physical work capacity is the product of musculoskeletal strength and endurance, aerobic fitness and the skill of the task. A worker can sustain a task when the physical, cardiovascular and postural demands stay within measured capacity across a working day.

3Pathophysiology

When capacity falls below the job's demands a gap — disability — opens between what the worker can sustain and what the task requires. The gap is widened by psychosocial flags: yellow flags (fear-avoidance and catastrophising), blue flags (the worker's perception of the workplace) and black flags (system barriers such as no light duty or pending compensation).

4Answer

The FCE is a standardised, two-day battery performed over four to five hours each day to capture fatigue. It tests the real demands of work: lifting from floor to waist and waist to shoulder, carrying, pushing and pulling, overhead reach, crouching and kneeling, hand grip and endurance, standing and sitting tolerance, and repeated trunk bending. Scores are recorded as safe maximum weights and tolerances. Equally important is validity: consistency of effort across dissimilar tests, physiological plausibility (does the heart rate rise with the load?), and behaviour during testing. A full FCE with inconsistency documented is a defensible report; a gym session is not.

Fig 9 — The FCE on the left feeding the return-to-work ladder on the right. Every rung of that ladder is a comparison between measured capacity and job demand — that comparison is the whole concept.

Job demand analysis breaks the worker's actual job into physical requirements: weights and frequencies of lifting, distances carried, postures held, walking and climbing hours, and grip demands. Physical demand levels then classify work from sedentary through light, medium and heavy to very heavy. Return-to-work decisions compare FCE results against these demands — a worker with a 15-kilogram safe lift returning to a 25-kilogram heavy job is not ready for full duty, whatever the MRI says.

Early, graded return beats prolonged rest — the strongest evidence in this field. The plan escalates capacity: work conditioning (physical reconditioning, two to four hours a day) progresses to work hardening (simulated job tasks, real tools, real pace, half to full day). On the job, the plan uses modified duties — reduced hours, restricted lifting, alternate tasks — reviewed every one to two weeks with the employer, and communicated in writing. Address yellow flags with graded exposure and reassurance, not more passive treatment.

Formal modified duty is rare outside large employers and the ESIC system; for the self-employed farmer, tailor or shopkeeper, build the same grading around their actual tasks — half-days at the counter, no overhead loading this month. Whatever the setting, the report must state safe limits in plain numbers (kilograms, minutes, postures), the gap to job demands, and the next review date.

One line carries the concept: "return to work is decided by matching capacity to job demands, not by the medical diagnosis." Write it once, then fill the page with the FCE and the plan.
One line carries the concept: "return to work is decided by matching capacity to job demands, not by the medical diagnosis." Write it once, then fill the page with the FCE and the plan.

5Recent advances

  • Steel et al. (2024) — a randomised controlled trial is evaluating the effectiveness of functional capacity evaluation on the return-to-work process for people on sick leave or work disability.
  • Gross & Battié (2004) — a prospective study found functional capacity evaluation performance predicted time to return to work in chronic low back pain claimants, but did not predict sustained return to work.
  • Bühne et al. (2020) — a cohort study found that patients whose measured functional capacity matched job demands had sixfold higher odds of returning to work, confirming the predictive validity of a customised FCE.
  • Villotti et al. (2024) — a systematic review identified work accommodations, return-to-work expectations, physical job demands and return-to-work self-efficacy as modifiable prognostic factors for return to work.
  • Bhupal et al. (2024) — a scoping review found information and communication technology (including sensors and machine learning) is emerging in return-to-work FCE but is not yet widely adopted, and no unified system exists.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — work evaluation chapters.
  2. King PM. Sourcebook of Occupational Rehabilitation (functional capacity evaluation).
  3. World Health Organization. ICF framework.
  4. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice.
  5. Predictive validity of a customized functional capacity evaluation in patients with musculoskeletal disorders. Int Arch Occup Environ Health. 2020;93(5).
  6. Technological interventions in Functional Capacity Evaluations: an insight into current applications. Work. 2024.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Work capacity evaluation and return to work

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: worker recovering from musculoskeletal injury or surgery (e.g., lumbar disc prolapse, fracture, ligament reconstruction) referred for functional capacity evaluation before return to work; job title and formal/actual physical demands (lifting, carrying, pushing, pulling, standing, sitting, climbing); date and details of injury; treatment received; current activity level. Chief concern: capacity to return to pre-injury work. Symptom analysis: pain on NPRS (0-10), its behaviour with specific tasks; aggravating and relieving factors. Psychosocial screen: fear of movement/re-injury, job dissatisfaction, litigation or compensation issues; Orebro Musculoskeletal Pain Questionnaire to identify risk of long-term disability. Vital signs recorded before testing.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Posture during interview; guarding/kinesiophobic behaviour; willingness to move; use of aids; body mechanics in undressing and chair rise.

On palpation. Tenderness and tissue tension in the involved region; signs of persistent inflammation or guarding.

1. Motor assessment

AROM/PROM, MMT and resisted isometrics of the involved region establishing baseline impairment.
