11. Functional diagnosis

Postural instability in an elderly faller driven by weak anti-gravity muscles, reduced distal sensation, kyphotic posture and poor postural reactions, limiting floor rise, stairs and outdoor walking and restricting activity through fear of falling.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Safe transfers; single-leg stance 5 s per side; anti-gravity strength MRC 3+/4; independent in drills.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Improved TUG with safe unaided outdoor walking; Berg gain ≥10 points; independent stairs; reduced fear of falling.

13. Treatment plan

Anti-gravity strengthening 3/week: heel raises 3×10 progressing to 3×20, weighted sit-to-stand, step-ups, trunk extension, gluteal bridging. Balance retraining: ankle- and hip-strategy work — tandem and single-leg stance, perturbation drills, foam-board training, head-turns while walking. Postural work: thoracic extension, wall angels, scapular setting.

14. Home programme

Daily kitchen-counter circuit (heel raises, chair stands, tandem walking); vitamin D and vision review; footwear and home-hazard advice.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe McKenzie's principles of mobilization.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 4 — manual therapy schools (mechanical diagnosis and therapy)

★ Memory hook — CENTRALISE, DON'T PERIPHERALISE — repeated end-range loading that pulls the pain towards the spine (centralisation) marks the direction to treat; pain that marches away (peripheralisation) marks the direction to avoid.

1Introduction

Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (MDT), the McKenzie method, rests on one radical idea: the patient's symptomatic response to repeated end-range loading is the most reliable guide to classification and treatment. Assessment begins with a full history and baseline symptom mapping (where the pain is now, how far it spreads, what makes it better and worse). The examiner then performs repeated movement testing — sagittal first (flexion, extension in lying and standing), then frontal plane if needed — five to ten repetitions at end range, and watches what happens to the DISTAL extent of symptoms. McKenzie deliberately says little about pathology; the behaviour of the pain under load is the diagnosis.

The answer then defines the key phenomena, the three syndromes with their matched treatment, and the force-progression and self-management rules.

2Physiology

Normally the lumbar intervertebral disc behaves as a hydrated, pressurised structure that shares load with the facet joints and the trunk muscles, and segmental movement is a smooth roll-and-glide. Repeated end-range loading in a single direction can hydraulically shift nuclear material within the disc, so the direction of loading — not a fixed recipe — governs how the segment behaves. That mechanical behaviour is the physiology that the McKenzie assessment deliberately provokes and reads.

3Pathophysiology

centralisation is the phenomenon by which referred or radicular pain retreats proximally towards the midline spine in response to a specific repeated movement — the single best prognostic sign in MDT and one of the best in spinal manual therapy overall. Peripheralisation is the opposite: the pain marches distally, and that movement is immediately withdrawn and avoided. Directional preference is the movement direction that produces centralisation or lasting relief — most commonly extension in the lumbar spine. A patient with a directional preference is treated in that direction; this is the operational core of the method.

The derangement is an internal displacement of nuclear material that makes the pain mechanically changeable and intermittent — centralising or peripheralising under load — and it is this abnormal, load-sensitive behaviour that the method classifies and treats.

4Answer

Derangement syndrome — the most common: internal displacement of nuclear material causing a mechanically changeable, intermittent pain that centralises or peripheralises. Treatment: repeated end-range movements in the directional preference (classically prone press-ups or standing extension for a posterior derangement); force is progressed only as far as needed to achieve centralisation. Postural syndrome — pain only on sustained end-range static loading (slumped sitting in a young, normal spine), relieved instantly by position change. Treatment: postural correction plus education; no hands-on needed. Dysfunction syndrome — shortening or scarring of tissue producing consistent end-range pain in a fixed direction that does not change with repetition (e.g., flexion dysfunction after a healed disc episode). Treatment: static end-range stretching in the restricted — and painful — direction, remodelling the adapted tissue over weeks. Any competent answer also mentions the "other" category (non-mechanical presentations, red flags, chronic pain states) for red-flag safety.

Force is progressed along a logical ladder only if the response is incomplete: patient-generated movement, then clinician overpressure, then sagittal mobilisation, then (rarely) manipulation — always re-testing centralisation after each step. The method's second pillar is that the patient treats the patient: the exercises are home exercises performed ten times a day, and the clinician's job is to find, teach and progress them. Maintenance — posture correction (lumbar roll, standing extension after prolonged sitting), regular self-mobilisation, and recurrence management — completes the principle of independence.

McKenzie and May's The Lumbar Spine is the primary reference; systematic reviews support directional preference as a real, clinically useful phenomenon, centralisation as a strong prognostic marker, and MDT as at least as effective as — and in some trials superior to for short-term pain — other conservative care for acute and subacute low back pain. In conclusion: MDT is a classification-driven, assessment-led system in which repeated end-range loading identifies a directional preference, defines one of three syndromes, and hands the treatment to the patient — mobilisation as the servant of a diagnosis, not a recipe.

Fig 4 — The MDT decision tree in one diagram: repeated movements, three possible responses, three syndromes. Reproduce it in the answer margin and the marks follow the branches.
Do not write "McKenzie means extension exercises" — that is the common wrong answer. The principle is RESPONSE-GUIDED loading: centralisation decides the direction, and the syndrome decides the technique. Name all three syndromes with one treatment line each.

5Recent advances

  • Lam et al. (2018) — their meta-analysis in JOSPT found moderate-to-high quality evidence that MDT is not superior for acute low back pain but is superior to other rehabilitation interventions for chronic low back pain.
  • Halliday et al. (2019) — this systematic review showed that trials delivering MDT consistent with its core principles produced larger reductions in pain and disability than "generic" delivery of the method.
  • Hennemann et al. (2024) — a meta-analysis in the Journal of Manual & Manipulative Therapy found low-to-moderate certainty evidence that credentialed-therapist McKenzie care reduces short-term pain and intermediate-term disability in chronic low back pain with directional preference.
  • Mbada et al. (2024) — a randomised controlled trial found telerehabilitation-based McKenzie therapy compared favourably with clinic-based manual therapy for chronic low back pain.

6References

  1. McKenzie R & May S, The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (24).
  2. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — spine mobilisation progression context.
  3. Butler & Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System (26) — contrast with neurodynamic schools.
  4. Lam OT, et al. Effectiveness of the McKenzie Method of Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy for treating low back pain: literature review with meta-analysis. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy 2018;48(6):476–490.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the role of various external appliances used for rehabilitation in patients following L2-L3 disc prolapse.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 4 — external applications (orthoses and supports)

★ Memory hook — HIGH LESION, HIGHER BRACE — L2-L3 is upper lumbar, so control must reach above the lesion (think TLSO, not a simple lumbar belt); brace during activity, wean over 4–6 weeks, and never let the brace replace exercise.

1Introduction

An L2-L3 prolapse is an UPPER lumbar lesion: the segment moves mainly in the sagittal plane, and the classical lumbar extension-biased loading taught for L4-S1 must be applied with more caution this high. The external appliance has four jobs: limit painful flexion (the position that increases posterior annular and nuclear stress), raise intra-abdominal pressure so the abdominal cylinder shares the spinal load — a well-fitted corset can reduce the load on the lumbar column by roughly a third during lifting — provide proprioceptive feedback ("posture reminder") that keeps the patient out of end-range flexion, and, in the acute phase, allow the patient to move and walk while protecting the healing annulus. An lumbosacral orthosis is a prescribed spinal support whose rigid panels and closure system control segmental motion; that is the umbrella term for most of what follows.

The answer sets out the orthotic menu, the ancillary appliances, and the prescription, schedule and weaning rules.

2Physiology

Normally the lumbar spine shares load between the disc, the posterior elements and the abdominal cylinder: raising intra-abdominal pressure lets the abdominal cavity act as a fluid-filled ball that transmits part of the load, reducing the force the lumbar column must carry. A well-fitted corset exploits this mechanism, and the upper lumbar segment (L2-L3) is loaded mainly in the sagittal plane, so flexion is the movement of concern.

3Pathophysiology

In an L2-L3 disc prolapse, nuclear material displaces posteriorly and the healing annulus is vulnerable to flexion, which increases posterior annular and nuclear stress. The appliance buys the annulus a protected interval and cues posture, while the segment heals.

4Answer

Soft canvas corset with abdominal binder: the commonest prescription in Indian practice — inexpensive, available off the shelf, gives abdominal compression and posture cueing with little true motion control; suits the comfort phase. Semi-rigid lumbosacral orthosis: corset with posterior moulded plastic or metal stays and paraspinal steels; controls flexion-extension partially and is the workhorse for the four-to-six-week protected phase after an acute upper lumbar prolapse. Rigid three-point lumbosacral orthosis (e.g., a chairback or Williams-type design): anterior and posterior panels with a three-point system — sternal/sacral and abdominal pads — that genuinely blocks lumbar flexion. Rigid thoraco-lumbo-sacral orthosis: for an L2-L3 lesion, control must extend above the lesion, so the orthosis must include a thoracic band (Boston-type overlap or custom-moulded TLSO); this is the key level-specific point that distinguishes an upper-lumbar answer from a generic one. Hyperextension orthosis (Jewett type): blocks flexion while allowing some extension, mainly post-fracture but worth naming. Each of these works WITH the physiotherapy programme, never instead of it.

During the acute phase: an adjustable walking aid (rollator or cane on the opposite side) to reduce axial load and improve confidence; firm mattress or bed board under a lumbar roll for sleeping; log-rolling technique taught rather than equipment. For daily activities to protect the healing disc: raised toilet seat and commode chair, long-handled reacher and shoe horn (dressing without trunk flexion), elevated chair with armrests, and a lumbar cushion for unavoidable sitting. These are the rehabilitation appliances examiners expect beyond the brace itself.

Prescription principles: fit at the level of the lesion with the pelvic band anchored on the sacrum, worn during activity and weaned at rest, checked for pressure areas in our hot climate, and paired from day one with an isometric abdominal and back programme — because every orthosis unloads the very muscles that must eventually take over. Wearing schedule typically tapers over four to six weeks; prolonged bracing produces trunk muscle atrophy and dependence, which is the classic complication the examiner wants you to warn about.

Chui and colleagues' orthotics text and Maxey and Magnusson detail the biomechanics; randomised evidence suggests orthoses add only modest benefit over exercise-plus-advice alone for uncomplicated disc prolapse, so the modern role is a short, well-defined protective and confidence-building phase — not a substitute for active rehabilitation. In conclusion: at L2-L3 the appliance must reach higher (TLSO logic), buy time for the annulus, use the abdominal cylinder to unload the segment, cue posture, and be withdrawn before dependency develops.

Fig 5 — Trunk outline, one yellow disc at L2-L3, corset band, and the three pads of a three-point orthosis with arrows. The level-specific detail (control must extend ABOVE L2) is what earns the distinguishing marks.
The trap in this question is writing a generic "lumbar belt" essay. L2-L3 is upper lumbar: mention that a standard LSO does not control it, so the orthosis must extend thoracically. Also state the weaning principle — orthosis plus exercise, never orthosis instead of exercise.

5Recent advances

  • Arienti et al. (2026) — this Cochrane review of lumbar supports found insufficient evidence to support their routine use for chronic low back pain; benefits were small and appeared mainly when supports were added to NSAIDs.
  • Azadinia et al. (2023) — a systematic review found external lumbar supports may improve joint position sense and postural control, though effects on motor control remain mixed.
  • Gignoux et al. (2022) — a literature review and meta-analysis found non-rigid lumbar supports may reduce pain in non-specific low back pain, with modest effects.
  • Vick et al. (2024) — a review confirmed that fears of trunk-muscle atrophy and deconditioning from non-rigid bracing are largely unfounded.

6References

  1. Chui et al., Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation (18) — spinal orthosis designs and control levels.
  2. Maxey & Magnusson (13) — orthotic prescription and wearing schedules.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — spinal intervention progression.
  4. McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine (24) — loading considerations at upper lumbar levels.
  5. Arienti C, et al. Lumbar braces and other assistive devices for treatment of chronic low back pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2024.

On the evaluation form — Q5: External appliances / bracing after fracture

I. Subjective examination

30-year-old labourer; template for post-fracture appliance selection. Index presentation: radius fracture out of plaster at 6 weeks with residual wrist stiffness; braced tibial and spinal scenarios are also discussed. Chief complaint: residual wrist stiffness after immobilization. No other past medical history, red flags or vitals are given in the template.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Forearm and calf disuse wasting; plaster-edge skin marks; ankle held plantigrade; no deformity of bony contours documented.

On palpation. Mild fracture-site tenderness; tight gastrosoleus; skin type and scar status noted from plaster-edge marks; no swelling or crepitus documented.

1. Motor assessment. MMT (MRC 0–5): wrist and finger muscles 3+ post-immobilization; knee and ankle groups 4. ROM: wrist flexion/extension 50% of normal; ankle dorsiflexion 10°. Muscle girth: calf circumference 2 cm less than the sound side.

2. Sensory assessment. Median, ulnar and radial territories intact; no cast-related nerve compression.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Grip for work tasks and independent donning and doffing of the appliance assessed. Outcome measures: NPRS 0–10; LEFS 0–80; goniometric ROM of immobilized joints; radiological union correlated with weight-bearing progression.

4. Gait analysis. Assisted gait with crutches — pattern, stair negotiation and endurance assessed.

5. Balance. Imbalance associated with assisted gait while using walking aids.

6. Hand function. Grip for work tasks; independent donning and doffing of the appliance (assistive device management).

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

Serial radiographs confirming fracture union, as per medical records, guide weight-bearing progression; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

No condition-specific special tests are documented for this post-immobilization presentation; assessment centres on ROM, strength, gait and appliance fit.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Post-immobilization stiffness
  • Weakness
  • Assisted-gait imbalance

Functional limitations

  • Weight-bearing
  • Grip

Disabilities

  • Cannot resume manual labour
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-fracture immobilization stiffness and weakness with assisted-gait imbalance, limiting weight-bearing and grip and preventing return to manual labour, requiring graded appliance-supported rehabilitation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Correct independent appliance use; NPRS ≤2; oedema controlled; protected ROM begun.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full pain-free ROM; MRC 4+ in immobilized groups; brace and assistive device weaned; return to heavy work by 3–4 months.

13. Treatment plan

Appliance selection (template):

ApplianceIndicationTypical condition
Arm sling / collar-and-cuffSupport the limb against gravityUpper-limb and shoulder-region fractures
Static cock-up wrist splintRest in functional positionDistal radius fracture after cast removal
Hinged ROM brace (knee/elbow)Controlled motion during healingPeri-articular fracture after fixation
Thoraco-lumbar-sacral orthosisLimit spinal flexion and extensionStable thoraco-lumbar vertebral fracture
Rigid walking bootProtected weight-bearing gaitTibia, ankle and foot fractures in union
Patellar tendon-bearing orthosisOff-load the tibiaTibial shaft and distal tibial fractures
Halo vestRigid cervical immobilizationUnstable upper cervical fracture
Crutches / walkerNon- or partial weight-bearingAny lower-limb fracture before full loading

Phase 1 (protection, 0–6 weeks): appliance fitting with pressure-area checks, isometrics in the brace, oedema control. Phase 2 (controlled motion, 6–10 weeks): supervised ROM, graded resisted exercise, weight-bearing per radiological union. Phase 3 (function, 10 weeks onward): strengthening, work-conditioning, lifting mechanics, staged brace weaning.

14. Home programme

Hourly active ROM of adjacent joints; isometric sets; ankle pumps; skin inspection under splints; wearing-time diary to guide brace reduction.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Describe the evidence-based electrotherapy management of fibromyalgia.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 5 — evidence-based electrotherapy

★ Memory hook — TENS FOR SYMPTOMS, EXERCISE FOR THE DISEASE — electrotherapy is an adjunct; graded aerobic exercise, sleep and education are the core, and each modality should be graded strong, moderate or weak.

1Introduction

Fibromyalgia, by the Wolfe et al. American College of Rheumatology criteria, is chronic widespread pain lasting at least three months with somatic and cognitive symptoms — classified by the widespread pain index and symptom severity scale (the older 1990 criteria counted tender points out of 18).

The answer then gives the physiological rationale, the current-based modalities, the thermal agents, and an honest grading of the evidence.

2Physiology

Mechanism first: according to the gate control theory of Melzack and Wall, stimulation of large-diameter A-beta afferents in the dorsal horn closes the gate on nociceptive transmission — high-frequency, sensory-intensity TENS exploits exactly this. Low-frequency, acupuncture-like TENS at motor intensity recruits endogenous opioid release. Both mechanisms are only plausible adjuncts in fibromyalgia because the problem is central sensitisation — so any modality must be judged by whether it increases activity and sleep, not by immediate pain relief alone.

3Pathophysiology

It is a disorder of central pain processing: diffuse hyperexcitability with reduced descending inhibition, fatigue and non-restorative sleep. Electrotherapy therefore never treats the disease; it treats pain and sleep symptoms as an ADJUNCT to the cornerstones — graded aerobic exercise, education and cognitive-behavioural therapy. An answer that promises cure by machine loses credibility at the first line.

Because the problem is central sensitisation with impaired descending inhibition, electrophysical agents cannot correct the disease; they can only dampen symptoms and enable activity, so they must be judged by whether the patient moves and sleeps better, not by immediate pain relief alone.

4Answer

Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation: the most studied; best used high-frequency (40–80 Hz per DeLisa; 70–100 Hz in practice), strong but comfortable, over the most symptomatic regions for 30 minutes, several times daily — self-applied for flares; trials show modest short-term pain reduction. Interferential therapy (four-pole; beat 20–80 Hz per DeLisa, commonly 90–100 Hz for pain in Indian clinics): widely used in Indian clinics with a similar gate-control rationale; comfort-oriented evidence, less trial support than TENS. Microcurrent therapy (microamperage currents): small trials suggest pain and sleep benefit; evidence remains weak. Electroacupuncture: systematic reviews find it better than sham for pain and stiffness in the short term — one of the better-supported electrical options. Frequency-specific magnetic stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation target the central component directly; promising for pain and fatigue in trials but not yet routine physiotherapy practice — mention them as emerging evidence.

Superficial heat (hot packs, warm showers before exercise to reduce stiffness) and warm-water balneotherapy or hydrotherapy are the strongest of the physical-agent options: randomised trials of warm pool exercise programmes show durable improvements in pain, function and quality of life. Cryotherapy has a role for local flares. Electrophysical agents, in short, are comfort-and-enabling tools wrapped around an exercise programme.

Grading the evidence honestly: strongest — warm-water exercise and graded land-based aerobic exercise (core, not adjunct); moderate — electroacupuncture, some TENS benefit for short-term pain; weak — interferential, microcurrent, static magnets. Conclusion: an evidence-based electrotherapy plan for fibromyalgia uses TENS or electroacupuncture for symptomatic relief and heat or hydrotherapy to enable activity, always subordinate to graded exercise, sleep and education — and is reviewed against function, not pain scores alone.

Fig 6 — One gate diagram does double duty: it is the mechanism for TENS in fibromyalgia AND revision for any pain question in this paper. Large fibres in, gate closes, pain falls.
The phrase that scores is "adjunct to exercise and education — never a substitute". Grade each modality as strong / moderate / weak evidence; examiners reward candidates who rank their own tools honestly rather than listing every machine in the department.

5Recent advances

  • Macfarlane et al. (2017) — the EULAR revised recommendations found that exercise was the only therapy with a strong recommendation in fibromyalgia, positioning electrotherapy as an adjunct within a graduated, non-pharmacological-first programme.
  • Johnson et al. (2022) — the meta-TENS study (381 RCTs) found moderate-certainty evidence of clinically important pain reduction with TENS across chronic pain conditions.
  • García-López et al. (2024) — a systematic review with meta-analysis (12 studies, 944 patients) found TENS improves pain, disability and physical quality of life in fibromyalgia, and works best when used as a stand-alone therapy.
  • Amer-Cuenca et al. (2023) — a dose-dependent meta-analysis showed TENS relieves fibromyalgia pain when applied at high or mixed frequency, at high intensity, for ten or more sessions.
  • Sahebari et al. (2026) — an umbrella review confirmed TENS is safe and gives short-term pain relief, with low-to-moderate certainty of evidence.

6References

  1. Wolfe F et al., American College of Rheumatology fibromyalgia criteria.
  2. Melzack R & Wall PD, Pain mechanisms: a new theory, Science 1965.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — pain physiology and descending inhibition.
  4. O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — chronic pain rehabilitation.
  5. Dailey DL, et al. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation reduces movement-evoked pain and fatigue: a randomized, controlled trial. Arthritis & Rheumatology 2020;72(5):824–836.

On the evaluation form — Q6: Fibromyalgia — evidence-based electrotherapy management

I. Subjective examination

38-year-old homemaker with widespread pain above and below the waist for over a year, non-restorative sleep, fatigue and “brain fog”. Pain 6/10 on NPRS (0–10), fluctuating with exertion and weather; analgesics gave only transient relief. Symptom analysis — site: widespread, above and below the waist; onset: over a year ago; type: diffuse widespread ache; severity: 6/10; aggravating factors: exertion, weather changes; relieving factors: transient relief with analgesics. No red flags or vitals are given in the record.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Guarded slow movements; difficulty rising from a chair; no swelling or deformity.

On palpation. Symmetric tenderness at the classical sites — suboccipital, lower cervical, trapezius, supraspinatus, second rib, epicondylar, gluteal, trochanteric and knee fat pad.

1. Motor assessment. Gross strength 4/5 but effort-dependent; endurance poor; cervical and shoulder ROM full but painful at end-range.

2. Sensory assessment. No focal deficit; allodynia over the trapezius and forearms; reflexes otherwise normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Reduced sit-to-stands; fatigue-limited stairs; flare–rest cycling of activity. Outcome measures: FIQ-R (overall impact of fibromyalgia on function and symptoms); NPRS 0–10; Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index.

4. Gait analysis. Slow but normal gait pattern.

5. Balance. Not documented; no imbalance reported.

6. Hand function. Not documented as affected.

7. Coordination. Not documented; no focal neurological deficit.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment — the diagnosis is made on clinical criteria (below).

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
ACR tender point examinationThumb pressure (~4 kg) on the 18 classical sitesPain at multiple sitesGeneralized hyperalgesia (ACR 1990)
Widespread Pain IndexBody-map count of painful regionsHigh regional pain countWidespread pain of fibromyalgia
Symptom Severity ScaleScore of fatigue, sleep, cognition and somatic symptomsElevated burdenSupports diagnosis (ACR 2016)
Thumb palpation algometryGraded pressure over defined pointsLowered pressure-pain thresholdCentral pain sensitization

In this patient the tender point examination is positive — symmetric tenderness at the classical sites. Numerical WPI, Symptom Severity Scale and algometry results are not documented.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Widespread hyperalgesia
  • Fatigue
  • Poor sleep
  • Deconditioning

Functional limitations

  • Sustained household activity

Disabilities

  • Role strain
  • Social withdrawal
11. Functional diagnosis

Fibromyalgia with widespread hyperalgesia, fatigue, non-restorative sleep and deconditioning, limiting sustained household activity and causing role strain and social withdrawal.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Daytime pain ≤4/10; sleep routine established; pacing diary understood.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). 30 minutes of tolerated aerobic activity on most days; FIQ-R improvement; reduced flare frequency; independent self-management.

13. Treatment plan

Electrotherapy is an adjunct, never the core. TENS — 80–100 Hz, sensory intensity, 20–30 min over the most painful regions during flares; interferential therapy for deep aching relief; superficial heat before exercise; warm-pool hydrotherapy 2–3 times a week. Laser and magnetotherapy have weak, inconsistent evidence and are used only within a graded-exercise framework. Core management: walking or cycling started at 10–15 min and progressed by about 10% weekly, stretching, pacing, sleep hygiene, and education about central sensitization.

14. Home programme

Warm bath followed by whole-body stretches; paced walking with a diary; relaxation breathing; fixed sleep–wake hours; flare plan of gentle movement rather than bed rest.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe adjuvant therapies in managing pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 4 — adjuvant methods; Unit 2 — pain management

★ Memory hook — THE MULTIPLIER, NOT THE ENGINE — adjuvants remove the barriers (pain, stiffness, fear, arousal) that block exercise; they are timed around the active programme and reviewed by what the patient can now do.

1Introduction

An adjuvant therapy is one administered ALONGSIDE the primary treatment to enhance its effect, address a component the primary therapy does not reach, or reduce overall drug burden. In pain management, where the primary tools are exercise, manual therapy, education and analgesics, adjuvants are the supporting cast.

The answer then works through the four shelves — physical, hands-on and movement-based, pharmacological, and psychosocial.

2Physiology

Mechanism first: most adjuvants work through segmental gate control, descending inhibitory pathways, altered tissue fluid dynamics, or psychological (attention and expectancy) mechanisms — which is why they relieve pain without changing the disease. Classify them as physical, hands-on and movement-based, psychosocial, and pharmacological — a four-shelf answer.

3Pathophysiology

Adjuvants matter most where pain has become persistent: peripheral and central sensitisation amplify nociceptive traffic, while catastrophising, fear-avoidance and poor sleep sustain the amplification. These are the barriers that block the primary active treatment, and each class of adjuvant is chosen to lower one of them.

4Answer

Superficial heat (hot packs, paraffin wax baths for hand pain) reduces muscle spindle excitability and stiffness before exercise; deep heat (ultrasound, 1 MHz) targets deeper fascia and tendon; cryotherapy reduces conduction velocity and acute inflammation after trauma. Topical counterirritation — menthol, methyl salicylate and capsaicin balms, the classic Indian household remedies — works by stimulating superficial receptors to compete with nociceptive input and, with capsaicin, by depleting substance P over days of use. TENS and interferential therapy act as electrical adjuvants through the gate mechanism. These are comfort-and-enabling tools that should be timed around the active programme: heat before stretching, cold after loading.

Massage (effleurage and petrissage) reduces perceived pain and muscle guarding via mechanoreceptor stimulation and improved local circulation; myofascial release and soft-tissue mobilisation address trigger points. Dry needling and acupuncture de-nociceptise trigger points and stir endogenous opioid release — moderate evidence in myofascial pain. Kinesio taping provides continuous cutaneous afferent input and tactile cueing of posture. Relaxation techniques (progressive muscle relaxation, diaphragmatic breathing), yoga and meditation modulate sympathetic arousal and improve pain coping — culturally resonant in India and increasingly evidence-supported for chronic low back pain and fibromyalgia.

The physiotherapist must know what the physician adds around our prescription: adjuvant analgesics — tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline at low dose for neuropathic and fibromyalgia pain), serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin), topical lidocaine and capsaicin patches — chosen when simple analgesics fail, especially in neuropathic and central pain states. Psychological adjuvants — cognitive-behavioural therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, guided imagery — target catastrophising and fear-avoidance, the strongest drivers of chronicity. Knowing this list keeps our language consistent with the multidisciplinary team.

Evidence pattern: adjuvants reliably deliver short-term symptomatic relief and rarely change long-term outcomes alone; their value appears when combined with exercise, education and graded exposure — Melzack and Wall's gate theory explains the neurophysiology of most of them. Conclusion: adjuvant therapies are the multiplier, not the engine, of pain management — selected to remove the barriers (pain, stiffness, fear, arousal) that block the primary active treatment, timed around it, and reviewed by whether the patient can now do more, not by the warmth or coolness of the modality itself.

Fig 7 — The wheel: primary care in the centre (exercise plus education), adjuvants arranged around it feeding in. Draw it as a circle of boxes; the examiner reads the structure in two seconds.
Definition marks are free: "administered alongside primary treatment to enhance effect or reduce drug burden" — write it in the first line. Then classify into four shelves (physical, hands-on, psychosocial, pharmacological) instead of a random list; structure is what turns a list into a 10-mark answer.

5Recent advances

  • Vickers et al. (2018) — this individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 39 trials and 20,827 patients found acupuncture was superior to both sham and no-acupuncture controls for chronic musculoskeletal, headache, shoulder and osteoarthritis pain, with effects persisting for about a year.
  • Kent et al. (2023) — the Lancet RESTORE randomised trial showed physiotherapist-led cognitive functional therapy produced large, sustained reductions in activity limitation and lower societal costs than usual care in chronic disabling low back pain.
  • Richmond et al. (2015) — this systematic review and meta-analysis (23 trials, 3359 patients) found cognitive behavioural approaches gave long-term improvements in pain, disability and quality of life in low back pain, supporting them as psychological adjuvants to exercise.
  • Johnson et al. (2022) — the meta-TENS study (381 RCTs) confirmed moderate-certainty, clinically important pain relief with TENS, a safe electrotherapy adjuvant that is timed around the active rehabilitation programme.

6References

  1. Melzack R & Wall PD, Science 1965 — gate control mechanism of most adjuvants.
  2. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — soft-tissue and physical agent adjuncts.
  3. Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — pain modulation pathways.
  4. Wolfe F et al., ACR fibromyalgia criteria — context for adjuvant use in widespread pain.
  5. Johnson MI, et al. Efficacy and safety of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation for acute and chronic pain in adults (the meta-TENS study). BMJ Open 2022;12(2):e051073.

On the evaluation form — Q7: Chronic MSK pain — adjuvant therapies

I. Subjective examination

55-year-old shopkeeper with chronic knee and neck pain for 2 years. Pain 5/10 on NPRS (0–10), worse with standing and shop work, disturbing sleep; apprehensive about movement after earlier exercise advice failed. Symptom analysis — site: knee and neck; onset: 2 years ago, persistent; severity: 5/10; aggravating factors: standing, shop work; relieving factors: not reported; associated features: sleep disturbance, movement apprehension. No red flags or vitals are given in the record.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Guarded posture; minimal knee flexion while loading; trapezius elevation; no wasting, swelling or scars documented.

On palpation. Taut bands with tender nodules in the trapezius and quadratus lumborum; cool, puffy skin over the painful regions.

1. Motor assessment. MMT (MRC 0–5): quadriceps 3+, scapular stabilizers 4. ROM: knee 10–100° with end-range pain; cervical ROM three-fourths of normal.

2. Sensory assessment. No radicular findings; regional hyperalgesia without dermatomal sensory loss.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Difficulty reaching overhead shelves. Outcome measures: NPRS 0–10; Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire — pain quality and intensity; WOMAC 0–96 for knee OA symptoms; Patient Global Impression of Change.

4. Gait analysis. Walking tolerance 15 minutes; guarded stair descent.

5. Balance. Not documented; not reported as affected.

6. Hand function. Reduced reaching to overhead shelves during shop work.

7. Coordination. Not documented; no neurological deficit.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

Local twitch responseSnapping palpation across the bandVisible local twitchActive trigger point
Pressure algometryDolorimeter over tender and control sitesLowered pressure-pain thresholdRegional hyperalgesia
Pain drawing / body mapPatient marks pain distributionDiffuse, non-anatomical shadingCentral pain component

In this patient trigger point palpation is positive — taut bands with tender nodules in the trapezius and quadratus lumborum. Local twitch response, pressure algometry and pain-drawing results are not documented.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Persistent pain
  • Myofascial trigger points
  • Lowered pain threshold
  • Deconditioning

Functional limitations

  • Standing
  • Overhead reach

Disabilities

  • Reduced shop hours
11. Functional diagnosis

Chronic musculoskeletal knee and neck pain with myofascial trigger points, lowered pain threshold and deconditioning, limiting standing tolerance and overhead reach and reducing shop hours.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain ≤3/10 at work; 20-minute standing tolerance; two self-applied adjuvant techniques used independently.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Pain ≤2/10 with full shop duty; graded strengthening routine established; reduced reliance on passive therapy.

13. Treatment plan

Adjuvants layered onto active management: TENS (80–100 Hz, 20–30 min, electrodes around the pain area, reassessed after 2 weeks); interferential therapy for deep aching; heat before exercise and cold after overload; ultrasound for localized tendon sites (low evidence, time-limited); dry needling or acupuncture for trigger points; massage for spasm; yoga- or tai-chi-based movement as mind–body adjuvants. Passive adjuvants are tapered as graded quadriceps and scapular strengthening build capacity.

14. Home programme

Ball self-massage over the trapezius; heat pack before exercises; TENS unit for flares; relaxation breathing; weekly symptom log showing function — not modality comfort — improving.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe wrist ergonomics for a computer operator.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 6 — interventions for work-related musculoskeletal disorders

★ Memory hook — HANDSHAKE POSITION — keep the wrist neutral (as in a handshake), the keyboard flat at elbow height, palm rests for pauses only, and audit the setup with a RULA grand score kept at 5 or below.

1Introduction

The goal of wrist ergonomics is to keep the hand working on a neutral wrist posture — forearm supported, wrist straight, no lean — while the bigger joints (elbow at about 90 degrees, shoulders relaxed) absorb the posture.

The answer then describes the workstation arrangement, the assessment of risk, and the work-organisation and education measures.

2Physiology

Mechanism first: carpal tunnel pressure rises steeply when the wrist leaves neutral — wrist extension beyond about 15 degrees, and sustained ulnar deviation and forearm pronation, increase pressure inside the tunnel, load the wrist extensors statically, and hold the finger flexors working at a poor length.

3Pathophysiology

Add repetition (fast keyboard work can reach 8,000 to 12,000 keystrokes per hour — the exposure the NUDATA study linked to arm and elbow pain), static loading, contact stress at the wrist rest, and cold or vibration from some devices, and you have the classic recipe for work-related disorders: carpal tunnel syndrome, De Quervain's tenosynovitis and non-specific forearm pain.

4Answer

Keyboard: flat or negatively tilted (the back feet folded DOWN, not up), directly in front, at elbow height, close to the body so the wrists need not extend to reach. Mouse: beside the keyboard at the same height, size matched to the hand, operated with the whole arm; a keyboard tray with a mouse platform prevents reaching. Wrist or palm rests: used during PAUSES, not while typing — leaning on them while typing creates contact stress. Chair: height so the forearms are parallel to the floor, feet flat, lumbar support; forearms lightly supported on the chair arms or desk edge. Monitor: top at or just below eye level, an arm's length away, so a flexed neck does not drag the whole kinetic chain down. Desk: adequate depth so the monitor is not pushed back into extension-heavy reaching. Document holder inline with the screen. In the Indian IT and back-office setting, the commonest faults are laptop use at a low table (forced wrist and neck flexion) and shared workstations never adjusted for the individual — say this and the examiner knows you have seen a real office.

Screen with the OSHA Computer Workstations eTool checklist, and quantify posture with RULA — the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment of McAtamney and Corlett, which scores posture, force and muscle use into an action list; a grand score above 5 demands prompt change. Symptom survey (discomfort charts), keystroke rates and overtime patterns complete the picture. Risk factors to hunt: deviation, extension, repetition, static hold, contact stress, cold and psychosocial pressure.

Micropauses of 30-60 seconds every 20-30 minutes; stretch the wrist flexors and extensors; alternate tasks; keep typing load realistic with software breaks reminders; early symptom reporting with a no-blame culture. Educate the operator in self-checking the neutral posture — the "handshake" position is the memory hook.

Evidence: ergonomic interventions (adjusted workstation plus education plus breaks) reduce discomfort and symptoms in office workers more consistently than exercise alone, and combined ergonomic-plus-exercise programmes are most effective; RULA gives a repeatable measure of improvement. Conclusion: wrist ergonomics for the computer operator is the marriage of a neutral-wrist workstation (keyboard and mouse at elbow height, flat keyboard, palm rests for pauses only) with regular breaks and posture education — engineering first, behaviour second, both audited by RULA.

Fig 8 — A side-view workstation with three annotated essentials: monitor height, desk at elbow height, straight supported wrist. Two minutes to draw, all the layout marks secured.
Numbers buy marks here: wrist extension beyond about 15 degrees is the danger zone; elbows near 90 degrees; RULA grand score above 5 needs prompt change. Also mention palm rests are for pauses, not typing — a favourite examiner discriminating detail.

5Recent advances

  • Hoe et al. (2018) — this Cochrane review (15 RCTs, 2165 office workers) found moderate-quality evidence that an arm support with an alternative mouse reduces neck and shoulder disorders; evidence for workstation adjustment alone was weak.
  • Sihawong et al. (2011) — this systematic review found strong evidence that muscle strengthening and endurance exercise reduce neck pain in office workers, with moderate evidence for endurance training reducing pain-related disability.
  • Gram et al. (2014) — this cluster randomised trial of 351 office workers showed that one hour a week of workplace neck/shoulder strength training for 20 weeks reduced neck pain and headache, independent of the level of supervision.
  • Sihawong et al. (2014) — this 12-month cluster randomised trial of 567 office workers found that a stretching and endurance exercise programme cut the incidence of neck pain by more than half (hazard ratio 0.45).

6References

  1. OSHA Computer Workstations eTool — workstation checklist.
  2. McAtamney L & Corlett EN, RULA: a survey method, Applied Ergonomics 1993.
  3. Cooper C, Fundamentals of Hand Therapy (21) — wrist pathology and activity modification.
  4. Saunders, Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation (20) — tendinopathy management context.
  5. Hoe VCW, et al. Ergonomic interventions for preventing work-related musculoskeletal disorders of the upper limb and neck among office workers. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2018.

On the evaluation form — Q8: Wrist / RSI in a computer operator

I. Subjective examination

28-year-old data-entry operator typing 8 hours daily, with 3 months of bilateral wrist pain and night numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers. Pain 4/10 on NPRS (0–10), worse late in the shift; shaking the hands relieves the symptoms. No trauma or neck pain. Symptom analysis — site: bilateral wrists with numbness in the radial three digits; onset: 3 months ago; type: activity-related pain with night numbness; severity: 4/10; aggravating factors: sustained typing, late shift; relieving factors: shaking the hands. No red flags or vitals are given in the record.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Wrists held extended over the keyboard; right wrist ulnar-deviated on mouse use; mild thenar puffiness; no thenar wasting, scars or bandages.

On palpation. Tenderness over the carpal tunnel and the first dorsal compartment; no local warmth or swelling documented.

1. Motor assessment. Grip strength 70% of normal; thumb abduction 4/5; wrist ROM full but painful at end-range.

2. Sensory assessment. Pins-and-needles in the median distribution after sustained typing; light touch mildly reduced over the radial three digits; neck screen normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Typing tolerance 2 hours before a flare; difficulty with mouse dragging; reduced work output. Outcome measures: QuickDASH 0–100 (higher = greater disability); NPRS 0–10; Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire — symptom severity and function; grip dynamometry.

4. Gait analysis. Not relevant to this upper-limb presentation.

5. Balance. Not relevant to this presentation.

6. Hand function. Reduced tolerance for sustained typing and mouse dragging (reaching, grasping and releasing during keyboard and mouse tasks); a neutral night splint is part of the management plan.

7. Coordination. Not separately documented; difficulty with mouse-dragging precision is noted under hand function.

8. Investigations

No electrodiagnostic studies mentioned; X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Phalen's testFull wrist flexion held for 60 sNumbness or tinglingCarpal tunnel syndrome
Tinel's sign (wrist)Percussion over the carpal tunnelTingling into the radial digitsMedian nerve irritability
Carpal compression (Durkan's)Sustained pressure on the tunnelSymptoms within 30 sCarpal tunnel syndrome
Finkelstein's testThumb held in the fist with the wrist ulnar-deviatedFirst compartment painDe Quervain's tenosynovitis

In this patient Finkelstein's test is positive — dorsoradial pain is reproduced. Phalen's, Tinel's and Durkan's tests are not documented as performed, although the median-distribution night numbness and sensory findings are consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Extended-wrist posture with median nerve irritation
  • Painful first-compartment tendons
  • Weak grip

Functional limitations

  • Typing
  • Mouse use

Disabilities

  • Reduced productivity
11. Functional diagnosis

Bilateral work-related wrist overuse with median nerve irritation and painful first-compartment tendons in an extended-wrist working posture, limiting typing and mouse use and reducing work productivity.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Night symptoms abolished with a neutral splint; pain ≤2/10 at work; workstation corrected.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Symptom-free 8-hour typing day; grip within 90% of normal; QuickDASH reduced; independent ergonomic self-management.

13. Treatment plan

Ergonomics: neutral-wrist keyboard position with the wrist rest used between (not during) typing; elbow at 90° close to the body; monitor at eye level; forearm support and a fitted mouse size; break software enforcing a 5-minute micro-break every 30 minutes. Therapy: neutral cock-up splint at night; tendon and median-nerve glides; grip and wrist strengthening with putty and bands; ice after overload.

14. Home programme

Nightly splint wear for 4–6 weeks; tendon glides ×3 daily; desk-posture reminders; workstation photographs reviewed at follow-up to confirm workplace transfer.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe the role of assistive devices in industrial setups which work with heavy loads.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 6 — assistive devices at work and work hardening

★ Memory hook — ELIMINATE, ENGINEER, THEN EDUCATE — push the fix up the hierarchy of controls; the device carries the load so the worker can carry the career. Dismiss the back belt: the evidence is against it.

1Introduction

Manual handling is the single largest source of occupational injury in Indian industry, from construction sites and godowns to warehouses and small-scale assembly units. The professional answer does not begin with "teach safe lifting"; it begins with the hierarchy of controls: eliminate the lift, engineer it away, redesign the task, change the work organisation, and only lastly rely on training and personal protective equipment. Assistive devices are the engineering tier — the most effective one.

The answer then lists the device menu by category, the assessment of manual-handling risk, and the training and work-hardening measures.

2Physiology

Mechanism first: during a freestyle stoop lift the lumbar disc compression can exceed the 3.4 kN action limit proposed for repeated loading — approaching the NIOSH maximum permissible limit of about 6.4 kN — because the spine acts as a long lever with a short, poor-efficiency erector spinae moment arm. The disc, not the muscle, is the weak link.

3Pathophysiology

The injured structure is usually the lumbar disc: a stoop lift loads the disc far beyond the safe repeated-loading action limit, and repeated manual handling is the largest single source of occupational injury in Indian industry. Assistive devices work by removing that load from the spine altogether.

4Answer

Load movement instead of load lifting: trolleys, hand trucks, pallet trucks, conveyor belts, roller tracks and chutes — the cheapest and highest-yield tier. Position the load at waist height: lift tables, scissor lifts, tilt tables, turntables and self-levelling dispensers so the worker never bends below knuckle height or reaches above shoulder height. Vertical handling: hoists, jib cranes, gantry cranes, vacuum tube lifters for sacks and sheet material, and powered stackers — removing the spine from the chain altogether. Tool-integrated supports: balancers and torque arms that absorb the weight and reaction of heavy power tools. Emerging: passive industrial exoskeletons that support the shoulders or trunk during sustained overhead or stooped work — promising for fatigue, still accumulating safety evidence. The back belt, by contrast, is NOT a reliable assistive device: evidence shows it does not prevent injury in untrained workers and may promote over-reliance; mention it to dismiss it correctly.

Quantify the job before choosing the device: the NIOSH lifting equation computes a recommended weight limit from the horizontal distance, vertical height, travel distance, asymmetry, frequency and coupling quality (a constant of 23 kg for an ideal lift under it), giving a lifting index — a value above 1 means the task exceeds the recommended limit. Supplement with postural screens (RULA or REBA) for the upper limb and whole body, and a walkthrough of the actual task in the actual shift pattern. The assessment drives the purchase — not the catalogue.

Devices change the job; people still need preparing: manual-handling training (load close to the body, neutral spine with hip hinge, pivot not twist, team lifts above about 25 kg per person), job rotation across loading tiers, and for the injured worker returning to heavy industry, a structured work hardening and work conditioning programme — simulated job tasks at real loads with cardiovascular conditioning and ergonomic education — which has good evidence for return-to-work outcomes.

Evidence: engineering controls (mechanical aids, adjustable workstations) show consistent reductions in manual-handling injury rates, whereas lifting-training-only interventions have small and short-lived effects; back belts do not prevent low back injury. Conclusion: in heavy-load industry the physiotherapist or ergonomist's role is to assess with the NIOSH equation and RULA, then push the fix up the hierarchy — eliminate, then mechanise (trolleys, conveyors, hoists, lift tables), then position (waist-height zones), then prepare the worker with training and work hardening. The device carries the load so the worker can carry the career.

Fig 9 — The zones diagram (green at waist, amber at shoulder, red at floor and above head) with a devices column that "empties" the red and amber zones. Simple, memorable, and it is the ergonomic thinking the examiner is testing.
Two scoring moves: open with the hierarchy of controls (eliminate, engineer, redesign, administrate, protect) and give the NIOSH numbers — 23 kg constant for an ideal lift, lifting index above 1 flags risk. Also dismiss the back belt explicitly; the examiner wants to see you know the evidence is against it.

5Recent advances

  • Qu et al. (2021) — a PLOS One study of an industrial passive exoskeleton found it reduced lumbar erector spinae activity by up to 21% and shoulder and arm activity by up to 38% during lifting, though contact pressure reduced comfort.
  • Schmalz et al. (2022) — a study of the Paexo Back exoskeleton showed reduced oxygen uptake (9%), back-muscle activation (up to 18%) and L4/L5 compression (21%) during repetitive lifting.
  • Rodzak et al. (2024) — a case series found elastic back exosuits increased lifting endurance by 28–75% while still reducing estimated cumulative low-back damage.
  • Di Natali et al. (2024) — the "Equivalent Weight" method translates an exoskeleton's erector-spinae reduction into a lower NIOSH lifting index, cutting it by up to 64% in real railway tasks.

6References

  1. Maxey L & Magnusson (13) — industrial rehabilitation and work hardening.
  2. McAtamney L & Corlett EN, RULA, Applied Ergonomics 1993 — postural risk assessment.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — work conditioning and functional progression.
  4. OSHA Computer Workstations eTool — assessment checklist principles (adapted to manual handling walkthrough).
  5. Baltrusch SJ, et al. The effect of a passive trunk exoskeleton on functional performance in healthy individuals. Applied Ergonomics 2018;72:94–106.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Industrial worker with heavy loads — assistive devices

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 40-year-old warehouse worker; occupation involves loading 50 kg sacks for 8 hours daily. Chief complaints: recurrent low back pain for 2 years, 5/10 on the NPRS (0–10) at shift end and absent on holidays; no radiation to the legs. He wants to protect his back “without losing wages”. Symptom analysis — site: low back; onset and duration: recurrent over 2 years; type: work-load-related; severity: 5/10 at shift end, 0/10 on holidays; aggravating factors: a full shift of sack handling and stoop lifting; relieving factors: rest and holidays. No past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history was given. Red-flag screen: negative. Vital signs not documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Jerky stoop lifting using the back rather than the legs, with guarded lumbar flexion. Built, wasting, oedema, scars/bandages, bony contours and deformity are not otherwise commented on.

On palpation. Myofascial tenderness of the paraspinal and gluteal muscles. Deep-tissue texture, spasm, skin type, scar, swelling and crepitus not documented.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: lumbar flexion limited by 25% (end-feel not recorded). MMT (MRC 0–5): trunk extensors 4, abdominals 3+, gluteus maximus 3+. No motor or reflex deficit on the neurological screen; muscle girth and limb length not documented.

2. Sensory assessment. No sensory, motor or reflex deficit; dermatomes and myotomes screened and intact.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Lifting-cycle observation: squat versus stoop quality, load distance from the trunk, and twisting. Outcome measures: NPRS (0–10); Oswestry Disability Index (0–100%) for back-related disability; REBA/RULA for the postural loading risk of the task.

4. Gait analysis. Gait parameters (stance/swing, base width, cadence, step and stride length) not documented; observation centred on the lifting cycle rather than walking.

5. Balance. Static and dynamic balance not documented at this assessment.

6. Hand function. Not separately documented; reaching, grasping and releasing are relevant to operating the handling devices listed in the treatment plan.

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Straight leg raisePassive hip flexion with the knee extendedPain radiating below the kneeNerve-root tension — negative in this patient (80° bilaterally)

No other provocative tests were documented.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Recurrent low back pain (5/10 at shift end)
  • Weak trunk extensors, abdominals and gluteus maximus
  • Lumbar flexion limited by 25%
  • Paraspinal and gluteal myofascial tenderness
  • Poor (stoop) lifting technique

Functional limitations

  • Heavy lifting
  • Prolonged standing

Disabilities

  • Risk of work loss and loss of wages
11. Functional diagnosis

Recurrent mechanical low back pain with trunk and hip extensor weakness and hazardous stoop-lifting technique, limiting heavy lifting and prolonged standing, threatening wage-earning capacity, and amenable to ergonomic (assistive-device) modification and work-conditioning.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain 2/10 or less at shift end; correct squat-lift and trolley technique demonstrated; job-task REBA score improved.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Trunk and gluteal strength MRC 5; a full shift managed with handling devices and job rotation without a pain flare-up.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (weeks 1–2): education on lifting mechanics — load close to the trunk, neutral spine, leg drive, no twisting under load — and supervised device practice on the shop floor. Phase 2 (weeks 3–6): work-conditioning — dead-lift and squat patterns with graded weights, core stabilisation, carrying drills. Phase 3 (weeks 7–12): work-hardening over a simulated shift, job rotation with the supervisor, participatory ergonomics review (scissor tables, trolley routes). Routine use of back belts remains controversial.

Assistive devices (the core of this case):

DeviceIndicationTypical task / condition
Hand truck / trolleyMove loads without carryingCartons and crates between bays
Pallet truck / scissor lift tableTransport pallets; raise load to waist heightWarehouses, packing stations
Conveyor, roller track, turntable / slidesEliminate carrying; rotate or slide, not twist-liftProduction lines; drum and bag handling
Hoist / gantryOverhead handling of heavy itemsMachine loading
Team-lift protocolTwo or more workers per loadLoads above the single-person limit
14. Home programme

Glute bridges, bird-dog and squat practice 4/week, a daily walk, and a fortnightly tally of lifts by device versus by hand.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe the role of evidence-based rehabilitation following arthroscopic meniscus repair.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3 — functional training and physical activity promotion

★ Memory hook — PROTECT SIX WEEKS, PROGRESS BY CRITERIA — repair is not meniscectomy; guard the suture line for about six weeks, then let limb-symmetry criteria (not the calendar) decide return to sport.

1Introduction

That single fact drives the entire programme — after meniscectomy you protect nothing but the effusion, but after repair you protect the suture line for about six weeks while fibrocartilaginous healing proceeds.

The answer then follows the three phases of rehabilitation and closes with the evidence.

2Physiology

Mechanism first: the meniscus is vascular only in its outer third. A repair (inside-out, all-inside or outside-in sutures) succeeds only where the tear sits in the red-red or red-white zone with blood supply to heal; a white-white tear is usually excised, not repaired.

3Pathophysiology

Complex or bucket-handle repairs, and repairs done with ACL reconstruction (common in the young Indian athlete with a twisting football or kabaddi injury), demand even more caution with rotation and deep flexion.

A white-white (avascular) tear cannot heal and is usually excised rather than repaired; a complex or bucket-handle tear, or a repair combined with ACL reconstruction, is mechanically less stable and needs even more guarded rotation and deep flexion.

4Answer

Brace locked in extension for ambulation, partial weight-bearing on crutches (toe-touch to 30-50 percent, surgeon-dependent), avoiding twisting, squatting and deep flexion — the positions that tear the repair apart. Goals: full knee extension (hyperextension matching the other side), control of effusion with ice and compression, patellar mobilisations to prevent retinacular adhesions, quadriceps re-education with isometrics, straight-leg raises (brace off once the quad controls the lift), ankle pumps, and gentle 0-90 degree flexion progressing per protocol. This phase is about PREVENTING stiffness and arthrogenic muscle inhibition without loading the repair.

Weight-bearing progresses to full, brace is weaned, gait normalises. Range moves beyond 120 degrees. Strengthening becomes closed kinetic chain dominant — mini-squats to 45 degrees, leg press in protected arcs, step-ups, calf raises, stationary cycling with a raised seat — because closed-chain loading compresses and stabilises the joint while protecting the repair from shear. Open-chain knee extension stays in the protected arc, avoiding the terminal 30-45 degrees of extension where shear is highest. Add proprioceptive retraining: single-leg balance, wobble board, perturbation work. Aquatic therapy in this phase is invaluable where available.

Progress to running from month three (for isolated repair) on level surfaces, then agility, plyometrics and sport-specific drills — cutting, pivoting, and change of direction — around months four to five, guided by limb-symmetry criteria rather than the calendar: quadriceps and hamstring strength within about 90 percent of the other limb, single-leg hop tests symmetric, no effusion, full painless range. Heavy-labour workers follow the same strength criteria with simulated task training. Education for maintenance: a repaired meniscus is a long-term investment — quadriceps strength, load management and avoiding deep squats under load in the first year protect it.

Evidence: Sihvonen and colleagues' FIDELITY trial in the New England Journal of Medicine showed that for DEGENERATIVE meniscal tears, arthroscopic partial meniscectomy was no better than sham surgery — rehabilitation, not surgery, is the first-line treatment there, which is precisely why repair of repairable traumatic tears is protected so carefully (Wilk and Brotzman's protocols supply the criteria-based progression). Conclusion: evidence-based rehabilitation after meniscus repair is a protection-then-progression story — six weeks guarding the sutured zone while regaining extension, then closed-chain loading and neuromuscular control, then criteria-based return to sport — with the modern message that for degenerate tears the rehab pathway, not the scope, is the treatment.

Fig 10 — One horizontal timeline, three phase boxes, and the two exam-winning lines written under it: protect for six weeks; criteria, not dates, decide return. Draw this even if you draw nothing else.
The examiner's favourite discriminator: repair is NOT meniscectomy. Say "protect the suture line six weeks, delay twisting and deep flexion" and then close with FIDELITY — the trial that flipped degenerate tears to rehab-first. Both lines together put you in the top band.

5Recent advances

  • Pujol et al. (2024) — the EU-US Meniscus Rehabilitation consensus recommends time- and criterion-based progression after repair, with a minimum of four months of rehabilitation for repaired vertical tears and six to nine months for complex radial or root tears.
  • Skou et al. (2022) — this NEJM Evidence randomised trial in young adults found that supervised exercise therapy and education was not inferior to early meniscal surgery for pain, function and quality of life at 12 months, with three of four patients avoiding surgery.
  • Lind et al. (2013) — this randomised trial in the American Journal of Sports Medicine showed that free (accelerated) rehabilitation after isolated meniscus repair did not increase failure rates compared with a restricted six-week protocol.
  • Calanna et al. (2022) — this evidence-based protocol review advised accelerated rehabilitation when the hoop tensile stress effect is preserved, and restricted protocols (no weight-bearing for six weeks) when circumferential fibres are disrupted.
  • Eberbach et al. (2017) — this systematic review reported return to sport typically at three to six months, with about 89% returning to preinjury level and a global failure rate of about 21%.

6References

  1. Wilk KE, Brotzman SB et al., Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation (14) — meniscus repair protocols.
  2. Sihvonen R et al., Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy versus sham surgery (FIDELITY), New England Journal of Medicine 2018.
  3. Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — closed-chain progression and criteria-based return.
  4. The EU-US Meniscus Rehabilitation 2024 consensus statement, JOSPT Open 2025.

On the evaluation form — Q10: Rehabilitation after arthroscopic meniscus repair

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 26-year-old footballer, 2 weeks after arthroscopic repair of a bucket-handle medial meniscus tear. Chief complaints: knee stiffness, quadriceps weakness and apprehension about weight-bearing; pain 3/10 on the NPRS (0–10). No locking since surgery; currently on crutches with a hinged brace. No past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history was given. Red-flag screen: negative. Vital signs not documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Healed portal wounds, quadriceps atrophy, minimal effusion, hinged brace in situ.

On palpation. Medial joint-line tenderness, no warmth, restricted patellar glide.

1. Motor assessment. MMT (MRC 0–5): quadriceps 3 with a 10° extension lag; hamstrings and hip groups 4+. ROM: flexion 0–90° by protocol, extension full; end-feel not recorded. Muscle girth: thigh circumference 2.5 cm less than the sound limb. Reflexes and limb length not documented.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation normal apart from slight hypoesthesia around the portal sites; no common peroneal involvement; dermatomes and myotomes intact.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Ambulation with two crutches at partial weight-bearing; stairs not negotiated reciprocally; sporting function suspended. Outcome measures: Lysholm knee scale (symptoms and function); IKDC subjective knee form; Tegner activity scale for sport level; goniometric ROM and thigh girth.

4. Gait analysis. Two-crutch partial weight-bearing gait; detailed stance/swing, base width, cadence and step/stride parameters not documented.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance held for 5 s with compensation on the operated side; eyes-open/eyes-closed testing not documented.

6. Hand function. Handles bilateral crutches (assistive device, with the hinged brace); reaching, grasping and releasing otherwise not documented.

7. Coordination. Knee-joint proprioception reduced (listed among the impairments); addressed in phase 3.

8. Investigations

Arthroscopy performed 2 weeks ago, confirming a bucket-handle tear of the medial meniscus as per the operative records; no further imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Joint-line tendernessPalpation along the medial joint lineFocal tendernessMeniscal pathology or post-repair irritation
McMurray's testKnee fully flexed, rotated while extendedClick with joint-line painMeniscal tear (test late in rehab)
Thessaly testStanding on the leg, knee 20° flexed, trunk rotationJoint-line pain or catchingMeniscal tear (deferred to late rehab)

In this patient: medial joint-line tenderness on palpation — positive; McMurray's and Thessaly tests deferred to the late rehabilitation phase and not performed at 2 weeks post-repair.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Quadriceps inhibition and atrophy
  • Restricted knee flexion (0–90° by protocol)
  • Joint-line pain
  • Poor proprioception

Functional limitations

  • Gait on crutches
  • Stairs
  • Squatting

Disabilities

  • Unable to play football
11. Functional diagnosis

Two weeks after arthroscopic medial meniscus repair, with quadriceps inhibition and atrophy, restricted knee flexion, joint-line pain and reduced proprioception, limiting ambulation, stair negotiation, squatting and sporting participation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Full pain-free extension; flexion 0–120°; full weight-bearing with normal gait; straight-leg raise without lag.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Full ROM; quadriceps and hamstrings 4+ or better; hop symmetry; running progression with return to sport by 4–6 months.

13. Treatment plan

Phase 1 (0–2 weeks): protected weight-bearing per the surgeon's protocol with a brace, cryotherapy 15–20 min 3–4 times daily, quad sets, straight-leg raises, patellar mobilisations. Phase 2 (2–6 weeks): weight-bearing to full, stationary cycling, closed-chain work — mini-squats 0–45°, step-ups, leg press, hamstring curls. Phase 3 (6–12 weeks): resisted strengthening, wobble-board proprioception, agility drills. Phase 4 (3–6 months): running progression, plyometrics, sport-specific cutting, graded return with clearance. Deep flexion beyond 90° and twisting only as healing allows.

14. Home programme

Quad sets and straight-leg raises 3×10 daily, heel slides, static cycle, ice after sessions.

Last-Hour Sheet · Paper IV

QP 8132 · 26-May-2025 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Ankle impaired mobility

  • ATFL most commonly torn; capsular pattern of ankle = more dorsiflexion restriction than plantarflexion.
  • Dorsiflexion needs posterior talar glide; 10 degrees minimum for normal gait.
  • Two-sided answer: hypomobility (effusion, capsule, glide loss) AND hypermobility (anterior drawer, talar tilt).
  • Verhagen: proprioceptive training roughly halves sprain recurrence.

2Education in low back pain

  • Education targets fear-avoidance, catastrophising and self-efficacy — the biopsychosocial flags.
  • Menu: individual advice, back school, printed media, pain neurosciences education, CBT-informed classes.
  • Advice alone = small effect; education + graded exercise = real effect.
  • Bed rest is harmful; stay active is the message.

3Anti-gravity muscles and stability

  • Soleus, quadriceps, gluteus maximus, erector spinae, neck extensors — tonic, type-I, fatigue-resistant.
  • Gamma system keeps spindles sensitive; postural tone is reflex-managed sway control.
  • Ankle strategy for small sway, hip strategy for fast, stepping strategy for large.
  • Anticipatory postural adjustments fire before the movement; single-leg stance under 10 seconds = fall risk.

4McKenzie principles

  • Repeated end-range loading is the assessment; the pain response is the diagnosis.
  • Centralisation retreats proximally — the best prognostic sign; peripheralisation = avoid.
  • Three syndromes: derangement (directional-preference loading), postural (correction), dysfunction (end-range stretch of shortened tissue).
  • Force ladder: self-movement, overpressure, mobilisation, manipulation; patient treats the patient.

5Appliances after L2-L3 disc prolapse

  • L2-L3 is UPPER lumbar — control must extend thoracically (TLSO logic, not a plain belt).
  • Corset raises intra-abdominal pressure, offloads the disc about a third while lifting, cues posture.
  • Menu: canvas corset, semi-rigid LSO, rigid three-point, TLSO; plus cane, reacher, raised toilet seat, firm bed.
  • Wean over 4-6 weeks with isometric trunk work — orthosis plus exercise, never instead.

6Electrotherapy in fibromyalgia

  • ACR criteria: widespread pain 3 months + symptom severity scale (old: 18 tender points).
  • Central sensitisation — machines are adjuncts; exercise, sleep, education are the core.
  • TENS 70-100 Hz gate-control: modest short-term pain relief; electroacupuncture moderate evidence.
  • Warm-water hydrotherapy is the strongest physical agent; interferential and microcurrent = weak.

7Adjuvant therapies in pain

  • Definition line: given ALONGSIDE primary treatment to enhance effect or cut drug burden.
  • Four shelves: physical (heat, cold, counterirritants, TENS), hands-on (massage, needling, taping), mind-body (relaxation, yoga, CBT), pharmacological (amitriptyline, pregabalin).
  • Mechanism: gate control + descending inhibition for most; capsaicin depletes substance P.
  • Adjuvants multiply the engine (exercise); they never replace it.

8Wrist ergonomics for computer operators

  • Neutral wrist: extension under about 15 degrees, no resting ulnar deviation — the handshake position.
  • Keyboard flat (feet DOWN), at elbow height; mouse beside it; palm rests for pauses only.
  • Monitor top at eye level, arm's length; micropauses every 20-30 minutes.
  • RULA (McAtamney & Corlett): grand score above 5 = prompt change; use the OSHA eTool checklist.

9Assistive devices in heavy-load industry

  • Hierarchy of controls: eliminate, engineer, redesign, administrate, protect — devices sit at the top.
  • Menu: trolleys, conveyors, hoists, lift tables, turntables, vacuum lifters, exoskeletons.
  • NIOSH: 23 kg constant for an ideal lift; lifting index above 1 = risk; back belts do NOT prevent injury.
  • Work hardening = simulated real loads + conditioning; criteria-based return to work.

10Rehab after arthroscopic meniscus repair

  • Repair needs vascular red-red or red-white zone; protect the suture line six weeks.
  • Phase I: brace, partial weight-bearing, full extension, 0-90 degrees, no twist or deep squat.
  • Phase II: full weight-bearing, closed-chain loading, proprioception.
  • Phase III: run from month three, return to sport on criteria — 90 percent limb symmetry; FIDELITY: degenerate tears = rehab first, sham-equivalent scope.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall.
