Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Explain in detail the basic assessment methods for diagnosis of musculoskeletal conditions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 1a — basic assessment methods and physical assessment as a screening tool

★ Memory hook — the ladder: Subjective → Look → Feel → Move → Special tests → Synthesise. Say it as “Some Lads Feel More Sure Standing.”

1Introduction

Every musculoskeletal diagnosis, however complicated the condition, is built on one disciplined sequence that you should be able to recite and demonstrate: subjective examination → look → feel → move → special tests → synthesis. The examiner is testing whether you can move from a complaint to a hypothesis to a confirmation without jumping to conclusions. In an Indian outpatient department, where a single therapist may screen forty or more patients in a morning, this sequence is what keeps the assessment complete even when it is fast — each rung of the ladder either confirms or eliminates a hypothesis, so no time is wasted on tests that cannot change your decision.

2Physiology

Musculoskeletal assessment rests on normal structure–function relationships that the examiner must know before any abnormality can be interpreted. A healthy joint moves through a painless active and passive range that ends in a characteristic end-feel — capsular, bony or a springy block; healthy muscle contracts to a firm, painless isometric hold; and healthy tissue tolerates graded load without swelling, guarding or night pain. Because the body works as linked segments, a normal examination of one region includes a screening check of the neighbouring regions and quadrants — the cervical spine for shoulder pain, the hip and foot for knee pain — so that a distant, symptomless dysfunction is not mistaken for the local one.

3Pathophysiology

Injury and disease alter this baseline in recognisable patterns. Inflammatory tissue produces pain on active and resisted movement but not on passive movement — the contractile pattern of Cyriax — whereas an inert structure such as capsule, ligament or joint reproduces pain only passively; a soft, springy or empty end-feel replaces the normal firm stop when a ligament or capsule is torn or inflamed; and muscle wasting, swelling, warmth and an antalgic gait mark the segment that has been injured or diseased. Reading these patterns is what converts a list of findings into a diagnosis.

4Answer

Begin with demographics and context: age and sex (degenerative disease in the elderly, inflammatory arthropathy in the young adult), occupation (a farmer lifting sacks, a tailor sitting cross-legged for hours, an IT professional at a poorly set-up desk), and hand dominance. Record the mechanism of injury — trauma versus insidious onset — and analyse the pain: site, onset, character, radiation, aggravating and relieving factors, behaviour over 24 hours, and night pain. Add past medical history (diabetes, steroid use suggesting osteoporosis, previous surgery), drug history, and family history. The classic teaching, worth quoting in the exam, is that a carefully taken history alone delivers roughly 80 per cent of the diagnosis; the objective examination is largely confirmatory.

Inspection covers posture in standing and sitting, gait, deformity, swelling, muscle wasting (compare sides — look at the supraspinatus fossa, the thenar eminence, the quadriceps above the patella), skin colour, scars and sinuses. Palpation follows a systematic order — skin temperature, swelling, and then bony and soft-tissue tenderness, always comparing with the unaffected side. Movement is tested in a fixed order: active range first (patient willing, physiology intact?), then passive range (end-feel — capsular, bony, springy block, empty), then resisted isometric testing. This is Cyriax's contribution at the bedside: pain on active and resisted movement but not passive suggests contractile tissue; pain reproduced only passively suggests inert structures — capsule, ligament, joint.

Only after the basic examination should region-specific special tests be selected — and they are selected, not sprayed: choose the tests that discriminate between your top two or three hypotheses. Add functional and dynamic assessment — gait analysis, squatting, stair negotiation, a timed up-and-go — because function, not range, is what the patient actually complains of. Where physiotherapy findings are inconclusive or the picture suggests systemic disease, adjuncts come in: plain radiographs, MRI, ultrasound, laboratory studies and electrodiagnosis. Remember also that a physical assessment in direct practice doubles as a screening tool for the neighbouring regions and quadrants — a shoulder pain deserves a cervical screen, a knee pain deserves a hip and foot screen.

Fig 1 — Draw the six-step ladder in under a minute; the structure mark is awarded for the correct order and the one-line justification under each box.

Finally, cluster the findings. The subjective and objective data must fit one another; when they do, you state a physiotherapy diagnosis at the level of impairment and function (for example, "subacromial pain syndrome with restricted and painful elevation and scapular dyskinesia"). Alongside it you commit to a differential diagnosis — a ranked short list of other conditions that could produce the same presentation, each one eliminated by a named finding. Close the loop by documenting baseline measures, setting goals, and planning re-assessment, because a diagnosis that is never re-tested is only an opinion.

Examiner's tip: students lose marks by listing everything they know about each method. Keep the sequence visible — the examiner is marking your diagnostic reasoning, not the page count. Name one Indian occupational example in the history to show contextual thinking.

5Recent advances

  • Bernhardsson et al. (2023) — systematic review in PLOS ONE finding digital (telehealth) physiotherapy assessment reliable for pain, range of motion and patient-reported measures but only fair validity for spinal posture, so remote assessment supplements rather than replaces hands-on examination.
  • De Sloovere et al. (2026) — scoping review identifying 23 diagnostic-reasoning tools for musculoskeletal care, most weighting environmental and personal factors, and calling for a tool that weighs several dimensions together.
  • Hamzeh et al. (2021) — validated the Diagnostic Thinking Inventory for musculoskeletal physiotherapy (test–retest ICC about 0.91), letting educators audit the effect of continuing education on diagnostic reasoning.
  • Hegedus et al. (2012) — systematic review with meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine showing no single shoulder special test is pathognomonic (Neer, Hawkins–Kennedy and painful arc all have limited accuracy) and that tests should be combined with history and physical examination.

6References

  1. Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment, 6th ed (syllabus ref 4), Ch. 1: the examination sequence and end-feels.
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH — Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System (ref 1): tissue response framework.
  3. Jones MA, Rivett DA — Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice: hypothesis generation and testing.
  4. De Sloovere M, Van Tiggelen D, De Ridder R, et al. Diagnostic reasoning in musculoskeletal healthcare: a scoping review. J Bodyw Mov Ther. 2026;47:295–303.
  5. Digital physiotherapy assessment versus conventional face-to-face physiotherapy assessment of patients with musculoskeletal disorders: a systematic review. PLOS ONE. 2023;18(5):e0283013.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Elaborate the assessment method with differential diagnosis for shoulder impingement syndrome.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2b — screening: shoulder and upper extremity

★ Memory hook — sensitive screen first (Neer, Hawkins), specific confirmer second (painful arc, Jobe, lag), and always clear the neck: N-H-P-J.

1Introduction

Subacromial impingement — today more precisely called subacromial pain syndrome or rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain — is the commonest cause of shoulder pain in adults and the commonest reason for a shoulder referral. This answer sets out the assessment method and the differential diagnosis that must accompany it, moving from mechanism to history, special tests and a discriminating short list of mimics.

2Physiology

In normal shoulder elevation the humeral head is depressed and centred in the glenoid by the force couple of the rotator cuff and deltoid, the scapula upwardly rotates and tilts posteriorly on the thorax in a coordinated scapulohumeral rhythm, and the subacromial interval stays clear throughout the arc. This clearance — a millimetre or two of glide between the humeral head and the coracoacromial arch — is the physiological state that every impingement test is trying to prove has been lost.

3Pathophysiology

The subacromial space is a functional interval between the coracoacromial arch above (acromion, coracoacromial ligament, AC joint) and the humeral head with its rotator cuff below. Everything inside it — the supraspinatus tendon, the subacromial bursa and the intra-articular portion of the long head of biceps — can be compressed during elevation. Quoting Neer's stages earns instant credibility: stage I, oedema and haemorrhage in the young overhead athlete; stage II, fibrosis and tendinopathy in the 25–40 age group; stage III, bone spurs and partial or complete cuff tears above 40. Distinguish primary impingement (intrinsic tendon degeneration or a hooked acromion) from secondary impingement, where the real driver is glenohumeral instability or scapular dyskinesia letting the head ride up — the treatment differs completely.

4Answer

Typical patient: an overhead worker — a painter, a batsman, a housewife lifting pots onto a high shelf — with pain over the deltoid insertion rather than the joint line, painful overhead reaching, and night pain when lying on the affected side. Inspect for forward-head rounded-shoulder posture, a prominent inferior angle of the scapula, scapular dyskinesia on repeated elevation (watch for the "shrug" sign), and wasting of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae, which suggests a chronic cuff tear rather than simple impingement.

The special test battery

Use a battery, never a single test. The Neer test (scapula stabilised, arm passively flexed in internal rotation) and the Hawkins-Kennedy test (90° flexion, forced internal rotation) are sensitive screens — pooled sensitivity is around 0.8 for both but specificity is only around 0.5, so they confirm suspicion, not the diagnosis. The painful arc between roughly 60 and 120 degrees of active abduction is more specific; note whether it is present in passive abduction too. Then test the cuff: the Jobe empty-can position for supraspinatus strength, resisted external rotation for infraspinatus, and an external rotation lag or drop-arm test — true weakness out of proportion to pain points towards a tear rather than impingement. Finish with the scapular assistance test: if symptoms improve when you assist the scapula upward, dyskinesia is a driver and rehabilitation must include scapular retraining.

Fig 2 — Draw the arc: two dashed thresholds at 60 and 120 degrees with pain rising inside the band and easing beyond it; label "painful arc" and say why it localises the lesion to the subacromial space.

Discriminate point by point. Cervical radiculopathy C5–C6: pain and paraesthesia below the elbow, worse with neck movement, positive Spurling test — always clear the cervical spine in every shoulder case. Adhesive capsulitis: global restriction of both active and passive external rotation and abduction, not just a painful arc. Acromioclavicular arthritis: pain localised on top of the joint, positive cross-body adduction test. Calcific tendinitis: dramatic night pain, radiograph confirms. Glenohumeral osteoarthritis: crepitus and capsular pattern of restriction. Superior labral (SLAP) lesion: deep click, biceps load test positive. Rotator cuff tear: persistent lag and true weakness. Suprascapular neuropathy: isolated fossa wasting without a painful arc. And the red flag you must name — a Pancoast tumour presenting as shoulder pain with hand wasting and Horner syndrome in a smoker.

Conclude the way an examiner wants: a consistent history of overhead pain with night pain, a positive Neer and Hawkins, a painful arc and preserved strength clusters into subacromial impingement syndrome with scapular contribution. Persistent pure weakness or a positive lag test upgrades the suspicion to a cuff tear and warrants ultrasound or MRI referral. Management begins with a three-month structured conservative trial — scapular control, posterior capsule mobility, rotator cuff loading — before any question of subacromial decompression is raised.

Examiner's tip: quote the pooled numbers — Neer about 0.79 sensitivity and 0.53 specificity — and say aloud what they mean: sensitive screen, poor confirmer, therefore use a cluster. That single sentence shows you understand diagnostic accuracy, which is what separates a 7 from a 9.

5Recent advances

  • Lafrance et al. (2022) — JOSPT clinical practice guideline on rotator cuff disorders recommending an active, task-oriented rehabilitation programme of exercise and education, restricting imaging to select circumstances, and — on high-certainty evidence — recommending against subacromial decompression for tendinopathy.
  • Hopewell et al. (2021) — GRASP trial (Lancet, 708 patients) showing a progressive physiotherapy exercise programme was not superior to a single best-practice advice session for rotator cuff disorders, and that subacromial corticosteroid injection gave no long-term benefit.
  • Pieters et al. (2020) — update of systematic reviews in JOSPT confirming exercise therapy, and multimodal physiotherapy including manual therapy, reduce pain and disability in subacromial shoulder pain, with evidence strongest for exercise.
  • Kuhn et al. (2013) — MOON Shoulder Group multicentre cohort showing a structured non-operative physical therapy programme succeeds in about 75 per cent of atraumatic full-thickness cuff tears at two years, so cuff repair is considered only after failed exercise-based therapy.

6References

  1. Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4), shoulder chapter.
  2. Neer CS II — J Bone Joint Surg Am, 1972: stages and anterior acromioplasty.
  3. Hawkins RJ, Kennedy JC — Am J Sports Med, 1980: the impingement test.
  4. Hertling D, Kessler RM — Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders (ref 15): impingement rehabilitation.
  5. Rotator cuff disorders: a clinical practice guideline. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2022;52(10):647–664.
  6. Dutch Orthopaedic Association. Update of the guideline for diagnosis and treatment of subacromial pain syndrome: a multidisciplinary review. Acta Orthop. 2025.

On the evaluation form — Q2: Subacromial impingement syndrome

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 45-year-old overhead worker / housewife. Chief complaints: right shoulder pain for 3 months, insidious onset. Symptom analysis — site: anterolateral shoulder; onset: insidious; duration: 3 months; type: dull ache with painful catches; severity: NPRS 6/10 on overhead activity, 2/10 at rest; aggravating factors: overhead reach, reaching behind the back, lying on the affected side; relieving factors: rest, arm supported. History: repetitive overhead activity; no trauma and no neck symptoms. Red-flag screen: negative. Vital signs: afebrile, blood pressure and pulse normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Protracted, rounded shoulders with scapular dyskinesia on the right; hollowing of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae (marked wasting would suggest a rotator cuff tear); no scar, sinus or oedema.

On palpation. Tenderness over the greater tuberosity and subacromial region; increased deep-tissue tension in the upper trapezius; no warmth; crepitus on shoulder elevation.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: painful arc of abduction at 60–120°; abduction and internal rotation behind the back limited. PROM: near-full but painful in the arc (a gross capsular-pattern loss would suggest adhesive capsulitis instead). End-feel: empty, due to pain. Resisted isometrics: painful weakness in abduction and external rotation (radiculopathy, by contrast, gives painless weakness). MMT: shoulder girdle 4/5. Reflexes normal; limb lengths equal.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact; C5–C6 dermatomes and myotomes (shoulder abduction, elbow flexion) screened to exclude cervical referral.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Dressing (hooking a blouse/dhoti), combing and overhead reach are limited, with overhead reach to about 120°. Outcome measures: SPADI (0–100, shoulder pain and disability), QuickDASH (0–100, upper-limb disability), NPRS (0–10), PSFS (0–10) — track one PSFS activity, e.g. hanging clothes.

4. Gait analysis. Gait normal — an upper-limb condition; formal parameters not documented.

5. Balance. Not affected and not documented — an upper-limb condition.

6. Hand function. Overhead reaching limited to about 120° and reaching behind the back limited (dressing, combing); grasping and releasing not documented.

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Neer testPassive forward elevation with the scapula stabilisedPain reproduced in the arcSubacromial impingement
Hawkins-Kennedy testShoulder at 90° elevation, forced internal rotationAnterosuperior painAnterosuperior impingement
Painful arcActive abduction through rangePain at 60–120°, easing beyondImpingement of subacromial structures
Jobe (empty can)Resisted abduction at 90° in the scapular plane, arm internally rotatedPain and/or weaknessSupraspinatus pathology
Drop arm testSlowly lower the arm from 90° abductionArm falls uncontrollablyRotator cuff tear
Gerber lift-offHand behind the back, push posteriorly against resistanceUnable to lift hand off the backSubscapularis weakness
Cross-body adductionHorizontal adduction at 90° elevationPain localised to the AC jointAC joint pathology (differential)

In this patient: painful arc positive (pain at 60–120° on active abduction, easing beyond); resisted isometrics showed painful weakness in abduction and external rotation, consistent with a positive Jobe-type response; the results of the Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy, drop arm, Gerber lift-off and cross-body adduction tests were not individually documented.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Shoulder pain
  • Reduced pain-free AROM (painful arc 60–120°)
  • Painful rotator-cuff weakness
  • Scapular dyskinesia

Functional limitations

  • Overhead and behind-back activities of daily living

Disabilities

  • Reduced household/work output at present
11. Functional diagnosis

Right subacromial impingement syndrome with a painful-arc restriction of active range, painful rotator-cuff weakness and scapular dyskinesia, limiting overhead and behind-the-back activities of daily living and reducing household and work output.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain 3/10 or less on the NPRS; pain-free AROM; scapular control initiated.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Cuff and scapular muscle MMT 5/5; full pain-free overhead function; QuickDASH 10 or less; return to work.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): relative rest, cryotherapy, pendulum exercises, postural correction. Stage 2 (weeks 2–4): isometric then Theraband strengthening of the cuff and scapular stabilisers in pain-free range. Stage 3 (weeks 4–12): eccentric loading, overhead functional retraining, graded return to activity.

14. Home programme

Pendulum swings, scapular retractions, side-lying external rotation with a small weight; avoid sustained overhead positions.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. How do you conclude while screening that the pain in the lumbar spine is due to disc herniation? Justify with differential diagnosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2a — screening: head, neck and back

★ Memory hook — the four-point disc cluster: dermatomal leg pain below the knee + a neurological deficit + a positive neurodynamic test + centralisation on movement.

1Introduction

The examiner is asking a specific question: not “describe the disc” but “how do you conclude, while screening, that this lumbar pain is discogenic and radicular?” The answer is built on a converging cluster of findings and a disciplined differential diagnosis, with the red-flag boundary drawn before anything else.

2Physiology

The intervertebral disc is a hydraulic shock absorber: a gelatinous nucleus pulposus enclosed by the concentric lamellae of the annulus fibrosus, sandwiched between cartilaginous end plates. It transmits and distributes compressive load while allowing segmental flexion, extension and rotation, and it is reinforced centrally and posteriorly by the posterior longitudinal ligament. Intradiscal pressure is posture-dependent — it is lowest in supine lying, rises on standing, and rises roughly 40 per cent above standing in relaxed sitting, which is why sustained sitting loads a degenerate disc.

3Pathophysiology

Because the posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the disc centrally, herniations track posterolaterally, exactly where the nerve root lies; over 90 per cent occur at L4–L5 (compressing L5) and L5–S1 (compressing S1). The pain profile is characteristic and worth writing verbatim: younger adult, 20–50 years; flexion- and sitting-intolerant pain (sitting raises intradiscal pressure roughly 40 per cent above standing); pain radiating below the knee in a dermatomal band — true sciatica, not the vague thigh ache of referred pain; often relief in supine lying or standing extension. State clearly that symptoms arise from both mechanical deformation and chemical inflammation of the dorsal root ganglion, which is why the severity of leg pain often outruns the MRI appearance.

4Answer

Screen dermatomes, myotomes and reflexes on both sides. Sensation: L4 over the medial malleolus, L5 over the dorsum of the first web space, S1 over the lateral foot. Motor: test a standard myotome pattern — ankle dorsiflexion (L4), great-toe extension (L5), ankle plantarflexion and rising on toes (S1) — as resisted isometric holds and compare sides, grading asymmetry rather than absolute strength. Reflexes: the knee jerk (L4) and ankle jerk (S1); L5 has no reliable reflex, so great-toe extension weakness plus an absent ankle jerk localises cleanly. A reproducible, side-to-side-documented deficit is the strongest clinical evidence that the pain is radicular and not merely referred.

The straight leg raise tensions the L5 and S1 roots; the classic pooled values (Deville et al., meta-analysis, Spine 2000) are sensitivity about 0.91 with specificity only about 0.26 — excellent for ruling out when negative, poor for ruling in. The crossed straight leg raise flips this: sensitivity about 0.28 but specificity near 0.90, so a positive crossed SLR is close to confirmatory. Add the slump test for sensitivity, and sensitizers — ankle dorsiflexion and cervical flexion — to prove the pain is neurogenic rather than hamstring or sacroiliac. Centralisation of symptoms during repeated movement testing is a further discogenic pointer: pain withdrawing from the foot towards the spine as the direction of preference is repeated.

Fig 3 — Draw the supine SLR: plinth, trunk, hip and raised leg, the angle arc marked between 35 and 70 degrees, and the two sensitizers (ankle dorsiflexion, cervical flexion). Labelling the sensitizers is the detail that earns the interpretation mark.

You conclude disc herniation by convergence, never by a single sign. The cluster to state in your answer: leg-dominant pain in a dermatomal band below the knee, plus at least one objective neurological deficit (sensory change, myotomal weakness or an absent reflex), plus a positive neurodynamic test, with symptom centralisation on movement testing. When all four converge, the clinical conclusion is "lumbar disc herniation with L5 (or S1) radiculopathy" — that sentence, with the level named, is the justification the question demands. Where the cluster is incomplete, say what is missing and what it means: a positive SLR without any deficit behaves like discogenic pain without root compression, which usually has a better prognosis.

Discriminate the mimics. Facet joint arthropathy: extension- and rotation-provoked localised back pain, no leg deficit. Sacroiliac joint pain: pain over the posterior superior iliac spine, positive Laslett cluster of provocation tests, negative SLR. Piriformis and deep gluteal syndrome: sciatica-like pain with a tender piriformis, SLR often positive but slump negative. Hip osteoarthritis: groin pain, restricted internal rotation, pain on FABER. Neurogenic claudication of spinal stenosis: leg symptoms that ease on flexion and walking uphill, in an older patient — the mirror image of discogenic flexion intolerance. Peripheral diabetic neuropathy: glove-and-stocking, symmetrical, non-dermatomal. Finally, before any of this, screen for the red flag: age under 20 or over 55 with new pain, night pain unrelieved by position, fever, weight loss, trauma, cancer history, steroid use, or any bowel-bladder change with saddle anaesthesia — the last one is cauda equina and is a same-day surgical referral, not an exercise prescription. Order imaging only for red flags or when invasive treatment is planned, remembering that a sizeable minority of asymptomatic adults show disc herniation on MRI — imaging must correlate with the clinical cluster, not replace it.

Examiner's tip: the question asks "how do you conclude", so structure the answer as a decision, not a description. Write the four-point cluster, then one line per differential with the single discriminating test for each. Quoting SLR sensitivity 0.91 / specificity 0.26 and crossed SLR 0.28 / 0.90 converts a pass answer into a distinction answer.

5Recent advances

  • El Melhat et al. (2024) — narrative review in the Journal of Clinical Medicine grading the evidence for conservative care: patient education, the McKenzie method, mobilisation and manipulation, exercise, neural mobilisation and epidural injection have moderate (Level B) support, while laser, ultrasound and electrotherapy have conflicting or no evidence.
  • Liu et al. (2023) — BMJ systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials finding surgery for sciatica gives only a small, short-lived benefit over conservative care, with no clinically important difference at one year, supporting physiotherapy-first management.
  • Kilpikoski et al. (2023) — randomised trial in patients with MRI-confirmed disc herniation and sciatica finding physiotherapist-directed McKenzie therapy and guideline-based advice produced similar improvements in pain and disability and similar low surgery rates at 24 months.
  • Ma et al. (2021) — randomised study finding about 84 per cent excellent outcomes with conservative care for large herniations, with greater protrusion actually increasing the likelihood of spontaneous resorption.

6References

  1. Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4), lumbar spine chapter.
  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC — Joint Structure and Function (ref 2): disc mechanics and loading.
  3. Deville WLJM et al. — Spine, 2000: pooled accuracy of SLR (meta-analysis).
  4. Laslett M et al. — Manual Therapy, 2005: sacroiliac cluster, used here for differential discrimination.
  5. WFNS Spine Committee. Consensus on the conservative treatment of lumbar disc herniations. 2024.
  6. Non-surgical approaches to the management of lumbar disc herniation associated with radiculopathy: a narrative review. J Clin Med. 2024;13(4):974.

On the evaluation form — Q3: Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 38-year-old manual labourer. Chief complaints: low back pain after lifting, sudden onset 2 weeks ago, radiating below the knee into the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot (S1) or the great toe (L5). Symptom analysis — site: low back with radiation to the leg; onset: sudden, 2 weeks ago, after lifting; type: sharp, shooting; severity: NPRS 7/10; aggravating factors: sitting, forward bending, coughing, sneezing and straining (conative pain); relieving factors: lying with the knees flexed, standing. Red-flag screen: negative — no fever, weight loss, cancer history, saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel change, or progressive weakness. No other medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history was given; vital signs not documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Antalgic list to the contralateral side; flattened lumbar lordosis; antalgic gait.

On palpation. Paravertebral spasm with tenderness at the L4–L5/L5–S1 level; no warmth.

1. Motor assessment. ROM: flexion limited and reproduces leg pain; extension may relieve or centralise symptoms (McKenzie directional preference). MMT by myotome — L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 great-toe extension, S1 plantarflexion — graded by side. Reflexes: ankle jerk diminished on the affected side (S1); knee jerk (L4) normal. SLR angle recorded (see special tests).

2. Sensory assessment. Dermatome screen: L4 medial leg, L5 first webspace, S1 lateral foot — diminished to pinprick along the affected root; plantar response normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Sitting tolerance, sit-to-stand, forward reach and walking distance recorded. Outcome measures: Oswestry Disability Index (0–100%), NPRS (0–10), PSFS (0–10); SLR angle tracked as an objective measure of neural mobility.

4. Gait analysis. Antalgic gait (see observation); formal stance/swing, cadence and step/stride parameters not documented.

5. Balance. Not documented at this assessment.

6. Hand function. Not documented; not directly involved in this lumbar condition.

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Straight leg raise (SLR)Passive hip flexion, knee extended, leg raised 10–70°Pain radiating along the dermatomeDural/nerve-root tension from a lower lumbar herniation
Crossed SLRRaise the unaffected legPain reproduced in the symptomatic legStrongly suggestive of disc herniation
Slump testSeated slump, knee extension with neck flexionLeg pain reproduced, eased by neck extensionNeural tension sign
Femoral nerve stretchProne knee flexion with hip extensionAnterior thigh painL2–L4 upper lumbar herniation
Bowstring signAfter SLR, add knee flexion and apply pressure over the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossaRadicular pain reproducedConfirmatory nerve-root tension

In this patient: SLR positive, reproducing radiating leg pain (angle recorded); positive tension signs are noted overall, but the individual results of crossed SLR, slump, femoral nerve stretch and bowstring sign were not separately documented.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Lumbago with radiating leg pain
  • Limited lumbar flexion
  • Possible segmental (myotomal) weakness
  • Diminished ankle jerk

Functional limitations

  • Unable to sit or lift for work

Disabilities

  • Loss of earning capacity
11. Functional diagnosis

Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy: symptoms that centralise with extension, single-root dermatome, myotome and reflex findings and positive tension signs — consistent with disc herniation rather than facet syndrome, spinal stenosis, SI joint or piriformis syndrome — currently limiting sitting, lifting and earning capacity.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Centralise and reduce leg pain to 3/10 or less on the NPRS; SLR angle up by 20°; independent home programme.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Symptom-free lumbar ROM; myotomes 5/5; ODI below 20%; return to manual work with lifting education.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): McKenzie extension if symptoms centralise, positional advice, pain-relieving modalities. Stage 2 (weeks 2–6): neural mobilisation (slump sliders), core stabilisation (dead bug, bird-dog, bridges), graded walking. Stage 3 (weeks 6–12): lifting mechanics, functional reconditioning, work hardening.

14. Home programme

Prone press-ups thrice daily, neutral-spine log rolling, avoid prolonged sitting; report any bladder or bowel change immediately.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Discuss autonomous practice and the decision-making process in musculoskeletal physiotherapy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 3 — direct access, primary care, autonomous practice, decision making

★ Memory hook — autonomy is a cycle: Screen → Diagnose → Decide (treat or refer) → Document. You are the gatekeeper.

1Introduction

Autonomous practice means the physiotherapist practises as a first-contact, primary-care professional: the patient may arrive without a physician referral, and the physiotherapist independently performs the examination, decides whether the problem belongs in physiotherapy or outside it, makes the diagnosis at the level of impairment and function, and sets the plan of care — while accepting full professional accountability for that decision. Direct access is the enabling mechanism. In the Indian context, referral requirements are not uniform; several states and institutional settings allow patients to approach physiotherapy directly, and musculoskeletal physiotherapists increasingly run first-contact clinics in metros. With that privilege comes the burden this question is really about: competent differential diagnosis, medical screening, and knowing when to send the patient on.

2Physiology

Describe three models and say who uses each. The hypothetico-deductive model is the novice pathway: from the first cues you generate a hypothesis list, test each hypothesis with selected questions and tests, and revise until one explanation survives — slow, conscious, and safe. Pattern recognition is the expert shortcut: thousands of stored illness scripts let the clinician match the presentation to a known pattern almost at sight — fast, but vulnerable to atypical presentations and to bias. Dual-process theory reconciles them: System 1 is the fast intuitive match, System 2 the slow analytic check, and expertise is knowing when to switch — especially when the pattern fit is imperfect or the patient is not responding as expected. Add that errors in musculoskeletal practice are rarely knowledge errors; they are reasoning errors — premature closure and confirmation bias — so the deliberate use of "what else could this be?" is a professional skill, not an academic ornament.

3Pathophysiology

The failure modes of clinical decision making are the pathology this question is really about. Errors in musculoskeletal practice are rarely knowledge errors; they are reasoning errors — premature closure (settling on the first plausible diagnosis) and confirmation bias (seeking only the findings that support it). In autonomous practice the consequence is sharper: a missed red flag or a medical mimic that is never screened becomes a delayed diagnosis, and non-response to treatment at two or three visits is itself a signal that the working hypothesis is wrong.

4Answer

Because no physician has pre-screened the patient, every musculoskeletal assessment under direct access begins with a medical screen. Screen for red flags of serious spinal pathology; screen for medical mimics — claudication presenting as calf pain on walking, diabetic neuropathy presenting as foot pain, visceral referral presenting as thoracic or shoulder pain; review medications (long-term steroids, anticoagulants, bisphosphonates); and check baseline vital signs when the history warrants. The screen is not a one-time event: a patient who fails to improve as expected at two or three visits is re-screened, because non-response is itself a red flag for a wrong diagnosis. In Indian practice this duty is sharpened by reality — patients may arrive having self-medicated, with undiagnosed diabetes or tuberculosis, and with late presentations; the autonomous physiotherapist is often the first health professional to notice the weight loss behind a "backache".

Fig 4 — Draw the gatekeeper flowchart: entry, the red-flag diamond, the refer box, and the treat-and-re-test loop. The diamond is what the examiner wants to see — autonomy means the referral decision is yours.

The autonomous clinician works on a clearly reasoned treat-or-refer axis. Refer urgently when red flags appear — suspected fracture, malignancy, infection, cauda equina, acute inflammatory arthritis; refer for medical opinion when the presentation is outside your differential, when the patient deteriorates, or when expected improvement does not occur within the agreed number of sessions. Within musculoskeletal practice itself you decide the pathway: classification-based treatment (for example, a treatment-based classification for low back pain), manual therapy versus exercise direction, and progression criteria governed by re-assessment rather than by habit. Autonomy also has a legal and ethical face: informed consent before assessment and treatment, truthfulness about the limits of your competence, record-keeping that would survive scrutiny, and honesty about prognostic uncertainty. With no physician standing between you and the patient, "I referred because I was not sure" is a defensible decision; "I treated because I did not check" is not.

Close the argument with the systems that keep autonomy safe. Document the reasoning, not just the findings — what you suspected, what you tested, what you concluded, and why the referral was or was not made. Anchor progress with validated outcome measures so continuation of care is justified by data. And maintain competence through continuing education and clinical audit, because autonomous practice is a licence granted to a professional who keeps proving it.

Examiner's tip: this question is failed by students who write only about treatment techniques. Marks live in the decision architecture — models of reasoning, the screening obligation, the referral trigger. Give one concrete Indian scenario (an undiagnosed diabetic presenting as foot pain) and you demonstrate applied autonomy rather than textbook recall.

5Recent advances

  • Bicker et al. (2024) — narrative synthesis in Musculoskeletal Care of musculoskeletal First Contact Physiotherapy in UK primary care finding high patient satisfaction and improved health status, with reduced GP musculoskeletal workload.
  • Walsh et al. (2024) — FRONTIER evaluation in the British Journal of General Practice finding First Contact Physiotherapy non-inferior to GP-led care at 6 months, with significantly more patients improved at 3 months, lower NHS costs and less opioid prescribing.
  • Gallotti et al. (2023) — systematic review finding direct access safe and cost-effective with higher patient satisfaction than physician-referred care, and no adverse events.
  • Ojha et al. (2014) — systematic review in Physical Therapy finding direct-access episodes of care had better outcomes and satisfaction, with fewer physiotherapy visits, imaging tests and medications than physician-referred episodes.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ — Physical Rehabilitation (ref 10): clinical decision making in physical therapy.
  3. Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4): screening principles in the introduction.
  4. Bicker J, et al. A narrative synthesis of the effectiveness and acceptability of musculoskeletal first contact physiotherapy practitioner roles in primary care. Musculoskeletal Care. 2024;22(2):e1875.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Distinguish the various special tests with interpretation for knee instability.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4b — special tests and interpretation

★ Memory hook — ACL: Lachman detects, pivot shift confirms, drawer grades. PCL: sag sign, posterior drawer, quadriceps active test.

1Introduction

Knee instability is not a diagnosis but a description of abnormal translation or rotation, and the examiner wants you to distinguish the special tests by what each detects and how it should be interpreted. This answer classifies the instabilities, presents the tests region by region, and closes with a grading and interpretation grammar.

2Physiology

The knee is stabilised by four principal ligaments working with the capsule and the surrounding musculature. The anterior cruciate ligament resists anterior translation of the tibia on the femur and controls rotatory laxity; the posterior cruciate ligament is the primary restraint to posterior translation; the medial and lateral collateral ligaments resist valgus and varus stress respectively; and the posterolateral corner restrains external rotation. In health these structures allow a smooth, firm-stopped arc of movement with no abnormal translation in any plane.

3Pathophysiology

Ligamentous instability is abnormal translation or rotation of the tibia on the femur, and you classify it by direction: straight instabilities (anterior, posterior, medial, lateral) versus combined or rotatory instabilities (anteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral). Mechanism predicts the torn structure: a non-contact pivot — valgus load with the foot planted and the body rotating, the classic kabaddi or football cutting injury — ruptures the ACL; a dashboard injury or a fall on a flexed knee with the foot planted drives the tibia backwards and ruptures the PCL; a blow to the lateral side opens the medial compartment and grades the MCL. An acute haemarthrosis within two hours of a pivot injury is ACL until proven otherwise — write that sentence.

4Answer

The Lachman test is the workhorse: knee at 20–30 degrees of flexion, one hand stabilising the femur, the other drawing the tibia anteriorly; pooled sensitivity about 0.85 with specificity about 0.94, and the end-feel matters — soft or mushy compared with the other side, with loss of the firm stop, is positive. The anterior drawer at 90 degrees is more familiar but weaker in the acute knee (about 0.55 sensitivity) because hamstring guarding blocks the translation — it is more useful in chronic tears. The pivot shift is the physiological test: under a valgus load the ACL-deficient knee subluxes anteriorly in extension and reduces with a clunk as it flexes; its sensitivity is low, around 0.24, but its specificity near 0.98, so a positive pivot shift is essentially confirmatory — provided the patient is relaxed and comfortable, which is why it is never your first test.

Fig 5 — Draw two bones meeting at a circle, the two hands as ellipses, and the anterior arrow on the tibia. Label "20–30 degrees of flexion" and the anterior drawer force — that single sketch carries the whole test.

The posterior sag sign (Godfrey): supine, hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees supported by the examiner, and the tibia visibly drops backwards — a quiet, high-yield observation that is often missed. The posterior drawer is the most sensitive PCL test (around 0.9): push the tibia posteriorly at 90 degrees and grade against the contralateral step-off of the medial tibial plateau. The quadriceps active test separates true from apparent laxity: asking the seated patient to slide the foot forward fires the quadriceps and visibly pulls a posteriorly-sagged tibia back into place — a PCL tear written in front of your eyes.

Valgus and varus stress testing is done twice — at 30 degrees of flexion, which isolates the collateral because the cruciates are slack, and at full extension, where the capsule and both cruciates also contribute, so laxity at 0 degrees means a more extensive injury. Grade the end-feel as you go. The dial test done at 30 degrees and 90 degrees of flexion separates an isolated posterolateral corner injury (increased external rotation at 30 degrees only) from a combined PCL plus posterolateral injury (increased at both angles). Rotatory tests such as the Slocum anteromedial drawer complete the picture for combined instabilities. Finally, mention the Ottawa knee rules as the clinical screen for when a radiograph is actually needed — age, isolated patella tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, and inability to bear weight for four steps.

Interpret in a fixed grammar: grade I — pain with stress but no laxity; grade II — laxity with a firm endpoint; grade III — laxity with a soft or absent endpoint. Then cluster: mechanism plus acute haemarthrosis plus a positive Lachman with a soft endpoint is an ACL rupture; add a positive pivot shift and the rotatory instability is clinically significant; a positive Lachman combined with laxity to valgus stress at 0 degrees signals a multi-ligament knee that needs urgent orthopaedic referral, not a programme sheet. Instrumented arthrometry and MRI confirm and quantify when surgery is contemplated, but the clinical cluster remains the reference standard at the bedside.

Examiner's tip: the verb is "distinguish" — so never present the tests as a list without contrast. Give each test a one-line accuracy figure and say what it is for: Lachman to detect, pivot shift to confirm, drawer to grade in chronic knees. A small comparison table written in the margin of your answer sheet reads like an examiner's own checklist.

5Recent advances

  • Sokal et al. (2022) — bivariate meta-analysis in Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy re-estimating ACL test accuracy and showing the Lachman test had been overestimated: pooled sensitivity about 81 per cent and specificity about 85 per cent, lower in post-acute and complete tears.
  • Sokal et al. (2022) — the same review confirmed the pivot shift is the best test to rule in a tear (specificity about 94 per cent, positive likelihood ratio about 10.7) but the least sensitive, so it should confirm rather than screen.
  • Reiman et al. (2018) — systematic review with meta-analysis in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy showing the Lever sign can moderately shift post-test probability to rule in or rule out an ACL tear and is simple to perform.
  • Abruscato et al. (2019) — meta-analysis in the International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy reporting pooled sensitivity about 0.77 and specificity about 0.90 for the Lever sign, comparable to Lachman and anterior drawer.
  • Sokal et al. (2022) — the same review concludes evidence continues to favour a test combination over any single examination, because no one clinical test achieves both a high positive and a high negative likelihood ratio.

6References

  1. Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4), knee chapter: ligament stress testing.
  2. Torg JS, Conrad W, Kalen V — Clin Orthop Relat Res, 1976: the Lachman test.
  3. Galway RD, Beaupré A, MacIntosh DL — Clin Orthop, 1972: the pivot shift phenomenon.
  4. Stiell IG et al. — JAMA, 1996: Ottawa knee rules for radiography.
  5. Sokal PA, Norris R, Maddox TW, Oldershaw RA. The diagnostic accuracy of clinical tests for anterior cruciate ligament tears are comparable but the Lachman test has been previously overestimated: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2022;30(10):3287–3303.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Knee ligament instability (ACL/PCL/MCL)

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 24-year-old footballer. Chief complaints after a non-contact twisting injury with an audible pop while pivoting: pain, swelling, inability to continue play, and giving way on pivoting and stairs; the knee swelled within 2–3 hours, suggesting the haemarthrosis typical of an ACL rupture. Pain history: NPRS 7/10 on the day of injury, 3/10 now. The mechanism directs suspicion: a valgus contact force — MCL; a dashboard-type posterior force — PCL. A locked knee or inability to extend would suggest a displaced meniscal tear and must be flagged to the surgeon. Red-flag screen: negative as above. No other history was given; vital signs not documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Suprapatellar fullness with obliterated peripatellar hollows (effusion); vastus medialis wasting noted at review; knee held in 20–30° of flexion for comfort.

On palpation. Warmth; joint-line tenderness (meniscus); tenderness along the medial femoral condyle to tibia (MCL); positive patellar tap.

1. Motor assessment. ROM: flexion and terminal extension limited by pain and effusion. MMT: quadriceps 3/5, hamstrings 4/5. Muscle girth: thigh circumference measured 10–15 cm above the patella, both sides. Reflexes normal; limb lengths equal.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact; the common peroneal distribution (dorsum of the foot) and active dorsiflexion are screened specifically after a varus injury — at risk with LCL/posterolateral corner injury. Dermatomes and myotomes otherwise intact.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Stairs non-reciprocal; single-leg squat shows dynamic valgus and giving way; single-leg hop not possible. Outcome measures: Lysholm knee scoring scale (0–100), IKDC subjective knee form (0–100), NPRS (0–10); thigh girth and single-leg hop distance as functional measures.

4. Gait analysis. Quadriceps-avoidance antalgic gait; formal stance/swing, cadence and step/stride parameters not documented.

5. Balance. Single-leg balance tested; eyes-open/eyes-closed results not documented.

6. Hand function. Ambulation is assisted with crutches (see goals for independent crutch ambulation); reaching, grasping and releasing otherwise not documented.

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Lachman testKnee at 20–30° flexion, anterior tibial translation on the femurSoft or absent end-pointACL rupture (most sensitive clinical test)
Anterior drawer testSupine, hip 45°, knee 90°, foot stabilised, tibia drawn forwardExcess anterior translationACL injury (may be negative acutely)
Pivot shift testValgus and internal rotation while moving the knee from extension to flexionClunk as the iliotibial band reduces the subluxed tibiaRotatory anterior instability (ACL)
Posterior sag signSupine, hip 45°, knee 90°, heels supportedTibia visibly sags posteriorlyPCL injury
Posterior drawer testSupine, knee 90°, tibia pushed backwardPosterior translationPCL injury
Quadriceps active testSupine, knee 90°, patient tries to extend the kneeTibia shifts anteriorlyPCL deficiency
Valgus stress at 30°Knee flexed 30°, abduction force appliedMedial joint openingMCL injury
Valgus stress at 0°Knee extended, abduction force appliedMedial opening even in extensionGrade III MCL or combined/bony injury
Varus stress testAdduction force at 0° and 30°Lateral joint openingLCL/posterolateral corner injury

In this patient: ligamentous laxity is present on the relevant stress test(s); the individual results for each test listed above were not separately documented.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Pain (NPRS 3/10 currently)
  • Effusion
  • Limited terminal extension
  • Quadriceps weakness
  • Ligamentous laxity on the relevant stress test

Functional limitations

  • Unable to run
  • Unable to pivot
  • Unable to climb stairs reciprocally

Disabilities

  • Loss of sporting participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Acute traumatic knee ligament injury (suspected ACL rupture with haemarthrosis) with effusion, quadriceps weakness and ligamentous instability, preventing running, pivoting, stair use and sporting participation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain 3/10 or less on the NPRS; full terminal extension; straight-leg raise without lag; independent crutch ambulation.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Quadriceps and hamstrings 5/5; thigh girth within 1 cm of the normal side; hop distance 90% of the uninjured limb; Lysholm above 85; criteria-based return to pivoting sport.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): protection, relative rest, ice, compression, elevation, hinged brace, isometric quadriceps. Stage 2 (weeks 2–6): closed-chain strengthening (mini-squats, step-ups), stationary cycling, wobble-board proprioception. Stage 3 (weeks 6–12): agility, plyometrics, sport-specific drills; after reconstruction the same phases follow with the surgeon's graft-protection protocol.

14. Home programme

Quad sets, straight-leg raises, heel slides, calf pumps, ice after exercise.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Explain exercise testing in musculoskeletal disease.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4e — exercise testing and prescription

★ Memory hook — never test before screening: Screen → Baseline → Load → Monitor → Stop criteria → Prescribe.

1Introduction

Exercise testing is the measurement of a patient's physical capacity under controlled, graded loading, and in musculoskeletal practice it serves three purposes: it quantifies the impairment (how weak, how unfit, how easily fatigued), it provides the baseline against which the whole rehabilitation programme is judged, and it is itself a motivational and educational tool — a patient who sees the number move believes in the treatment. It also screens for function beyond the index joint: the knee may be the complaint, but aerobic capacity and global strength determine whether the patient returns to work or the field.

2Physiology

Exercise testing measures the integrated response of the cardiovascular, respiratory and musculoskeletal systems to graded load. In a healthy person oxygen uptake rises linearly with work rate until a plateau (VO2max) is reached, heart rate and systolic blood pressure climb together, ventilation tracks carbon-dioxide production, and perceived exertion (Borg 6–20 or CR10) rises in step with the load. Muscular performance is expressed as maximal force (strength), the ability to sustain repeated contractions (endurance), and side-to-side symmetry.

3Pathophysiology

Disease distorts these normal responses and sets the boundaries of safe testing. Deconditioning in musculoskeletal disease lowers aerobic capacity and strength before the index joint is even loaded, so the patient fatigues early; a beta-blocker flattens the heart-rate response so perceived exertion must replace pulse as the gauge; and a falling blood pressure, angina, marked dyspnoea, dizziness or an abnormal gait during a test are the physiological markers of a system that must be stopped. These are the reasons a contraindication list and termination criteria precede every test.

4Answer

No test before screening. Take the cardiovascular history, use a structured self-report such as the PAR-Q+ as a first filter, measure baseline heart rate and blood pressure, and review medications — a beta-blocker flattens the heart-rate response, so rating of perceived exertion becomes your gauge instead of pulse alone. Stratify risk and list contraindications explicitly: uncontrolled hypertension (above 180/110), unstable angina, recent infarction, uncontrolled arrhythmia, acute deep-vein thrombosis, acute inflammation or fever, and uncontrolled metabolic disease are absolute stops; significant musculoskeletal pain, recent surgery and severe osteoporosis are relative ones that modify the modality. Obtain informed consent and explain stop signals before you start.

Maximal graded exercise testing on a treadmill or cycle ergometer directly measures VO2max, but it is rarely needed in musculoskeletal clinics; more often you use submaximal prediction — the Åstrand-Rhyming or YMCA cycle protocols, or a treadmill test terminated at a target heart rate or an RPE of about 15 — to estimate VO2max from the heart-rate response. Field tests bring the same logic to resource-limited Indian settings: the six-minute walk test for endurance in elderly and post-operative patients, the two-minute walk or the shuttle walk for higher-functioning patients, and the sit-to-stand test for lower-limb power in older adults. Record the mode, because numbers are not interchangeable across tests.

Strength is quantified in a hierarchy: manual muscle testing for grading 0–5 where weakness is marked; handheld dynamometry for an objective force reading; one-repetition maximum or its safer estimate from a 6–10 repetition maximum (the Brzycki equation) for prescribing progressive resistance; and isokinetic dynamometry where velocity-controlled torque data are needed — the classic use is the hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, conventionally about 0.6, with asymmetry beyond about 10 per cent between limbs flagged as a reinjury risk after ACL reconstruction. Muscular endurance is measured by timed holds or repetition counts, and functional composite tests — the timed up-and-go, stair climb, single-leg hop battery — translate muscle data into capability.

Fig 6 — Draw the test loop: stage, monitor, decision diamond, and the stop box with four termination criteria listed. Examiners give the safety mark specifically for the stop criteria being visible.

Interpret against expected responses: heart rate and blood pressure should rise together, perceived exertion should track the load (Borg 6–20 scale, or CR10), and a falling blood pressure, angina, marked dyspnoea, dizziness, an abnormal gait or RPE above 17 are absolute termination criteria. In musculoskeletal interpretation, compare side-to-side symmetry of strength and endurance, and record the distance walked, the claudication or pain onset distance in osteoarthritis and vascular insufficiency, and the load tolerated. The results then write the prescription: intensity from the heart-rate reserve or RPE zone, volume from the repetition maximum, progression by documented increments. Re-test under identical conditions every few weeks — same time of day, same mode, same instructions — because only a comparable number can prove progress.

Examiner's tip: safety content separates grades here. Every answer must contain a named contraindication list and termination criteria — in many Indian clinics there is no crash trolley next to the physiotherapy department, and saying that out loud in your answer shows you understand why the list exists.

5Recent advances

  • Kabbadj et al. (2024) — review establishing cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), analysing respiratory gases alongside ECG and haemodynamic monitoring, as the recognised gold standard for cardiorespiratory fitness and for prescribing and monitoring exercise in rehabilitation populations.
  • Holland et al. (2014) — European Respiratory Society/American Thoracic Society technical standard and systematic review confirming the six-minute walk test and incremental shuttle walk test are valid, reliable and responsive field measures of functional exercise capacity when CPET is unavailable.
  • Crook et al. (2017) — multicentre validation in the European Respiratory Journal showing the one-minute sit-to-stand test is reliable, valid and responsive with a minimal important difference of three repetitions, making it practical where space and time are limited.
  • Kabbadj et al. (2024) — review repositioning exercise testing as a prognostic and risk-stratification tool across chronic disease, not merely a measure of fitness.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ — Physical Rehabilitation (ref 10): exercise testing and prescription chapters.
  2. Nordin M, Frankel VH — Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System (ref 1): load-response principles.
  3. Magee DJ — Orthopedic Physical Assessment (ref 4): functional testing of the lower limb.
  4. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing: methodology and interpretation in cardiac rehabilitation — a review. 2024.
  5. Musculoskeletal limitation in preoperative cardiopulmonary exercise testing favours the use of submaximal metrics. The Physiological Society. 2023.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Outline the orthotic devices with indications for spinal conditions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5b — orthotics prescription

★ Memory hook — match the force to the fault: three-point extension (Taylor, Jewett), circumferential (TLSO), correction (Milwaukee, Boston, Charleston), compression (SI belt).

1Introduction

An orthosis is an externally applied device that supports, aligns, prevents or corrects a body segment while improving function — distinguished from a prosthesis, which replaces a missing part. Spinal orthoses work through a small set of biomechanical levers worth naming: the three-point pressure system (an anterior force balanced by two posterior counter-forces, or the reverse), distraction or offloading to reduce axial load on healing bone, motion restriction in selected planes (flexion is easiest to block, rotation hardest), and postural cueing by proprioceptive reminder. Prescription follows the diagnosis, the stage of healing, and the patient: a device that cannot be tolerated in a humid Indian summer will not be worn, and an unworn orthosis is a failed prescription.

2Physiology

The normal spine is a curved, load-bearing column in which the vertebral bodies carry compression, the discs distribute it, and the surrounding musculature and ligaments provide dynamic and passive stability; the sagittal profile alternates cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis to centre the line of gravity. In health the trunk tolerates axial load, bends in all planes and returns to alignment without external support.

3Pathophysiology

Orthoses are prescribed when that self-supporting system fails: a vertebral compression or burst fracture with compromised stability, a healing fusion or osteoporotic segment that must be offloaded, a progressive scoliotic curve in a growing child, a symptomatic spondylolysis or listhesis, or pelvic-ring dysfunction. In each case the pathology defines the direction of force the orthosis must supply — extension moment, circumferential control or correction — and the stage of healing defines how long it is worn.

4Answer

The soft collar gives comfort and a reminder effect but almost no motion control — prescribe briefly for acute sprains, and wean within one to two weeks to avoid dependency. The Philadelphia two-piece foam collar with plastic shell restricts flexion-extension modestly: suitable for stable fractures and post-fusion support. The sterno-occipital-mandibular-immobiliser (SOMI) adds chin and occipital control with a sternal plate, better for flexion control, usable even in the supine patient with a headboard attachment. The Guilford four-poster adds similar control from a pelvic base. At the top of the hierarchy, the halo vest — ring fixed to the skull by pins, attached to a vest — provides the most rigid cervical immobilisation and is the choice for unstable cervical fractures and post-operative fixation, but demands pin-site care, so physiotherapy follow-up is mandatory.

The Taylor and cruciform anterior hyperextension orthoses apply a three-point system — a sternal pad and a pubic pad anteriorly, a thoracic pad posteriorly — creating an extension moment; classic indications are stable anterior compression fractures and posture support in healing kyphoplasty patients, with the Jewett hyperextension brace offering the same principle in a lighter, more tolerable frame for stable thoracolumbar compression fractures, generally from about T8 to L3. The custom-moulded or prefabricated thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO) gives circumferential control of the trunk: indicated after spinal fusion, for burst fractures with an intact posterior wall, and for situational offloading in osteoporotic patients. Note the trade-off honestly — better control costs greater discomfort, heat intolerance and trunk-muscle disuse, so the weaning plan is part of the prescription, not an afterthought.

Fig 7 — Draw the curved spine with the three pads and arrows: sternal anterior, thoracic and pubic posterior. Label "one anterior force, two posterior counter-forces, extension moment" — this sketch explains every orthosis in the answer.

Bracing in scoliosis prevents progression of an immature curve, and the choice follows curve apex and maturity. The Milwaukee cervico-thoracolumbosacral orthosis with its neck ring and throat mould is the historic prototype, still used for high thoracic curves with the apex above about T8 where an underarm brace cannot reach. The underarm TLSO family (Boston-type) covers curves with apexes below T8 and is the commonest modern prescription, with full-time wear (16–23 hours) while the child grows, guided by the Risser sign: bracing helps until skeletal maturity, not after. The Charleston night-time bending brace, fabricated in maximal correction for single flexible thoracolumbar or lumbar curves, trades daytime freedom for night-only wear. Bracing is prevention, not correction of an established structural curve — and the psychological load of full-time wear on a teenager is a clinical problem in itself, which is why counselling and sport continuation are part of the orthotic plan.

The lumbosacral corset raises intra-abdominal pressure to offload the lumbar spine: indicated for mechanical low back pain, symptomatic spondylolysis and listhesis, and post-operative support. The sacroiliac belt compresses the pelvic ring: indicated for sacroiliac joint dysfunction, and commonly in India for pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain where it lets the mother keep working. Close every orthotic answer with the honest limitations: prolonged rigid bracing weakens the trunk musculature it replaces, causes heat rash and pressure sores in our climate, may reduce bone density with long use, and can create psychological dependency — therefore prescribe with a defined duration, an exercise programme to maintain what the brace is resting, and a written weaning schedule.

Examiner's tip: the question says "with indications", so every device earns its mark only through a named indication. The examiner's test of depth is the limitations paragraph and the weaning plan — most students can list braces; fewer can say when to stop one.

5Recent advances

  • Vick et al. (2024) — retrospective study of back bracing in chronic low back pain finding it significantly improved pain (visual analogue scale falling from about 6.3 to 3.2 over 12 months) and function when combined with physiotherapy, with no evidence of orthosis-induced muscle atrophy.
  • Borg et al. (2024) — mini-review in Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences of spinal orthoses in osteoporotic vertebral fractures finding dynamic hyperextension orthoses (Spinomed, Spinfast) outperformed rigid three-point braces, improving back extensor strength and reducing pain, though trial quality remains limited.
  • Weinstein et al. (2013) — BrAIST randomised trial in the New England Journal of Medicine showing bracing prevented progression to the surgical threshold in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (72 versus 48 per cent success), with benefit increasing with hours of brace wear.
  • Negrini et al. (2018) — SOSORT international guidelines for orthopaedic and rehabilitation treatment of idiopathic scoliosis, recommending disease-specific bracing matched to the curve and physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises alongside brace wear.
  • Landauer & Trieb (2022) — indication-based concept concluding that spinal orthoses work only when the diagnosis is specific and the orthosis is matched to it — non-specific bracing of non-specific back pain shows no measurable effect.

6References

  1. Chui K, Jorge M, Yen S-C, Lusardi MM — Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation (ref 18): spinal orthoses chapters.
  2. Maxey L, Magnusson JA — Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient (ref 13): post-operative bracing timelines.
  3. McKinnis LN — Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging (ref 8): imaging follow-up of braced fractures.
  4. Freeman J, Nikjou D, Maloney J, et al. The role of orthoses in chronic axial spinal conditions. Curr Pain Headache Rep. 2024;28:501–506.
  5. De Sire A, et al. Efficacy of different spinal orthoses for pain, function and quality of life in osteoporotic vertebral fractures: a mini review. Front Rehabil Sci. 2024;5:1506279.

On the evaluation form — Q7: Spinal orthoses

I. Subjective examination

Typical orthotic-clinic patient: a 40-year-old man with a stable thoracolumbar burst fracture after a road traffic accident, or a growing child with an idiopathic scoliosis curve of 25–40°. Record the diagnosis, level of injury or curve magnitude, the surgeon's prescription, occupation, home environment and who will assist with the brace; document neurological status before and after every brace check. Red-flag screen: watch for any new neurological deficit after brace application. Vital signs not documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Posture; any kyphotic deformity or list; bed mobility and transfers; skin over bony prominences (iliac crests, spinous processes, ribs) inspected before fitting and at every follow-up — pressure sores are the commonest complication.

On palpation. Spinous tenderness and paraspinal spasm.

1. Motor assessment. Trunk ROM permitted by the injury and brace (flexion is the restricted plane); MMT of all four limbs; transfers and gait with the brace on and off. Reflexes documented serially.

2. Sensory assessment. Dermatome and myotome screen of the lower limbs at every visit; any new deficit after brace application is reported immediately.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Transfers, bed mobility, sitting and standing tolerance; brace donning/doffing independence scored on a FIM-type scale. Outcome measures: Oswestry Disability Index (0–100%) and NPRS (0–10) for adults; serial Cobb angle for braced scoliosis; a compliance diary of daily wearing hours.

4. Gait analysis. Gait with the orthosis, tested on and off; formal stance/swing, cadence and step/stride parameters not documented.

5. Balance. Balance tested with the brace on; eyes-open/eyes-closed results not documented.

6. Hand function. Donning and doffing the orthosis (straps, pads) requires reaching, grasping and releasing; independence is scored on a FIM-type scale. No other assistive devices documented.

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

Serial radiographs (fracture alignment and healing, or the Cobb angle in braced scoliosis) per the surgeon; none reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

No provocative special tests are performed at an orthotic review; assessment centres on the neurological screen above and on device checks (see the orthosis selection table under the treatment plan).

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Spinal pain
  • Restricted trunk mobility
  • Altered breathing mechanics under a rigid shell

Functional limitations

  • Transfers and self-care need assistance

Disabilities

  • Temporary loss of the occupational role
11. Functional diagnosis

A spinal condition (stable thoracolumbar burst fracture or growing idiopathic scoliosis) requiring orthotic control, presently limited by brace-related pain, restricted trunk mobility and dependence in transfers and self-care, with temporary loss of the occupational role and recovery expected through graded weaning.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Brace tolerated for the prescribed hours; skin intact; pain 3/10 or less on the NPRS; independent transfers and brace management.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Maintained alignment with radiological healing or a non-progressive curve; graded weaning per the surgeon; trunk strength restored for return to work or school.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (fitting): wear time built up gradually to the prescribed hours (up to 23 hours daily in scoliosis bracing); daily skin inspection; education on numbness or new pain. Stage 2: in-brace diaphragmatic breathing, isometric trunk and limb exercises; brace-free scoliosis-specific exercises. Stage 3 (weaning): progressive reduction of hours guided by radiographs and postural re-education. Complications monitored: pressure ulcers, skin maceration, deconditioning, non-compliance. Orthosis selection:

DeviceIndicationTypical condition
Soft cervical collarMild soft-tissue strain, night comfort, weaning aidCervical sprain/whiplash; weaning from rigid orthoses
Rigid cervical collar (Philadelphia, Miami J)Temporary cervical immobilisationStable cervical fracture, post-operative fusion
Halo vestRigid upper-cervical immobilisationType II odontoid fracture, C1–C2 instability
SOMI / Minerva cervicothoracic orthosisControl extending to the lower cervical/upper thoracic spinePost-fusion support, unstable lower cervical injury
Jewett hyperextension braceThree-point extension control of the thoracolumbar spineStable burst fracture, osteoporotic compression fracture
Taylor / Knight-Taylor braceHyperextension force and trunk supportThoracic compression fracture, Scheuermann kyphosis

Lumbosacral corsetSymptomatic support, proprioceptive reminderMechanical/degenerative low back pain
