14. Home programme

Skin checks twice daily, hourly breathing exercises, log rolling, follow-up radiographs.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe the assessment method for a two-year-old child who developed excessive lateral curvature of the thoracic spine.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5f — pediatric orthopedic assessment

★ Memory hook — the two-year-old curve turns on two numbers: RVAD (under/over 20 degrees) and Mehta phase (1 or 2). Double thoracic curves resolve; single phase-2 curves progress.

1Introduction

A lateral curvature presenting at two years of age is early-onset scoliosis; within that label, scoliosis first appearing up to three years is called infantile idiopathic scoliosis, and the history-taking is dominated by separating it from the three dangerous mimics: congenital scoliosis (a hemivertebra or failure of segmentation visible on radiographs, often linked with cardiac and renal anomalies), neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, myelodysplasia, spinal dysraphism — always confirmed or excluded by neurological examination), and syndromic scoliosis (neurofibromatosis, Marfan, muscle disease). Take a birth history — breech delivery and first-born status associate with infantile idiopathic scoliosis; ask about milestones, whether the mother noticed a persistently tilted posture, a hump, or an asymmetrical skin crease; and ask about family history. A breastfed toddler in an Indian joint family will usually have a grandmother's observation already — take it.

2Physiology

The infant spine grows rapidly in the first years of life, and normal growth is symmetrical: the thoracic vertebrae and ribs develop in step, and the curve of the spine stays balanced as the child begins to sit, crawl and walk. Because growth velocity is highest before the third birthday, any asymmetry that appears in this window is amplified by growth itself — which is why a lateral curvature at two years of age is treated as a different problem from one appearing after the growth spurt of adolescence.

3Pathophysiology

State the classic facts: the majority of infantile idiopathic curves — historically quoted at around 90 per cent — resolve spontaneously, especially double thoracic curves with a low RVAD. The resolving pattern shows a flexible curve, RVAD under 20 degrees, rib phase 1, and no vertebral anomaly. The progressive pattern shows a single curve, RVAD above 20 degrees, phase 2 changes, and often early radiographic deterioration on serial films — the determination is made by comparing measurements, which is why the first follow-up at about four months is part of assessment itself.

4Answer

Examine on the mother's lap if the child will not cooperate, and undress adequately while keeping the room warm. Inspect standing (if the child stands reliably) and sitting: shoulder level, scapular prominence, waist crease asymmetry, pelvic level, and head position. The Adam's forward-bend test shows a rib hump on the convex side of a structural thoracic curve — in a two-year-old, perform it across your lap and use a scoliometer if the child allows. Then the screen that most candidates forget: the skin — café-au-lait patches of neurofibromatosis, a hairy patch, dimple or sinus over the spine suggesting dysraphism. Complete neurological examination — tone, gait if walking, muscle bulk and reflexes, and check the abdomen for a neurological bladder pattern. Examine the hips (developmental dysplasia or an adduction contracture can produce a compensatory apparent curve) and measure leg lengths. Infantile idiopathic scoliosis characteristically shows a left thoracic curve in a boy — remember that a left thoracic curve at any age warrants the most thorough neurological screen.

Request a full-length posteroanterior spine radiograph (supine if standing films are impossible at this age), and read it systematically. Measure the Cobb angle — the angle between the most tilted end vertebra above and below the curve, with 10 degrees the conventional diagnostic threshold for scoliosis. For prognosis at this age, use Mehta's rib-vertebral angle difference: draw a line perpendicular to the end plate of the apical vertebra and lines along the necks of the ribs on each side; an RVAD above about 20 degrees marks a curve at risk of progression, and Mehta's phase 2 — the rib head on the convex side overlapping the vertebral body — is a progression marker even at normal angles. Look specifically for congenital anomalies: hemivertebrae, bars, fused ribs. Where neurological signs coexist, an MRI of the entire spine is indicated before any management decision.

Fig 8 — Draw a curved spine, two lines along the most tilted end vertebrae, and the angle where their extensions meet. Label the 10-degree threshold — one clean sketch earns the radiology marks.

Resolving and low-risk curves are observed with radiographs every four to six months, with parental education on symmetry of carrying and play positioning. Progressive curves are referred without delay to a paediatric orthopaedic spine surgeon — at this age, definitive management is serial Mehta casting under anaesthesia (elongation-derotation-flexion), followed by bracing once walking age is established, with growth-friendly surgical options such as magnetically controlled growing rods for severe curves. Screening of associated systems matters in congenital cases — echocardiography and renal ultrasound. The physiotherapist's assessment output is therefore a classification: idiopathic-resolving, idiopathic-progressive, congenital, neuromuscular or syndromic — each with a different urgency of referral.

Examiner's tip: the age is the question. Everything that makes this answer distinctive — infantile onset, left thoracic male predominance, RVAD, Mehta phases, serial casting — flows from the child being two. Any general scoliosis answer without Mehta's method will read as a missed question.

5Recent advances

  • Johnson & Lark (2024) — review confirming Mehta (elongation-derotation-flexion) serial casting as the mainstay for progressive infantile curves, with cure rates of 45–49 per cent at over 5 years and the rib-vertebral angle difference (over 20 degrees, rib phase 2) as the key progression indicator.
  • Negrini et al. (2018) — SOSORT international guidelines recommending casting or very rigid bracing as the first step for infantile idiopathic scoliosis and disease-specific physiotherapy for juvenile curves, with follow-up until skeletal maturity.
  • Li et al. (2024) — study in Scientific Reports finding bracing corrected idiopathic early-onset curves by about 49 per cent versus about 17 per cent for congenital curves, and delayed surgery by a mean of about 69 months.
  • Thometz et al. (2018) — reported that CAD/CAM-designed elongation-derotation-flexion braces deliver casting-type three-dimensional correction without repeated anaesthesia, achieving about 50 per cent correction in infantile curves.
  • Schreiber et al. (2016) — randomised controlled trial in PLOS ONE showing Schroth physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises added to standard care produced better Cobb angle outcomes than standard care alone, supporting exercise as part of conservative management.

6References

  1. McKinnis LN — Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging (ref 8): scoliosis measurement on radiographs.
  2. Greenspan A, Beltran J — Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach (ref 9): congenital vertebral anomalies.
  3. Mehta MH — J Bone Joint Surg Br, 1972: the rib-vertebral angle difference in infantile scoliosis.
  4. Maxey L, Magnusson JA — Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient (ref 13): paediatric orthopaedic rehabilitation context.
  5. Current concepts in the treatment of early-onset scoliosis. 2024.
  6. The efficacy of bracing in the treatment of progressive early-onset scoliosis. Sci Rep. 2024;14:10213.

On the evaluation form — Q8: Excessive lateral spinal curvature in a 2-year-old

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 2-year-old child (sex not stated). Chief complaints: the parent noticed asymmetry — one shoulder higher or a rib hump — for 4 months. Birth history: full-term, breech delivery (breech associates with infantile idiopathic scoliosis, which is more common in boys and typically has a left thoracic curve). Development: walked at 13 months, now runs; bladder and bowel normal (screens for dysraphism). No pain — spinal pain in a toddler is a red flag. Vital signs and growth normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. With the nappy off: shoulder and pelvic level asymmetry, rib hump. The spinal skin is inspected for dimples, hair tufts, a fatty pad or naevi (occult dysraphism); a cavus foot would suggest a neuromuscular cause.

On palpation. Spinous process deviation.

1. Motor assessment. Spinal ROM observed during play; limb lengths equal; squat-to-stand, walking and running appropriate for age. The Babinski response may be physiological up to about 2 years; no clonus; abdominal reflexes symmetric (asymmetry suggests syringomyelia).

2. Sensory assessment. Withdrawal to touch symmetric in all four limbs. Any neurological abnormality means the curve is not idiopathic — refer for spinal MRI.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Play-based: rising from the floor, walking, running, squatting, stairs with hand-holding; milestones age-appropriate. Outcome measures: serial Cobb angle and scoliometer angle of trunk rotation are the standard measures; no validated self-report scale exists at this age, so parent-reported function is used.

4. Gait analysis. Play-based observation of walking and running; formal gait analysis is not applicable at 2 years.

5. Balance. Not formally testable at this age; balance is observed during play (walking, running, stairs with hand-holding).

6. Hand function. Age-appropriate play observed; formal hand-function testing not applicable at this age.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed; developmental milestones age-appropriate.

8. Investigations

AP spinal radiograph for the Cobb angle and Mehta RVAD is planned as part of the work-up; MRI is reserved for any neurological abnormality; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Adams forward-bend test with scoliometerChild bends forward; inclinometer placed over the rib prominenceAngle of trunk rotation at or above 5–7°Rotational scoliosis; refer for radiographs
Cobb angle measurementAP radiograph; angle between the most tilted end vertebrae10° or moreDefines and grades scoliosis; serial value tracks progression
Mehta rib-vertebral angle difference (RVAD)Measured on the AP radiograph of an infantile curveRVAD of 20° or moreHigh risk of progression in infantile scoliosis
Leg-length assessment with blocksMeasured blocks under the short limb until the pelvis levelsCurve disappears with levellingFunctional (leg-length) scoliosis, not structural
Dysraphism/developmental screenSkin inspection, abdominal reflexes, milestone review, spinal ultrasound in infancyCutaneous stigmata, reflex asymmetry, delayed milestonesNon-idiopathic cause — refer for MRI and paediatric opinion

In this child: Adams forward-bend test positive (rib hump present); limb lengths equal, so functional (leg-length) scoliosis is unlikely; Cobb angle and RVAD awaited (radiographs pending); dysraphism/developmental screen negative to date.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Lateral spinal curvature with rib rotation
  • Progression risk if the RVAD is raised

Functional limitations

  • None — milestones appropriate for age

Disabilities

  • Potential future cardiopulmonary restriction if a severe curve progresses
11. Functional diagnosis

Probable infantile idiopathic scoliosis in a 2-year-old (breech delivery, painless curve, normal neurological screen, age-appropriate milestones), with the risk of curve progression to be quantified by the Cobb angle and RVAD.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Complete the work-up (radiograph, RVAD, neurological screen); baseline Cobb angle documented; family educated.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks and beyond). Curve stable or resolving (no increase of 5° or more between radiographs); milestones maintained; skin intact under any cast or brace; surgery avoided if possible.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: observation — most infantile curves resolve spontaneously; radiographs every 4–6 months. Stage 2: for progressive curves, serial Mehta derotational casting under anaesthesia every 2–3 months, then a custom TLSO once the child stands reliably. Stage 3: surgery (growing rods or magnetically controlled growing rods) only for severe progressive deformity.

14. Home programme

Prone play, symmetric carrying, skin checks under any cast or brace; report new weakness, limp or bladder/bowel change.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Explain the pre- and post-operative assessment of fracture neck of femur.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5a — assessment of fractures: pre-operative and post-operative

★ Memory hook — Garden I–II fix, III–IV replace; pre-op = Function/cognition, Regional, Cardiorespiratory, Teaching; post-op = general, DVT, fixation-specific, measure.

1Introduction

Fracture neck of femur is the classic fragility fracture of the elderly, and the physiotherapist meets it on both sides of the operating theatre. This answer moves from the classification and medical picture through a structured pre-operative assessment and a post-operative assessment shaped by the surgical choice, to complications, outcome measures and discharge planning.

2Physiology

The femoral neck is a short, oblique strut that transmits body weight from the femoral head to the shaft at a neck–shaft angle of about 125–135 degrees, with the trabecular arcades of the proximal femur distributing load. Its blood supply is precarious: the medial circumflex femoral artery and its retinacular (lateral epiphyseal) branches run along the neck and supply most of the femoral head, so a displaced fracture can interrupt the supply and cause avascular necrosis. The hip's deep socket and strong capsule make it a weight-bearing joint whose function depends on abductor strength and pain-free rotation.

3Pathophysiology

Fracture neck of femur is the classic fragility fracture of an elderly woman after a trivial fall; in Indian practice, expect osteoporotic bone, comorbid diabetes or hypertension, and often a delay before admission from a village home. Classify with the Garden system: types I and II are undisplaced (valgus impacted or incomplete) and are usually treated by fixation — cancellous screws or a dynamic hip screw; types III and IV are displaced and typically treated by arthroplasty — hemiarthroplasty in the frail or cognitively impaired, total hip replacement in the active elderly — with cemented stems allowing immediate weight-bearing. The physiotherapist's pre-operative assessment is embedded in this medical picture: note the comorbidities, American Society of Anesthesiologists grade, frailty and nutritional status, medications (anticoagulants, steroids), and remember that this same fall may reflect a FRAX-level osteoporotic risk that will need addressing after the hip heals.

4Answer

Four clusters. Function and cognition: pre-injury mobility level (walking to the field? using a stick?), independence in activities of daily living, cognitive state — delirium risk predicts rehabilitation success more than the fracture pattern does. Regional examination: the injured hip held in shortening and external rotation, pain, skin integrity over the heel and sacrum (pressure ulcers begin in the first hours on the ward), bilateral hip range of motion and strength to serve as the patient's own baseline, peripheral pulses. Cardiorespiratory: chest expansion, breath sounds, baseline effort tolerance — elderly supine patients decondition within days. Pre-operative teaching — which is assessment turned therapeutic: deep-breathing and incentive spirometry, ankle pumps and circulation exercises, log-rolling technique, and rehearsing the first transfers, so the post-operative day is not the first teaching day.

Assess systematically on day one and document daily. General: vital signs, pain score, wound and dressing, drain if present, hydration, and a delirium check. DVT screen: daily calf circumference and tenderness — calf pain on dorsiflexion alone is unreliable, so examine for swelling, warmth and circumference difference, and remember pharmacological prophylaxis is the main protection. Regional by fixation: after internal fixation, weight-bearing is often restricted (touch or partial) until union is shown radiographically at about six to twelve weeks, and assessment focuses on protecting the fixation while maintaining mobility; after cemented arthroplasty, weight-bearing as tolerated usually begins day one, and assessment focuses on the dislocation precautions of a posterior approach — no hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation — while an anterolateral approach relaxes these. Then measure: hip range of motion, abductor and quadriceps strength, sitting and standing balance, and gait with the correct aid — frame first, then stick. Above all, re-assess daily, because a post-operative hip deteriorates fast when it is not looked at.

Fig 9 — Draw the timeline with four nodes and the two weight-bearing tracks (fixation versus arthroplasty) beneath it. Showing that the surgical choice changes your assessment is the mark-scoring insight of the figure.

Screen at every session for the five classical complications: deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (sudden dyspnoea is an emergency), wound infection, dislocation of an arthroplasty (shortened, internally rotated limb after an awkward movement), avascular necrosis and non-union after fixation (persistent groin pain with late failure to progress), and pressure ulcers plus chest infection from immobility — the last two are the physiotherapist's own preventable complications. Outcome measurement should be named and specific: the Harris Hip Score (100 points — 44 for pain, 47 for function, 4 for absence of deformity, 5 for range of motion) is the classic post-operative hip instrument, complemented by the timed up-and-go test and an activities-of-daily-living scale for the geriatric picture.

Phase the programme: bed mobility and breathing on day zero; sitting and transfers day one; standing and walking with a frame days two to three; progression to a stick and stairs within the first fortnight; then strengthening of abductors and quadriceps, balance re-education, and endurance. Discharge planning is assessment applied to the house: most Indian homes have floor-level toilets, squatting baths and possibly stairs — teach the patient and family accordingly, supply a raised toilet seat if needed, train a caregiver in safe handling, and arrange follow-up for osteoporosis management, because the fracture that predicts the next fracture is this one.

Examiner's tip: the question asks for both pre- AND post-operative assessment — students who rush the pre-operative half cap themselves at half marks. Pre-operative teaching is physiotherapy assessment with a therapeutic intent; say exactly that, and split your answer visibly fifty-fifty.

5Recent advances

  • Bökeler et al. (2024) — matched-pair study of 9,580 patients finding geriatrician-led multiprofessional rehabilitation after proximal femur fracture reduced 7-day mortality (2.89 versus 5.11 per cent) and improved early walking ability compared with standard orthogeriatric care.
  • Kimmel et al. (2016) — HIP4Hips randomised trial in the Medical Journal of Australia showing intensive acute physiotherapy (three sessions daily) after hip fracture was safe and shortened hospital length of stay by more than 10 days without increasing complications.
  • Sylliaas et al. (2011) — randomised controlled trial in Age and Ageing showing a three-month supervised progressive strength-training programme improved balance, mobility and activities of daily living in home-dwelling older hip fracture patients.
  • Fairhall et al. (2022) — updated Cochrane review concluding that mobility strategies after hip fracture — especially gait, balance and functional training — produce clinically meaningful gains in mobility and walking speed both in hospital and after discharge.
  • Dakhil et al. (2021) — pooled analysis of two Norwegian randomised trials showing comprehensive orthogeriatric care improves activities of daily living up to 12 months after hip fracture, with the effect strongest in home-dwelling patients.

6References

  1. Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL — Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures (ref 16): neck of femur management and rehabilitation.
  2. Maxey L, Magnusson JA — Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient (ref 13): post-operative hip protocols.
  3. Garden RS — J Bone Joint Surg Br, 1961: the classification of femoral neck fractures.
  4. Harris WH — J Bone Joint Surg Am, 1969: the hip rating score.
  5. Kanis JA et al. — Osteoporos Int: FRAX and fracture-risk context.
  6. Intensive multiprofessional rehabilitation is superior to standard orthogeriatric care in patients with proximal femur fractures: a matched-pair study of 9,580 patients. J Clin Med. 2024;13(21):6343.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Fracture neck of femur — pre- and post-operative

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 72-year-old woman; slipped in the bathroom; groin pain and unable to bear weight (pre-operative presentation). Risk screen: comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, ischaemic heart disease), anticoagulant use (inform the surgical team), last meal, bladder and bowel habits, pressure areas, cognition and delirium risk, previous falls, home layout and support. The Garden classification (I–IV) drives fixation versus arthroplasty; watch for dehydration and hypothermia.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Pre-op: limb shortening with external rotation and adduction; cannot lift the heel. Post-op: scar clean and dry; sacral and heel skin checked every session.

On palpation. Pre-op groin tenderness; post-op calf tenderness screened for DVT.

1. Motor assessment. Post-op ROM: after a posterior-approach arthroplasty avoid combined adduction–internal rotation and flexion beyond 90°; the fixation group follows the surgeon's protocol. MMT: hip abductors, extensors and quadriceps graded serially; limb length re-measured after arthroplasty. End-feel and reflexes not documented.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation over the foot and lateral leg (sciatic/peroneal territory) and ankle power; any new deficit is reported immediately. Dermatomes and myotomes screened accordingly.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Pre-op: bed mobility and spirometry teaching. Post-op: transfers, walker gait and stairs before discharge. Outcome measures: Oxford Hip Score (0–48), Harris Hip Score (0–100), TUG (seconds), Berg Balance Scale (0–56), NPRS (0–10).

4. Gait analysis. Post-op walker gait, weight-bearing per the plan — protected after screw/DHS fixation, as tolerated after cemented arthroplasty; stairs before discharge. Formal stance/swing, cadence and step/stride parameters not documented.

5. Balance. Berg Balance Scale recorded (0–56); balance retraining included in the plan.

6. Hand function. Grips the walking frame (assistive device); weaning off the frame is planned; reaching, grasping and releasing otherwise not documented.

7. Coordination. Not documented.

8. Investigations

Radiographs with the Garden classification (I–IV) of the femoral neck fracture guide fixation versus arthroplasty; no films reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Log roll testGentle passive internal rotation of the extended hipSharp groin pain, guardingIntracapsular hip pathology — NOF fracture
Axial heel percussionTap along the long axis of the leg through the heelGroin pain on the affected sideFemoral neck fracture
Patellar-pubic percussion (auscultatory) testStethoscope on the pubis, tap each patellaDuller note on the fractured sideOccult NOF fracture when radiographs are negative
True and apparent leg lengthASIS to medial malleolus (true); umbilicus to medial malleolus (apparent)Shortening on the affected sideDisplaced fracture pre-op; limb length after arthroplasty
Trendelenburg testSingle-leg stance on the operated sideContralateral pelvis dropsGluteus medius insufficiency post-operatively

In this patient: limb-length assessment positive pre-op (shortening with external rotation and adduction on the affected side); the individual results of the log roll, axial heel percussion, patellar-pubic percussion, Trendelenburg and Thomas tests were not separately documented (Trendelenburg is reassessed serially after surgery).

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Post-surgical pain
  • Hip abductor and quadriceps weakness
  • Precaution-limited ROM

Functional limitations

  • Transfers and ambulation with an aid

Disabilities

  • Temporary loss of independent living
11. Functional diagnosis

Status post fracture neck of femur (fixation or arthroplasty) in an elderly woman, with post-surgical pain, hip abductor and quadriceps weakness and precaution-limited range, dependent for transfers and walker-assisted ambulation, and a temporary loss of independent living.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks). Pain 3/10 or less on the NPRS; independent bed exercises, ankle pumps, breathing exercises and safe walker ambulation.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks). Ambulation with a stick or unaided; abductors 4–5/5 with a negative Trendelenburg; Berg and TUG at age-normal level; safe return home.

13. Treatment plan

Pre-op: chest care and incentive spirometry, ankle pumps, log rolling, pressure-area care, counselling. Post-op days 1–7: phased weight-bearing per fixation type; isometric quadriceps and hip abduction within precautions. Weeks 2–12: resisted strengthening, balance retraining, scar mobilisation, stairs, weaning off the frame. After a posterior-approach arthroplasty, dislocation precautions for 6–12 weeks: no low chairs or floor sitting, no crossing legs, no bending past 90°. Complications monitored: DVT, pressure ulcer, chest infection, dislocation, re-fall.

14. Home programme

Daily exercises, raised toilet seat, good lighting, loose rugs removed, osteoporosis follow-up and fall prevention.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Determine the use of ICF in musculoskeletal diagnosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6a — functional assessment and ICF

★ Memory hook — five boxes around the health condition: body functions and structures, activity, participation, environment, personal — every arrow bidirectional.

1Introduction

The ICF — the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, published in 2001 — is the framework that describes a health condition not only as pathology but as a lived experience. Its architecture is worth drawing: at the centre sits the health condition; around it, two components of functioning — body functions and structures (impairment at this level) and activity (limitation) — together with participation (restriction); and around everything, the contextual factors: environmental (products, people, attitudes, policies — barriers or facilitators) and personal (age, sex, coping style, occupation). Every arrow between these boxes is bidirectional, which is the whole point: disability is an interaction, not a property of the person, and the ICF replaced the older ICIDH's linear, consequence-based model with this dynamic one.

2Physiology

In health, functioning is the dynamic interaction between a person's body functions and structures, their capacity to carry out activities, their involvement in life situations, and the environmental and personal context. A person without a health condition performs the same tasks — walking, dressing, working, taking part in family and community life — without impairment, limitation or restriction, and the contextual factors act only as background.

3Pathophysiology

Apply it with one worked example and the abstract becomes marks. A 58-year-old farmer with knee osteoarthritis: at the level of body functions and structures — knee pain, crepitus, restricted flexion, quadriceps weakness (impairments). At the level of activity — limited walking distance, difficulty squatting, and — write the culturally specific ones, they earn marks — difficulty sitting cross-legged at meals, squatting over an Indian toilet, and climbing into a bus. At the level of participation — cannot plough his fields, cannot attend the temple festival or family functions, loses his role as breadwinner. Environmental factors: the house is on a hillock with steps (barrier), the village bus has high steps (barrier), a supportive joint family (facilitator), distance from a physiotherapy centre (barrier). Personal factors: 58 years, high pain tolerance, fear of surgery. Notice the diagnostic shift: the biomedical diagnosis says "knee osteoarthritis"; the ICF profile says what that disease does to this person's life — and physiotherapy is the profession whose whole value lies in that second statement.

Fig 10 — Draw the classic ICF box diagram with double-headed arrows in every direction and "knee osteoarthritis" in the centre. Writing the worked example into the boxes converts the diagram from decoration into the answer itself.

4Answer

To make the classification practical at the bedside, the WHO's ICF research branch developed comprehensive and brief ICF core sets — agreed short lists of the categories most relevant to a condition, so that two clinicians assess the same things. Core sets exist for several musculoskeletal problems, notably chronic low back pain and osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. Using a core set turns the ICF from theory into a checklist: the clinician rates each category (for instance, pain, joint mobility, walking, remunerative employment) with a qualifier from 0 (no problem) to 4 (complete problem), producing a functioning profile at first assessment and a re-testable measure of change thereafter.

Merits: it completes the diagnosis — the pathology plus what the pathology does; it creates a common professional language across orthopaedics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and social work; it justifies holistic intervention to funders and insurers; it is patient-centred because activity and participation are the patient's own goals; and it supports the legal and administrative documentation of disability, which in India matters for certification and benefits. Limitations: completeness costs time — a full ICF profile is heavy for a busy OPD; coding requires training; personal factors are deliberately not classified, so their use is inconsistent; and it does not name pathology — it grades the consequences of pathology, so the ICF supplements but never replaces the biomedical and movement-system diagnosis.

Conclude the way the verb "determine" invites: use the ICF as the second half of every musculoskeletal diagnosis. Pair the impairment diagnosis (subacromial pain syndrome, L5 radiculopathy, knee osteoarthritis) with an ICF profile of activity limitation and participation restriction, and let environmental and personal factors be assessed explicitly. Set SMART goals at the activity and participation level — "walk to the temple without a stick" beats "improve hip abduction by 10 degrees" as a goal a patient understands — and choose outcome measures that map to those levels. Re-assess with the same qualifiers, and the ICF becomes the audit trail of the entire treatment.

Examiner's tip: the commonest failure is describing the ICF in the abstract. One named patient with culturally grounded examples — cross-legged sitting, squat toilet, farming, a festival — used consistently through every component, takes this answer from definition-recall to distinction.

5Recent advances

  • Cieza et al. (2004) — consensus process establishing the Comprehensive and Brief ICF Core Sets for low back pain (78 and 35 categories), giving musculoskeletal practice a standardised biopsychosocial framework for assessment.
  • Hernández-Lázaro et al. (2023) — multicentre study in the Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine confirming the content validity of the ICF Core Set for post-acute musculoskeletal conditions in primary-care physiotherapy, with pain (b280) and joint mobility (b710) the most prevalent impairments.
  • Ponzano et al. (2025) — comprehensive ICF Core Set for vertebral fragility fracture (Disability and Rehabilitation), adding a biopsychosocial assessment framework for spinal fractures.
  • Mukaino et al. (2020) — operationalised the ICF Generic-30 and Rehabilitation Set into national rating tools with interrater-reliability studies, moving the framework from theory toward routine clinical scoring.
  • Schwarzkopf et al. (2008) — analysis of commonalities across the ICF Core Sets for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, low back pain and chronic widespread pain, identifying shared categories that allow a common musculoskeletal assessment language.

6References

  1. World Health Organization — International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), Geneva, 2001.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ — Physical Rehabilitation (ref 10): disablement frameworks and outcome measurement.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH — Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System (ref 1): linking impairment to mechanical limitation.
  4. Hernández-Lázaro H, et al. Multicentre cross-sectional study assessing content validity of the ICF core set for post-acute musculoskeletal conditions in primary care physiotherapy services. J Rehabil Med. 2023;55:jrm11950.
  5. An ICF comprehensive core set for vertebral fragility fracture. Disabil Rehabil. 2025;48(4):1046–1059.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper III

QP 8131 · 14-Nov-2025 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1The assessment ladder

  • Subjective → look → feel → move → special tests → synthesis; history alone gives about 80 per cent of the diagnosis.
  • Cyriax order: AROM, then PROM with end-feel, then resisted — separates contractile from inert tissue.
  • Inspection: compare sides; wasting, swelling, gait, posture before ever touching.

2Shoulder impingement

  • Neer stages I–III: under 25 oedema, 25–40 fibrosis, over 40 spurs and tears.
  • Neer and Hawkins: sensitivity about 0.8, specificity about 0.5 — screen, never confirm alone.
  • Painful arc 60–120°; persistent weakness or lag sign = think cuff tear.

3Lumbar disc herniation

  • SLR: sensitivity 0.91, specificity 0.26; crossed SLR: 0.28 and 0.90 — rule out versus rule in.
  • L4–L5 hits L5 root; L5–S1 hits S1; L5 has no reflex — use great-toe extension.
  • Conclude on a cluster: dermatomal leg pain + objective deficit + positive neurodynamic + centralisation.

4Autonomous practice

  • First-contact physiotherapy under direct access: you decide treat-or-refer, and you own the decision.
  • Novice = hypothetico-deductive; expert = pattern recognition; wisdom = knowing when to switch.
  • Red-flag screen on day one AND whenever the patient fails to improve as expected.

5Knee instability

  • Lachman 0.85 / 0.94 at 20–30°; pivot shift 0.24 / 0.98 — confirm, never screen; anterior drawer weak acutely.
  • Valgus at 30° = MCL; at 0° = cruciate involved too; posterior sag = PCL.
  • Grades: I pain only, II laxity with endpoint, III laxity without endpoint; acute haemarthrosis after a pivot = ACL.

6Exercise testing

  • Purpose: quantify impairment, set baseline, prove progress; PAR-Q+ and vitals first.
  • Stop criteria: BP drop, angina, RPE above 17, dizziness — memorise all four.
  • 6-minute walk for endurance; 6–10 RM to estimate 1 RM; H:Q ratio about 0.6.

7Spinal orthoses

  • Three-point pressure and extension moment explain Taylor, Jewett and TLSO at one stroke.
  • Halo = unstable cervical; Jewett / TLSO = stable thoracolumbar; Milwaukee = apex above T8.
  • Every brace named must carry one indication and one limitation; wean to prevent disuse.

8The two-year-old with a thoracic curve

  • Under three = infantile idiopathic; left thoracic curve in a boy; most resolve spontaneously.
  • Cobb 10° threshold; Mehta RVAD above 20° or rib phase 2 = progression risk.
  • Always: skin (café-au-lait, hairy patch), neurological exam, hips and leg lengths; congenital needs cardiac and renal screening.

9Fracture neck of femur

  • Garden I–II undisplaced → fixation; III–IV → arthroplasty; cemented stem = weight-bearing day one.
  • Posterior precautions: no flexion beyond 90°, no adduction past midline, no internal rotation.
  • Harris Hip Score: 44 pain + 47 function + 4 deformity + 5 motion = 100; watch DVT, dislocation, AVN, non-union, pressure sores.

10ICF in musculoskeletal diagnosis

  • Five boxes around the health condition: body functions and structures, activity, participation, environmental, personal — all arrows bidirectional.
  • Impairment / limitation / restriction is the vocabulary triplet examiners look for.
  • Indian worked examples: squatting, cross-legged sitting, floor-level toilet, festival participation, farm work.
keep-if-nothing-else: the ladder (look-feel-move-test-synthesize), Neer-Hawkins-painful arc, SLR 0.91/0.26 with crossed SLR 0.28/0.90, Lachman 0.85/0.94, Cobb 10 degrees and RVAD 20 degrees, Garden I–IV with the fifty-fifty pre/post split, and the five ICF boxes with one knee-osteoarthritis worked example — that is the minimum cargo for the exam hall.
