Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Discuss the interventions to improve the mobility of the shoulder joint following adhesive capsulitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 1 — Interventions for physiologic impairments: mobility

★ Memory hook — “Grade for pain, stretch for stiffness, sustain for range”: match the Maitland grade to the stage (I–II freezing, III–IV frozen, sustained IV thawing).

1Introduction

Adhesive capsulitis (“frozen shoulder”) is a painful, progressive loss of glenohumeral motion that can take one to three years to settle. Because the loss is driven by a contracted, fibrotic capsule rather than by muscle guarding, the interventions that restore mobility are those that progressively lengthen the capsule mechanically — and the stage of the disease decides how aggressively you may do so. This answer sets out the graded mobilization, stretching and self-management package and the logic that sequences them.

2Physiology

The glenohumeral joint is a ball-and-socket joint whose stability depends on a relatively loose, redundant capsule and the surrounding rotator cuff. The capsule is composed largely of type I collagen with a small amount of elastin, giving it extensibility rather than elasticity. Under sustained tensile load, collagen exhibits creep and, with repeated low-load stretch, permanent elongation by plastic deformation; raising tissue temperature a few degrees increases collagen extensibility and reduces its failure load. Normal capsular length permits roughly 90° external rotation, 180° flexion and abduction, and 70° internal rotation. The posterior and inferior capsule and the coracohumeral ligament are the structures that most limit external rotation and elevation — which is why they are the targets of mobilization.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanism first: what has actually stiffened?

Adhesive capsulitis is an idiopathic contracture of the glenohumeral joint capsule with a chronic inflammatory-fibrotic cascade — the capsule thickens, folds in, and loses its normal extensibility. The restriction follows the capsular pattern: external rotation is lost most, then abduction, then internal rotation. Screen for the common Indian associations — diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and postmenopausal women in their fifth and sixth decades — because they change prognosis and the pace of recovery. Clinically stage it: freezing (pain more than stiffness, about 0–3 months), frozen (stiffness more than pain, 3–9 months), thawing (slow spontaneous recovery, 9–24 months). The stage decides how aggressive you dare to be.

Fig 1 — Capsular pattern on the left, three stages on the right; the stage tells you how aggressively to mobilize.

4Answer

Graded joint mobilization — the spine of treatment

Use Maitland grades I–II oscillations purely for pain in the freezing stage, then move to grade III–IV stretching oscillations, and finally sustained grade IV glides in the directions of lost range — inferior glide for abduction, posterior glide for internal rotation and flexion, anterior glide for external rotation. Sustained glides of 20–30 seconds produce more creep in the contracted capsule than brief oscillations. Add Mulligan's mobilization-with-movement: a lateral glide of the humeral head combined with the patient's own elevation gives an immediate pain-free range gain that you then tape to hold.

Prolonged end-range stretching and PNF

Heat (hot pack or whirlpool) over the posterior capsule for 10 minutes before stretching makes the tissue more extensible. Follow with prolonged end-range stretches held 30–60 seconds: pendulum (Codman) exercises in the early painful stage, wall-climbing, overhead pulley, towel stretch for internal rotation behind the back, and finger-ladder for flexion. Add PNF hold-relax (contract-relax) of the internal rotators and adductors to exploit post-isometric relaxation before the final stretch. Each stretch should end-range the capsule, not just swing the arm.

Self-mobilization, home program and progression

Teach self-sustained inferior glide with a belt or towel while elevating, so the patient treats the capsule three times daily at home — the supervised session alone will never win this two-year disease. Progress by hold time, not by force: 30 seconds to 60 seconds, then add gentle weighted hangs in the thawing stage. Hydrotherapy in a warm pool is superb in India — the buoyancy and warmth allow pain-free end-range work.

Examiner's tip: name the stage and justify the force from it — forceful stretching in the freezing stage worsens pain and loses marks; the same force in thawing earns them.

5Recent advances

  • Rangan et al. (2020) — the UK FROST randomised trial in 503 patients found early structured physiotherapy with steroid injection, manipulation under anaesthesia and arthroscopic capsular release all improved shoulder scores substantially at 12 months, with no clearly superior treatment, supporting a stepped approach beginning with physiotherapy.
  • Wang et al. (2023) — a randomised controlled trial found neuromuscular exercise plus physical therapy superior to strengthening exercises for pain and active range of motion in idiopathic frozen shoulder.
  • Çelik & Kaya Mutlu (2016) — a randomised controlled trial found glenohumeral joint mobilisation added to a stretching programme produced significantly greater gains in external rotation, abduction and shoulder function than stretching exercises alone in frozen shoulder.
  • Page et al. (2014) — a Cochrane review of manual therapy and exercise for adhesive capsulitis found the combination safe and broadly comparable to glucocorticoid injection over the medium term, while calling for higher-quality trials to define the optimal protocol.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 10th ed.
  3. Wilk KE, Brotzman SB. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation.
  4. Rangan A, Brealey S, Keding A, et al. Management of adults with primary frozen shoulder in secondary care (UK FROST): a multicentre, pragmatic, three-arm, superiority randomised clinical trial. Lancet. 2020;396(10256):977–989.
  5. Mertens MG, Meert L, Struyf F, et al. Exercise therapy is effective for improvement in range of motion, function, and pain in patients with frozen shoulder: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2022;103(5):998–1012.

On the evaluation form — Q1: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)

I. Subjective examination

A 52-year-old female homemaker with an 8-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with four months of progressive right shoulder pain and stiffness. Chief complaints: she cannot hook her blouse, comb her hair or sleep on the affected side. Past medical history: type 2 diabetes of eight years' duration. Symptom analysis — site: right shoulder; onset: progressive, no trauma; duration: four months; type: dull ache, worst at night; severity: NPRS 6/10 at rest, 8/10 on movement; aggravating factors: shoulder movement and lying on the right side; relieving factors: not reported. Pain evaluation: night-dominant pain with a mechanical pattern on movement. Red-flag screen: no trauma and no radicular symptoms reported. Vital signs normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. The arm is held adducted and internally rotated; deltoid wasting with loss of the normal shoulder contour.

On palpation. Tenderness over the anterior capsule, the coracoid process and the deltoid insertion; no local warmth.

1. Motor assessment

Passive ROM follows the capsular pattern: external rotation most limited (20°), then abduction (80°), then internal rotation, all with a capsular end-feel. MMT 3+/5 through the available range. Biceps, triceps and brachioradialis reflexes normal. Deltoid girth 1.5 cm less than on the uninvolved side.

2. Sensory assessment

Sensation intact over the C4–T1 dermatomes; together with the normal reflex screen this excludes cervical radiculopathy and axillary nerve involvement.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Hand-behind-back and overhead reach markedly limited; dressing, grooming and side-sleeping affected; transfers independent. Outcome measures selected: SPADI (0–100, higher = worse), QuickDASH (0–100), NPRS (0–10) and goniometric passive ROM.

4. Gait analysis

Gait independent; transfers independent; no assistive device used.

5. Balance

Static and dynamic balance not documented in this case.

6. Hand function

Reaching overhead and taking the hand behind the back markedly limited; hooking the blouse and combing the hair are restricted by shoulder range rather than hand dexterity. No assistive device.

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Coracoid pain testFirm thumb pressure over the coracoid, sides comparedMarked pain on the affected sidePositive in this patient (matches the palpated coracoid tenderness) — anterior capsular inflammation
Passive ROM patternPassive glenohumeral external rotation, abduction, internal rotationGlobal restriction, external rotation worstPositive — confirms capsular restriction
Drop arm testArm passively abducted to 90°, then lowered slowlyUncontrolled descentResult not stated in the case record; a positive test would suggest rotator cuff tear
Spurling's testCervical extension, lateral flexion and axial compressionArm pain reproducedResult not stated; absence of radicular symptoms and a clear neurological screen argue against cervical referral, which would need re-examination if positive
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Pain (6/10 at rest, 8/10 on movement)
  • Capsular restriction of glenohumeral ROM in the capsular pattern
  • Weak shoulder musculature (3+/5) with deltoid wasting

Functional limitations

  • Dressing and grooming (hooking blouse, combing hair)
  • Side-sleeping on the affected side

Disabilities

  • Reduced household and social participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform overhead and hand-behind-back activities of daily living secondary to pain and capsular restriction of the right glenohumeral joint (adhesive capsulitis).

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): reduce night pain from 6/10 to 3/10; gain 15° passive external rotation; independent in home stretches.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain ≤2/10; functional ROM (external rotation 60°, abduction 150°); SPADI reduced by 30%; independent dressing and grooming.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1, painful (weeks 1–2): hot pack 15 minutes, pendulum exercises, grade I–II mobilizations, TENS; sleep supine with a pillow under the arm. Stage 2, stiff (weeks 3–6): sustained grade III–IV posterior and inferior glenohumeral mobilizations; passive external rotation, abduction and internal rotation stretches. Stage 3, functional (weeks 7–12): elastic-band strengthening 3 × 10, closed-chain weight-bearing, functional reaching; progress stretch range by 5–10° weekly as pain allows.

14. Home programme

Passive ER, abduction and IR stretches held 30 s × 5, twice daily; home pulleys, wall climbing, towel stretch behind the back and rod exercises, 10 repetitions thrice daily; continue into stage 3 with elastic-band strengthening and functional reaching; sleep supine with a pillow under the arm.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Explain the adjunct therapies in managing chronic heel pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 2 — Management of pain: adjuvant methods

★ Memory hook — “Load it, don’t rest it”: orthosis and tape to off-load, shockwave or needling for pain, high-load heel raises as the base.

1Introduction

Chronic heel pain lasting more than three months is usually plantar fasciopathy at the medial calcaneal tubercle. “Adjunct therapies” are the passive and semi-active measures applied alongside — never instead of — loading exercise: they reduce pain and improve tolerance so that the patient can do the loading that actually changes the tissue. This answer covers the biomechanical, electrotherapy, needling and exercise adjuncts and how to rank them.

2Physiology

The plantar fascia is a thick aponeurosis of longitudinally arranged collagen running from the medial calcaneal tubercle to the metatarsal heads and toes. It acts as a tie-rod that supports the medial longitudinal arch and stores and returns elastic energy during gait, tightening with toe extension in the windlass mechanism. Like other collagenous tissue, it adapts to load by remodelling — progressive tensile load stimulates fibroblast activity and matrix turnover — and it tolerates load poorly when load is suddenly increased without preparation. The heel fat pad provides the primary shock absorption under the calcaneus.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanism first: why does the heel stay painful for months?

Chronic heel pain (beyond 3 months) is most often plantar fasciopathy at the medial calcaneal tubercle, but the differential includes fat pad atrophy, calcaneal stress reaction, and Baxter's nerve entrapment — mention them and you separate yourself from the average script. Histology in chronic cases shows degenerative, mucoid change with fibroblast proliferation, not acute inflammation, so the word "fasciitis" is a misnomer for the chronic stage — treat it as a loading problem, not an inflammation problem.

4Answer

Biomechanical adjuncts

Off-load the origin of the fascia: soft heel cups or silicone heel pads for fat pad symptoms, prefabricated medial arch orthoses for the pronated foot, and firm-soled footwear — in India, flat chappals and hard bathroom tiles at home are common perpetuators worth asking about. Low-Dye taping supports the medial arch and gives immediate, measurable pain relief; if tape helps, an orthosis usually will. A night splint holding the ankle in about 5 degrees of dorsiflexion with toes dorsiflexed prevents the classic first-step morning pain by keeping the fascia lengthened overnight.

Electrotherapy and shockwave adjuncts

Therapeutic ultrasound (1 MHz, around 0.5–1.0 W/cm²) over the calcaneal insertion is the traditional Indian OPD choice; evidence is modest, so frame it as a pain-relieving adjunct during the loading phase. Iontophoresis with dexamethasone gives short-term relief superior to placebo in some trials. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy is the best-evidenced of the passive adjuncts for chronic plantar fasciopathy — three sessions, roughly 2000 impulses — and is worth committing for recalcitrant cases.

Dry needling and soft-tissue work

Trigger points in gastrocnemius-soleus and the plantar intrinsic muscles refer to the heel and maintain the pain; dry needling or ischemic compression of the gastroc-soleus complex plus stretching of the triceps surae reduces fascial strain at the calcaneal origin. This link between calf tightness and heel pain is a favourite viva question.

The base under the adjuncts: exercise and evidence

Adjuncts palliate; loading cures. Progressive eccentric loading — heel drops off a step — has been the standard, and Rathleff and colleagues showed that high-load strength training (weighted heel raises with a towel under the toes, every second day for 3 months) produced markedly better results than stretching alone at 3 and 12 months. Conclusion: correct footwear and taping to off-load, shockwave or dry needling for pain, and a progressive high-load strengthening program as the definitive base.

Fig 2 — Strength training is the base; taping, shockwave and needling sit on top of it, never instead of it.
Examiner's tip: spend two lines on differential diagnosis before jumping to treatment — fat pad atrophy is worsened by stretching and steroid injection, and missing it costs the answer its clinical realism.

5Recent advances

  • Koc et al. (2023) — the JOSPT clinical practice guideline (Heel Pain — Plantar Fasciitis, Revision 2023) recommends therapeutic exercise including resistance training for the foot and ankle musculature, and notes that plantar-fascia-specific stretching is superior to calf stretching alone.
  • Rathleff et al. (2015) — a randomised trial found high-load progressive heel-raise strength training (with a towel under the toes to engage the windlass mechanism) produced a significantly better foot function index than plantar-specific stretching at 3 months in plantar fasciitis.
  • Lippi et al. (2024) — a systematic review with meta-analysis found both focal and radial extracorporeal shock wave therapy reduce pain in plantar fasciopathy, with effect related to energy and number of impulses, and generally minor adverse effects.
  • Heide et al. (2024) — a four-arm randomised trial (n = 200, British Journal of Sports Medicine) found radial shockwave, sham shockwave and a high-load strength program each added no benefit over advice plus customised foot orthoses alone at 6 months, a caution against over-relying on any single adjunct.

6References

  1. Rathleff MS et al. High-load strength training versus stretching for chronic heel pain (BJSM / RSM series).
  2. Chui K et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  4. Martin RL, Davenport TE, Reischl SF, et al. Heel pain — plantar fasciitis: revision 2023. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2023;53(12):CPG1–CPG39.
  5. Riel H, Vicenzino B, Jensen MB, et al. Radial extracorporeal shock wave therapy, sham, or exercise for plantar fasciopathy: a four-arm randomised trial. Br J Sports Med. 2024;58(16):910–919.

On the evaluation form — Q2: Chronic heel pain (plantar fasciopathy)

I. Subjective examination

A 48-year-old male shopkeeper whose work involves standing 10–12 hours daily (BMI 29) presents with seven months of right heel pain. Chief complaint: classical first-step pain on waking and after sitting. Symptom analysis — site: right heel; onset: insidious; duration: seven months; type: sharp on first steps, dull by evening; severity: NPRS 7/10 on first steps; aggravating factors: first steps after rest, prolonged standing; relieving factors: not reported. Red-flag screen: no night pain and no numbness. Vital signs normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Pes planus with arch collapse on weight bearing and calcaneal valgus; type of gait: antalgic.

On palpation. Point tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle and over the proximal plantar fascia; tight gastrocnemius-soleus complex (increased deep tissue tension).

1. Motor assessment

Ankle dorsiflexion 5° with the knee extended. MMT: plantarflexors and invertors 4/5; hallux flexors 4/5. Functional strength: single-leg heel raises 8 (fewer than the expected 20). Achilles reflex intact. Girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment

Plantar sensation intact; tarsal tunnel Tinel's test negative — excludes tarsal tunnel syndrome, and with an intact Achilles reflex excludes S1 radiculopathy.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Standing tolerance 30 minutes; painful first steps limit occupational walking. Outcome measures selected: NPRS (0–10) for first-step pain, LEFS (0–80, higher = better) and the Foot Health Status Questionnaire (foot-specific quality of life).

4. Gait analysis

Antalgic gait with reduced push-off on the right.

5. Balance

Single-leg balance normal.

6. Hand function

Not relevant to this case.

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Windlass testGreat toe passively dorsiflexed, loading the fasciaHeel pain reproducedPositive in this patient — confirms plantar fasciopathy (consistent with medial calcaneal point tenderness)
Silfverskiöld testDorsiflexion with the knee extended, then flexedLimited only with the knee extendedPositive — isolated gastrocnemius tightness (consistent with the documented 5° dorsiflexion with knee extended)
Heel squeeze testCalcaneus compressed between the palmsFocal bony painResult not stated in the case record; a positive test would raise suspicion of calcaneal stress fracture
Navicular drop testNavicular height sitting versus standingDrop ≥10 mmFindings consistent with the observed arch collapse and calcaneal valgus — excessive pronation; numerical drop not recorded
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Insertional heel pain
  • Restricted ankle dorsiflexion
  • Weak foot intrinsics

Functional limitations

  • Painful first steps
  • Poor standing tolerance

Disabilities

  • Difficulty sustaining shop work
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to stand and walk for occupational demands secondary to insertional plantar-fascia pain with restricted ankle dorsiflexion.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): first-step pain from 7/10 to 4/10; gain 5° dorsiflexion; stand 60 minutes.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain ≤2/10 on morning steps; 15 heel raises; full shop duties; LEFS up ≥9 points.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): ice massage 5–10 minutes after work, contrast bath, ultrasound 1 MHz over the fascial origin, IFT for analgesia. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): plantar fascia stretch (ankle dorsiflexed, toes extended, 30 s × 3, thrice daily); eccentric heel drops off a step 3 × 15 daily; heel raises over a towel roll 3 × 8–12 on alternate days. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): towel curls, short-foot holds 10 s × 10, progressive loading, graded return to prolonged standing.

14. Home programme

Morning arch ball-rolling; night splint if morning pain persists; silicone heel cups; weight-management advice; continue the stretching and eccentric regimen above daily.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. How do you determine the methods to promote physical activity in musculoskeletal conditions?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3 — Functional training and physical activity promotion

★ Memory hook — determine the method with “A-M-P-M”: Assess activity and readiness, Match the behaviour-change method, Prescribe to WHO/FITT, Monitor weekly.

1Introduction

Musculoskeletal pain is one of the commonest reasons for physical inactivity, yet inactivity itself worsens pain, function and cardiometabolic risk — the very outcomes we treat. The question is not which exercise to give but how to determine, for a given person, the method that will actually raise their activity level. This answer sets out a four-step decision process.

2Physiology

Regular physical activity produces adaptation across every system relevant to musculoskeletal care: it improves aerobic capacity and mitochondrial function, increases muscle strength and mass, enhances tendon and bone load tolerance, raises endogenous opioid and endocannabinoid tone (an analgesic effect), and improves mood, sleep and self-efficacy. The WHO 2020 guidelines summarise the dose-response: 150–300 minutes of moderate (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous) aerobic activity per week, plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days, reduces all-cause mortality and improves pain and function in most musculoskeletal conditions; importantly, some activity is better than none.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanism first: why inactivity is the disease

In every musculoskeletal condition — osteoarthritis, low back pain, rheumatoid arthritis — pain triggers a downward spiral of avoidance, deconditioning, weight gain and more pain: the fear-avoidance cycle. Physical activity is therefore not a health footnote but the primary disease-modifying intervention. The question asks how you determine the method, so your answer must be a decision process, not a shopping list.

4Answer

Step 1 — assess the person, not just the joint

Quantify current activity (steps per day, minutes of moderate activity per week, a simple activity diary or IPAQ-short), then grade readiness to change using the transtheoretical model — precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance. Next, list the barriers honestly: pain and fear, fatigue, comorbidity, and the Indian realities — heat, traffic, unsafe walking roads, the belief that "rest is best" after joint pain, and women's household time constraints. The barrier profile selects the method.

Step 2 — prescribe against a standard

Anchor the target to the WHO activity guidelines (2020): 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week in bouts that can be as short as a few minutes, muscle-strengthening on two or more days, and for older adults, balance training on three or more days. Critically, WHO states that some activity is better than none — start where the person is. Build the FITT plan: frequency, intensity (Borg rating of perceived exertion 11–13, or the talk test — able to talk, not sing), time and type. Walking is the cheapest and most culturally acceptable aerobic mode in India; yoga doubles as flexibility and balance training.

Step 3 — match the behaviour change method to readiness

For someone in precontemplation, education about pain and deconditioning (not scare tactics) plus motivational interviewing — open questions, reflective listening, rolling with resistance — moves them to contemplation. In preparation, set SMART goals with the patient ("30-minute walk before work, five days a week") and write them down. In action, use graded activity, self-monitoring (pedometer or phone step counter), feedback and social support — walking groups, family involvement. In maintenance, plan for relapse: pain flares are setbacks, not failures.

Step 4 — monitor, progress, and conclude

Review every 2–4 weeks: recheck steps, symptoms (pain during and 24 hours after activity should settle to baseline), and confidence. Progress intensity and duration by roughly 10% per week when symptoms allow. Conclusion: the method is determined by assessing activity status and readiness, matching the behaviour-change technique to the stage, prescribing to the WHO standard with FITT, and monitoring — the therapist is a coach, not a machine operator.

Fig 3 — A four-step ladder: assess, match, prescribe, monitor. Drawing the ladder itself answers "how do you determine".
Examiner's tip: the verb in this question is "determine" — marks sit in the decision logic (readiness staging, barrier analysis), not in listing exercise types.

5Recent advances

  • Bull et al. (2020) — the WHO 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour recommend 150–300 minutes of moderate activity per week and muscle-strengthening twice weekly, dropped the 10-minute minimum bout rule, and stressed that some activity is better than none.
  • Rausch Osthoff et al. (2018) — the EULAR recommendations for physical activity in inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis found public-health physical-activity recommendations applicable and safe in these conditions, and that physical activity should be an integral part of standard care.
  • Rausch Osthoff et al. (2025) — the 2025 EULAR update emphasises reducing sedentary behaviour and breaking it up with short, frequent "exercise snacks", and recognises the role of technology for measurement and intervention.

6References

  1. WHO. Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 10th ed.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  4. Rausch Osthoff AK, Niedermann K, Braun J, et al. 2018 EULAR recommendations for physical activity in people with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis. Ann Rheum Dis. 2018;77(9):1251–1260.
  5. EULAR. 2025 update of the EULAR recommendations for physical activity in people with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis. Ann Rheum Dis. 2025.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. What alternative intervention would you suggest for lateral elbow pain, based on biomechanical concepts, for a patient who has already undergone conventional physiotherapy treatment?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 3 — Biomechanical concepts in rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — failed elbow: “L-G-N-T” — fix the Load path, Glide (Mulligan MWM), Nerve (radial slider), Tendon (Tyler twist).

1Introduction

Lateral elbow pain in a patient who has already had conventional physiotherapy is a diagnostic and biomechanical problem, not a modality problem. When ultrasound, massage, stretching and bracing have failed, the therapist must ask why the load keeps returning and whether the pain has a source outside the elbow. This answer offers biomechanically reasoned alternatives for such a resistant case.

2Physiology

The common extensor origin is a relatively hypovascular enthesis where the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) transmits high tensile loads during gripping and wrist extension. Tendon is built of parallel collagen fascicles with a small proteoglycan-rich matrix; it adapts to progressive load by increasing collagen cross-linking and fibril diameter, but repetitive submaximal load without adequate recovery produces the degenerative, non-inflammatory tendinopathy picture — disorganised collagen, increased ground substance and neovascularisation — rather than true inflammation. The radial nerve and its branches, and the cervical spine, share the lateral elbow’s sensory territory, so both can refer pain there.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanism first: why did conventional treatment fail?

Lateral epicondylalgia ("tennis elbow", and in India far more often a housewife's or mechanic's elbow from repetitive wringing and wrenching) is an overload tendinopathy of the extensor carpi radialis brevis at its origin. If ultrasound, friction massage, stretching and counterforce bracing have failed, three causes stand out: the load keeps coming back through faulty mechanics; cervical or radial nerve involvement is feeding the lateral elbow pain; and the tendon has never been properly strengthened. Your alternative intervention must attack these.

4Answer

Biomechanical analysis of the load path

Work along the kinetic chain: wrist position during grip (a flexed wrist during gripping spikes ECRB demand), grip size and tool handle diameter, technique in the patient's actual occupation or sport — racket grip and backhand mechanics, or in the kitchen, knife-sharpening and wet-clothes wringing. Correct the movement that loads the tendon, or every treatment below is temporary.

Mulligan mobilization-with-movement

A lateral glide of the ulna (or a squeeze of the forearm) applied while the patient makes a fist or grips pain-free gives an immediate increase in pain-free grip strength. Reapply for three sets of ten or more, then tape the forearm to sustain the glide — classically left on for two days without exercises (Mulligan). The immediate-on, immediate-off pain relief is the biomechanical signature that distinguishes MWM from passive modalities.

Neurodynamics — the missing link

Lateral elbow pain can be a cervical referral or a radial nerve sensitization that no amount of local elbow treatment will fix. Screen the cervical spine and conduct a neurodynamic test; if radial nerve bias tests are positive, treat with sliders (gentle alternating elbow extension with wrist flexion, keeping tension "on-off" without stretching the nerve) as described by Butler and Jones and Shacklock. This is the classic "alternative intervention" the examiner has in mind for a resistant case.

Re-load the tendon: Flexbar Tyler twist

Finish with eccentric training using the crooked Flexbar — the Tyler twist, performed with the unaffected arm assisting — which in a randomized trial beat standard eccentric wrist-extension exercise for pain and strength. Progress resistance over 4–6 weeks, then return the patient to sport or work with the corrected technique. Conclusion: resistant lateral elbow pain needs a biomechanical diagnosis — correct the load path, mobilize with movement, treat the nerve, then re-load the tendon.

Fig 4 — One elbow, four targets: load path, joint glide, nerve, tendon. Each gets one intervention in the answer.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "already undergone conventional physiotherapy" is the cue to look outside the elbow — cervical and radial nerve screening earns the discriminating marks.

5Recent advances

  • Bisset et al. (2006) — a randomised trial found physiotherapy combining Mulligan mobilisation with movement and exercise was superior to wait-and-see in the short term and to corticosteroid injection after six weeks in tennis elbow, with fewer recurrences than injection.
  • Coombes et al. (2013) — a placebo-controlled 2 × 2 factorial trial (JAMA, n = 165) found multimodal physiotherapy (elbow mobilisation with movement plus exercise) benefited lateral epicondylalgia in the short term, whereas corticosteroid injection gave poorer one-year outcomes and higher recurrence.
  • Coombes et al. (2016) — a trial in people with lateral epicondylalgia found isometric wrist-extensor exercise performed above the individual pain threshold reduced pain perception, supporting isometric loading as an analgesic adjunct to a graded programme.
  • Karanasios et al. (2021) — a systematic review and meta-analysis (30 trials, 2123 participants) found exercise, with or without other interventions, outperformed corticosteroid injection and passive treatments for pain and function in lateral elbow tendinopathy, though the effect size was small.

6References

  1. Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System.
  2. Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics.
  3. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient.
  4. Bateman M, Littlewood C, Rawson B, et al. Platelet-rich plasma or autologous blood do not reduce pain or improve function in patients with lateral epicondylitis: a randomized controlled trial. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 2020;478(8):1892–1900.
  5. Coombes BK, Bisset L, Vicenzino B. Management of lateral elbow tendinopathy: one size does not fit all. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2015;45(11):938–949.

On the evaluation form — Q4: Lateral elbow pain (lateral epicondylalgia)

I. Subjective examination

A 40-year-old right-dominant male machine operator and weekend cricketer presents with five months of right lateral elbow pain. Chief complaints: pain worse on gripping spanners and lifting a full bottle (coffee-cup sign); weak grasp. Onset: after intensified batting practice. Symptom analysis — site: right lateral elbow; onset: post-training, no acute trauma; duration: five months; severity: NPRS 6/10 with gripping; aggravating factors: gripping and lifting; relieving factors: not reported. Red-flag screen: no radicular symptoms. Vital signs not documented.

II. Objective examination

On observation. No swelling; the arm is carried slightly flexed.

On palpation. Tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and the common extensor origin (extensor carpi radialis brevis); cervical spine non-tender.

1. Motor assessment

Wrist and elbow ROM full. MMT: wrist extensors 4/5 with pain on resistance. Resisted grip isometrically painful; grip strength approximately one-third less than the left, worse with the elbow extended. Brachioradialis reflex normal. Girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment

Sensation intact in the radial territory, including the C6 dermatome; radial nerve non-tender on palpation.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Mobility normal; limitation is confined to gripping tools, turning keys and the batting grip. Outcome measures selected: NPRS (0–10) with gripping; PRTEE (0–100, higher = greater pain and disability); grip dynamometry in kg.

4. Gait analysis

Gait and mobility normal.

5. Balance

Not documented in this case.

6. Hand function

Reaching unaffected; grasping and releasing limited by painful grip — difficulty gripping spanners, turning keys, holding a full bottle and the batting grip. No assistive device.

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Cozen's testResisted wrist extension with the fist clenchedSharp pain at the epicondylePositive in this patient (matches pain on resisted wrist extension) — extensor carpi radialis brevis tendinopathy
Mill's testPassive forearm pronation, wrist flexion and elbow extensionPain over the epicondyleResult not stated in the case record; if positive, indicates common extensor origin involvement
Maudsley's testResisted middle-finger extensionLateral elbow painResult not stated in the case record; if positive, indicates extensor origin involvement
Chair lift testLifting a chair by the backrest with the forearm pronatedElbow pain on liftingResult not stated; if positive, provides functional confirmation
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Elbow pain on loading
  • Reduced grip strength
  • Reduced wrist extensor strength

Functional limitations

  • Tool use and lifting

Disabilities

  • Reduced work and sport participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to grip and lift secondary to lateral epicondylalgia of the right common extensor origin.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain with gripping from 6/10 to 3/10; grip strength up 10%; brace worn at work.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): pain ≤1/10 with daily gripping; grip within 10% of the left; PRTEE halved; full work and batting duties.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): isometric wrist extension held 45 s × 5, three to four times daily, pain kept ≤3/10; ice after work; padded gloves. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): eccentric wrist extensor training — lift the wrist up with the other hand and lower slowly over 3–4 s; 3 sets of 15 daily. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): concentric-eccentric and functional loading — wrist deviations, wrist curls, pronation-supination with a rod; return to batting.

14. Home programme

Daily isometrics or eccentrics as above; brace during gripping tasks; self-massage over the tender point twice daily.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. How do you distinguish and prioritize the various external application techniques for correction of forward neck posture?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV Unit 4 — External applications in musculoskeletal rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — “the more the device works, the less you use it”: exercise > kinesio cue > rigid tape > brace.

1Introduction

Forward head posture is extremely common in people who work at screens and phones, and “external applications” — tape and braces — are widely marketed for it. The examiner’s real question is how to tell these techniques apart by mechanism and how to rank them. This answer does exactly that.

2Physiology

The cervical spine supports a head of about 5 kg; the deep cervical flexors (longus capitis and colli) provide segmental stability, while the superficial extensors and upper trapezius maintain the head’s position against gravity. Muscle length and strength are use-dependent: sustained flexion and a protracted scapular posture inhibit and lengthen the deep flexors and lower scapular stabilizers while shortening the upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals and pectoralis minor (Janda’s upper crossed syndrome). Cutaneous and fascial mechanoreceptors, stimulated by tape or a brace, feed into cervical proprioception and can cue postural correction.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanism first: what is forward neck posture?

Forward head posture is part of upper crossed syndrome: deep neck flexors and lower scapular stabilizers become inhibited and elongated while upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals and pectoralis minor tighten. For every inch the head translates forward, the load on the cervical extensors multiplies, producing chronic upper back and neck ache, suboccipital headaches and rounded shoulders. External applications do not strengthen anything — they provide proprioceptive cueing, brief support, or correction of the scapular position while the exercise program does the real work.

4Answer

Distinguishing the techniques

Kinesiology taping is elastic (up to about 140% stretch) and works by proprioceptive input and light tissue lift, not by holding the head back. Apply an inhibition-facilitation pair: a vertical strip over the upper trapezius with light tension (10–15%) from insertion to origin, and facilitation strips over the deep cervical flexor region or a Y-strip along the thoracic spine. The patient feels a gentle "reminder" when the head drifts forward. Rigid (sports or zinc oxide) taping mechanically pulls the scapulae into retraction and holds the correction, but irritates skin within 3–4 days and cannot be worn in Indian heat and sweat through a full work week. Postural braces — figure-of-eight elastic supports with a thoracic strap — hold the shoulders back externally; they transfer the work to the garment, weaken the scapular muscles if overused, and are best reserved for short high-load exposure such as long two-wheeler commutes or a week of examination invigilation.

Prioritizing: a decision rule worth writing

Priority one is always the active program — deep neck flexor training (craniocervical flexion, 10 repetitions of 10-second holds), scapular retraction and thoracic extension — because posture is a habit of muscle, not of strap. Priority two is kinesiology tape as a wearable cue for 3–5 days at a time during retraining; it is comfortable in our climate, tolerates bathing, and reinforces the correction between sessions. Priority three is rigid taping for short, defined periods when stronger cueing is needed. Braces come last and only as a time-limited bridge, never as the treatment. Contraindications across all of them: skin allergy, loss of sensation over the taped area, and open wounds.

Evidence and conclusion

Studies of taping combined with exercise in forward head posture show better reduction of pain and neck disability than exercise alone in the short term, but tape without exercise does not hold its gain — exactly what the mechanism predicts. Conclusion: distinguish the techniques by mechanism (elastic cue versus rigid hold versus brace), and prioritize them in inverse proportion to how much work they do for the patient: the more the device works, the less the patient's muscles do.

Fig 5 — Priority ladder climbs from exercise at the base to brace at the top of the drawing's list — the device works more as you go up, and that is exactly why you use it less.
Examiner's tip: the phrase "distinguish AND prioritize" wants two things — a comparison of mechanisms, then an explicit order with justification. Scripts that only describe taping techniques score half.

5Recent advances

  • Alahmari et al. (2020) — a placebo-controlled randomised trial (n = 66) found Kinesio tape reduced cervical joint-position error and pain more than sham tape in mechanical neck pain at 3 and 7 days, with no difference in neck disability, supporting a proprioceptive-cue role.
  • Balthillaya et al. (2025) — a randomised trial from India (Manipal) found posture-correction taping in forward head posture with mechanical neck pain reduced pain and upper-trapezius EMG activity and increased serratus anterior and middle-trapezius activity immediately.
  • Augustsson et al. (2022) — a randomised controlled trial of a three-week Balance Body Tape postural-taping program found it reduced neck, shoulder and back pain intensity but did not change the craniovertebral angle, so it helped pain rather than posture.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  2. Chui K et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  3. OSHA. Computer Workstations eTool.
  4. Alahmari KA, Reddy RS, Silvian PS, et al. The effect of Kinesio taping on cervical proprioception in athletes with mechanical neck pain — a placebo-controlled trial. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2020;21:660.
  5. Balthillaya G M, Bhat SN, Shalini H, Rao BK. Immediate effects of posture correction taping on pain, cervical range of motion, and scapulothoracic muscle activity in individuals with forward head posture and mechanical neck pain: a randomized controlled trial. 2023.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Choosing external support techniques (taping and bracing)

I. Subjective examination

A 26-year-old recreational badminton player presents with a twelfth episode of right ankle giving way. Chief complaints: apprehension while landing and ache after play; pain 3/10. Symptom analysis — site: right ankle; onset: recurrent episodes; type: giving way with post-play ache; severity: NPRS 3/10. No locking and no instability at rest. No skin allergy present — essential to confirm before adhesive taping. Red-flag screen: none identified.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Swelling absent between episodes; mild forefoot abduction on squatting.

On palpation. Anterior talofibular tenderness only in the post-injury week; peroneal tendons and hindfoot alignment normal; distal pulses normal.

1. Motor assessment

Ankle ROM full. MMT: peroneals 4/5 with fatigue on repeated eversion. Single-leg heel raise and hop normal. Deep tendon reflexes normal. Girth equal.

2. Sensory assessment

Plantar and dorsal sensation intact.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Apprehension with hop-and-land activity; competitive participation modified. Outcome measures selected: PSFS (0–10 per activity), NPRS (0–10) and the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (ankle-instability severity).

4. Gait analysis

Gait not specifically documented in this case; single-leg hop is normal.

5. Balance

Single-leg balance stable with eyes open; unstable on a tilt board; hop-and-land apprehension (dynamic balance affected).

6. Hand function

Not relevant to this case (lower-limb condition).

7. Coordination

Not documented in this case.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

No ligamentous stress-test results are documented for this patient; the table below records how the external support techniques are selected.

TechniqueIndicationTypical condition
Rigid sports taping (stirrup, figure-of-six)Rigid end-of-range support for an eventAcute ankle sprain; return to play
Kinesio tapingProprioceptive cueing, oedema facilitationPatellofemoral pain; subacute swelling

11. Functional diagnosis

Recurrent right ankle giving way during sport secondary to chronic ligament laxity with poor peroneal endurance.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): independent application of tape or brace before play; 5 seconds of stable tilt-board balance on each side.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): full badminton without giving way; peroneals 5/5; PSFS mean ≥9/10.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): rigid taping during sport while proprioceptive retraining begins — single-leg balance, eyes open then closed, 5 minutes twice daily. Stage 2 (weeks 3–6): a lace-up brace when protection must last weeks; elastic-band eversion 3 × 12 daily plus heel raises. Stage 3 (weeks 7–12): taper support to high-risk matches as strength and balance normalize.
