Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Define probability and normal distribution.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3 — research methodology and biostatistics: probability and distributions

★ Memory hook — Probability lives between 0 and 1; the normal curve is fixed by just µ and σ — remember 68.27–95.44–99.73 per cent and Z = (X − µ) / σ.

1Introduction

Probability is a number between 0 and 1 (equivalently 0 to 100 per cent) that quantifies the chance that an event occurs; 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, and every real-world event lives strictly in between. Three definitions coexist, and a good answer separates them. Classical or a priori probability applies when outcomes are equally likely: probability equals favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes — the chance of a coin landing heads is one in two, with no experiment required. Empirical or frequentist probability is the limit of the relative frequency in a long series of trials: if 60 of our last 200 frozen-shoulder patients recovered full abduction within 12 weeks, our best estimate of that event is 0.3. Subjective probability is a degree of belief — the clinician's gut number before data arrive, honest enough to be labelled as such.

2Background and principles

Kolmogorov's axioms: probability of any event lies between 0 and 1; probability of the certain event (the whole sample space) is 1; and mutually exclusive events add. Hence the addition rule, probability of A or B equals probability of A plus probability of B minus probability of A and B; for independent events the multiplication rule, probability of A and B equals the product; and conditional probability, probability of A given B, which is the doorway to Bayes' theorem — how a test result should update our belief about the patient in front of us.

3Key concepts — the normal distribution

The normal (Gaussian) distribution is a continuous probability distribution for a variable that results from the sum of many small independent influences; its density curve is the symmetric, bell-shaped curve defined entirely by two parameters — the mean (µ), which fixes its centre, and the standard deviation (σ), which fixes its spread. Properties worth writing: it is unimodal and symmetric, so mean equals median equals mode; total area under the curve is 1, so areas are probabilities; the curve is asymptotic — the tails approach but never touch the axis; points of inflection lie one σ either side of the mean; and there is a family of curves, one for each µ-σ pair.

4Answer

For any normal distribution, roughly 68.27 per cent of values lie within one σ of the mean, 95.44 per cent within two σ, and 99.73 per cent within three σ. Converting any normal variable by Z equals X minus µ divided by σ maps it onto the standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, whose areas are tabulated — this one transformation lets us compare a patient's haemoglobin, a class's exam score and a study's sample mean on a single scale.

Normal distributions generate laboratory reference ranges (the central 95 per cent), underpin quality-control flagging of outlier results, and — most importantly — form the sampling distribution of the mean that the central limit theorem guarantees, which is the mathematical licence for the t-test and ANOVA. Conclusion: probability is the grammar, the normal curve is the commonest sentence, and parametric statistics is a conversation conducted almost entirely in that sentence.

Fig 5 — the bell curve with the three empirical bands shaded. Practise drawing this until the 68-95-99.7 labels are muscle memory; it is the most frequently sketched figure in biostatistics papers.
Examiner's tip: marks are lost in the definitions, not the picture — keep probability "between 0 and 1" and normal "defined by two parameters, µ and σ" stated crisply, then give one numeric example (a laboratory range) to prove you can use it, not just recite it.

5Recent advances

  • Wang et al. (2018) — provided US population-based hand-grip strength normative reference values, percentiles and regression equations (JOSPT), showing how age, height and weight define the expected normal distribution of a key physiotherapy outcome measure.
  • Enright & Sherrill (1998) — established the widely used reference equations and lower limit of normal for the six-minute walk distance (Am J Respir Crit Care Med), the classic clinical application of the normal distribution to interpreting walking capacity.
  • de Vet et al. (2006) — clarified the distinction between the minimal detectable change (based on the standard error of measurement) and the minimal important change (Health and Quality of Life Outcomes), showing how measurement error and the normal curve guide interpretation of change scores.

6References

  1. Indrayan A. Medical Biostatistics.
  2. Hulley SB, Cummings SR, Browner WS, et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  3. Wang CC, Lee WC. Evaluation of the Normality Assumption in Meta-Analyses. Am J Epidemiol 2020;189(3):235-242.
  4. US Food and Drug Administration. Guidance for the Use of Bayesian Statistics in Medical Device Clinical Trials. Silver Spring: FDA; 2018.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Instrumentation of NMES (neuromuscular electrical stimulation).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 5 — electrotherapy fundamentals: NMES instrumentation and application

★ Memory hook — NMES dose: 45 Hz · 300 µs · ramp 2 s · 10 s on : 50 s off · 12–15 contractions · 3×/week. One memorised full column beats ten knob names.

1Introduction

NMES is the use of a pulsed electrical current to evoke a visible muscle contraction through its motor nerve — as distinct from TENS, which aims at sensory nerves. The instrument, whatever the brand, is one chain: mains through a power supply (step-down transformer, rectification, smoothing) to an oscillator and master timer that set pulse rate and treatment time; a pulse-shaping circuit that fixes pulse duration and waveform; an output amplifier that delivers current at the set amplitude with a ramp generator shaping the rise time; and an isolation transformer separating the patient circuit from the mains, so no fault can pass wall power to the patient. Modern clinical units make the ramp an explicit knob because comfort, and therefore treatment tolerance, lives at the leading edge of the pulse train.

2Background and principles — controls and waveforms

Frequency: 30 to 50 Hz for tetanic strengthening contractions; lower rates suit sensory and endurance goals. Pulse duration: 200 to 400 µs to preferentially depolarise motor axons. Amplitude: raised slowly to a strong but tolerable contraction, and because units operate close to constant-current behaviour, the machine pushes the voltage needed to keep the programmed milliamperes flowing as skin impedance changes — which is why amplitude, not voltage, is the honest measure of dose. Waveform: charge-balanced biphasic rectangular pulses, so each cathodic phase is cancelled by an anodic one and no net direct current chemically burns the skin; classic Russian current is a 2.5 kHz carrier delivered in bursts at 50 per second. Rhythm: the duty cycle alternates contraction and rest (about 10 seconds on to 50 seconds off for strengthening) because stimulated muscle, recruited in reverse order, fatigues earlier than voluntary muscle.

3Patient circuit and electrodes

Self-adhesive hydrogel electrodes sized to the target muscle, the active electrode placed over the motor point for the strongest contraction at the least current; inter-electrode distance shapes the current path; skin must be clean and intact, and poor contact concentrates current density into a burn. Impedance varies with sweating, oedema and electrode age, which is why a session started at a comfortable amplitude in a sweating patient can drift uncomfortable within minutes — check back, do not set and walk away.

4Answer

Hardware safety: isolation of the patient circuit, current-limited output, charge balance, timer cutoff, and periodic calibration against a test load in the biomedical department. Patient safety: contraindications include demand pacemakers and implanted electronic devices, the abdomen during pregnancy, active malignancy in the region, deep vein thrombosis in the limb (risk of embolus), and over anesthetic or absent skin sensation. Never place electrodes so current crosses the heart, and never assume a ward machine is calibrated because its display lights up.

Worked setting for quadriceps strengthening after knee immobilisation: biphasic pulses, 300 µs, 45 Hz, ramp 2 seconds, 10 seconds on with 50 seconds off, 12 to 15 contractions, three sessions weekly for 4 to 6 weeks, amplitude to strong visible contraction — parameters documented in the record exactly like a drug prescription. Conclusion: the instrument exists to deliver a reproducible dose; the therapist who understands each block knows exactly which knob changes which physiological outcome, which is the whole point of studying instrumentation.

Fig 6 — the NMES chain with the dose box underneath. In the practical exam, drawing this and then stating one complete, defensible parameter set is the difference between knowing the machine and using it.
Examiner's tip: when asked instrumentation of NMES, candidates list knob names; examiners reward the map from knob to physiology — frequency to tetany, pulse duration to axon selectivity, duty cycle to fatigue protection. One sentence per knob.

5Recent advances

  • Happ & Behringer (2022) — meta-analysis (J Strength Cond Res) showing that at matched training volume NMES matches conventional strength training for strength development.
  • Alqurashi et al. (2023) — systematic review and meta-analysis (Age and Ageing) showing that NMES in hospitalised adults improves muscle size moderately and strength slightly, with only minor adverse effects.
  • Nakashima et al. (2023) — systematic review and meta-analysis (PLOS ONE) of NMES after thoracic and abdominal surgery found a slight increase in lower-limb strength without serious adverse events, though superficial burns can occur with incorrect settings.
  • Rathore (2026) — an Indian practice guideline (IJPOT) proposing standard calibration and quality-assurance criteria for electrotherapy devices aligned with IEC 60601.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA, et al. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  2. Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  3. Happ KA, Behringer M. Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation Training vs. Conventional Strength Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. J Strength Cond Res 2022;36(12):3527-3540.
  4. The effects of neuromuscular electrical stimulation on hospitalised adults: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Age Ageing 2023;52(12):afad236.
Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Testing of hypothesis (null and alternative hypotheses, type I and type II errors, p-value, steps, one-tailed and two-tailed tests).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 3 — research methodology and biostatistics: hypothesis testing

★ Memory hook — The p-value is the probability of data this extreme or more if the null is true — never the probability that the null is true.

1Introduction

A hypothesis is a testable statement about a population parameter; the null hypothesis asserts no difference or no association (the new mobilisation technique is no better than standard care) and the alternative hypothesis asserts that a difference or association exists. Because we can never prove anything with a sample, we try to reject the null. The ritual has five steps: state H0 and H1; choose the significance level α (conventionally 0.05); select the right test for the data type and design (paired t-test, independent t-test, chi-square, ANOVA); compute the test statistic and its p-value; and decide — reject H0 if the p-value is less than or equal to α, otherwise fail to reject it. Note the wording: we never "accept" H0, we only fail to reject it; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

2Background and principles — one-tailed versus two-tailed

A two-tailed test looks for a difference in either direction and splits α across both tails — use it unless a difference in one direction is meaningless or impossible. A one-tailed test places all of α in a single tail and is justified only when the alternative hypothesis was directional before the data were seen (our new protocol is claimed to reduce pain-score; nobody cares if it is better in only one direction). The ethics: choosing one tail after seeing the trend is not statistics, it is story-telling, and it inflates the apparent significance.

3Key concepts — errors, power and the decision

A type I error is rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true — a false positive, the "fooling yourself" error; its probability is α, the significance level we set. A type II error is failing to reject a null that is false — a false negative; its probability is β. Power equals 1 minus β, the chance of detecting a real difference, and is conventionally targeted at 80 per cent or more. The levers: increasing sample size and effect size raises power, and reducing measurement noise tightens it; α and β trade off against each other for a fixed sample size, which is exactly why the α of 0.05 is a social contract rather than a law of nature. Underpowered pilot studies reported as negative are the commonest type II error habitat in student theses — say this aloud in the viva and watch the examiner smile.

4Answer

The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Small p means "such data would be surprising if the null held," which is evidence against the null — nothing more. It is not the probability that the null is true, not the probability the result is due to chance in general, and p of 0.04 versus 0.06 is not a cliff edge. Report it with the confidence interval, which shows the size and uncertainty of the effect — the question the clinician actually needs answered.

Example: does six weeks of mobilisation plus exercise beat exercise alone for frozen shoulder? H0: no difference in SPADI change scores; H1: a difference exists (two-tailed); α 0.05; independent t-test on change scores; suppose p equals 0.03 with a mean difference of 9 points on the 0-100 scale — we reject H0, then immediately ask whether 9 points clears the minimal clinically important difference; if it does, statistical and clinical significance agree. Conclusion: hypothesis testing is a filter for chance, not a verdict on usefulness — the number that matters after the p-value is whether the patient can feel the difference.

Fig 7 — the decision table. Fill the four cells from memory: gold cells are errors (α and β), green cells are correct decisions; power lives in the bottom-left green cell.
Examiner's tip: the single most-rewarded sentence in this answer is the definition of p — "the probability of data this extreme or more if the null is true." Follow it with the misconception (p is not the probability that the null is true) and you have secured the discriminator marks.

5Recent advances

  • Elkins et al. (2022) — the International Society of Physiotherapy Journal Editors recommended moving physiotherapy research from null-hypothesis significance testing toward estimation with confidence intervals (Journal of Physiotherapy), directly reshaping how physiotherapy trials test hypotheses.
  • Kamper (2019) — JOSPT evidence-to-practice paper explaining how to interpret statistical significance alongside clinical meaningfulness when reading physiotherapy trials.
  • Christiansen et al. (2018) — benefit-harm trade-off study (J Clin Epidemiol) estimating the smallest worthwhile effect of primary care physiotherapy for musculoskeletal pain, informing the target difference and power of physiotherapy trials.
  • Hinman et al. (2024) — the PEAK non-inferiority randomised controlled trial (The Lancet) showed telerehabilitation was non-inferior to in-person physiotherapy for chronic knee pain, a landmark use of non-inferiority hypothesis testing in physiotherapy.

6References

  1. Indrayan A. Medical Biostatistics.
  2. Hulley SB, Cummings SR, Browner WS, et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  3. Amrhein V, Greenland S, McShane B. Retire statistical significance. Nature 2019;567:305-307.
  4. Wasserstein RL, Schirm AL, Lazar NA. Moving to a world beyond p < 0.05. Am Stat 2019;73(sup1):1-19.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Discuss the psychometric properties of SPADI (Shoulder Pain and Disability Index).

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 1 — standardized scales and psychometric properties

★ Memory hook — 13 items (5 pain + 8 disability) ÷ 130 × 100; quote the quartet together — Cronbach α 0.86–0.96, ICC 0.84–0.95, MCID ~8–13, MDC95 ~18.

1Introduction

A patient-reported outcome measure earns its place only if its measurements can be trusted — that is what psychometric properties mean. SPADI, developed by Roach and colleagues in 1991, is a self-administered, region-specific shoulder scale of 13 items in two subscales: five pain items (pain at its worst, lying on the involved side, reaching to a high shelf, touching the back of the neck, pushing with the involved arm) and eight disability items (washing hair, washing the back, pulling on a sweater, buttoning a shirt, putting on pants, placing an object on a high shelf, carrying a 10-pound object, removing something from the back pocket). Each item is scored on an 11-point numerical rating scale from 0 to 10; the total (out of 130) is expressed as a percentage, 0 meaning a perfect shoulder and 100 the worst imaginable — a design that suits busy Indian OPDs because it takes two to three minutes.

2Background and principles — reliability

Internal consistency is high: Cronbach's alpha has ranged from about 0.86 to 0.96 across studies, above the 0.7 floor and below the 0.95 zone where items merely repeat each other. Test-retest reliability is likewise high in later studies — intra-class correlation coefficients commonly between about 0.84 and 0.95 for the total score (the original 1991 development sample reported more modest values around 0.64). Measurement error must be quoted alongside: on the 0-100 scale, the minimal detectable change (MDC95) is about 18 points, so a repeated-measurement difference smaller than that is indistinguishable from noise.

3Validity and responsiveness

Construct validity: factor analysis supports the two-factor (pain and disability) structure, though some studies find a single dominant factor — worth one honest line in an exam answer. Convergent validity: SPADI correlates strongly with other upper-limb measures such as the DASH (correlations around 0.7 to 0.9 across validation studies) and moderately with pain ratings and generic measures like SF-36 physical scores, as expected for a region-specific tool. Criterion validity is the soft spot — there is no universally accepted gold standard for shoulder disability, so SPADI anchors itself against ROM and clinical change; in the original study it correlated negatively with shoulder range of motion, and it detects change in clinical status over short intervals.

SPADI is responsive in conditions from adhesive capsulitis to post-arthroplasty follow-up. The minimal clinically important difference — the smallest change a patient would actually notice — has been estimated at roughly 8 to 13 points on the 0-100 scale across studies (8, 10 and about 13 have all been reported), with values near the higher end after procedures such as arthroplasty. Read the numbers together: statistical significance decides whether the treatment beat noise; crossing the MCID decides whether the patient cares; and change below the MDC cannot be claimed as change at all.

4Answer

Cross-cultural adaptation matters in a multilingual country: validated Indian versions include the Hindi SPADI (translated per AAOS guidelines; in overhead athletes with impingement, internal consistency about 0.75, test-retest ICC about 0.87, convergent correlation 0.94 with Hindi DASH, MDC95 about 14), and a Tamil version validated in Hong Kong Physiotherapy Journal, 2012. Conclusion: SPADI is a short, reliable, valid and responsive shoulder-specific measure whose numbers are only interpretable through its psychometric properties — the same 9-point improvement can be noise in one context and a patient-felt success in another.

Fig 8 — SPADI at a glance: two subscales funnelling into a percentage score, with the psychometric quartet (alpha, ICC, MCID, MDC) boxed and quotable.
Examiner's tip: never quote a reliability number without naming its statistic, and never quote MCID without MDC — the pair shows you understand measurement error, and that distinction is precisely what this question is set to test.

5Recent advances

  • Salvatore et al. (2025) — defined the MCID, Patient Acceptable Symptom State and Substantial Clinical Benefit thresholds for SPADI after rotator-cuff repair (J Back Musculoskelet Rehabil).
  • Munir et al. (2022) — cross-cultural validation of the Urdu SPADI (BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders) reporting Cronbach's alpha 0.94 and test-retest ICC 0.89.
  • Porollan et al. (2024) — cross-cultural adaptation of the Argentine SPADI (JSES International) reporting reliability, validity, responsiveness and interpretability values.
  • Abdul-Karim et al. (2023) — validated the Malay SPADI (Malaysian Orthopaedic Journal), confirming construct validity, internal consistency, test-retest reliability and responsiveness.

6References

  1. Roach KE, Budiman-Mak E, Songsiridej N, Lertratanakul Y. Development of a shoulder pain and disability index. Arthritis Care Res 1991;4:143-9.
  2. Jeldi AJ, Aseer AL, Dhandapani AG, Roach KE. Cross-cultural adaptation, reliability and validity of an Indian (Tamil) version for the SPADI. Hong Kong Physiother J 2012;30:99-104.
  3. Sharma N, Sharma S, Kataria C. Translation and adaptation of SPADI into Hindi. Indian J Physiother Occup Ther 2011;5(4):142-5.
  4. Herbert RD, Jamtvedt G, Mead J, Hagen KB. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Bloom's Taxonomy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 6 — professional practice, pedagogy and entrepreneurship: Bloom's taxonomy and intended learning outcomes

★ Memory hook — 1956: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation. 2001: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create — crossed with factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive.

1Introduction

A taxonomy is a classification that orders things by complexity, and Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives (Bloom and colleagues, 1956) orders cognitive learning outcomes from simple recall to the highest forms of thinking. The original six levels, each requiring those below it: knowledge (recall facts — name the ulnar nerve roots), comprehension (explain in your own words), application (use the rule in a new patient), analysis (break a gait pattern into its deviations), synthesis (assemble a treatment plan), and evaluation (judge which plan is best, and defend the choice). Two claims matter for teaching: the hierarchy is cumulative — a student cannot analyze what they do not understand — and it pushes teachers to aim above the recall level where most exams quietly live.

2Background and principles — the revised taxonomy

The revision, led by Krathwohl and Anderson, renamed the levels as verbs and swapped the top two: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create — creation now sits at the apex. Its deeper change is that it is two-dimensional: the cognitive process dimension is crossed with a knowledge dimension of four types of content — factual (terminology, details), conceptual (classifications, principles), procedural (techniques, methods), and metacognitive (knowledge of one's own thinking, and of oneself as a learner). A learning outcome is therefore a cell in a grid: "design (create) a graded eccentric loading programme (procedural)" is a different cell from "list the contraindications (factual, remember)", and postgraduate physiotherapy training lives almost entirely in the right-hand, higher cells.

3The other two domains

Cognitive is only one of Bloom's three domains. The affective domain (Krathwohl's hierarchy: receiving, responding, valuing, organizing, characterizing) tracks how attitudes form — the student who first attends to patient counselling, then practises it, then values it, until professional empathy is character. The psychomotor domain (Simpson's and Harrow's versions: perception, set, guided response, mechanism, complex overt response) is where manual skills progress from clumsy imitation to automatic mastery — obviously the physiotherapist's home domain. A complete lesson plan touches all three: the student must know, must care, and must do.

4Answer

This is where the taxonomy earns its syllabus place. Intended learning outcomes should be written with observable verbs at the intended level: "list" and "define" sit at remember; "differentiate" at analyze; "construct" or "justify" at create and evaluate — while verbs like "know", "understand" and "appreciate" are unmarkable because nobody can observe them. Assessment must then align with the outcome (constructive alignment): an ILO promising analysis cannot be tested by a recall MCQ, and a viva that only asks "define TENS" has silently lowered the level of the whole course. Use the grid as a checklist when preparing a class: name the cell you are aiming at before writing the slide.

For clinical competence, Bloom's cognitive domain pairs naturally with Miller's pyramid of assessment: knows (the base, Bloom's remember), knows how (apply and analyze), shows how (psychomotor domain under observation) and does (performance in real practice). Conclusion: Bloom's taxonomy is the operating system of physiotherapy education — it decides what we ask in vivas, what our MCQs actually test, and whether we are training recallers of electrotherapy lists or clinicians who can create and defend a treatment decision.

Fig 9 — the revised pyramid (note the 2001 swap: create at the apex), flanked by the four knowledge dimensions and Miller's assessment ladder. One sketch covers the whole answer.
Examiner's tip: quote one physiotherapy-specific verb pair at each level (define SPADI at remember, justify the treatment plan at evaluate) — examiners marking a pedagogy paper reward the ability to use the taxonomy, not to recite its ladder.

5Recent advances

  • Zainuldin & Tan (2021) — developed the first set of core entrustable professional activities (EPAs) for an undergraduate physiotherapy programme (Physiotherapy), mapping Bloom-style competencies to the observable tasks students must perform unsupervised.
  • Ndacayisaba et al. (2026) — systematic review (Physiotherapy Theory and Practice) showing that simulation-, digital- and case-based learning most consistently build clinical reasoning in physiotherapy students and clinicians.
  • Hall et al. (2021) — proposed a taxonomy for shared language in competency-based medical education (Medical Teacher) that organises outcomes across focus, level and timeline.
  • Nakanishi & Nakanishi (2025) — applied the Revised Bloom's taxonomy table (knowledge and cognitive-process dimensions) to reorganise the 2022 model core curriculum in medical education.

6References

  1. Anderson LW, Krathwohl LH, et al. A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing: A Revision of Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives. New York: Longman; 2001.
  2. Bloom BS, et al. Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, Handbook I: The Cognitive Domain. New York: David McKay; 1956.
  3. Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Acad Med 1990;65:S63-7.
  4. Outcomes of competency-based medical education: a taxonomy for shared language. Med Teach 2021;43(7):794-800.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Describe the different methods used in strength training.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper I Unit 4 — exercise physiology and prescription: strength training methods

★ Memory hook — Four methods, one engine: isometric (angle-specific), isotonic (con/ecc), isokinetic (fixed velocity), plyometric (power) — all run on progressive overload + specificity.

1Introduction

Classify by what happens to muscle length and joint angle. In isometric training the muscle develops tension without changing length — the joint does not move; the strength gain is angle-specific (plus a small spill-over of roughly 10 to 20 degrees either side), so several angles must be trained. It is the method of choice when movement is prohibited or painful: post-operative limbs, painful arthritic joints, and in the classic setting of a patient in a cast — brief maximal holds, for example a six-second contraction repeated several times at multiple angles. In isotonic (dynamic) training the joint moves: the concentric phase shortens the muscle to lift, the eccentric phase lengthens it under load to lower. Eccentric loading produces greater force per unit of activation and better hypertrophy stimulus, at the price of delayed-onset muscle soreness — which is exactly why it is both the tool of choice in tendinopathy rehabilitation (heavy slow resistance, eccentric decline protocols) and something to grade carefully in the untrained.

2Background and principles — isokinetic and plyometric

Isokinetic training keeps limb velocity constant while the machine accommodates resistance moment to moment, so the muscle works maximally through the whole range — free weights are hardest only where leverage is worst. Computerised dynamometers (Cybex, Biodex) also quantify torque, making this the reference standard for strength testing as well as a training mode, across a spectrum of angular velocities. Plyometric training works the stretch-shortening cycle: a rapid eccentric pre-load stores elastic energy, and the immediate concentric recoil spends it — depth jumps, bounding, medicine-ball throws. It trains power rather than pure strength, demands a strength base and sound landing mechanics first, and belongs to late-stage athletic rehabilitation.

3Dosage and prescription principles

Every method is a vehicle; the dose is the engine. Intensity: a novice begins around 60 to 70 per cent of one repetition maximum, advanced lifters train at 80 per cent and above. Volume: about 8 to 12 repetitions per set for general strengthening (heavier loads, fewer repetitions for pure strength; lighter loads to muscular failure for hypertrophy), typically 2 to 4 sets per muscle group. Rest: 2 to 3 minutes between sets for strength work. Frequency: 2 to 3 sessions per week per muscle group, because the muscle grows between sessions, not during them. And every plan runs on progressive overload — small systematic increases in load, volume or frequency as adaptation allows — paired with the principle of specificity: you get precisely what you train.

4Answer

Variable-resistance equipment (cam-and-lever machines) varies resistance to match the natural strength curve through the range. Circuit resistance training strings stations together with short rests for combined strength and conditioning in limited time. Bodyweight and elastic-resistance training deliver progressive overload without a gym — the practical backbone of Indian home programmes. Periodisation structures training into phases (hypertrophy, strength, power, deload) so peak performance arrives at the right competition or season, and the same logic phases a rehabilitation programme from control, to capacity, to power.

Prescription is a matching exercise: post-operative knee — isometric quadriceps setting, progressing to eccentric work; anterior knee pain — closed-chain weight-bearing work; older adults — power training, because the ability to react quickly fades faster than strength and predicts falls; metabolic risk — the Misra JAPI 2009 consensus for Asian Indians explicitly prescribes muscle-strengthening activity on most days as part of daily physical activity, not an optional extra. Conclusion: there is no best method — there is a best match between method, stage of healing, and goal, held together by measurable dosage and progressive overload.

Fig 10 — the four-method grid with use-cases and one dosage line beneath. In a 10-mark answer this figure is the skeleton the paragraphs hang on.
Examiner's tip: whichever method you describe, end its paragraph with "so it is used when...". A method without a clinical indication is trivia; a method matched to a patient phase is prescription — and that is the difference the marks table is measuring.

5Recent advances

  • ACSM (2026) — Position Stand updating the 2009 guidance after synthesising 137 systematic reviews (more than 30,000 participants): strength favours loads of at least 80 per cent 1RM for 2-3 sets, hypertrophy favours at least 10 sets per week, and power favours 30-70 per cent 1RM.
  • ACSM (2026) — the same review found that non-traditional methods - elastic bands, bodyweight and home-based training - deliver marked gains, and that training to failure, equipment type and complex periodisation do not consistently affect outcomes.
  • Prudencio et al. (2023) — systematic review and meta-analysis (BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil) supporting eccentric loading, with eccentric and heavy-slow-resistance loading giving similar results, as first-line for lower-limb tendinopathy.
  • Breda et al. (2021) — randomised trial (Br J Sports Med) showing progressive tendon-loading exercise outperforms isolated eccentric exercise for patellar tendinopathy, refining loading-method selection.

6References

  1. McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA, et al. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  3. Misra A, Chowbey P, Makkar BM, et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. J Assoc Physicians India 2009;57:163-70.
  4. American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(4):851-872.
  5. McLeod JC, Currier BS, Lowisz CV, Phillips SM. The influence of resistance exercise training prescription variables on skeletal muscle mass, strength, and physical function in healthy adults: an umbrella review. J Sport Health Sci 2024;13(1):47-60.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper I

QP 8129 · 28-May-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1History taking

  • History generates hypotheses; objective exam tests them.
  • OPQRST: onset, provocation, quality, radiation, severity, timing.
  • Red flags: night pain, weight loss, fever, carcinoma, trauma, neuro deficit, bladder-bowel.
  • Record in ICF: body function, activity, participation, environment, personal.

2Instrumentation techniques

  • Chain: power supply to oscillator/timer to pulse shaper to output amplifier to isolation to patient.
  • Difference: therapeutic chain sends energy to patient; EMG chain takes signal away, differential amplifier with high CMRR cancels 50 Hz.
  • Needle EMG filter band roughly 10 Hz to 10 kHz; gain in µV per division.
  • Safety: macroshock vs microshock; applied parts B/BF about 100 µA, CF about 10 µA.

3MSK adaptations to training

  • Order: skill, then neural drive (weeks 2-8), then hypertrophy (8+), matrix last (months).
  • Type IIx shifts to IIa with any regular training.
  • Wolff's law: bone along lines of strain; cartilage eats cyclic compression.
  • Detraining unwinds fastest first: drive and capillaries within weeks.

4Muscle plasticity with ES

  • Stimulated recruitment: non-selective, spatially fixed, temporally synchronous — reversed size principle, fatigues fast.
  • Chronic 10-20 Hz for weeks transforms fast to slow (Salmons and Vrbova, 1969).
  • Dose: 30-50 Hz, 200-400 µs, ramped, 1:5 on-off; denervated muscle needs millisecond pulses.
  • Electrode over motor point: most contraction for least current.

5Probability and normal distribution

  • Probability 0 to 1; classical (equally likely), empirical (long-run frequency), subjective (belief).
  • Addition rule subtracts the overlap; independent events multiply.
  • Normal: µ and σ only; mean = median = mode; total area 1; asymptotic tails; inflection at µ ± 1σ.
  • 68.27 — 95.44 — 99.73 per cent within 1, 2, 3σ; Z = (X - µ)/σ.

6Instrumentation of NMES

  • Blocks: PSU, oscillator + timer, pulse shaper (µs, waveform), output amp (mA, ramp), isolation + current limit, electrodes at motor point.
  • Charge-balanced biphasic pulses prevent electrolytic burns.
  • Worked dose: 45 Hz, 300 µs, ramp 2 s, 10 s on : 50 s off, 12-15 contractions, 3 times weekly.
  • Contraindications: pacemaker, pregnancy over uterus, DVT, malignancy, insensate skin.

7Testing of hypothesis

  • Steps: state H0/H1, set α 0.05, choose test, compute, decide.
  • Type I = reject true H0 (α, false positive); Type II = keep false H0 (β, false negative); power = 1 - β, target 80 per cent.
  • P-value: probability of data this extreme or more if H0 true — never "probability H0 is true".
  • One-tailed only if the direction was declared in advance.

8SPADI psychometrics

  • 13 items: 5 pain + 8 disability, each 0-10; total ÷ 130 × 100 = 0-100.
  • Reliability: alpha 0.86-0.96; ICC 0.84-0.95.
  • MCID about 8-13 points; MDC95 about 18 points — change below MDC is noise.
  • Validated Indian versions: Hindi (2011) and Tamil (2012).

9Bloom's taxonomy

  • 1956: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation.
  • 2001: remember, understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, create (create on top).
  • Knowledge dimension: factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive.
  • Miller: knows, knows how, shows how, does; write ILOs with observable verbs.

10Strength training methods

  • Isometric (angle-specific, post-op), isotonic (concentric/eccentric, tendon rehab), isokinetic (fixed velocity, testing), plyometric (stretch-shortening, power).
  • Dose: 60-70% 1RM novice, 8-12 reps, 2-4 sets, rest 2-3 min, 2-3 days per week.
  • Principles: progressive overload + specificity.
  • Misra 2009: strengthening exercise is prescription for Asian Indian metabolic risk.
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall.
