10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Posterior knee pain
  • Posterior tibial laxity
  • Quadriceps weakness
  • Dynamic instability on stairs

Functional limitations:

  • Descending stairs, squatting and prolonged sitting

Disabilities:

  • Reduced driving and sport
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform stair descent, squatting and single-leg loading secondary to PCL insufficiency.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain reduced from 5/10 to 2/10; full pain-free extension; quadriceps isometric activation with electrical stimulation; independent crutch walking and home programme.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): quadriceps 5/5 with girth within 1 cm; controlled single-leg squat and step-down; KOOS and LEFS within 10 points of age norms; clinical stability 0–1+; return to driving and recreational sport.

13. Treatment plan

Acute (0–2 weeks): relative rest; extension brace for comfort in grade 2–3; cryotherapy; isometric quadriceps (avoid early isolated hamstring work — the hamstrings pull the tibia posteriorly); patellar mobilisations. Subacute (2–6 weeks): closed-chain strengthening — mini-squats 0–45°, step-ups, high-seat cycle, proprioceptive drills. Advanced (6–12 weeks): single-leg strengthening, plyometric and quadriceps-dominant sport drills, stair-descent retraining; reconstruction reserved for grade 3 or combined PCL–posterolateral corner injuries.

14. Home programme

Quad sets, straight-leg raises, heel slides, step-ups, single-leg balance; review 2-weekly.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Describe in detail the assessment following Symes amputation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5 — Amputations: assessment and prosthetic prescription

★ Memory hook — The five advantages: end bearing, long lever, self-suspension, near-normal energy, bare-stump standing.

1Introduction

What a Symes amputation is, and why it is loved

A Symes amputation is a disarticulation at the ankle joint with removal of the malleoli, the heel pad sutured over the end of the tibia to create a durable, end-bearing stump. Its advantages: virtually full end bearing (the heel pad is made for load), an intact long tibial lever arm with preserved knee and good muscle control, self-suspension from the bulbous distal end, a shorter but fully end-bearing limb (a leg-length discrepancy is expected), lower energy cost of walking than transtibial amputation, and — uniquely — the patient can hobble short distances on the bare stump (a real advantage for night bathroom use in Indian homes). Disadvantages to mention: the bulbous end is cosmetically bulky in a prosthesis, and heel pad migration can occur.

2Physiology

At the ankle the talus sits in the mortise formed by the tibia and fibula, and the heel pad — the thick fibrofatty tissue beneath the calcaneus — is specialised for load bearing and proprioception. An intact tibia provides a long lever arm, the knee remains intact, and the plantar skin tolerates direct pressure: the anatomical reasons a Symes stump works so well as an end-bearing limb.

3Pathophysiology

A Symes amputation is performed for trauma, infection or dysvascular and diabetic disease when the foot cannot be salvaged but the heel pad is viable. The pathological risks after surgery are heel-pad migration, skin breakdown and cysts on the end-bearing surface, and wound failure in dysvascular patients; in children, distal stump overgrowth can occur.

4Answer

Residual limb assessment

Assess in the examiner's order — look, feel, measure, move. Shape: the classical Symes stump is bulbous with a narrow shaft above; note any dog-ears or prominences that the socket must accommodate. Skin and heel pad: intact plantar skin, no breakdown or wart-like cysts on the end; check whether the pad is stable over the tibia or migrates on weight bearing (pinch and glide it distally). Scars: posterior heel-flap scar placement and maturity. Circulation and sensation: palpable pulses proximal and at the flap margins, protective sensation of the pad — critical for an end-bearing limb. Measurements: residual length from medial tibial plateau to end, circumference at defined levels, and comparison with the sound side; the bulbous diameter determines prosthetic design. Palpate the bony end for tenderness and heterotopic bone. Volume stability: oedema versus mature stump — sockets are prescribed on mature volume.

Proximal segment and whole patient

Because the knee is intact, the big wins are hip and quadriceps power, full knee range, and absence of hip flexion contracture; assess manually and functionally (sit-to-stand). Balance, upper limb strength for aids, cardiovascular endurance, vision, and the systemic disease that caused the amputation (diabetes control, Hansen's disease status) frame the prognosis. Document the pre-prosthetic stage: stump conditioning, shrinker socks, walking with crutches.

Fig 6 — Stump silhouette on the left with the three assessment boxes on the right; the look-feel-measure-move order is what examiners tick off.

Prosthetic considerations

The bulbous end must pass through a narrow shank, so socket designs manage this: posterior-opening or medial-window sockets (Canadian type), expandable-wall closed sockets, or bivalve designs. The socket gives total contact, distributes load between the end-bearing pad and the proximal tibia, and the bulbous flare provides suspension; a suprapatellar strap is added when the flare is insufficient. Because the space between stump end and floor is small, a thin SACH or solid-ankle cushioned foot is standard — few modern Symes prostheses use articulated ankles. Check in with the prosthetist's goals: end bearing, suspension during swing, rotation control, cosmesis (the unavoidable compromise).

Gait analysis

With the prosthesis: near-normal gait is expected because limb length is preserved and the knee is intact; look for shortened stance phase, reduced push-off, vaulting on the sound side, and early knee flexion issues. Check socket pistoning (pad migration or volume loss), pressure areas over the malleolar remnants, and stairs, slopes and floor sitting — cross-legged sitting and squatting matter to the Indian patient. Without the prosthesis: short-distance bare-stump walking is one of the level's unique advantages, assess skin tolerance for it.

Complications, outcomes and conclusion

Watch for heel pad migration, skin breakdown and cysts, stump overgrowth in children, and wound failure in dysvascular or diabetic patients. Reported outcomes are strong: roughly four in five adults walk with their prosthesis, energy cost is close to normal, and most need minimal therapy. Conclude: the assessment revolves around the end-bearing pad and the intact knee — protect the first and strengthen the second.

Examiner's tip: the five advantages — end bearing, long lever, self-suspension, near-normal energy, bare-stump standing — is a guaranteed marks list. Write it.

5Recent advances

  • Gailey et al. (2002) — The Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) was validated as a quick (under 15 minutes), highly reliable performance measure of ambulatory potential with or without a prosthesis, and now helps guide prosthetic prescription (K-levels) in Symes and other lower-limb amputations.
  • Morrison et al. (2020) — This survey of people with Symes amputation using the TAPES-R and LCI-5 found bare-stump walking depends on the floor environment and declines into adulthood, and that a moderate limb-length discrepancy was not functionally inferior to a very short residual limb.
  • Slater et al. (2023) — This within-participant study found high-profile "crossover" prosthetic feet increased prosthetic ankle range of motion and push-off power compared with traditional low-profile energy-storing feet in people with Symes amputation.

6References

  1. Maxey L, Magnusson M. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. Mosby.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 5th ed. FA Davis.
  3. Kanas JL, Stevens PM. Syme ankle disarticulation: prosthetic management. Atlas of Amputations and Limb Deficiencies. AAOS.
  4. Chui J et al. Syme amputation: a systematic review. Foot Ankle Int. 2018.
  5. Effects of high-profile crossover feet on gait biomechanics in 2 individuals with Syme amputation. Prosthet Orthot Int. 2023.
  6. Morrison SG, Thomson P, Lenze U, et al. Syme amputation: function, satisfaction, and prostheses. J Pediatr Orthop. 2020;40(6):e532-e536.

On the evaluation form — Q6: Assessment following Symes amputation

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 44-year-old farmer. Chief complaints: stump pain, walking only with crutches (no prosthesis yet) and difficulty sitting on the floor. History: right Symes amputation (ankle disarticulation with heel-pad preservation) 6 weeks ago after a farm-thresher crush injury; non-painful phantom toe sensations. Past medical history: type 2 diabetes, controlled. Symptom analysis: site — right stump (with phantom sensations in the toes); onset — since surgery 6 weeks ago; type — stump pain with non-painful phantom sensations; severity — stump pain 4/10 on the NPRS; aggravating and relieving factors not specified. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented; the sound foot is monitored for diabetic complications. Vital signs: stable.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Well-healed bulbous stump with a retained heel pad; healthy scar; mild distal oedema after dependency; sound left foot inspected for callosities and diabetic skin changes.

On palpation. Mild tenderness over the stump end; heel pad mobile and well centred over the tibial end (critical for end-bearing); scar mobility adequate; no neuroma nodule or warmth; calf bulk 1 cm less on the right.

1. Motor assessment. ROM: right knee and hip full and pain-free. MMT: knee extensors 4+/5, knee flexors 4+/5, hip flexors and abductors 4+/5 (disuse weakness); sound limb 5/5. Reflexes intact; no clonus. Serial stump girth measured from the tibial tuberosity; functional limb length recorded for prosthetic prescription.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch and pinprick over the stump (tibial and sural nerve territories); phantom sensation documented; Tinel's percussion for neuroma; the sound foot is screened with a 10 g monofilament and a 128 Hz tuning fork given the diabetes.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Ambulates with axillary crutches, non-weight-bearing; transfers independent; difficulty sitting on the floor; stairs with supervision. Outcome measures: NPRS (0–10) for stump and phantom pain; Patient-Specific Functional Scale (0–10); Locomotor Capabilities Index — an amputee-specific measure of basic and advanced walking ability; Timed Up and Go; serial stump girth for volume; 6-minute walk test for prosthetic endurance; post-fitting Timed Up and Go, 2-minute walk test, prosthetic gait observation and FIM (18–126) for overall independence.

4. Gait analysis. Axillary-crutch gait, non-weight-bearing; prosthetic gait observation planned after fitting.

5. Balance. Single-leg (sound-limb) stance 20 seconds; sound-limb balance training is part of the programme.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not formally assessed at this stage.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Heel-pad (end-bearing) assessment (heel pad mobile and well centred; only mild distal tenderness in this patient)Graded axial compression of the stump endPain or lateral shift of the padPoor end-bearing tolerance; defer or grade weight-bearing
Tinel's over the distal stump (no neuroma nodule palpated; percussion response not documented)Grid-pattern percussion over the stump endFocal sharp shooting tinglingNeuroma or nerve-ending irritation
Scar mobility (pinch-roll) (negative — scar mobility adequate)Lift and roll the skin over the scarTethered, painful skinAdherent scar needing mobilisation
Stump attitude check (no contracture documented; position monitored as a risk)Observe the stump position supine and standingFlexion–abduction contractureHip contracture risk; needs positioning and stretching
Prosthetic fit / socket tolerance (not applicable yet — no prosthesis fitted)Don the Symes prosthesis; stand and loadPistoning, distal pressure pain, persistent rednessSocket-fit problem for prosthetist review
Sound-foot monofilament test (screened; deficits not documented)10 g Semmes-Weinstein monofilament on plantar pointsInability to feel the filamentDiabetic neuropathy; ulcer and falls risk on the remaining foot
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Stump pain
  • Deconditioned hip and knee musculature
  • Phantom sensation
  • Risk of flexion–abduction contracture
  • Non-prosthetic status

Functional limitations:

  • Cannot walk bipedally or sit on the floor

Disabilities:

  • Unable to return to farm work
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to ambulate and perform standing occupational activities secondary to Symes amputation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): stump pain reduced to 1–2/10; full pain-free hip and knee ROM with contracture-prevention stretching; stump conditioning begun; independent crutch gait indoors.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): full-time prosthetic use; gait without aids on level ground; hip and knee strength 5/5; continuous 500 m walk; return to modified farm duties.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (pre-prosthetic): stump conditioning and desensitisation (tapping, towel rubbing), shrinker sock, prone lying and hip extensor stretching, progressive resisted strengthening, sound-limb balance, scar massage, crutch gait, phantom-limb education. Stage 2 (prosthetic training): temporary then definitive prosthesis; progressive weight-bearing; gait re-education from parallel bars to level surfaces, stairs, donning/doffing and skin hygiene. Stage 3 (community/vocational): uneven-ground mobility, energy conservation for farm work, foot-care education for the sound limb given the diabetes.

14. Home programme

Daily stump washing and inspection, shrinker wear, strengthening and desensitisation.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe the role of demographic data and history taking in assessment.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 1 — Introduction to assessment: demographic data and history

★ Memory hook — Every variable must rule something in or out: 80% of the diagnosis is reached before you touch the patient.

1Introduction

Demographic data and history taking are the first and most powerful steps of the physiotherapy assessment. Demographics (age, sex, occupation, dominance, residence, socioeconomic status, habits and family structure) are not administrative trivia — each item shifts the probability of pathology before a single test is performed. History taking then develops the patient's story into a set of testable hypotheses.

Together they are the "diagnosis before the examination": a well-taken history shortens the physical examination, avoids unnecessary investigations and is the single cheapest diagnostic instrument available to the therapist. In a long-essay answer the marks are earned by showing what each datum rules in or out, not by listing items.

2Physiology

History taking is the "physiology" of clinical reasoning: it is the input that generates the hypotheses the examination will test. A good history works like a filter — demographic and historical data narrow a large list of possibilities to two or three, and each subsequent examination manoeuvre either confirms or refutes one of them.

The process has a defined structure: the patient's own words for the main complaint and its duration; then each symptom dissected along the standard ladder — onset (sudden or gradual, trauma), character and distribution, aggravating and relieving factors, timing and diurnal pattern, associated features (stiffness, swelling, paraesthesia) and response to treatment so far. Pain is analysed by site, character, severity on a VAS, radiation, temporal pattern and behaviour with posture and activity.

The temporal pattern is a diagnostic shortcut: inflammatory pain is worse at rest and in the second half of the night, with morning stiffness lasting over an hour; mechanical pain worsens with load and eases with rest. Eliciting this history is what makes the later tests meaningful.

3Pathophysiology

When history taking is skipped or shallow, the reasoning process fails. The most serious consequence is a missed red flag: unexplained weight loss, night pain unrelieved by position, fever, loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological deficit, a history of carcinoma, or trauma in the osteoporotic or anticoagulated patient. A positive red flag changes the whole plan — stop, document, refer.

In the Indian context, chronic low back pain with evening fever, night sweats and weight loss must raise spinal tuberculosis (still a common spine pathology in India); a middle-aged smoker with unremitting night pain needs malignancy excluded. Relying on demographic stereotypes, or accepting the patient's own diagnosis, produces anchoring and premature closure.

4Answer

Demographic data — the diagnosis before the examination:

  • Age shifts probability — osteochondritis in the young, osteoarthritis after fifty, osteoporotic fracture in the postmenopausal woman, tendon degeneration in mid-life.
  • Sex modifies it again — osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia are commoner in women; ankylosing spondylitis in young men.
  • Occupation predicts the tissue — a farmer's knee, a tailor's shoulder, a software engineer's neck, a construction worker's low back with a flexion-loading history.
  • Hand dominance localises the symptomatic limb and sets functional expectations.
  • Residence and socioeconomic status shape diagnosis (brucellosis and spinal tuberculosis in endemic areas) and the plan (travel distance, ability to attend, home help).

History of present illness: main complaint in the patient's words and its duration; each symptom dissected along onset, character, distribution, aggravating/relieving factors, timing, associated features and treatment so far. Red-flag screen is performed inside the history (see above).

Past, drug, family and social history: past medical history (diabetes, tuberculosis, malignancy, previous surgery) and past physiotherapy with its result; drugs (steroids and osteoporosis, anticoagulants and bleeding risk, analgesic dependence); family history (rheumatological disease, ankylosing spondylitis, haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell in central India); social and occupational history (workload, posture, sports, and even sleep surface — a thin cotton mattress on the floor versus a hard cot changes spine advice).

Documentation and the link to reasoning. The history is where shared goals are set — ask what the patient expects and what function must be recovered (fetching water, sitting cross-legged for meals, riding a scooter). Record in a standard format (SOAP or the departmental assessment sheet) so that the data steer hypothesis testing: the history chooses the tests, the tests confirm or reject, and both set the treatment.

Examiner's tip: do not merely list "age, sex, occupation" — state what each one rules in or out. Value, not vocabulary.

Conclusion

Demographic data and history taking convert the patient's story into a ranked list of hypotheses and a red-flag screen, guiding every later test; used actively rather than recorded passively, they are the most efficient diagnostic tool in physiotherapy.

5Recent advances

  • Hill et al. (2011) — This Lancet randomised trial showed that stratifying primary care low back pain management using the 9-item STarT Back prognostic screening tool (built from history and psychosocial items) improved disability outcomes and was cost-effective compared with usual best practice.
  • Finucane et al. (2020) — The International Framework for Red Flags for potential serious spinal pathologies moved red-flag practice from single-sign screening towards weighing combined clinical patterns and urgency.
  • Maselli et al. (2022) — This systematic review confirmed that single red flags have low diagnostic accuracy, while combining multiple flags improves detection of serious pathology in thoracolumbar pain.
  • Shultz et al. (2015) — This systematic review of history-taking items found no single subjective question reliably identifies low-back-related leg pain, but clustering key history items sharpens the clinical picture.
  • Paling (2021) — This professional-issue paper stressed that red flags are notoriously unreliable and advocated safety-netting, guidelines and referral pathways to manage clinical risk.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function: A Comprehensive Analysis. FA Davis.
  3. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
  4. Finucane LM, Downie A, Mercer C, et al. International framework for red flags for potential serious spinal pathologies. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2020;50(7):350-372.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe various outcome measures used for knee pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6 — Functional assessment, outcome scales and ICF

★ Memory hook — WOMAC 24 (high = bad), KOOS 42 (high = good), Lysholm 8, Kujala 13 — the score direction is the mark most candidates lose.

1Introduction

An outcome measure converts the patient's knee into a number that can be tracked across visits and reported to surgeons, insurers and researchers. Because knee pain spans impairment, activity and participation, a defensible evaluation combines a self-report scale with objective impairment measures.

A usable instrument needs reliability (same score on repeat testing), validity (measures what it claims), responsiveness (detects real change) and interpretability — the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), which for KOOS subscales is roughly 8–10 points. Each tool is mapped to the ICF: impairment-level measures such as VAS, activity-level measures such as WOMAC and KOOS, and participation-level measures such as the Tegner activity scale. That single sentence ties this answer to the Paper III Unit 6 framework.

2Physiology

Normal knee function is a modified-hinge movement of the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints, stabilised by the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, the medial and lateral collaterals and the capsule, and driven by the quadriceps and hamstrings. Normal values are 0° of extension to about 135° of flexion, a pain-free, symmetric gait, and knee-extensor strength within about 10% of the opposite side.

Knee function spans the levels of the ICF — impairment (pain, stiffness, weakness, reduced range), activity limitation (walking, stairs, squatting, rising from a chair) and participation restriction (sport, work) — so a good outcome measure captures one or more of these levels and lets change be tracked objectively across visits.

3Pathophysiology

Different knee pathologies demand different instruments. Osteoarthritis and post-arthroplasty care are dominated by pain and function; ligament and sports injuries by instability, sport and quality of life; patellofemoral pain by anterior-knee and squatting symptoms; and inflammatory arthritis by systemic disease activity alongside joint function.

Mechanistically, OA is a whole-joint disease with cartilage loss, subchondral sclerosis, synovitis and arthrogenic muscle inhibition; ligament rupture produces laxity, giving-way and altered joint mechanics; and patellofemoral pain reflects maltracking and load intolerance. Because the clinical picture differs, the choice of scale follows the pathology — the selection logic that the answer must demonstrate.

4Answer

WOMAC — the osteoarthritis classic

The Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index: 24 items in three domains — pain (5 items), stiffness (2 items) and physical function (17 items) — scored 0-100 where higher means worse. Validated in knee osteoarthritis, available in translated Indian-language versions, responsive to change. Its limits: no sport or quality-of-life domain, ceiling effects in younger or higher-function patients, and poor performance in patellofemoral problems.

KOOS — the expanded successor

The Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score: 42 items across five subscales — symptoms, pain, activities of daily living, function in sport and recreation, and knee-related quality of life — each scored 0-100 where higher means better (note the reversal from WOMAC; examiners love this trap). It captures the young athletic patient where WOMAC ceilings out, making it the preferred measure after ACL reconstruction and for sports injuries.

Lysholm score and the Tegner activity scale

The Lysholm knee scoring scale, originally for ligament injuries and later broadened, is a knee-specific 8-item questionnaire — limp, support, locking, instability, pain, swelling, stair climbing, squatting — scored 0-100, higher is better. It is short, so it suits busy Indian OPDs, but it has a ceiling in high-functioning athletes. It pairs with the Tegner activity level scale, which grades current and pre-injury activity from 0 (sick leave, desk work) to 10 (competitive sports at national level): together they answer two different questions — how the knee feels and what the patient can do.

Fig 8 — Item counts on one bar chart with the scoring-direction note beneath; that note is the mark most candidates lose.

Kujala score — the patellofemoral tool

The Kujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale: 13 items covering limp, walking, stairs, squatting, running, jumping, prolonged sitting, pain and swelling, all weighted to patellofemoral complaints, scored 0-100 with higher being better. It is the instrument of choice for patellofemoral pain and patellar instability studies.

Generic anchors and the complete toolkit

The Visual Analogue Scale (0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable) or its numeric cousin is the universal impairment measure — quick, repeatable, but one-dimensional. The Knee Society Score (Insall, 1989) combines a knee score (pain, range, stability, alignment — clinician-rated) with a functional score (walking, stairs), originally built for total knee arthroplasty follow-up. Selection logic closes the answer: osteoarthritis or post-arthroplasty means WOMAC or KSS; sports injury or young active knee means KOOS with Lysholm-Tegner; patellofemoral pain means Kujala; and every patient gets a pain scale plus objective measures (goniometry, manual muscle testing, timed walk or stair tests) — because patient-reported and performance-based numbers together tell the whole story.

Examiner's tip: score direction and item counts are the discriminating marks: WOMAC 24, KOOS 42, Lysholm 8, Kujala 13 — and opposite directions of "better".

Selection summary:

ConditionPreferred measure(s)
Knee osteoarthritis / post-arthroplastyWOMAC, Knee Society Score
Sports injury / young active knee (ACL, meniscus)KOOS with Lysholm + Tegner
Patellofemoral pain / instabilityKujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale
Every patientPain scale (VAS/NRS) + objective measures (goniometry, MMT, timed walk or stair test)

Patient-reported and performance-based numbers together tell the whole story; report baseline → discharge change against the MCID of the chosen scale.

Conclusion

Outcome measurement for knee pain should match the instrument to the pathology and the ICF level — WOMAC/KSS for arthritis and arthroplasty, KOOS with Lysholm–Tegner for sports injury, Kujala for patellofemoral pain, and a pain scale plus objective tests for everyone — so that change is measured, not assumed.

5Recent advances

  • Gandek et al. (2019) — This study developed and validated KOOS-12, a 12-item short form cutting respondent burden by 70% while preserving pain, function and quality-of-life domain scores and a summary knee-impact score.
  • Baré et al. (2021) — This multicentre study found KOOS-12 shows no ceiling effect, good construct validity and responsiveness after total knee arthroplasty, where the full-length KOOS and KOOS-JR did show ceiling effects.
  • Roos (2023) — This 30-year review of the KOOS documented the KOOS-12 and established minimal-important-difference and patient-acceptable symptom-state thresholds (KOOS-12 MID about 14–16 points at six months after knee arthroplasty).
  • Quintana et al. (2024) — This factor-analytic study found the original KOOS did not meet structural-validity criteria and proposed a refined 12-item structure as a more psychometrically sound instrument.
  • Lyman et al. (2019) — Culturally adapted versions (for example the JKOOS+) now add floor-based activities such as squatting and using a squat toilet, relevant to Asian populations.

6References

  1. Bellamy N et al. Validation study of WOMAC. J Rheumatol. 1988.
  2. Roos EM et al. KOOS — Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther / JBJS. 1998.
  3. Lysholm J, Gillquist J. Evaluation of knee ligament surgery results. Am J Sports Med. 1982.
  4. Tegner Y, Lysholm J. Rating systems in the evaluation of knee ligament injuries. Clin Orthop. 1985.
  5. Kujala UM et al. Scoring of patellofemoral disorders. Arthroscopy. 1993.
  6. Insall JN et al. Rationale of the Knee Society clinical rating system. Clin Orthop. 1989.
  7. Roos EM, Lohmander LS. 30 years with the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Osteoarthritis Cartilage. 2023.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe screening of the ankle following ankle subluxation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2 — Screening: lower quadrant (ankle and foot)

★ Memory hook — Inversion failure order: ATFL first, CFL second, PTFL last — drawer tests the ATFL, talar tilt the CFL, and never forget the pulses.

1Introduction

An ankle subluxation is a momentary partial dislocation of the talus in the mortise, usually during an inversion episode, that signals failure of the lateral ligament complex. Screening after such an episode asks which ligaments are torn, what else is injured, and whether the dynamic stabilisers can compensate.

2Physiology

The lateral ankle is stabilised by three ligaments — the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL) — supported by the peroneal muscles and the proprioceptive system. The ATFL is the weakest and is tested by the anterior drawer; the CFL crosses both the tibiotalar and subtalar joints and is tested by talar tilt.

3Pathophysiology

Anatomy and mechanism: what a subluxation tells you

An ankle subluxation — a momentary partial dislocation, almost always the talus shifting under the tibiofibular mortise during an inversion or eversion episode — means the restraining ligaments failed: the anterior talofibular ligament (weakest, fails first in inversion), the calcaneofibular ligament (next, crosses both the tibiotalar and subtalar joints), and the posterior talofibular ligament (last). Repeated subluxation equals chronic instability, so screening asks three questions: which ligaments are loose, what else is injured, and can the dynamic stabilisers compensate.

4Answer

History and observation

Mechanism (inversion-plantarflexion for lateral), previous episodes — the single strongest predictor of chronic instability — inability to bear weight, swelling and bruising pattern, and functional giving way on uneven ground or stairs. Observe swelling, ecchymosis over the lateral ligaments, hindfoot alignment, arch posture, and gait (antalgic, avoidant push-off). Palpate systematically: distal fibula, ATFL and CFL course, base of the fifth metatarsal (avulsion), anterior syndesmosis, deltoid, and the proximal fibula — a Maisonneuve pattern referred up the leg.

Anterior drawer test — the ATFL test

Patient sitting with leg hanging, ankle relaxed in about 10 to 20 degrees of plantarflexion; the examiner stabilises the tibia with one hand and grips the calcaneus with the other, drawing the hindfoot forward while the talus is distracted from the mortise. Excessive anterior translation with a soft end-feel compared with the other side indicates ATFL insufficiency. Best after five to seven days, once acute spasm has settled; a side-to-side difference of about 3 mm or more on stress imaging is the laboratory counterpart, and manual grading is subjective — hence always compare with the uninjured ankle.

Fig 9 — Lateral ligament map with the two stress-test arrows; knowing ATFL fails first and CFL second turns a drawing into marks.

Talar tilt (inversion stress) test

Stabilise the tibia and calcaneus together, then invert (adduct) the talus in the mortise — a comparison test for the CFL and subtalar restraint. Increased tilt with a soft end-feel against the other side indicates lateral ligament laxity; pure talar tilt also loads the subtalar joint, so attribute carefully. Both tests can be done with an arthrometer or stress ultrasound/radiographs for objectivity when surgery is contemplated.

Clearing the rest of the ring

After a subluxation the examiner must clear the neighbours: the squeeze test (compress the calf mid-shaft; pain distally at the syndesmosis is positive) and external rotation test (dorsiflex the ankle and externally rotate — syndesmotic pain) rule out a high sprain; deltoid palpation and eversion stress rule out the medial side; the Ottawa ankle rules guide radiography (malleolar or midfoot bone tenderness plus inability to bear four steps); the Thompson test clears the Achilles; and the neurovascular check (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial pulse, sensation) is mandatory after any subluxation episode.

Functional screening and conclusion

Test what the instability actually steals: single-leg balance with eyes open and closed, the Star Excursion Balance Test, hopping and figure-of-eight running, stair descent. Quantify with the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool or FAAM for outcome tracking. Conclude the screening by grading: mechanical laxity (positive stress tests) plus functional instability (positive balance and giving-way) with muscle weakness means a structured proprioceptive-peroneal rehabilitation programme; bony avulsion, syndesmotic injury or neurovascular deficit means immediate referral. That closing sentence is what a 10-mark answer is judged by.

Examiner's tip: "compare with the other ankle" after each stress test, and never forget the pulses — the viva question hiding at the end of this paper.

5Recent advances

  • Delahunt et al. (2019) — The International Ankle Consortium ROAST consensus defined a structured, equipment-free clinical assessment of acute lateral ankle sprain (mechanism, bony and ligamentous integrity, swelling, range, strength, balance, gait) to identify impairments that lead to chronic instability.
  • Vasconcelos et al. (2018) — This meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials found proprioceptive/balance training reduced the incidence of ankle sprains by 38% and improved dynamic neuromuscular control (Star Excursion Balance Test) in athletes.
  • Jiang et al. (2022) — This meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials found balance training significantly improves dynamic postural stability (Star Excursion Balance Test) in people with chronic ankle instability.
  • Mollà-Casanova et al. (2021) — This meta-analysis found balance training significantly improves function, instability and dynamic balance in chronic ankle instability, outperforming strength training for the functional outcome.
  • Tang et al. (2023) — This systematic review found elastic orthoses, kinesiotaping and textured insoles can improve postural stability in chronic ankle instability, although evidence for semi-rigid braces and arch-support insoles remains mixed.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  2. Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott.
  4. Jiang C, Huang D, Li X, et al. Effects of balance training on dynamic postural stability in patients with chronic ankle instability: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2022;62(12):1707-1715.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Recurrent ankle instability / subluxation

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 21-year-old female college basketball player. Chief complaints: repeated giving way of the right ankle on uneven ground with the joint slipping out and back; persistent lateral swelling; apprehension on landing and cutting; walks with slight antalgia on uneven ground. History: three right-sided inversion sprains in 14 months, the latest 3 weeks ago. No other past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history is given. Symptom analysis: site — anterolateral aspect of the right ankle; onset — after the initial sprain 14 months ago, recurrent since; duration — current episode 3 weeks; type — sharp pain; severity — 3/10 on the NPRS; aggravating factors — uneven surfaces, jumping and flat unsupportive chappals; relieving factor — taping. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented. Vital signs: normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Mild anterolateral swelling with resolving ecchymosis; slight pes planus with dynamic valgus on single-leg stance; the patient watches her foot during stance (visual dependency of chronic instability).

On palpation. Tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament, milder over the calcaneofibular ligament; the fifth metatarsal base, syndesmosis and medial structures are non-tender; no effusion or crepitus.

1. Motor assessment. AROM full, with pain at end-range inversion; dorsiflexion 5–10° less than on the left side. PROM: increased inversion laxity. MMT: peroneals 4/5 (the key finding in chronic instability); other muscles 5/5. Resisted isometrics painful for eversion. Ankle jerk intact; calf girth 1 cm less on the right.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch and pinprick intact in the L4–S1 dermatomes, including the peroneal territories; ankle position sense commonly impaired after repeated sprains; eyes-closed single-leg stance reduced on the right — the proprioceptive deficit central to functional instability.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Running, cutting, jumping and landing are limited; single-leg hop is limited by apprehension; the LEFS documents the overall activity limitation. Outcome measures: Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool — a condition-specific questionnaire for chronic ankle instability; Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) with ADL and sport subscales; NPRS (0–10); LEFS (0–80); Patient-Specific Functional Scale (0–10); single-leg stance time and Star Excursion Balance Test as performance measures.

4. Gait analysis. Slight antalgia on uneven ground; dynamic valgus on stair descent.

5. Balance. Eyes-open single-leg stance normal; eyes-closed single-leg stance clearly reduced; Star Excursion Balance Test reach reduced posteromedially and anteriorly.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately tested; the proprioceptive and balance deficits above are the relevant coordination-related findings.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Anterior drawer test (result not documented)Ankle relaxed in about 20° plantarflexion; stabilise the tibia, translate the talus anteriorlyExcessive anterior translation or soft end-feelAnterior talofibular ligament laxity
Talar tilt (inversion stress) test (positive — increased inversion laxity on PROM in this patient)Ankle neutral; stabilise the leg, invert the hindfootExcessive inversion laxity versus the sound sideCalcaneofibular ligament laxity / subluxation
Squeeze test (negative — syndesmosis non-tender)Compress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calfPain over the syndesmosisSyndesmotic (high ankle) injury
External rotation (Kleiger) test (negative — no syndesmotic or medial joint pain)Stabilise the leg, externally rotate the foot with the knee at 90°Syndesmotic or medial joint painSyndesmosis injury, possible deltoid involvement
Thompson / Simmonds test (result not documented)Prone; squeeze the calfNo plantarflexionAchilles rupture (exclude in ankle trauma)
Cotton test (result not documented)Anteroposterior drawer with the ankle in neutralIncreased translation with a mushy end-feelGeneralised talar instability
Single-leg balance, eyes closed (positive — clearly reduced on the right)Timed unilateral stance, eyes closedReduced time or increased sway versus the leftProprioceptive deficit of functional instability
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Anterolateral ligament laxity with recurrent subluxation
  • Peroneal weakness
  • Impaired proprioception and balance
  • Dorsiflexion tightness

Functional limitations:

  • Running, cutting, jumping and landing

Disabilities:

  • Reduced basketball and college outdoor participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform running, cutting and single-leg stability tasks secondary to chronic ankle instability.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain reduced from 3/10 to 1/10; swelling controlled; peroneal isometric activation; eyes-closed single-leg balance progressing toward 30 seconds.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): peroneal strength 5/5; Star Excursion Balance Test within 5–10% of the left side; confident hop, side-hop and cutting; full return to basketball with preventive bracing.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): relative rest; balance retraining from single-leg stance to eyes-closed and foam surfaces; peroneal isometrics; taping. Stage 2 (weeks 2–4): elastic-band peroneal strengthening, wobble-board balance, calf stretching, reactive peroneal drills, hopping in place. Stage 3 (weeks 4–8): plyometrics, agility ladder, cutting and landing mechanics, uneven-surface training, sport reintegration with a semi-rigid orthosis. Stage 4 (weeks 8–12): full return with a twice-weekly prevention programme and footwear advice (supportive shoes rather than loose sandals).

14. Home programme

Band eversion, single-leg balance progressions, heel raises off a step; surgery is considered only after failed 3–6-month rehabilitation.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Write in detail about clinical reasoning in manual therapy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4 — PT diagnosis, special tests and red flags; Unit 3 — decision making

★ Memory hook — Hypothesis → test → treat → re-assess: reasoning is a cycle, not a list, with the red-flag gate at the top.

1Introduction

What clinical reasoning is

Clinical reasoning is the thinking process that converts patient data into decisions — diagnosis, prognosis and intervention. Modern understanding is dual-process: System 1 is fast, automatic pattern recognition born of experience; System 2 is slow, deliberate, analytic hypothesis testing. The novice must live in System 2 deliberately; the expert runs System 1 and audits it with System 2 when the pattern does not fit. In manual therapy, reasoning decides not only which technique, but whether manual therapy belongs in the plan at all.

2Physiology

Hypothesis-oriented examination

The Jones model structures the examination around hypotheses generated from the very first history sentence. From the referral, demographics and opening complaint the clinician frames candidate hypotheses across categories: the pain source (pathology, tissue), movement impairment, contributing factors (biomechanical, psychosocial), precautions and contraindications, prognosis, and management. Each question and each test then deliberately seeks information that confirms or rejects a hypothesis, and the therapist reweights with every finding. In manual therapy this shows as: does the movement reproduce the pain (a concordant sign), does repeated movement centralise or abolish it, which direction of mobilisation changes it immediately. Hypothesis orientation is what separates an examination from a checklist.

3Pathophysiology

Red flags and the reasoning to refer

Before any mobilisation, reasoning screens for red flags: unexplained weight loss and night pain, fever, history of malignancy, sphincter disturbance or saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological deficit, trauma in the osteoporotic, anticoagulated or pregnant patient, upper cervical ligament laxity (RA), and vascular claudication. Manual therapy is contraindicated or requires modification in osteoporosis, acute fracture, inflammatory flare, hypermobility and vertebrobasilar insufficiency for cervical techniques. The clinician's reasoning must distinguish nociceptive mechanical pain from systemic or visceral mimicry — in the Indian clinic, spinal tuberculosis and malignancy present late, so vigilance is high.

4Answer

Schools of thought and their reasoning fingerprints

The Maitland concept (Australian) is hypothesis-driven, movement-based, with Maitland's famous dictum that the therapist needs a hypothesis only until the next piece of data arrives; grades I-IV of oscillation are chosen by irritability and stiffness versus pain. The McKenzie method (mechanical diagnosis and therapy) classifies by directional preference — derangement responds to repeated movements in one plane, dysfunction to end-range loading, postural syndrome to education. The Kaltenborn-Evjenth/OMPT tradition reasons by arthrokinematics and grades of translation to restore roll-glide. Paris's reasoning emphasises segmental dysfunction and soft-tissue signs. The modern synthesis (Jones and Rivett) makes reasoning itself explicit: narrative, diagnostic, procedural, interactive, collaborative and predictive reasoning streams run in parallel during one consultation.

Fig 10 — The reasoning cycle with the red-flag gate at the top; the loop from re-assessment back to cues is the sentence that earns full marks.

Re-assessment: the manual therapist's stethoscope

Immediate re-assessment after a treatment trial is the core manual-therapy reasoning skill: the pre-post comparison of the concordant sign — pain on movement, range, or the patient's functional task. Improvement validates the hypothesis and the technique; no change rejects it and redirects the reasoning. Sustained reassessment over visits separates real progress from short-term analgesic effects, and treatment-based classification systems (for example, the Pittsburgh low-back classification) formalise this logic into subgroups: mobilisation responders, specific-exercise responders, centralisation, control-dysfunction groups.

Expert versus novice, and the honest conclusion

Experts reason by organised patterns, tolerate uncertainty, self-monitor for bias, and change course early; novices gather indiscriminately and anchor on first impressions. Clinical reasoning in manual therapy, concluded properly, is not the decoration of technique selection — it is the safety system that decides who should be mobilised, who should be exercised, and who should be sent to a surgeon today.

Examiner's tip: name Jones, Maitland, McKenzie and Kaltenborn in one paragraph with one reasoning idea each, then close with "immediate re-assessment validates every hypothesis". That paragraph alone is a third of the marks.

5Recent advances

  • Blanpied et al. (2017) — This APTA clinical practice guideline (Neck Pain: Revision 2017) recommends manual therapy (thoracic and cervical manipulation/mobilisation) combined with targeted exercise for neck pain, with the technique chosen according to the patient's impairment classification.
  • Beyer et al. (2022) — This summary review placed the overall evidence for manual medicine/manual therapy at EBM level III, with manipulation and mobilisation more effective than no treatment, placebo or usual care for neck and low back pain.
  • Short et al. (2023) — This clinical commentary argued that the value of manual therapy lies in reasoned, individualised symptom modification alongside exercise, rather than as a standalone passive treatment.
  • Veenstra et al. (2024) — This cross-sectional study using the Diagnostic Thinking Inventory found hypothetical-deductive reasoning skills develop with professional experience and education, supporting structured reasoning training.

6References

  1. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  3. Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
  4. A clinically-reasoned approach to manual therapy in sports physical therapy. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2023.
  5. Evidence (-based medicine) in manual medicine/manual therapy: a summary review. Manuelle Medizin. 2022.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper III

QP 8131 · 03-Jun-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Elbow special tests

  • Cozen's = resisted wrist extension, pain at lateral epicondyle
  • Mill's = passive stretch (elbow ext, forearm pronated, wrist flexed)
  • Reverse both for golfer's elbow (medial)
  • Valgus at ~25 deg = MCL; varus = LUCL
  • Tinel cubital tunnel = ulnar; Maudsley = radial tunnel trap

2Decision-making steps

  • Examine, evaluate, diagnose, prioritise, prognose (SMART), intervene, re-examine, modify
  • Novice = analytic; expert = pattern recognition + audit
  • Bias list: anchoring, confirmation, availability

3Both-bone forearm fracture

  • ORIF plate = motion-first rehab
  • Phase 1 (0-2 wk): protect, elevate, finger/shoulder AROM, watch 6 Ps
  • Phase 2 (2-6 wk): elbow, wrist, pro-sup, scar mob
  • Phase 3 (6-12 wk): resistance; 3-6 months: work/sport
  • Enemies: stiffness, radioulnar synostosis, compartment syndrome, re-fracture after plate removal

4SCI investigations

  • ASIA: 10 key muscles 0-5, 28 dermatomes x 2 modalities 0-2, plus DAP and VAC
  • AIS A = no sacral sparing; C = less than half key muscles 3 or more; D = half or more
  • 2019 revision: ZPP now allowed in incomplete injuries; star tag for non-SCI deficits
  • MRI = cord (haemorrhage = poor prognosis); CT = bone and canal
  • Myelography when MRI contraindicated or unavailable
  • SSEP tests dorsal columns, gives prognosis; urodynamics protects the kidneys

5PCL screening

  • Posterior drawer at 90 deg = gold standard (about 90 percent sensitive, 99 percent specific)
  • Grade I anterior (0-5 mm), Grade II flush (5-10 mm), Grade III behind (over 10 mm + suspect PLC)
  • Sag sign: tibia drops by gravity; quadriceps active: tibia shifts forward on quad contraction
  • Dashboard mechanism; sag makes ACL drawer falsely positive — reduce first

6Symes amputation

  • Ankle disarticulation, malleoli removed, heel pad over tibia end
  • Advantages: end bearing, long lever, self-suspending, near-normal energy, bare-stump standing
  • Socket: posterior door or expandable wall; thin SACH foot
  • Assess: pad migration, bulbous diameter, knee ROM, quads strength

7Demographics and history

  • Every variable must rule something in or out (age, sex, occupation, dominance, locality)
  • Inflammatory pain: rest + second half of night + morning stiffness over 1 hour
  • Red flags: weight loss, night pain, fever, sphincter loss, saddle anaesthesia, progressive deficit
  • India context: spinal TB with evening fever and weight loss

8Knee outcome measures

  • WOMAC 24 items (5 pain, 2 stiffness, 17 function); high = worse
  • KOOS 42 items, 5 subscales; high = better
  • Lysholm 8 items x 100; Tegner 0-10 activity level; Kujala 13 items patellofemoral
  • KSS = knee score + function score (arthroplasty); VAS 0-10 for all

9Ankle after subluxation

  • Inversion order of failure: ATFL first, CFL second, PTFL last
  • Anterior drawer in 10-20 deg plantarflexion tests ATFL; talar tilt tests CFL
  • Squeeze + external rotation = syndesmosis; Ottawa rules for X-ray
  • Pulses and sensation after every subluxation episode

10Clinical reasoning in manual therapy

  • Hypothesis categories: pain source, movement impairment, contributing factors, precautions, prognosis, management
  • Schools: Maitland (movement, grades), McKenzie (directional preference), Kaltenborn (arthrokinematics), Paris (segmental)
  • Immediate re-assessment of the concordant sign = validate or reject the hypothesis
  • Red flag gate before any mobilisation
