Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Explain the special tests of knee complex used in musculoskeletal system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit III — Screening of the knee complex

★ Memory hook — Lachman for the ACL, McMurray for the meniscus, valgus and varus for the collaterals — name the test, position, force and positive sign.

1Introduction

Special tests of the knee are the standardised manual procedures used to confirm which structure is injured or dysfunctional after the history and general examination have narrowed the field. They form part of the objective assessment of the knee complex — ligaments, menisci, patellofemoral joint and capsule.

Each test applies a specific force in a specific position to a specific structure, and its result is interpreted together with other findings rather than in isolation, because no single test is perfectly accurate.

2Physiology

The knee is a modified hinge joint stabilised by four main ligaments: the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments (ACL, PCL) controlling antero-posterior translation and rotation, and the medial and lateral collateral ligaments (MCL, LCL) controlling varus and valgus stress. The medial and lateral menisci distribute load, improve congruence and aid rotational stability.

The patellofemoral joint depends on balanced quadriceps and VMO activity and on the Q-angle for normal tracking. The screw-home mechanism and normal proprioception complete the functional picture, and each of these structures has a corresponding test that loads it selectively.

3Pathophysiology

Injury patterns include ligament sprains (ACL rupture from a non-contact pivot, PCL from a dashboard injury, collateral sprains from valgus/varus stress), meniscal tears from twisting under load, and patellofemoral pain or instability from maltracking or overload. Combined injuries and associated instability are common.

The special tests are designed to reproduce the specific mechanical fault — abnormal translation, rotation or pain — and to associate it with the structure responsible, so that the examination points to the correct diagnosis.

4Answer

Knee special tests — position, force and positive sign:

TestPosition & forcePositive sign
LachmanSupine, knee 20–30° flexion; anterior tibial translationSoft/lax endpoint, increased translation
Anterior drawerSupine, knee 90° flexion; anterior pullExcess anterior glide of tibia
Pivot shiftExtension, valgus and internal rotation then flexionVisible clunk/reduction of subluxation
Lever signFist under calf; downward force on femurHeel does not rise (positive)
Posterior drawer / sag signKnee 90°; posterior push / observationExcess posterior translation, sagging tibia
Valgus stressKnee 20–30° flexion; medial forceMedial laxity/pain (MCL)
Varus stressKnee 20–30° flexion; lateral forceLateral laxity/pain (LCL)
McMurraySupine, full flexion; rotation and extensionClick/pain over joint line
ThessalyStanding, 20° flexion, rotate bodyJoint-line pain/discomfort
ApleyProne, knee 90°; compression and rotationPain or clicking (meniscus)
Patellar apprehensionSupine, quadriceps relaxed; lateral glideApprehension/fear of dislocation
Clarke'sSupine; quadriceps contraction with patellar pressurePain at patella

Meniscal and ligament tests should be clustered, because no single test is perfectly accurate. The diagnostic accuracy of the ACL tests is comparable, and the pivot shift is the most specific for ruling in a tear.

Conclusion

The special tests of the knee complex are structure-specific provocation and laxity manoeuvres — Lachman and pivot shift for the ACL, posterior drawer and sag sign for the PCL, valgus/varus stress for the collaterals, McMurray/Thessaly/Apley for the menisci and apprehension/Clarke's for the patellofemoral joint — interpreted as a cluster, not singly.

5Recent advances

  • Sokal et al. (2022) — this bivariate meta-analysis found the Lachman test's accuracy had been previously overestimated and that the pivot shift and lever sign are best for ruling in and ruling out ACL tears respectively.
  • Hu et al. (2024) — this diagnostic meta-analysis of the lever sign reported pooled sensitivity of about 0.81 and specificity of about 0.78, supporting it as an adjunct rather than a stand-alone test.
  • Smith et al. (2015) — this systematic review and meta-analysis found McMurray's, joint-line tenderness and the Thessaly test have only modest accuracy for meniscal tears, cautioning against relying on any single special test.
  • Vaidya et al. (2020) — showed that a smartphone accelerometer can quantify the pivot shift reliably, part of a move to objective laxity devices that reduce examiner variability.
  • Karachalios et al. (2005) — introduced and validated the Thessaly test, a weight-bearing meniscal test with good diagnostic performance.

6References

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Exercise testing and prescription in arthritis patient.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit V — Exercise testing and prescription in arthritis

★ Memory hook — Test safely, prescribe FITT-VP, and remember low-impact, land or water — movement is medicine for the arthritic joint.

1Introduction

Exercise is the cornerstone of non-pharmacological management of arthritis, both osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Exercise testing establishes the patient's baseline capacity and safety, and exercise prescription translates that into a specific, individualised programme.

In arthritis the goal is to improve pain, function and quality of life while protecting the joint, so both testing and prescription must be adapted to the disease, its activity and the patient's comorbidities.

2Physiology

Regular exercise improves aerobic capacity, muscle strength, joint stability and proprioception, and helps control weight and cardiovascular risk — all of which reduce load on arthritic joints. Cartilage nutrition depends on intermittent loading, so appropriate movement is beneficial rather than harmful.

In RA, exercise must be balanced against systemic inflammation and fatigue, but the muscle weakness and deconditioning of inflammatory arthritis respond well to supervised, moderate-intensity training. The physiological target is to build strength and aerobic capacity without provoking a disease flare.

3Pathophysiology

In OA, cartilage loss, synovitis and muscle weakness produce pain and reduced function; arthrogenic muscle inhibition further weakens the quadriceps. In RA, chronic synovitis erodes cartilage and bone, and systemic inflammation causes muscle wasting (rheumatoid cachexia) and fatigue.

Both conditions are associated with sedentary behaviour and increased cardiovascular risk, so exercise testing must also screen for cardiac limitation. This pathophysiology dictates that testing be graded and that prescription be modified during flares.

4Answer

Exercise testing. Begin with pre-participation screening (ACSM algorithm / PAR-Q+): current activity level, signs or symptoms, known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and desired intensity. Then measure:

  • Aerobic capacity — 6-minute walk test, submaximal cycle or treadmill test, or a symptom-limited test where indicated.
  • Muscular strength — handheld dynamometry, grip strength, 1-RM or estimated 1-RM.
  • Range of motion — goniometry of the affected joints.
  • Function and pain — WOMAC or KOOS for OA, HAQ or DAS-28 for RA, and a numerical pain rating scale.
  • Perceived exertion — Borg RPE to monitor intensity.

Exercise prescription (FITT-VP):

ComponentRecommendation in arthritis
FrequencyAerobic 3–5 days/week; strengthening 2–3 days/week
IntensityModerate (RPE 11–14); start low if joints are inflamed
TimeBuild towards 150–300 min/week aerobic, in bouts
TypeLow-impact: walking, cycling, swimming, aquatic therapy, resistance
Volume/ProgressionProgress gradually; avoid overloading acutely inflamed joints

Include flexibility and neuromotor/balance work. Educate the patient about expected soreness versus a flare, and modify the programme during disease flares. Re-test periodically to document change.

Conclusion

Exercise testing in arthritis establishes safe baseline capacity and screens for cardiac risk, while prescription follows the FITT-VP principle with low-impact, progressive, individualised exercise — adapting dose to disease activity so that movement improves pain and function without provoking a flare.

5Recent advances

  • Moseng et al. (2023) — the 2023 EULAR recommendations emphasise exercise of adequate dosage with progression tailored to physical function, preferences and services, and support varied delivery modes including digital technology and aquatic exercise.
  • Bannuru et al. (2019) and Holden et al. (2022) — the 2019 OARSI guidelines and 2022 OARSI Rehabilitation Discussion Group consensus give detailed, practical guidance on dose, progression and adherence in hip and knee OA.
  • de Jong et al. (2003) — the RAPIT multicentre randomised trial showed a 2-year high-intensity exercise programme improved functional ability in rheumatoid arthritis without increasing radiographic joint damage, establishing that intensive exercise is safe in RA.
  • Bartels et al. (2016) — this Cochrane review found aquatic and land-based exercise have comparable benefits in knee and hip OA, with aquatic exercise useful when land exercise is painful.
  • Rodriguez-Sanchez-Laulhe et al. (2022) — a randomised trial of a smartphone app (CareHand) showed app-supported exercise and self-management improve hand function in rheumatoid arthritis, supporting telerehabilitation in chronic arthritis.

6References

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe in detail about the post operative assessment in Head of femur fracture in 58 year old female. Add note on its complications.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit VI — Post-operative assessment in hip fracture

★ Memory hook — After a femoral neck fracture, assess the surgery, the wound, the weight-bearing status and the function — and hunt for the classic complications.

1Introduction

Fracture of the head/neck of the femur is a common fragility fracture in older adults and a major cause of morbidity and mortality. In a 58-year-old female, the fracture is usually treated by internal fixation or by arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement), depending on displacement and bone quality.

Post-operative physiotherapy assessment determines what the patient can safely do and guides progressive rehabilitation. In this age group the goal is not merely survival but return to work and community function.

2Physiology

The femoral head receives its blood supply mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery via the retinacular vessels and the artery of the ligamentum teres. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint that transmits body weight from the pelvis to the femur; the abductor muscles (gluteus medius and minimus) stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance.

Normal hip function requires an intact capsule, good muscle strength and a stable, congruent joint. Arthroplasty replaces the joint surfaces, so the rehabilitation focus shifts to protecting the prosthesis and restoring function.

3Pathophysiology

Intracapsular femoral neck fractures disrupt the retinacular blood supply, risking avascular necrosis and non-union; displaced fractures are therefore often treated with arthroplasty in older patients. Extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures heal more reliably with fixation.

After surgery, muscle atrophy from disuse, post-operative pain, and the risk of dislocation (after arthroplasty) shape the clinical picture. In a 58-year-old, the goal is return to work and community function, not just survival.

4Answer

Post-operative assessment should cover:

  • History: fracture type, surgery performed (fixation, hemiarthroplasty, THR), approach, weight-bearing status, surgeon's precautions, comorbidities and pre-fracture function.
  • Observation: wound and dressing, swelling, limb position, leg-length discrepancy, deformity, skin condition.
  • Pain and wound: pain score, signs of infection, drain sites.
  • Range of motion: active and passive hip ROM, respecting precautions after arthroplasty (avoid flexion beyond 90°, adduction and internal rotation).
  • Strength: hip abductors, extensors, quadriceps, using MMT or dynamometry.
  • Gait and mobility: transfer ability, weight-bearing status, use of aids, gait pattern, balance (Berg Balance Scale, Timed Up and Go).
  • Function and outcome: Harris Hip Score or HOOS, Barthel Index, 6-minute walk test.
  • Circulation and neurology: distal pulses, sensation, signs of deep vein thrombosis.

Complications to watch for:

ComplicationClinical clue
Deep vein thrombosis / PECalf pain, swelling, breathlessness
Dislocation (arthroplasty)Sudden pain, deformity, leg shortening
Avascular necrosisPersistent pain, collapse on imaging
Non-union / fixation failureContinued pain, inability to weight-bear
InfectionWound discharge, fever, raised CRP
Pressure sores, pneumoniaImmobility-related
DeliriumAcute confusion, common post-operatively
Conclusion

Post-operative assessment after a femoral neck fracture in a 58-year-old combines history, wound and neurovascular checks, ROM, strength, gait and function against a background of surgical precautions — with vigilant screening for the classic complications (DVT, dislocation, AVN, non-union, infection, delirium) that determine recovery.

5Recent advances

  • Min et al. (2021) — this clinical practice guideline for post-operative rehabilitation in older patients with hip fractures strongly recommends multidisciplinary care, progressive resistance exercise and balance training, and supports early ambulation.
  • NICE (2023) — NICE guideline CG124 (updated 2023) requires rehabilitation to start no later than the day after surgery, at least once a day.
  • Diong et al. (2016) — this systematic review and meta-analysis found structured exercise improves mobility after hip fracture, with progressive resistance training and non-hospital settings giving the largest effects.
  • Kimmel et al. (2016) — the HIP4Hips randomised trial found intensive hospital physiotherapy is safe and shortens length of stay after an isolated hip fracture.
  • AAOS (2021) — the AAOS Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults guideline recommends surgery within 24-48 hours and immediate full weight-bearing as tolerated after surgical treatment.

6References

Q8. Write in detail about the musculoskeletal assessment method and screening in congenital dislocation of hip.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit VI — Paediatric musculoskeletal screening

★ Memory hook — Ortolani reduces, Barlow dislocates, Galeazzi reveals the shortening — screen the newborn hip early.

1Introduction

Congenital dislocation of the hip, now called developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), is a spectrum of abnormal development ranging from a mildly dysplastic acetabulum to frank dislocation of the femoral head. Early detection is critical because treatment in the first months of life is simple and effective, whereas late diagnosis requires major surgery.

The physiotherapist's role is in clinical screening, in supporting surveillance, and in post-treatment rehabilitation.

2Physiology

At birth the acetabulum is shallow and the femoral head is largely cartilaginous, so the hip is developmentally immature. Normal development requires the femoral head to remain concentrically reduced within the acetabulum, providing the stimulus for acetabular deepening.

Ligamentous laxity is normal in the newborn and usually resolves; the hip must be kept in a position that maintains concentric reduction for normal growth. This is why positioning (avoiding extended-hip swaddling) and early harness treatment are effective. On ultrasound the normal acetabular alpha angle is greater than 60°; values below this define the Graf type II–IV dysplasia that screening aims to detect.

3Pathophysiology

In DDH, capsular laxity, a shallow acetabulum and abnormal femoral head position produce instability, subluxation or dislocation. Risk factors include breech presentation, female sex, first-born status, family history, oligohydramnios and swaddling with the hips extended.

Left untreated, DDH leads to limping, leg-length discrepancy, early osteoarthritis and disability. Most mild dysplasia detected at birth resolves spontaneously, which complicates screening and is why universal ultrasound remains controversial.

4Answer

Clinical screening tests (newborn):

TestMethodPositive sign
OrtolaniHips flexed and abducted, femoral head lifted into socketA palpable clunk of reduction
BarlowHips flexed and adducted, gentle posterior pressureA palpable clunk of dislocation
GaleazziHips and knees flexed, compare knee heightsLower knee on the affected side
Abduction rangePassive abductionLimited or asymmetrical abduction
Skin creasesInspect thigh/gluteal creasesAsymmetry

Imaging: ultrasound is the investigation of choice before ossification (Graf method, using the alpha angle to classify types I–IV); plain radiography is used after about 4–6 months of age.

Older-child assessment: gait (Trendelenburg, limping), leg-length measurement, hip range of motion and the Trendelenburg test.

Screening strategy: every newborn has a clinical hip examination within the first days of life and again at 6–8 weeks. Infants with risk factors or an abnormal examination undergo targeted hip ultrasound; universal ultrasound screening remains controversial because most detected abnormalities resolve. Confirmed DDH is treated with a Pavlik harness in early infancy, and the physiotherapist reinforces safe hip positioning (avoiding tight swaddling with the hips extended) and monitors harness wear.

Indian context: in settings where routine newborn ultrasound is not universal, repeated clinical examination at the immunisation visits (6, 10 and 14 weeks) is the practical safety net, and delayed presentation with a limping toddler remains common — so the physiotherapist must keep DDH on the differential in any child with a limp or leg-length discrepancy.

Conclusion

Screening for DDH is a clinical examination — Ortolani and Barlow for instability, Galeazzi and crease/asymmetry checks — supported by targeted ultrasound (Graf) and repeated at 6–8 weeks, so that dysplasia is caught early, when a Pavlik harness can restore normal hip development.

5Recent advances

  • Marletta et al. (2025) — this systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed that early Pavlik-harness treatment, ideally in the first months of life, gives the best outcomes for Graf IIb-IV hips.
  • Bewick et al. (2025) — this multicentre UK study showed physiotherapy-led DDH clinics achieve high Pavlik-harness success (96%) and low residual dysplasia, matching medically-led clinics.
  • Sharma et al. (2022) — this scoping review found early, structured, individualised physiotherapy improves hip function and reduces complications in children with developmental dysplasia of the hip.
  • Ho et al. (2025) — this case report highlights the physiotherapist's role in detecting delayed DDH and in post-casting rehabilitation, restoring movement, strength and age-appropriate function.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Explain the uses of ICF in diagnosis of musculoskeletal disorders.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit II — ICF framework in musculoskeletal diagnosis

★ Memory hook — ICF turns a diagnosis into a profile: what is impaired, what the patient cannot do, and what the environment allows.

1Introduction

The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), published by the WHO in 2001, provides a standard language and framework for describing health and health-related states. In musculoskeletal practice it moves the clinician beyond a purely tissue-based diagnosis towards a biopsychosocial profile of the patient's functioning.

It is used in assessment, goal setting, outcome measurement and communication across disciplines, and it underpins modern physiotherapy diagnosis.

2Physiology

The ICF describes functioning across two parts. The first is Functioning and Disability, comprising Body Functions and Structures (physiological and anatomical status) and Activities and Participation (execution of tasks and involvement in life situations). The second is Contextual Factors, comprising Environmental Factors and Personal Factors.

These components interact dynamically with the health condition, so that a musculoskeletal disorder is understood as the result of the interaction between the pathology and the person's context, not the pathology alone.

3Pathophysiology

A musculoskeletal disorder — for example, knee osteoarthritis — produces impairment at the level of body function and structure (pain, reduced joint mobility, muscle weakness), activity limitation (difficulty walking or climbing stairs) and participation restriction (unable to work or socialise).

Environmental factors (stairs at home, workplace demands) and personal factors (age, coping, beliefs) modulate the impact. Recognising all these domains prevents the common error of treating only the tissue and ignoring the person.

4Answer

Uses of the ICF in musculoskeletal diagnosis and management:

  • Comprehensive assessment: it provides a checklist of domains to examine — body functions and structures, activities, participation and contextual factors — so nothing important is missed.
  • Core Sets: condition-specific ICF Core Sets (low back pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, post-acute musculoskeletal conditions) define the categories most relevant to each condition and make the framework practical.
  • Qualifiers: each category is graded from 0 (no problem) to 4 (complete problem), giving a quantitative profile that can be tracked over time.
  • Goal setting: goals can be set at impairment, activity and participation levels, aligning treatment with what matters to the patient.
  • Outcome measurement: the profile serves as a baseline and a measure of change.
  • Interdisciplinary communication: it provides a common language across physiotherapy, medicine, occupational therapy and social services.
  • Rehabilitation planning: it links identified problems to interventions and to the responsible professional.
ICF componentExample in low back pain
Body functionsb280 Sensation of pain
Body structuress760 Structure of trunk
Activities & participationd430 Lifting and carrying objects
Environmental factorse580 Health services, systems and policies
Conclusion

The ICF turns a musculoskeletal diagnosis into a biopsychosocial profile across body function, activity, participation and context — making assessment comprehensive, goals meaningful, outcomes measurable and communication shared across the rehabilitation team.

5Recent advances

  • Hernandez-Lazaro et al. (2023) — this multicentre study confirmed the content validity of the comprehensive ICF Core Set for post-acute musculoskeletal conditions in primary care physiotherapy services.
  • Selb et al. (2022) — developed an ICF-based assessment schedule to facilitate assessment and reporting of functioning in manual medicine, using low back pain as a model.
  • Cieza et al. (2004) — produced the ICF Core Sets for low back pain, which are now used as starting points for examination and outcome measurement in musculoskeletal conditions.
  • Bickenbach et al. (2020) — published the ICF Core Sets Manual for Clinical Practice (2nd edition), giving clinicians a step-by-step method and documentation tool for applying ICF Core Sets.
  • WHO (2001) — published the ICF framework, which is now increasingly embedded in national rehabilitation policies and primary care musculoskeletal pathways.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. What are the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit V — Fitness evaluation and exercise prescription

★ Memory hook — Screen before you test: check activity level, symptoms, known disease and intended intensity, then measure the five components of fitness.

1Introduction

Fitness evaluation in adults is the structured assessment of health status and physical fitness before an exercise programme is prescribed. Its purposes are to detect individuals at risk of exercise-related cardiovascular events, to establish a baseline, and to guide safe, effective prescription.

The evaluation has two parts: pre-participation health screening and the measurement of the components of fitness.

2Physiology

Physical fitness is the ability to perform daily tasks with vigour and without undue fatigue. It has five health-related components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition; balance is an important additional component in older adults.

Regular exercise improves all of these and reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and all-cause mortality. The body's acute response to exercise — heart rate, blood pressure, ventilation and oxygen uptake — is the basis of the tests used to assess capacity.

3Pathophysiology

The main risk of exercise testing is an exercise-related cardiovascular event, particularly sudden cardiac death or myocardial infarction, which is more likely in people with known or occult cardiovascular disease who undertake unaccustomed vigorous exercise.

Sedentary lifestyle, obesity, hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia increase this risk. Screening therefore aims to identify who needs medical clearance, while avoiding excessive referral that discourages physical activity.

4Answer

Criteria for fitness evaluation in adults:

  • Pre-participation health screening — using the ACSM algorithm based on (a) current level of structured physical activity, (b) presence of major signs or symptoms or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and (c) the desired exercise intensity. The PAR-Q+ may be used as a self-administered tool. The outcome is whether medical clearance is needed before starting.
  • Resting measures — heart rate, blood pressure, body mass index, waist circumference and resting ECG where indicated.
  • Cardiorespiratory fitness — a submaximal or maximal test (cycle or treadmill, or a field test such as the 6-minute walk) to estimate VO2max.
  • Muscular fitness — grip strength, push-up or sit-up tests, and 1-RM or estimated 1-RM.
  • Flexibility — sit-and-reach or goniometric measures.
  • Body composition — BMI, waist girth and, where available, body-fat percentage.
  • Balance and functional capacity — relevant in older adults (Berg Balance Scale, Timed Up and Go).

Indications to stop a test include chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness, pallor, a drop in systolic blood pressure, or a hypertensive response. Interpretation compares results with age- and sex-based norms and forms the basis of the FITT-VP prescription.

ComponentTest example
CardiorespiratorySubmaximal cycle, 6-minute walk
Muscular strengthGrip dynamometry, 1-RM
FlexibilitySit-and-reach
Body compositionBMI, waist girth
Conclusion

The criteria for fitness evaluation in adults are: pre-participation screening (ACSM algorithm / PAR-Q+) to decide on medical clearance, resting measures, and measurement of the five health-related components of fitness (plus balance in the elderly) — interpreted against age- and sex-based norms to prescribe exercise safely.

5Recent advances

  • Bull et al. (2020) — the WHO 2020 guidelines recommend 150-300 minutes of moderate or 75-150 minutes of vigorous activity per week for adults, plus muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days.
  • Piercy et al. (2018) — the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans (2nd edition) formalised the 150-300 minute aerobic target and, for the first time, recommended balance training alongside aerobic and strengthening activity in older adults.
  • Riebe et al. (2015) — the ACSM pre-participation screening model removed routine cardiovascular risk-factor profiling and now bases medical clearance on activity level, symptoms/disease and intended intensity, reducing unnecessary physician referrals.
  • Ross et al. (2016) — showed that cardiorespiratory fitness is a clinical vital sign that predicts cardiovascular and all-cause mortality independent of traditional risk factors.
  • Sherrington et al. (2019) — this Cochrane review found that balance and strength training reduces falls in older adults, so multicomponent training is now specifically recommended for them.

6References

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the impaired endurance seen in bed ridden patients with spinal cord injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Exercise physiology and management of the immobile patient (spinal cord injury).

★ Memory hook — Bed rest steals the pump, the pipes and the pressure — in SCI the damage is faster because the nervous system that runs them is already cut.

1Introduction

Endurance is the ability to sustain a physical task over time and reflects integrated cardiorespiratory, vascular, muscular and autonomic function. In a bed-ridden patient with spinal cord injury (SCI) this system is challenged twice over: once by the lesion itself and again by prolonged recumbency. The result is a steep fall in aerobic capacity, early fatigue and poor activity tolerance that delays rehabilitation and raises long-term cardiovascular risk.

2Physiology

Normal endurance depends on peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak), the product of cardiac output and the arteriovenous oxygen difference. Cardiac output depends on stroke volume, heart rate and venous return, maintained by the leg muscle pump and sympathetic vasoconstriction. Muscle contributes oxidative capacity through mitochondria, capillaries and type I fibres; VO2peak is about 35-45 ml/kg/min in trained people and 25-30 in sedentary adults.

3Pathophysiology

Immobility alone causes deconditioning: within days there is a fall in plasma volume, reduced left ventricular mass and compliance, loss of the leg muscle pump, reduced capillary density and a shift of muscle fibres towards fast, glycolytic type IIx. In SCI these changes are amplified and lesion-specific. A lesion above T6 removes supraspinal sympathetic control, causing neurogenic chronotropic incompetence (a blunted heart-rate response), impaired vasomotor tone and orthostatic hypotension; loss of the leg pump and venous pooling further reduce venous return, while cardiac atrophy lowers stroke volume. High lesions also impair respiratory function and cough. Spasticity, pressure ulcers, pain and depression reduce activity further. The net effect is a VO2peak that may fall to 10-20 ml/kg/min, with a disproportionate rise in perceived exertion, fatigue at low workloads and reduced endurance for transfers and arm work.

4Answer

Impaired endurance in the bed-ridden SCI patient is assessed and treated in the same framework.

Assessment. Record heart rate, blood pressure (watch for autonomic dysreflexia), respiratory rate and perceived exertion (RPE/Borg); use the 6-minute arm test or arm-crank ergometry for VO2peak, with the Fatigue Severity Scale for function.

Management (early, while on bed rest).

  • Positioning and early passive/active-assisted range of motion, four to six times daily, to preserve joint and muscle length.
  • Respiratory muscle training and incentive spirometry to preserve ventilation and cough.
  • Supine arm-crank ergometry using a bed-mounted ergometer, starting at 40-60% of predicted heart-rate reserve for 15-20 minutes, progressing to 30 minutes, three to five times weekly.
  • Functional electrical stimulation (FES) cycling or FES rowing of the paralysed legs to restore the muscle pump, increase venous return and recruit oxidative fibres; 30-45 minutes, three times weekly.
  • Graded tilt-table or standing programme to re-train orthostatic tolerance; abdominal binders and compression stockings as adjuncts.

Dosage and progression. Apply overload with recovery; evidence-based SCI guidelines recommend at least two aerobic and two strength sessions weekly. Progress duration before intensity and monitor autonomic signs.

Outcome measures. VO2peak/peak power, 6MAT distance, RPE at a fixed load, Fatigue Severity Scale and functional independence scores.

5Recent advances

  • Hodgkiss et al. (2023) — A PLOS Medicine systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression confirmed that exercise improves VO2peak, relative VO2peak and peak power output in SCI, with upper-body aerobic and resistance training among the most effective modes.
  • Pelletier et al. (2015) — A 16-week randomised controlled trial in Spinal Cord showed that following the SCI physical-activity guidelines raised relative VO2peak by about 17% and upper-body strength by 11.5-38.9%, validating the minimum exercise dose for the deconditioned patient.
  • Martin Ginis et al. (2018) — The evidence-based scientific exercise guidelines for adults with SCI (Spinal Cord) recommend at least 20 min of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise twice weekly plus strength training of the major muscle groups twice weekly.
  • Lutfy et al. (2021) — Pilot-tested supine arm-cycle ergometry (the multi-purpose arm cycle ergometer, M-PACE) to safely reduce deconditioning during the four to six weeks of complete bed rest after flap surgery for pressure injuries in SCI.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. Philadelphia: F.A. Davis; 2018.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. Philadelphia: F.A. Davis; 2019.
  3. American College of Sports Medicine. ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. 11th ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2021.
  4. Martin Ginis KA, van der Scheer JW, Latimer-Cheung AE, et al. Evidence-based scientific exercise guidelines for adults with spinal cord injury. Spinal Cord. 2018;56(4):308-321.
  5. Dolbow DR, Gorgey AS, et al. Exercise and health-related risks of physical deconditioning after spinal cord injury. Top Spinal Cord Inj Rehabil. 2017.
  6. Nightengale E, et al. Supine arm cycling during the post-flap recovery period for persons with spinal cord injuries: the multi-purpose arm cycle ergometer (M-PACE) safety and pilot testing. 2021.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the physiological mechanism of analgesia effect in the management of pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Pain mechanisms and electrotherapeutic/physiotherapeutic modulation of pain.

★ Memory hook — Pain is turned down at two gates: one in the spinal cord (gate control) and one in the brainstem (descending control).

1Introduction

Analgesia is the reduction of the perception of pain without loss of consciousness. Physiotherapists produce analgesia through several overlapping physiological mechanisms rather than by a single switch. Understanding these mechanisms explains why techniques as different as TENS, manual therapy, exercise, acupuncture and cryotherapy all relieve pain, and how to choose and dose them.

2Physiology

Nociception has four stages: transduction (a noxious stimulus becomes an electrical signal in free nerve endings), transmission (conduction along A-delta and C fibres to the dorsal horn and then via the spinothalamic tract), modulation (alteration of the signal at the spinal cord and brainstem) and perception (the subjective experience). The dorsal horn is a key control point. Melzack and Wall's gate control theory (1965) proposed that large-diameter A-beta fibres, excited by touch or non-noxious stimulation, activate inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) that presynaptically inhibit the A-delta and C fibres carrying nociceptive input, closing the gate. The brain also sends descending control: the periaqueductal grey matter (PAG) and the rostral ventromedial medulla project to the dorsal horn through serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways, and activate the endogenous opioid system. Endogenous opioids - endorphins (mu receptors), enkephalins (delta) and dynorphins (kappa) - inhibit transmitter release (including substance P) and hyperpolarise neurons, raising the pain threshold. Diffuse noxious inhibitory controls (DNIC), measured clinically as conditioned pain modulation, form another endogenous inhibitory system.

3Pathophysiology

When nociceptive input is intense or prolonged the modulation systems fail. Repeated C-fibre firing causes wind-up and central sensitisation, with increased excitability of dorsal-horn neurons, enlarged receptive fields, hyperalgesia (painful response to mildly painful stimuli) and allodynia (pain from non-painful stimuli). Descending inhibition may become less effective, and peripheral sensitisation lowers nociceptor thresholds through inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins, bradykinin and substance P. This is the state of persistent musculoskeletal and neuropathic pain that physiotherapy must modulate.

4Answer

Each physiotherapeutic agent works through one or more of these mechanisms.

  • Conventional (high-frequency) TENS - 80-120 Hz, low intensity, comfortable paraesthesia; selectively excites A-beta fibres and closes the spinal gate (segmental, fast onset, short duration).
  • Acupuncture-like (low-frequency) TENS - 2-10 Hz, high intensity, visible muscle twitch; activates A-delta fibres, the PAG and endogenous opioid release (mu and delta), giving slower onset but longer-lasting analgesia; reversed by naloxone.
  • Burst TENS - combines both mechanisms, stimulating A-beta and A-delta fibres.
  • Interferential and other currents - stimulate large fibres and reduce nociceptive transmission; the rhythmical, non-painful input closes the gate.
  • Manual therapy and mobilisation - stimulate mechanoreceptors and activate descending inhibition; part of the effect is contextual and expectation-driven.
  • Exercise and aerobic activity - produce exercise-induced hypoalgesia through endogenous opioids, endocannabinoids and descending inhibition.
  • Acupuncture/dry needling - A-delta stimulation, DNIC and endogenous opioid release.
  • Cryotherapy and thermotherapy - reduce nociceptor firing, slow conduction and reduce oedema, reducing peripheral input.

Clinical implications. Choose the mechanism that matches the pain state: segmental TENS for acute localised pain, acupuncture-like or burst TENS for chronic pain, exercise-induced hypoalgesia for widespread persistent pain. Apply electrodes over the painful segment or the related dermatome and check sensation. Reassess after each session and combine modalities with active therapy, since pain relief alone does not restore function.

5Recent advances

  • Sluka et al. (2018) — Described exercise-induced hypoalgesia and its opioid, endocannabinoid and descending-inhibition mechanisms, supporting exercise as an analgesic in its own right.
  • Hoegh & Bannister (2024) — A Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy review of the descending pain modulatory system explained how counter-stimulation techniques such as acupuncture and manual therapy, plus patient expectation and context, influence pain.
  • Johnson et al. (2022) — The meta-TENS systematic review and meta-analysis of 381 randomised trials (BMJ Open) found moderate-certainty evidence that strong non-painful TENS at the site of pain reduces pain intensity versus placebo, supporting TENS as a physiotherapy adjunct.
  • Naugle et al. (2012) — A meta-analytic review in the Journal of Pain showed that acute aerobic, isometric and dynamic-resistance exercise all reduce experimentally induced pain, with isometric exercise producing the largest hypoalgesic effect.
  • Dailey et al. (2020) — A randomised controlled trial showed that TENS reduced movement-evoked pain and fatigue in women with fibromyalgia.

6References

  2. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2018.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St. Louis: Elsevier; 2021.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the concept of functional rehabilitation following total knee replacement.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Rehabilitation following joint replacement surgery.

★ Memory hook — A knee replacement buys you the joint; only functional rehabilitation teaches you how to use it.

1Introduction

Total knee replacement (TKR) relieves pain and restores alignment in advanced knee arthritis, but it only provides a pain-free, stable joint - it does not by itself restore movement, strength or the ability to walk, climb stairs and work. Functional rehabilitation is a structured, goal-directed, phase-based programme that translates the new joint into real-life activity, guided by the patient's goals.

2Physiology

The knee is a modified hinge whose function depends on the interplay of the extensor mechanism (quadriceps and patella), the hamstrings, the joint capsule and the surrounding proprioceptors. The quadriceps is the key muscle: its strength determines stair climbing, rising from a chair and normal gait. Normal knee flexion for daily living is 0-110 degrees, and full extension is essential to avoid a flexed, inefficient gait. Healing after TKR proceeds through the inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases, and bone ingrowth into the cement or porous surface takes weeks. Because the patient is weight-bearing early, rehabilitation must protect the implant while progressively loading the soft tissues.

3Pathophysiology

TKR creates a predictable set of impairments: post-operative pain and swelling, quadriceps weakness and arthrogenic muscle inhibition (the joint refuses to let the muscle fire fully), restricted range of motion, a risk of arthrofibrosis (excessive scar formation) if movement is not regained early, altered proprioception and gait, and reduced function. If extension is not regained quickly, the patient develops a flexed-knee gait with increased energy cost; if flexion stalls, stair and toilet transfers are difficult. Persistent weakness and kinesiophobia delay return to activity.

4Answer

Functional rehabilitation follows four overlapping phases, individualised to the patient's goals.

Phase 1 - Pre-operative (prehabilitation). Education about the procedure and expected milestones, quadriceps and range-of-motion exercises, cardiovascular conditioning and smoking cessation. Pre-operative education reduces anxiety and improves early outcomes.

Phase 2 - Acute post-operative (day 0-3). Control pain and swelling (cryotherapy 15-20 minutes several times daily, elevation, compression, adequate analgesia); ankle pumps and active-assisted knee flexion/extension; isometric quadriceps, straight-leg raise and terminal knee extension to counter arthrogenic inhibition; sit-to-stand and safe transfer practice; begin walking with a frame or crutches and full weight-bearing as allowed. Goal: safe mobilisation and 0-90 degrees of movement.

Phase 3 - Early functional (weeks 2-6). Progress strengthening (open- and closed-chain quadriceps, hamstrings, hip abductors and calf), stationary cycling, step and stair practice, balance and proprioceptive work, and gait re-education. Aim for 0-120 degrees of flexion and independent household mobility.

Phase 4 - Advanced and return to function (weeks 6-12 and beyond). Progressive resistance training, endurance work (walking, cycling, aquatics), agility and task-specific training for work, driving, gardening or sport. Outcome is judged by function, not by the implant.

Dosage. Exercise should be performed most days, with strengthening three to five times weekly, one to three sets of 8-15 repetitions, progressed by load and complexity. Supervised rehabilitation is most intense in the first six weeks and then tapered.

Outcome measures. Range of motion, quadriceps and hamstring strength, timed up-and-go (TUG), 30-second sit-to-stand, 6-minute walk test, stair test, and patient-reported measures such as the Oxford Knee Score, WOMAC, KOOS and the Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) knee score.

5Recent advances

  • Jiao et al. (2023) — A randomised controlled trial showed that enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS)-based quantitative rehabilitation training improved knee function, shortened hospital stay and improved satisfaction after TKR.
  • Tousignant et al. (2015) — A non-inferiority randomised controlled trial in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery showed that in-home telerehabilitation was not clinically inferior to face-to-face rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty (WOMAC), supporting remote delivery of supervised exercise.
  • Piqueras et al. (2013) — A randomised controlled trial in the Journal of Rehabilitation Medicine found that an interactive virtual telerehabilitation programme after TKR was at least as effective as conventional outpatient physiotherapy.
  • Gränicher et al. (2020) — A pilot randomised controlled trial in Archives of Physiotherapy found that preoperative physiotherapy improved the level of physical activity before and after TKA and reduced analgesic use and overall costs.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe the principles of Butler's mobilization and methods of performing the lower limb tissue tension tests.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Neural tissue mobilisation / neurodynamics.

★ Memory hook — Treat the nerve like a delicate thread through a tight sleeve: slide it, do not tug it.

1Introduction

David Butler's concept of neural mobilisation (neurodynamics) treats the nervous system as a continuous, mechanically sensitive and mobile tissue. Injury, inflammation or entrapment makes a nerve mechanosensitive, so normal movement becomes painful. Butler's approach uses graded movement to restore the nerve's ability to glide and tolerate load. The lower limb tissue tension tests identify this mechanosensitivity and guide treatment.

2Physiology

Peripheral nerves must stretch and glide relative to their bed. During limb movement a nerve both elongates (tension) and slides within its sheath (excursion); sciatic excursion during a straight-leg raise is about 10-12 mm. Nerves tolerate modest elongation of roughly 6-8% before intraneural blood flow is impaired. Neurodynamic tests load the neural and surrounding non-neural tissues, and sensitising movements add load to the nervous tissue to confirm neural involvement.

3Pathophysiology

Mechanosensitivity develops when a nerve is compressed, stretched, inflamed or its surrounding tissue is injured; inflammatory mediators sensitise the nerve and dorsal root, so tension provokes pain. Common situations are lumbar radiculopathy, piriformis-related sciatica, tarsal tunnel syndrome and post-operative or scar-related restriction. In these states the neurodynamic test reproduces the patient's symptoms, the involved side differs from the uninvolved side, and structural differentiation (adding or removing a distal or proximal movement) changes the response.

4Answer

Principles of Butler's mobilisation.

  • The nervous system is treated as a continuum; the site of symptoms is not always the site of the problem.
  • Techniques are graded from least to most provocative, and are always within the patient's tolerance.
  • Sliders move the nerve in one direction while the opposite end moves away, producing excursion with little increase in tension - used when the nerve is very sensitive.
  • Tensioners move both ends apart, increasing neural tension - used later to build tolerance.
  • Slow, rhythmic, oscillatory movement is preferred; avoid prolonged end-range stretch.
  • Assess before and after every session (symptom response and test range) and progress load gradually.
  • Combine with education and active movement; avoid aggravating positions such as prolonged sitting or slump.

Lower limb tissue tension (neurodynamic) tests.

TestNerve / structureHow performed
Straight leg raise (Lasègue)Sciatic nerve, L4-S3 rootsSupine; passively raise the straight leg with the knee extended; positive if symptoms reproduce between 30 and 70 degrees.
Slump testMeninges, spinal cord, sciatic nerveSitting; thoracic and lumbar flexion, then cervical flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion; symptoms relieved by cervical extension confirm neural involvement.
Bragard / sensitised SLRSciatic nerveLower the leg slightly from the painful SLR angle then add ankle dorsiflexion; reproduction confirms neural tension.
Bowstring testTibial and common peroneal nervesAt the SLR limit, flex the knee slightly and press in the popliteal fossa over the nerve.
Femoral nerve stretch (prone knee bend)Femoral nerve, L2-L4Prone; passively flex the knee, then extend the hip; anterior thigh symptoms reproduce.
Slump with knee extension / tibial nerve testTibial nerveSlump position plus ankle dorsiflexion and eversion to load the tibial nerve.

Record the range at which symptoms appear, whether they are the patient's familiar symptoms, and whether sensitising movements change them. Repeat the same test after treatment to measure the response.

5Recent advances

  • Basson et al. (2017) — A systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy found that neural mobilisation (slump and straight-leg-raise mobilisation) significantly reduced pain and disability in people with neurogenic low back pain.
  • Neto et al. (2017) — A systematic review of lower-body-quadrant neural mobilisation confirmed reductions in pain and disability in low back pain and improved flexibility in healthy adults.
  • Cuenca-Martínez et al. (2022) — An umbrella review with meta-meta-analysis in Physical Therapy found moderate-to-large effects of neural mobilisation on pain and disability in musculoskeletal disorders and on mechanosensitivity in asymptomatic people.
  • Pellicciari et al. (2019) — A study of contralateral limb mobilisation in the slump position (Acta Biomedica) showed increased ipsilateral knee-extension range, supporting the neurodynamic principle of treating the opposite limb.

6References

  2. Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics: A New System of Musculoskeletal Treatment. Edinburgh: Elsevier; 2005.
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021.

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the role of cognitive behavioral therapy for a subject with neck pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Biopsychosocial management of neck pain.

★ Memory hook — Neck pain lives in the tissues, but it grows in the thoughts - CBT treats the thoughts.

1Introduction

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a structured, goal-oriented psychological approach that targets the thoughts, beliefs and behaviours that maintain pain and disability. In neck pain - especially chronic, non-specific and whiplash-associated neck pain - fear of movement (kinesiophobia), catastrophising and passive coping drive avoidance, deconditioning and persistence of pain. CBT is therefore not an alternative to physical therapy but a partner to it, helping the patient re-engage with activity.

2Physiology

Pain is not a simple reflection of tissue damage; it is produced by the brain in a biopsychosocial context. Descending modulation from the brainstem can either inhibit or facilitate nociception, and psychological state influences this balance. Stress and anxiety increase sympathetic activity and muscle guarding, and negative beliefs about pain amplify the perceived threat, sensitising the system. Normal cervical function depends on mobility, deep flexor and extensor endurance, and proprioceptive control, all of which deteriorate with inactivity driven by fear.

3Pathophysiology

In chronic neck pain, central sensitisation and impaired descending inhibition make the pain system hypersensitive. Kinesiophobia leads to avoidance of movement and work, which causes muscle weakness, reduced endurance and further disability. Catastrophising (ruminating on the worst outcome) and low self-efficacy predict poor recovery, and in whiplash-associated disorders these psychological factors are among the strongest predictors of chronicity. The goal of CBT is to break this fear-avoidance cycle.

4Answer

Role and components of CBT in neck pain.

  • Education and reconceptualisation - explain the biopsychosocial model and pain neuroscience so the patient understands that hurt does not always equal harm.
  • Cognitive restructuring - identify and challenge unhelpful thoughts ('my neck is fragile', 'movement will damage me') and replace them with realistic beliefs.
  • Graded exposure and graded activity - gradually reintroduce feared movements, postures and tasks, setting a baseline and progressing by time and load rather than by pain.
  • Relaxation and coping skills - diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation and pacing to reduce muscle guarding and stress.
  • Goal setting and self-management - collaborative, meaningful goals and problem-solving to build self-efficacy.
  • Behavioural activation - reducing pain behaviour and increasing healthy, functional behaviour.

Delivery and dosage. CBT is usually delivered in 6-12 individual or group sessions of 45-60 minutes, weekly or twice weekly, either by a psychologist or by a physiotherapist trained in psychologically informed practice. It is most effective when integrated with exercise and manual therapy in a multimodal programme, and when it addresses work-related and ergonomic factors.

Outcome measures. Neck Disability Index (NDI), Numerical Pain Rating Scale, Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK), Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Pain Anxiety Symptoms Scale, and measures of quality of life and work ability.

Clinical message. CBT is most valuable in chronic or whiplash-associated neck pain with high fear, catastrophising or distress. It reduces kinesiophobia, anxiety and depression and improves function; its effect on pain intensity itself is modest, so it should always be combined with active physical rehabilitation.

5Recent advances

  • Javdaneh et al. (2020) — A randomised controlled trial showed that scapular exercise combined with cognitive functional therapy was superior to scapular exercise alone for reducing chronic neck pain and kinesiophobia.
  • Monticone et al. (2022) — Designed a randomised controlled trial of a multidisciplinary programme combining task-oriented exercise with CBT for working patients with chronic neck pain, with one-year follow-up.
  • Monticone et al. (2015) — A Cochrane review of cognitive-behavioural treatment for subacute and chronic neck pain found low-quality evidence of benefit, mainly for kinesiophobia and psychological outcomes when CBT was combined with other treatment.
  • Ploutarchou et al. (2023) — A systematic review with meta-analysis in Cognitive Behaviour Therapy found low-certainty evidence of short-term pain reduction with CBT and clinically significant improvements in kinesiophobia, anxiety and depression when CBT formed part of a multimodal programme.
  • Ragab et al. (2019) — A randomised study adding CBT to physical therapy for chronic cervical radiculopathy reported greater improvement in pain anxiety, neck disability and range of motion than physical therapy alone.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write in detail about extra corporeal shock wave therapy used for tissue healing.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Electrotherapy / therapeutic modalities for tissue healing.

★ Memory hook — Shock waves are controlled micro-trauma: they wake a sleeping tendon and make it heal itself.

1Introduction

Extracorporeal shock wave therapy (ESWT) delivers high-energy acoustic (pressure) waves to a tissue from outside the body. Originally used to break kidney stones (lithotripsy), it is now an established non-invasive modality for chronic tendinopathies and other musculoskeletal conditions that have failed standard care. Its value lies in stimulating the body's own repair processes rather than simply masking pain.

2Physiology

Tendon healing passes through an inflammatory phase (days), a proliferative phase (weeks, with tenocyte proliferation and type III collagen) and a remodelling phase (months, with maturation to type I collagen and realignment). ESWT is applied at an energy flux density measured in millijoules per square millimetre (mJ/mm2). Low-energy ESWT stimulates healing, whereas excessive energy can itself cause structural injury, so dose matters. The acoustic wave creates mechanical stress at tissue interfaces and triggers a biological cascade.

3Pathophysiology

In chronic tendinopathy the tendon is degenerative rather than simply inflamed: disorganised collagen, increased matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and cytokines, neovessels with accompanying nerve ingrowth and failed healing. ESWT disrupts this failed cycle through mechanotransduction - converting mechanical energy into a cellular response - and by inducing controlled micro-trauma that restarts healing.

4Answer

Mechanisms of action.

  • Mechanotransduction - the pressure wave is converted into biochemical signals in tenocytes and other cells.
  • Neovascularisation - release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other growth factors promotes new capillary formation and improves blood supply.
  • Tenocyte stimulation - increased tenocyte proliferation, upregulation of proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA), transforming growth factor beta-1 (TGF-beta1) and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and accelerated collagen synthesis and maturation.
  • Matrix and cytokine modulation - reduced MMP-1, MMP-13 and IL-6, contributing to metabolic normalisation.
  • Disruption of calcification - breaks down calcium deposits in calcific tendinitis.
  • Analgesia - altered nociceptor input and central mechanisms reduce pain.

Types. Focused ESWT (f-ESWT) concentrates energy at a defined focal point; radial ESWT (r-ESWT) spreads a lower-energy pressure wave over a larger area and is simpler and cheaper. Evidence does not clearly favour one over the other for most tendinopathies.

Dosage parameters. Energy flux density typically 0.1-0.3 mJ/mm2 for low-energy and up to about 0.5 mJ/mm2 for high-energy treatment; 1,500-3,000 pulses per session; frequency around 4-15 Hz; three to five sessions at weekly intervals. Parameters are set according to the tendon, the tissue depth and patient tolerance.

Indications. Chronic plantar fasciitis, calcific and non-calcific rotator cuff tendinopathy, lateral epicondylalgia, Achilles and patellar tendinopathy, and delayed fracture or tendon-bone healing. Contraindications and precautions include application over malignancy, infection, open wounds, over the lung or major nerves and vessels, coagulopathy, pregnancy, and in children over growth plates. Transient skin reddening, bruising and discomfort are common and usually minor.

Clinical use. ESWT is usually an adjunct to loading exercise, not a stand-alone cure. Best results occur when it is combined with progressive eccentric and concentric exercise and load management. The evidence is strongest for plantar fasciitis and mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy and weaker for insertional Achilles tendinopathy.

5Recent advances

  • Paantjens et al. (2022) — A systematic review in Sports Medicine - Open found that adding ESWT to a tendon-loading programme produced clinically important improvement in mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, but could not support its use for insertional Achilles tendinopathy.
  • Charles et al. (2023) — A systematic review and meta-analysis in Frontiers in Immunology found high-quality evidence of a large effect for plantar fasciitis, but only low-to-moderate evidence with small effects for patellar and Achilles tendinopathy.
  • Majidi et al. (2024) — A systematic review and meta-analysis in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation of 45 trials found that ESWT significantly reduced pain across tendinopathies, with the largest effects for plantar fasciitis and rotator cuff tendinopathy.

6References

  2. Prentice WE. Therapeutic Modalities in Rehabilitation. 5th ed. McGraw-Hill; 2017.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2018.
  4. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for mid-portion and insertional Achilles tendinopathy: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Sports Med Open. 2022;8:68.
  5. Biological effects of extracorporeal shockwave therapy in tendons: a systematic review. 2022.
  6. The effectiveness of shockwave therapy on patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy and plantar fasciitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Immunol. 2023;14:1193835.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Describe work related musculoskeletal disorders seen in rock drillers.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Occupational health and work-related musculoskeletal disorders.

★ Memory hook — The drill shakes the hand, the hand shakes the nerve, and the nerve shakes the whole arm.

1Introduction

Rock drillers use heavy, hand-held percussive and rotary tools that expose them to intense hand-arm vibration, repetitive gripping, awkward postures, whole-body vibration and heavy manual handling. The resulting work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a well-recognised occupational problem, dominated by hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS) but also including disorders of the shoulder, elbow, wrist and spine. These are dose-related and largely preventable.

2Physiology

Hand-transmitted vibration is measured as the frequency-weighted, eight-hour energy-equivalent acceleration (A(8)) and governed by the ISO 5349 standard. Vibration at the frequencies generated by percussive drills (largely 20-500 Hz) is absorbed mainly by the fingers and hand but lower-frequency components travel to the arm, shoulder and neck. Repeated gripping and vibration cause vascular, neurological and musculoskeletal changes. Sustained static grip, awkward wrist and shoulder positions and whole-body vibration during drilling add further load.

3Pathophysiology

HAVS has three components. The vascular component is vibration-induced white finger: episodic blanching of the fingers after cold exposure, caused by vasospasm of the digital arteries and arterioles. The sensorineural component is vibration-induced neuropathy, with numbness, tingling, reduced tactile and thermal sensation and impaired dexterity. The musculoskeletal component includes reduced grip strength, carpal tunnel syndrome, tenosynovitis, epicondylalgia, shoulder tendinopathy and degenerative joint changes, and vibration exposure is associated with cysts and osteoarthritis. The condition is dose-dependent: prevalence and severity rise with years of exposure, and a classic study of rock drillers found vibration white finger in about half, with a median latent period of roughly seven to eight years and blanching in up to 80% of those exposed for sixteen years or more. Whole-body vibration and awkward postures contribute to low back and neck pain.

4Answer

Recognising the disorders. Stage HAVS using the Stockholm workshop scales for the vascular (white finger) and sensorineural components, and record the history of exposure, latency and cold provocation. Measure grip strength, and test sensation (vibration and thermal thresholds). Screen for carpal tunnel syndrome, lateral epicondylalgia, shoulder impingement and spinal pain.

Prevention and exposure control (first-line).

  • Reduce vibration at source: choose low-vibration tools, maintain and service equipment, and use the correct tool for the task.
  • Limit exposure time and rotate workers so that daily A(8) stays within ISO 5349 limits; avoid piecework that drives over-exposure.
  • Use anti-vibration gloves and supports, and warm, dry gloves to reduce vasospasm.
  • Keep hands warm, avoid smoking (which worsens vasoconstriction) and avoid cold after exposure.
  • Health surveillance with regular examination so that early signs are detected and the worker is redeployed before permanent damage.

Physiotherapy management.

  • Advise on stopping or reducing exposure and on self-monitoring of white-finger attacks.
  • Graded strengthening and endurance training of the forearm and shoulder muscles; tendon gliding and nerve mobilisation for the upper limb.
  • Desensitisation and sensory re-education for the sensorineural component.
  • Ergonomic advice on grip technique, wrist posture, rest breaks and tool handling; work-station and task redesign.
  • Treat secondary conditions - carpal tunnel, epicondylalgia, shoulder tendinopathy and spinal pain - with the appropriate modality and exercise.
  • Educate on the importance of early reporting, since once the vascular damage is established it is largely irreversible.

Outcome measures. Stockholm staging, grip strength, monofilament and vibration thresholds, symptom diaries and work-ability measures.

5Recent advances

  • Tanveer et al. (2025) — A cross-sectional study in the Journal of Hand Therapy reported a high prevalence of hand-arm vibration syndrome in mine workers at the Khewra salt mines, with hand discolouration, tingling and loss of grip strength among the most common symptoms.
  • Bovenzi et al. (1994) — Studies of quarry drillers and stone workers showed a dose-response relation for vibration-induced white finger, with prevalence rising with the lifetime vibration dose.
  • Marufa et al. (2023) — A pre-experimental study in the Physical Therapy Journal of Indonesia found that neurodynamic (neural) mobilisation significantly reduced sensorineural symptoms on the Stockholm Workshop Scale in workers with HAVS, supporting manual therapy in physiotherapy management.
  • Tekavec et al. (2023) — A clinical study in Occupational and Environmental Medicine found that the International Consensus Criteria regrade HAVS severity lower than the Stockholm Workshop Scale and stressed assessing small and large nerve fibres and cold intolerance, refining physiotherapy assessment.

6References

  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Write in detail about the work conditioning program for mason following a rotator cuff injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Work conditioning / vocational rehabilitation.

★ Memory hook — Do not just treat the shoulder - rebuild the mason, task by task.

1Introduction

A mason performs heavy overhead and repetitive work: laying bricks above shoulder height, carrying blocks, mixing and lifting mortar and gripping trowels. After a rotator cuff injury these demands exceed the shoulder's capacity, so a clinic-based programme alone is not enough. Work conditioning is a structured, work-oriented, progressive programme that rebuilds the strength, endurance and task tolerance needed for the mason's job and returns the worker safely to duty.

2Physiology

The rotator cuff - supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis and teres minor - centres the humeral head and provides dynamic stability, while the deltoid produces the lifting force. Overhead work loads the cuff and subacromial space, and repeated lifting needs both strength and endurance. Tendon healing passes through inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases, tolerating increasing load over time. Cardiovascular fitness and general work capacity also determine how many hours a mason can sustain.

3Pathophysiology

Rotator cuff injury ranges from tendinopathy and partial tears to full-thickness tears, producing pain, weakness (especially with elevation and external rotation), night pain and functional loss. In a mason this means difficulty lifting a brick, working overhead and sustaining a full shift; deconditioning and fear of movement add to the disability. Unmanaged, weakness and poor scapular control perpetuate subacromial irritation and prevent return to work.

4Answer

Assessment and job demands analysis first. Measure pain (NPRS), range of motion, cuff and scapular strength, and function (DASH, SPADI, Constant score). Perform a functional capacity evaluation (FCE) and a job-demand analysis of the mason's tasks - weights lifted, heights worked, repetition, duration and postures - to set objective return-to-work targets.

Programme structure. Work conditioning is usually delivered three to five days per week, two to four hours per day, for four to eight weeks, combining physical conditioning with simulated work tasks.

  • Pain and symptom control - relative rest, activity modification, appropriate modalities and education, without prolonged immobilisation.
  • Mobility - restore glenohumeral and scapulothoracic range, then thoracic mobility.
  • Strengthening - progressive cuff and scapular strengthening, then larger pushing, pulling and overhead patterns; begin with isometrics, progress to bands, then free weights, one to three sets of 8-15 repetitions, three to five times weekly.
  • Endurance and cardiovascular conditioning - arm ergometry, circuit training and general aerobic work to build shift tolerance.
  • Work simulation / job-specific training - graded lifting (brick boxes or weighted crates from floor to waist, then chest, then overhead), carrying, reaching, trowel use, and sustained overhead work; increase weight, repetitions and duration gradually.
  • Ergonomics and education - correct lifting mechanics, keeping loads close, using scaffolds and hoists, pacing, and the value of graded activity.
  • Psychosocial support - address fear-avoidance, catastrophising and work confidence, with CBT or psychologically informed practice where needed.

Progression and return-to-work criteria. Progress by time before load, and by load before speed. Return to work when strength is at least about 80% of the uninvolved side, pain is controlled, the worker can complete the simulated task at the required weight and duration, and cardiovascular fitness is adequate. Use modified duties or a graded return (partial hours, no overhead work) as a bridge.

Outcome measures. DASH/QuickDASH, SPADI, grip and shoulder strength, FCE task performance, pain scores, and work-ability or lost-time measures.

5Recent advances

  • Cullen et al. (2017) — A systematic review in the Journal of Occupational Rehabilitation found strong evidence that multi-domain return-to-work interventions (combining health care, service coordination and work modification) reduce lost time for musculoskeletal conditions.
  • Cheng & Hung (2007) — A randomised controlled trial found that workplace-based work hardening returned 71% of workers with work-related rotator cuff disorder to work versus 37% for clinic-based work hardening, and lowered self-reported shoulder problems.
  • Dyer et al. (2022) — A clinical practice guideline in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy recommended an active, task-oriented rehabilitation programme plus early, multi-stakeholder return-to-work planning for adults with rotator cuff disorders.
  • Schaafsma et al. (2013) — A Cochrane review of physical conditioning as part of a return-to-work strategy found that workplace-based or workplace-visited programmes may reduce sickness absence, especially in chronic back pain.
  • Skamagki et al. (2026) — A systematic review in BMJ Open of workplace interventions for chronic musculoskeletal disorders found that multicomponent programmes combining exercise, ergonomics and education gave the most consistent benefits.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe the management and rehabilitation following total Patellectomy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit — Rehabilitation following knee surgery / extensor mechanism.

★ Memory hook — No patella, no lever - so you must rebuild the brake and the spring with muscle.

1Introduction

Total patellectomy is the complete removal of the patella, now performed only as a last resort for severe patellofemoral destruction, comminuted fracture, infection or tumour. It is radical because the patella is the fulcrum of the extensor mechanism. Management is therefore both surgical (reconstruction) and rehabilitative, aiming to restore extension, strength and function despite the lost lever.

2Physiology

The patella increases the moment arm of the quadriceps, centralises the extensor mechanism and protects the front of the knee. Removing it reduces the quadriceps lever arm by roughly a third and lowers extensor efficiency, so more quadriceps force is needed for the same task. Normal knee function depends on the quadriceps (extension, shock absorption, stair and sit-to-stand control) and the hamstrings (flexion and dynamic stability). Healing after patellectomy involves repair of the reconstructed extensor mechanism, and the surrounding muscles must compensate for the lost patella.

3Pathophysiology

Loss of the patella produces a characteristic set of problems: reduced extensor moment arm and quadriceps strength (reported losses of 45-60% in some series), extensor lag or difficulty achieving full extension against gravity, reduced range of motion (active flexion often around 110 degrees), anterior knee pain, instability, altered gait (with compensatory early soleus activity) and reduced function. Weakness of the hamstrings correlates with poorer outcomes, and loss of quadriceps function of more than about 40% is associated with functional impairment.

4Answer

Post-operative rehabilitation is phase-based and must protect the reconstructed extensor mechanism while rebuilding strength.

Phase 1 - Protection and early motion (weeks 0-2). Immobilise or brace as the surgeon directs; control swelling with cryotherapy, elevation and compression; isometric quadriceps and hamstring setting; ankle pumps; passive and active-assisted knee flexion within safe limits; and protected weight-bearing. Goal: protect the repair, control pain and swelling, and begin muscle activation.

Phase 2 - Early strengthening (weeks 2-6). Progress active-assisted to active range of motion; straight-leg raises; terminal knee extension; closed-chain work such as mini-squats and step-ups as tolerated; patellar-mobilisation equivalent is not applicable, but soft-tissue and scar mobilisation around the knee is important. Begin gait re-education.

Phase 3 - Progressive strengthening and function (weeks 6-12). Progressive resistance training for quadriceps and, importantly, the hamstrings; eccentric quadriceps work; proprioceptive and balance training; stationary cycling; stair practice. Aim for full functional range and good eccentric control.

Phase 4 - Advanced and return to activity (3-6 months and beyond). Sport- or job-specific training, plyometrics as appropriate, and endurance work. Quadriceps and hamstring strengthening continues for many months.

Key principles.

  • Strengthen the hamstrings as well as the quadriceps - hamstring function is a strong predictor of a good outcome.
  • Train eccentric control and full knee extension against gravity.
  • Restore a normal gait pattern to reduce energy cost and compensations.
  • Reinforce the extensor mechanism, where the surgeon has reconstructed it, before aggressive loading.

Outcome measures. Range of motion, isokinetic quadriceps and hamstring strength, extensor lag, gait analysis, the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS), Knee Society Score and functional tests (sit-to-stand, stairs, 6-minute walk).

5Recent advances

  • Tozzi et al. (2026) — A case report of physical rehabilitation after total patellectomy described recovery to 110 degrees of active flexion, quadriceps strength of about 57% of the other side, independent gait and large gains on the Lower Extremity Functional Scale.
  • Kuster & Blatter (1996) — An isokinetic study in Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy showed that loss of quadriceps function greater than 40% after patellectomy correlates with proportional hamstring loss and a poorer functional result, so peak flexion torque can guide rehabilitation targets.
  • Watkins et al. (1983) — A classic isokinetic study in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery quantified the quadriceps and hamstring strength deficits after patellectomy, establishing the muscle-function losses that physiotherapy must target.

6References

  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. F.A. Davis; 2019.
  3. Brotzman SB, Manske RC, eds. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation: A Team Approach. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2018.
  4. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw-Hill; 2020.
