Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults following total knee replacement.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 10 – Pre- and postoperative evaluation and screening for arthroplasty

★ Memory hook — "Fitness for TKR is H-E-A-R-T-S: History, Exercise capacity, Anaemia, Risk (cardiac), Thrombosis risk, Screening & function."

1Introduction

Total knee replacement (TKR) is offered to adults with advanced knee arthritis when pain and disability are no longer controlled by conservative care. Fitness evaluation around TKR has two complementary purposes. The first is preoperative fitness assessment — determining whether the patient is medically and functionally fit to undergo anaesthesia and surgery, and optimising modifiable risk factors to reduce complications. The second is postoperative evaluation of fitness — judging whether the patient is fit to progress through rehabilitation, to bear weight, to be discharged and to return to activity. Both are structured, criteria-based processes that combine medical risk assessment with functional and psychological evaluation, and both rely on objective, validated tools rather than impression alone.

2Physiology

Undergoing and recovering from TKR demands physiological reserve. The heart must tolerate the stress of surgery and of early mobilisation, the lungs must maintain oxygenation, the blood must carry sufficient oxygen (adequate haemoglobin), and the renal, endocrine and coagulation systems must remain stable. Functionally, the patient needs adequate quadriceps and hip strength, a stable and balanced gait, sufficient range of knee motion for walking and transfers, and enough aerobic capacity to walk and exercise. Normal knee function after TKR approximates 0 degrees of extension to about 110–120 degrees of flexion, with good quadriceps control. These physiological requirements define the targets of fitness evaluation.

3Pathophysiology

Adults awaiting TKR often carry comorbidities — ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, obesity, chronic lung disease and venous thromboembolism risk — that increase the chance of perioperative complications such as myocardial infarction, stroke, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, infection and delayed wound healing. Reduced preoperative fitness and functional capacity are independently associated with slower recovery, longer hospital stay and poorer outcomes. Postoperatively, stiffness, quadriceps weakness, poor balance and cardiopulmonary deconditioning limit the ability to mobilise safely. Fitness evaluation targets these mechanisms so that risk can be quantified and modified before surgery and progress can be judged safely afterwards.

4Answer

(a) Preoperative fitness evaluation

  1. Cardiovascular risk assessment: structured evaluation of venous thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk factors (history of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia and stroke) within 30 days of surgery. For patients aged 65 or older, those aged 45–64 with significant cardiovascular disease, or those with a Revised Cardiac Risk Index of one or more, measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP is recommended to refine risk.
  2. Functional capacity screening: screen all patients with a validated tool such as the Duke Activity Status Index, Godin-Shephard questionnaire or International Physical Activity Questionnaire. Reduced capacity warrants objective assessment — cardiopulmonary exercise testing is the gold standard, with simpler alternatives (incremental shuttle walk test, 6-minute walk test, one-minute sit-to-stand, Timed Up and Go) where it is unavailable.
  3. Comorbidity optimisation: control of diabetes, hypertension, anaemia, heart failure, lung disease, renal and liver impairment, and sleep-disordered breathing; review of opioids and dependency-forming drugs; and referral of complex chronic-pain patients to a pain team.
  4. Thrombosis and infection risk: assess venous thromboembolism risk and screen for active infection or colonisation (including dental and skin sources) before implantation.
  5. Nutrition, obesity and smoking: identify modifiable factors; a body mass index threshold is often used to prompt referral to weight management, and smoking cessation is advised.
  6. Psychological and educational assessment: screen for anxiety and depression and provide pre-operative education and prehabilitation to set realistic expectations and improve outcomes.

(b) Postoperative fitness evaluation for progression and discharge

  1. Medical stability: stable vital signs, controlled pain, no signs of infection, DVT or pulmonary embolism, adequate wound healing and haemoglobin.
  2. Functional criteria: ability to perform safe transfers and to mobilise with the prescribed aid, independent or assisted ambulation, and adequate knee extension and flexion for function.
  3. Strength and balance: sufficient quadriceps control and standing balance for safe walking and stair use.
  4. Wound and skin: clean, dry, healing wound and no skin breakdown.
  5. Outcome measures: Oxford Knee Score or Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, knee range of motion, quadriceps strength, Timed Up and Go and 6-minute walk test to document function.
  6. Education and self-management: competence with home exercises, precautions and recognition of warning signs.

5Recent advances

  • UK Centre for Perioperative Care (2021) — guidance established that all surgical candidates should be screened for reduced functional capacity with a validated tool such as the Duke Activity Status Index, and that improving fitness before surgery (prehabilitation) reduces complications and length of stay.
  • Anderson et al. (2021) — a UK modified Delphi consensus produced recommendations for pre-operative TKR education and prehabilitation, including exercise, weight management and psychological support.
  • Nguyen et al. (2022) — a landmark multicentre randomised trial (EDEX, 262 patients) found that multidisciplinary prehabilitation before TKR did not improve short-term functional independence or midterm activity limitations versus usual care, tempering claims for routine prehabilitation although uptake of the intervention was low.
  • Konnyu et al. (2022) — a systematic review of 13 TKA trials found prehabilitation may increase strength and reduce length of stay (low certainty) without added harms, but has little effect on pain, range of motion or activities of daily living.
  • Wu et al. (2026) — a network meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials found prehabilitation effects are outcome-specific: resistance training best improved functional reserve (Timed Up and Go, quadriceps strength), neuromuscular and aerobic training best reduced pain, and multimodal exercise best improved knee flexion range of motion.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2018.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2019.
  3. Centre for Perioperative Care. Preoperative Assessment and Optimisation for Adult Surgery. London: CPOC; 2021.
  4. Halvorsen S, Mehilli J, Cassese S, et al. 2022 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular assessment and management of patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery. Eur Heart J. 2022;43(39):3826–3924.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Discuss the interventions to improve muscle performance following flexor tendon repair of the hand.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Hand and Tendon Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Repair the tendon, then make it glide before you make it strong.

1Introduction

Flexor tendon injuries of the hand, especially in zone II (Bunnell's "no man's land"), are among the most demanding problems in hand rehabilitation. Surgery restores continuity, but the final result depends on rehabilitation that restores tendon glide, prevents adhesion and rupture, and rebuilds muscle performance — that is, strength, endurance and coordinated grip. Muscle performance after repair is therefore the product of controlled early motion, graded loading and functional retraining, not of immobilisation.

2Physiology

Tendon healing passes through three overlapping phases: an inflammatory phase (0–7 days), a fibroblastic or proliferative phase (5–21 days) and a remodelling phase (beyond 21 days). The repaired tendon is nourished both intrinsically (synovial fluid diffusion through the vincula and sheath) and extrinsically (from the surrounding tissues). Controlled tension and motion align collagen fibres along lines of stress, raise tensile strength and discourage adhesions, whereas prolonged immobilisation allows adhesions to mature and muscle to waste. Flexor muscles are also highly sensitive to disuse: within weeks of immobilisation there is measurable loss of cross-sectional area, strength and endurance, so mobilisation is simultaneously a tendon and a muscle intervention.

3Pathophysiology

When motion is inadequate or excessive, complications appear. Adhesions between tendon and sheath cause loss of glide and flexion contractures; excessive load causes gap formation or rupture, which is most likely in the first 7–10 days when repair strength is lowest; and immobilisation produces muscle atrophy, joint stiffness and a weak, poorly coordinated grip. Zone II repairs are the most vulnerable because both flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus lie within a tight fibro-osseous tunnel.

4Answer

Interventions are organised into four overlapping phases. The therapist works with the surgeon, since the allowed load depends on the number of core suture strands (typically four to six for early active motion).

Phase 1 (0–3/4 weeks) — protection and glide. A dorsal blocking orthosis holds the wrist in 20–30° extension, MCP joints in 50–70° flexion and IP joints in extension. Oedema is controlled with elevation and compression. The classic programme (modified Duran) uses passive finger flexion with active finger extension; the Kleinert programme uses a dynamic traction splint. Place-and-hold (active hold in the passively flexed position) and tenodesis (wrist extension with finger relaxation, wrist flexion with finger flexion) encourage glide. Exercise is performed 10 repetitions every hour, in 4–6 sessions daily.

Phase 2 (3–6 weeks) — early active motion. Active finger flexion is begun through a partial range (the first third to two-thirds), because the tendon is smoothest and bending forces are lowest in mid-range. Tang's passive-active protocol recommends at least 40, ideally 60–80, cycles of active flexion per session — roughly 200–300 cycles daily — before progressing to full range by weeks 4–6. The orthosis is weaned.

Phase 3 (6–12 weeks) — strength and differential glide. Full active range is regained, and gentle resistance, blocking exercises to isolate FDS and FDP, tendon-gliding exercises and grip strengthening are added. Resistance begins at 3 sets × 10 repetitions and progresses weekly.

Phase 4 (beyond 12 weeks) — work conditioning. Progressive resistance training, endurance work, power and pinch grip and job-specific tasks restore muscle performance for daily living and occupation.

ProgrammeMotion allowedLoad on repairTypical use
ImmobilisationNoneMinimalUnreliable repair/patient
Passive (Duran/Kleinert)Passive flexion, active extensionLowWeaker repairs
Place-and-holdActive hold in flexed positionModerate2–6 strand repairs
Early active motionTrue active partial-range flexionHigherStrong 4–6 strand repairs

Outcome measures: total active motion (TAM) and the Strickland formula, grip and pinch strength (Jamar dynamometer), and the DASH questionnaire track muscle and hand performance.

5Recent advances

  • Mortada et al. (2024) — systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies (1414 patients) showing early active motion gives greater range of motion than passive protocols after zone II repair, with comparable re-operation rates, so strongly repaired tendons can be mobilised actively.
  • Starr et al. (2013) — systematic review of 34 studies found early passive protocols had a lower rupture rate but greater loss of digital motion, while early active protocols gave better motion, supporting active mobilisation as suture technique and repair strength improved.
  • Tang (2021) — the Nantong partial-range active flexion protocol glides the repaired tendon through only the initial one-third to two-thirds of flexion, where bending forces are lowest, protecting the repair while preventing adhesions.
  • Peck et al. (2014) — the Manchester short splint permits earlier wrist motion than the traditional forearm-based splint, reducing PIP flexion contracture and improving the digital flexion arc without increasing rupture.
  • Groth (2004) — the "Pyramid of Progressive Force Application" grades eight exercises from lowest to highest tendon load and guides progression by tissue response rather than by time alone.

6References

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Explain the educational and behavioural strategies in managing osteoarthritis of knee pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Osteoarthritis — Education and Behaviour

★ Memory hook — OA is not wear-and-tear; it is load-and-learn.

1Introduction

Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint, biopsychosocial condition, not simply a worn-out cartilage surface. Education and behavioural strategies are now recognised as core treatments, alongside exercise, because pain and disability in OA are shaped as much by beliefs, fear, coping and self-management as by the joint itself. The physiotherapist's task is to change how the patient understands and lives with OA, not only to strengthen the quadriceps.

2Physiology

Normal cartilage is avascular and nourished by synovial fluid through cyclic loading and unloading. Regular, moderate joint movement improves cartilage nutrition, strengthens periarticular muscle, improves proprioception and maintains joint range. Mild inflammation is part of normal tissue repair. These facts matter because they underpin the message that sensible activity protects rather than harms the knee.

3Pathophysiology

In OA, cartilage fibrillation, subchondral bone remodelling and synovitis produce nociceptive input. Persistent pain leads to central sensitisation, pain catastrophising, kinesiophobia and fear-avoidance, which reduce activity, decondition the quadriceps and worsen disability — a self-reinforcing cycle. The therapist therefore treats the maladaptive beliefs and behaviours, not just the joint.

4Answer

Educational and behavioural strategies work best when combined with exercise and delivered over several sessions.

Education. Pain neuroscience education explains that pain is a protective output of the nervous system rather than a direct readout of damage; that OA is not a fixed "wear-and-tear" process; and that graded activity is safe. Arthritis education is a core treatment in the OARSI 2019 guidelines. Simple, reassuring explanations, written material and clear prognosis reduce fear and improve adherence.

Self-management programmes. Structured programmes such as the Arthritis Self-Management Programme teach patients to monitor symptoms, pace activity, use heat or cold, manage flare-ups and solve problems. OARSI 2019 conditionally recommends self-management programmes across all comorbidity subgroups.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). CBT targets unhelpful thoughts and behaviours through cognitive restructuring, activity pacing, graded activity, relaxation and coping-skills training. OARSI 2019 recommends CBT with an exercise component, particularly for patients with widespread pain or depression.

Behaviour-change techniques. Goal setting (specific, measurable, achievable), motivational interviewing, self-monitoring with activity diaries or apps, feedback, prompts and relapse-prevention planning all increase exercise adherence. Shared decision-making and a therapeutic alliance improve outcomes.

Weight and lifestyle. Dietary weight management combined with exercise is a core treatment for knee OA; even modest weight loss reduces knee load and pain. Aquatic exercise, Tai Chi and yoga are safe adjuncts.

DomainStrategyTarget
EducationalPain neuroscience education, arthritis educationBeliefs, understanding
BehaviouralCBT, pacing, graded activity, self-monitoringCoping, adherence
Self-managementStructured programmes, flare-up plansIndependence
LifestyleWeight management, mind–body exerciseJoint load, general health

Outcome measures: WOMAC or KOOS, numeric pain rating, the Pain Catastrophising Scale, Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia and measures of adherence and self-efficacy.

5Recent advances

  • OARSI (2019) guideline — makes arthritis education and structured land-based exercise core treatments for knee OA, with CBT and self-management programmes conditionally recommended across comorbidity groups.
  • NICE (2022) guideline — the NG226 guideline recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the person, combined with an education or behaviour-change package as core care for osteoarthritis, and reassures patients that exercise-related pain does not mean joint harm.
  • Nelligan et al. (2021) — a randomised trial of 206 people found a self-directed web-based strengthening programme supported by automated behaviour-change text messages improved knee pain and function at 24 weeks compared with information alone.
  • Supe et al. (2023) — a randomised trial showed pain neuroscience education added to exercise via telerehabilitation reduced pain catastrophising and pain intensity in knee OA, supporting education as an active treatment.
  • Hurley et al. (2007) — structured self-management programmes retain benefit on pain and quality of life in knee OA and are now embedded in stepped-care pathways.

6References

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. How do you apply the functional concepts in rehabilitation of adhesive capsulitis of shoulder.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Shoulder Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Freezing means calm it, frozen means stretch it, thawing means use it.

1Introduction

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is a painful, progressive loss of glenohumeral movement caused by capsular fibrosis and contracture, usually in three overlapping phases — freezing (painful), frozen (stiff) and thawing (recovering). Because the disability is functional (dressing, reaching, sleeping), rehabilitation must be stage-matched and functionally oriented, not simply a set of passive stretches.

2Physiology

The glenohumeral joint is a mobile ball-and-socket whose stability depends on the capsule, the coracohumeral ligament and the rotator interval. Normal movement requires arthrokinematics (roll and glide) and a scapulohumeral rhythm of roughly two degrees of humeral to one degree of scapular motion. Capsular extensibility is maintained by regular end-range movement; when this is lost, connective tissue shortens and the muscle and capsular mechanoreceptors alter their input.

3Pathophysiology

In frozen shoulder, fibroblastic proliferation and myofibroblast activity, driven by cytokines such as TGF-beta and PDGF, thicken and contract the capsule, reducing joint volume and producing pain and stiffness. Pain and capsular tightness alter scapular mechanics, rotator cuff activation and proprioception, so the shoulder becomes functionally limited. Diabetes and thyroid disease are common associations and worsen prognosis.

4Answer

Functional rehabilitation is organised by stage, with the functional goal (for example dressing, hair care, reaching a shelf, hand behind back) agreed with the patient from the outset.

Freezing (painful) phase. The priority is pain relief and maintaining range, not aggressive stretching. Use gentle pendular exercises, active-assisted range, pain-free mobilisation (Maitland grades I–II), scapular mobility, and modalities such as heat, laser or TENS. Vigorous mobilisation is avoided because it aggravates inflammation.

Frozen (stiff) phase. With pain settling, the aim shifts to regaining range. Progress to end-range mobilisation (grades III–IV), sustained stretching of the posterior capsule (cross-body adduction, sleeper stretch), anterior capsule stretch, and proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation (PNF) patterns. Mobilisation-with-movement (Mulligan) and muscle energy techniques are useful. Cane or wand exercises, wall slides and pulleys let the patient self-stretch at home, 3–4 sessions a day of 10–15 minutes.

Thawing phase. Range returns spontaneously; the focus is on strengthening the rotator cuff and scapular stabilisers and on functional, task-specific practice — reaching overhead, behind the back, dressing and carrying.

Functional concepts applied throughout. Train movements the patient actually needs (hand behind back for toileting and dressing, hand to mouth for feeding, overhead reach for shelves). Use task-specific practice, closed- and open-chain exercise, scapular stabilisation and rotator cuff rehabilitation, and home exercises in the functional ranges. Outcome measures include the SPADI and DASH questionnaires and goniometry of flexion, abduction and rotation.

PhasePain/stiffnessPriorityMain methods
FreezingHigh pain, early stiffnessPain relief, maintain rangePendulum, grade I–II mobilisation, modalities
FrozenLow pain, marked stiffnessRegain rangeGrade III–IV mobilisation, PNF, stretching, MWM
ThawingMinimal pain, improving rangeStrength, functionRotator cuff and scapular strengthening, task training

5Recent advances

  • Rangan et al. (2020) — the UK FROST multicentre randomised trial found physiotherapy with steroid injection, manipulation under anaesthesia and arthroscopic capsular release were not clinically superior to one another, supporting a trial of conservative, stage-matched physiotherapy first.
  • Page et al. (2014) — the Cochrane review of 32 trials (1836 participants) synthesised the evidence on manual therapy and exercise for adhesive capsulitis, showing mobilisation with supervised exercise gives worthwhile short-term gains in pain and function.
  • Zhang et al. (2021) — an updated network meta-analysis ranked capsular distension (hydrodilatation) highly for short-term pain relief and function, with extracorporeal shockwave and laser therapy showing promise.
  • Lin et al. (2022) — a pilot randomised trial showed proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation improved shoulder range and reduced pain, with MRI evidence of reduced coracohumeral ligament and capsular thickening.
  • Itoi et al. (2016) — the ISAKOS Upper Extremity Committee consensus prefers the term "frozen shoulder" over "adhesive capsulitis", since true adhesions are not present, and guides treatment by clinical stage.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. How would you analyze the selection of exercises to improve postural stability and balance in chronic ankle instability.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Ankle and Foot Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Find the deficit, then train that deficit — stable to unstable, eyes open to closed.

1Introduction

Chronic ankle instability (CAI) is the persistence of "giving way", pain and reduced function after lateral ankle sprain. It combines mechanical instability (ligament laxity) with functional instability (impaired proprioception and neuromuscular control). Exercise selection to improve postural stability and balance must therefore be driven by a careful assessment of the specific deficits, then progressed systematically from easy to demanding.

2Physiology

Postural control depends on sensory input from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint and cutaneous receptors, integrated centrally and expressed through feed-forward and feedback muscle activation. The ankle evertors (peroneals) and dorsiflexors are critical for resisting inversion, and their reaction time and strength determine how well the joint is protected. Balance is thus a sensorimotor skill, trainable through repetition.

3Pathophysiology

After sprain, ligament laxity, damaged mechanoreceptors, delayed peroneal reaction time, reduced dorsiflexion range, altered arthrokinematics and, in some patients, cortical sensorimotor changes produce recurrent instability and reduced dynamic balance. The therapist must identify which component dominates in each patient, because this determines which exercises are chosen.

4Answer

Step 1 — Assess the deficits. Use the Star Excursion Balance Test or Y-Balance Test for dynamic balance, single-leg stance (eyes open/closed, firm/foam) for static balance, the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT) and Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) for self-reported function, and isokinetic or handheld dynamometry for evertor and dorsiflexor strength.

Step 2 — Match exercise to deficit.

  • Static balance deficit: single-leg stance progressions.
  • Dynamic balance deficit: reach tasks, wobble board, BOSU.
  • Reactive deficit: perturbation, hop-and-stick, drop landings.
  • Strength deficit: peroneal and dorsiflexor resistance work.

Step 3 — Progress the challenge. Move from bilateral to unilateral, eyes open to eyes closed, firm to unstable surface, static to dynamic, single task to dual task (adding a cognitive task), and finally to sport-specific and plyometric work. Dosage of roughly 4–6 weeks, three times weekly, three to four sets per exercise, is supported by the literature.

Deficit foundExercise choiceProgression
Static balanceSingle-leg stanceEyes closed → foam → perturbation
Dynamic balanceSEBT reaches, wobble boardStable → unstable surface
Reactive controlHop-and-stick, drop landingPlanned → unplanned direction
StrengthPeroneal/dorsiflexor resistanceIsometric → dynamic → eccentric

Step 4 — Reassess and progress. Re-test balance and function regularly; progress only when the current level is mastered without pain or giving way, and maintain a long-term home programme, because gains partly decline after six months.

5Recent advances

  • Mollà-Casanova et al. (2021) — a meta-analysis of 15 trials confirmed balance training significantly improves function, instability and dynamic balance in CAI, and is superior to general exercise for functional outcomes.
  • Koshino & Kobayashi (2023) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of conservative interventions found both balance and strength training improve static and dynamic balance in CAI, supporting exercise-based rehabilitation as first-line care.
  • Hou et al. (2022) — a one-year prospective study showed three months of supervised balance training improved postural control and strength in CAI, but some gains declined by six months, and high Beighton scores and initial inversion weakness predicted re-sprain, so dorsiflexion and eversion strengthening should be added.
  • Wang et al. (2023) — a meta-analysis of dual-task training in CAI found it improved dynamic balance and reduced centre-of-pressure area, supporting the addition of cognitive tasks to balance work.
  • Sierra-Guzmán et al. (2018) — a randomised trial found whole-body vibration added to balance training improved sensorimotor balance outcomes in recreational athletes with CAI.

6References

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the functional training methods in treatment of musculoskeletal conditions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Functional Training

★ Memory hook — Train the task, not just the tissue.

1Introduction

Functional training is a task-oriented, activity-based approach in which the patient practises the movements and activities they actually need, rather than isolated muscle actions alone. It is a top-down strategy: instead of only strengthening an impairment, it trains the whole functional task, promoting transfer to daily life, work and sport. In musculoskeletal rehabilitation it is used across fracture, joint replacement, back pain, tendon and sports injuries.

2Physiology

Functional training rests on motor learning and neuroplasticity. Skills are acquired through repeated, meaningful practice with feedback, and the nervous system reorganises in response to that practice. Training is specific: the body adapts to the exact task, load and context trained, so the closer the exercise is to the real task, the greater the transfer. Progressive overload, practice variability and part-to-whole learning drive adaptation.

3Pathophysiology

Musculoskeletal injury produces pain, weakness, loss of range and altered movement strategies. Prolonged protection and fear of movement (kinesiophobia) lead to deconditioning and maladaptive movement habits, so patients may regain strength without regaining function. Functional training directly addresses this gap by retraining the tasks that are limited.

4Answer

Functional training methods are applied along a continuum, from isolated to integrated to truly functional work.

Task-oriented training. The patient practises real, meaningful tasks — reaching, lifting, carrying, dressing, stair climbing, working — with difficulty graded to the current ability.

Motor skill training. For chronic low back pain, person-specific training changes how the patient performs a pain-provoking activity (for example, bending to pick up an object), using motor-learning principles rather than strength exercises alone.

Occupational and work simulation. Job-specific tasks, lifting technique and work conditioning prepare the patient for return to work.

Progressive functional exercise. Isolated strengthening is integrated into functional patterns; closed-chain, balance, perturbation and plyometric exercises are added as tolerated.

Graded activity and graded exposure. Activity is increased in a planned way to overcome fear-avoidance and build tolerance.

Principles. Specificity, overload, progression, individualisation, feedback, practice variability and part-to-whole sequencing govern the programme. Outcome measures include the Patient-Specific Functional Scale, DASH, WOMAC and job-related measures.

LevelExamplePurpose
IsolatedQuadriceps settingRestore activation
IntegratedSit-to-standCombine muscle groups
FunctionalStair climbing, liftingDaily-life transfer
Work/sportJob simulation, plyometricsReturn to role

5Recent advances

  • Monticone et al. (2021) — a randomised controlled trial showed task-oriented exercises based on patients' specific job activities plus occupational therapy produced clinically important, durable improvements in disability, pain and quality of life after surgically treated proximal humeral fracture.
  • Dudonienė et al. (2023) — a randomised trial found task-oriented exercise superior to conventional physiotherapy for hip function and dynamic balance in early rehabilitation after total hip replacement.
  • van Dillen et al. (2021) — a randomised trial found person-specific motor skill training in functional activities produced greater and more durable functional improvement than strength and flexibility exercise in chronic low back pain.
  • Nieves-Silva et al. (2025) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 trials reported functional task training significantly improves balance (Berg Balance Scale), mobility (Timed Up and Go) and endurance (6-minute walk test) in older adults.
  • Newington et al. (2024) — a systematic review of work-participation interventions for upper-limb musculoskeletal conditions found exercise-based, task-focused programmes had the most consistent benefit for return to work.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. How do you distinguish and prioritize the selection of different manual therapy methods for chronic non-specific neck pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Spine — Manual Therapy

★ Memory hook — Classify first, then choose the technique — and always pair it with exercise.

1Introduction

Chronic non-specific neck pain is neck pain without a specific pathological cause. Manual therapy is one component of a multimodal, classification-based approach and is never used in isolation. Distinguishing between the available manual therapy methods, and prioritising them, depends on the patient's impairment classification, irritability and stage, and on safety screening.

2Physiology

Manual therapy produces neurophysiological rather than purely mechanical effects. Mobilisation and manipulation stimulate joint and muscle mechanoreceptors — Ruffini endings, Pacinian corpuscles, Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles — which fire into the dorsal horn and trigger both segmental (gate-control) inhibition and descending pain-inhibitory pathways from the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla. This gives immediate hypoalgesia (a rise in pressure-pain threshold) within minutes of a cervical or thoracic technique. Cervical and thoracic techniques also influence segmental mobility and sensorimotor control, including joint position sense and deep cervical flexor endurance, and may transiently alter muscle tone and pain sensitivity. Because these effects are short-lived — hypoalgesia often lasts only 30–60 minutes — manual therapy opens a window in which exercise and education work, which is why it is combined with them rather than relied on alone.

3Pathophysiology

Persistent neck pain involves altered motor control (deep cervical flexor weakness with superficial flexor overactivity), reduced segmental mobility or hypermobility, myofascial trigger points, and central sensitisation with psychosocial contributors. The JOSPT neck pain guideline classifies patients into mobility deficits, movement coordination impairments (including whiplash), cervicogenic headache and radiating pain, because the appropriate manual therapy, its target region and its dosage differ for each. Chronicity also changes the tissue response: a stiff, hypomobile segment tolerates stronger mobilisation, whereas a sensitised, highly irritable segment needs gentle low-grade input.

4Answer

Distinguishing the methods.

  • Mobilisation vs manipulation: mobilisation uses low-velocity, graded oscillatory or sustained movements (Maitland grades I–V); manipulation is a single high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust beyond the physiological range.
  • Region: cervical versus thoracic mobilisation/manipulation; thoracic manipulation is often added for cervical mobility deficits.
  • Technique family: Maitland mobilisation, Mulligan sustained natural apophyseal glides (SNAGs), muscle energy technique, myofascial release and soft-tissue massage, and neural mobilisation.
  • Target tissue: articular (joint glides), myofascial (soft-tissue techniques) or neural (neurodynamic techniques).

Prioritising the selection.

  • By classification: mobility deficits → cervical and thoracic manipulation or mobilisation; movement coordination impairments (including whiplash) → mobilisation with a progressive exercise programme using cognitive behavioural principles; cervicogenic headache → C1–2 SNAG or upper cervical mobilisation/manipulation; radiating pain → intermittent mechanical cervical traction plus mobilisation.
  • By irritability: highly irritable conditions start with grade I–II mobilisation; less irritable conditions tolerate grade III–IV and manipulation.
  • By safety: screen for upper cervical instability, vertebrobasilar insufficiency and red flags before any thrust technique.
  • Always combined: manual therapy plus exercise and education, because manual therapy alone gives only short-term benefit.
FeatureMobilisationManipulation
VelocityLowHigh
AmplitudeGraded (I–V)Low, single thrust
Patient comfortGenerally comfortableMay cause brief soreness
Typical useIrritable or stiff jointsNon-irritable mobility deficits

Dosage parameters. Mobilisation is graded I–V (Maitland): grades I–II (small oscillations near the start of range, about 2–3 Hz for 30–60 seconds, repeated 3–4 times) for pain and high irritability; grades III–IV (larger oscillations to the limit of range, or a sustained stretch) for stiffness. Manipulation is a single high-velocity low-amplitude thrust, one to three per session, to the thoracic spine first. SNAGs are 6–10 pain-free repetitions, 3–5 times daily; muscle energy technique uses 3–5 repetitions of a 3–5 second submaximal contraction. A course is typically 6–12 sessions over 3–6 weeks.

Indian practice context. Indian patients often present late and expect passive treatment, so emphasise that the durable gains come from the home programme. Where supervised sessions are limited, teach a carer simple grade II self-mobilisation, prescribe daily SNAGs with walking, and review fortnightly — a low-contact model suited to busy government and rural clinics.

5Recent advances

  • Blanpied et al. (2017) — the JOSPT neck pain clinical practice guideline recommends a multimodal approach (thoracic and cervical manipulation or mobilisation, mixed exercise and education) for chronic neck pain with mobility deficits, rather than relying on passive techniques alone.
  • Gross et al. (2015) — the Cochrane review of 51 trials (2920 participants) found cervical manipulation and mobilisation give similar benefit and thoracic manipulation improves pain and function, but manipulation carries rare serious risk, so mobilisation is preferred.
  • Bussières et al. (2016) — the Canadian chiropractic clinical practice guideline recommends multimodal manual therapy including manipulation, mobilisation and soft-tissue therapy for persistent neck pain, with high-dose massage over no treatment.
  • Cleland et al. (2007) — developed a clinical prediction rule identifying patients with neck pain likely to benefit from thoracic spine thrust manipulation, supporting classification-based matching of technique to patient.

6References

  1. Blanpied PR, Gross AR, Elliott JM, et al. Neck pain: revision 2017. Clinical practice guidelines linked to the ICF from the Orthopaedic Section of the APTA. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2017;47(7):A1–A83.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Elaborate the neurological concepts and functional methods in rehabilitation of musculoskeletal dysfunctions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Neurological Concepts in MSK Rehabilitation

★ Memory hook — Pain lives in the brain; retrain the brain to retrain the movement.

1Introduction

Musculoskeletal dysfunction is not only a tissue problem. Persistent pain and injury change the nervous system — altering cortical body maps, sensorimotor control and movement strategies. Rehabilitation therefore applies neurological concepts (neuroplasticity, pain neuromatrix, sensorimotor integration) together with functional methods (task-oriented training, motor control retraining, graded motor imagery) to restore both movement and the brain's representation of it.

2Physiology

Movement is represented in the brain in distributed, overlapping cortical maps — the primary motor and somatosensory cortices, the premotor and supplementary motor areas, the cerebellum and the basal ganglia — and these maps are not fixed. Every skilled movement strengthens the synapses that produced it (long-term potentiation) and prunes those that were unused, so the map of a limb enlarges with training and shrinks with disuse or pain. Motor learning proceeds through three stages — cognitive, associative and autonomous — driven by task-specific, repetitive, meaningful practice with intrinsic (proprioceptive) and extrinsic (visual, verbal) feedback. Descending pathways from the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla modulate nociception, and normal movement depends on accurate sensory input, an intact body schema and feed-forward postural control.

3Pathophysiology

Chronic pain and injury produce maladaptive neuroplasticity. The cortical representation of the affected part shrinks and becomes smeared, so the brain’s map of the hand or the back loses precision, with cortical disinhibition and a disrupted body schema. Clinically this appears as reduced two-point discrimination, impaired left/right limb recognition and graphesthesia errors over the affected region, together with sensory loss and learned non-use — the patient stops using the limb even after the tissues have healed. Descending inhibition becomes less effective, so central sensitisation keeps the pain going. These changes persist after tissue healing and explain why some patients remain painful despite a healed injury; they are nevertheless reversible with targeted training.

4Answer

Neurological concepts applied.

  • Pain neuroscience education: explain pain as a protective output of the nervous system, reducing threat and fear.
  • Neuroplasticity: use repeated, meaningful practice to drive beneficial reorganisation.
  • Sensorimotor integration: restore accurate sensory input and coordinated motor output.
  • Central sensitisation: graded, non-threatening input to reduce nervous system sensitivity.

Functional methods.

  • Graded motor imagery (GMI): sequential laterality training (left/right recognition), explicit motor imagery, then mirror therapy — used in complex regional pain syndrome, chronic shoulder pain and after joint replacement.
  • Sensory retraining: tactile localisation, two-point discrimination and graphesthesia training to restore body maps.
  • Motor control retraining: re-educating movement patterns and segmental control.
  • Task-oriented and functional training: practising meaningful activities to embed new strategies.
  • Cognitive functional therapy: combining movement retraining with behavioural and cognitive approaches.
ConceptMethodExample condition
Pain neuromatrixPain neuroscience educationChronic low back pain
Cortical reorganisationGraded motor imageryCRPS, chronic shoulder pain
Body schemaSensory discrimination trainingChronic pain, post-surgery
Motor learningTask-oriented trainingPost-fracture, joint replacement

Dosage and progression. Graded motor imagery is delivered in three stages of about two weeks each (roughly six weeks in total): (1) laterality training — recognising left from right in photographs, aiming for speed and accuracy within two seconds; (2) explicit motor imagery — imagined movements, 10–20 repetitions several times daily; (3) mirror therapy — 5–10 minute sessions several times a day. Sensory retraining uses short, frequent, pain-free sessions (5–10 minutes, several times daily) progressing from gross localisation to fine two-point discrimination. Motor control and task-oriented training is dosed as high-repetition, variable practice with difficulty set so the patient succeeds about 70–80% of the time. Outcome measures include NPRS, two-point discrimination distance, the DASH and the Patient-Specific Functional Scale.

Indian practice context. Mirror therapy and graded motor imagery need only a mirror, a set of limb photographs and a willing patient, so they are inexpensive and well suited to Indian outpatient and home settings. Explain the neuroscience in the patient’s own language and use familiar analogies, because comprehension drives adherence. Where literacy or smartphone access is limited, provide printed left/right photographs and a simple daily tally sheet, and involve the family so the frequent short sessions actually happen.

5Recent advances

  • Moseley (2004) — introduced graded motor imagery, a movement-representation technique using laterality, motor imagery and mirror therapy to achieve cortical reorganisation and reduce pain.
  • Louw et al. (2016) — a systematic review of randomised trials found pain neuroscience education reduces pain, improves function, lowers disability, reduces psychosocial factors and cuts healthcare use in chronic musculoskeletal pain.
  • Bagg et al. (2022) — the RESOLVE randomised trial found pain education integrated with graded sensorimotor precision training significantly reduced pain intensity in chronic low back pain at 18 weeks.
  • Candiri et al. (2023) — a randomised trial found graded motor imagery added to rehabilitation after total knee arthroplasty improved pain, motor imagery ability, pain catastrophising and kinesiophobia.
  • Wand et al. (2010) — showed that two-point discrimination and graphesthesia (cortical sensory tests) are impaired over the lumbar spine in chronic low back pain, supporting their use as clinical markers of cortical body-map disruption.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2019.
  2. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2018.
  3. Moseley GL. Graded motor imagery for pathologic pain: a randomized controlled trial. Neurology. 2006;67(12):2129–2134.
  4. Moseley GL, Butler DS. Fifteen years of explaining pain: the past, present and future. J Pain. 2015;16(9):807–813.
  5. Graded motor imagery in orthopedic and neurological rehabilitation: a systematic review of clinical studies. 2023.
  6. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw Hill; 2020.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. How do you determine the importance of physical agents in rehabilitation of low back pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Physical Agents and Electrotherapy

★ Memory hook — Physical agents are helpers, not heroes — active exercise leads.

1Introduction

Physical agents in low back pain (LBP) include thermal agents (heat, cold), electrotherapeutic agents (TENS, interferential, electrical muscle stimulation), mechanical agents (traction, ultrasound, laser) and electromagnetic agents. Determining their importance means placing them correctly within the evidence-based, biopsychosocial management of LBP: they are adjuncts that may give short-term symptom relief, while exercise, manual therapy and education remain the core.

2Physiology

Thermal agents work by altering tissue temperature and blood flow. Superficial heat (hot packs, paraffin, infrared) raises skin and subcutaneous temperature by about 1–3 °C, increasing collagen extensibility and reducing muscle spasm and pain; cold (ice, cryotherapy) lowers tissue temperature, reduces acute inflammation, oedema and nerve conduction velocity, and raises the pain threshold. TENS acts largely through the gate-control mechanism (large-diameter Aβ fibres inhibiting small-diameter Aδ and C fibres in the dorsal horn) and through descending inhibition; low-frequency (2–4 Hz) TENS releases endogenous opioids while high-frequency (80–150 Hz) works more by segmental gating. Ultrasound produces thermal (deep heating) and non-thermal (cavitation, acoustic microstreaming) effects that may aid tissue healing. Traction distracts and separates spinal segments, reduces intradiscal pressure and may relieve nerve-root compression. These are physiological effects on symptoms, not on the underlying course of low back pain.

3Pathophysiology

Low back pain is classified by duration (acute under 6 weeks, subacute 6–12 weeks, chronic over 12 weeks) and by mechanism (nociceptive, neuropathic or centrally sensitised). Most acute low back pain is self-limiting, resolving in 4–6 weeks without specific treatment, and most chronic low back pain has biopsychosocial contributors — fear-avoidance, catastrophising, deconditioning and central sensitisation — rather than ongoing tissue damage. Physical agents target symptoms and short-term irritability, making the patient more comfortable, but they do not address deconditioning, fear-avoidance or central sensitisation, and over-use can reinforce the passive mindset that predicts chronicity. This mismatch between what agents treat and what drives chronicity is precisely why their role is limited.

4Answer

How to determine importance.

  1. Follow the guidelines. The JOSPT 2021 LBP guideline and the WHO 2023 guideline make exercise, manual therapy and education the priorities; physical agents are adjuncts.
  2. Match agent to stage and classification. Acute, highly irritable LBP may benefit from short-term heat or TENS for comfort; chronic LBP needs active exercise, not passive agents.
  3. Use evidence honestly. Heat has modest short-term benefit; TENS evidence is mixed and it is not recommended as routine care by the WHO 2023 guideline; ultrasound is not recommended; traction is not recommended for chronic LBP with leg pain (conflicting evidence) but may help a selective radicular subgroup.
  4. Combine with active therapy. Agents should enable exercise and function, not replace them, and should not foster passive dependence.
  5. Respect patient preference and safety, and reassess effect; discontinue agents that give no measurable benefit.
AgentMechanismEvidence in LBP
Superficial heatBlood flow, extensibility, spasm reliefShort-term relief
TENSGate control, descending inhibitionMixed; not routine (WHO 2023)
UltrasoundThermal/non-thermal tissue effectsNot recommended
TractionSegmental distractionNot for chronic LBP with leg pain; selective radicular use
Laser / interferentialPhotobiomodulation / currentAdjunct, limited evidence

Typical dosage: TENS 80–150 Hz or 2–4 Hz, 20–30 minutes per session; superficial heat 15–20 minutes; ultrasound 0.5–1.5 W/cm² for 5–8 minutes (not recommended for LBP); lumbar traction approximately 25–40% of body weight, intermittent, for 15–25 minutes. Agents are timed to precede exercise so that movement is easier.

Indian practice context. In Indian clinics patients often arrive expecting electrotherapy and may view an exercise-only plan as no treatment at all. The physiotherapist should therefore explain the evidence honestly, use an agent briefly as a trust-building bridge into active care, and shift the emphasis to exercise and education within the first few visits. Where a machine is shared across many patients, as in government hospitals, prescribe short, high-yield sessions with a clear home programme rather than long passive sittings, and avoid creating dependence on daily electrotherapy attendance.

5Recent advances

  • JOSPT/AOPT (2021) guideline — recommends exercise and manual therapy as core interventions for low back pain and states mechanical traction should not be used for chronic LBP with leg pain because it adds no benefit.
  • WHO (2023) guideline — for chronic primary low back pain conditionally recommends structured exercise and education, and conditionally recommends against routine traction, therapeutic ultrasound and TENS.
  • NICE (2016) guideline — the NG59 guideline recommends group exercise programmes for low back pain and advises against ultrasound, TENS, PENS and acupuncture, embedding active rehabilitation and de-emphasising passive electrotherapy.

6References

  1. George SZ, Fritz JM, Silfies SP, et al. Interventions for the management of acute and chronic low back pain: revision 2021. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2021;51(11):CPG1–CPG60.
  2. World Health Organization. WHO guideline for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults in primary and community care settings. Geneva: WHO; 2023.
  3. Watson T, ed. Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice. 12th ed. Elsevier; 2008.
  4. Robertson V, Ward A, Low J, Reed A. Electrotherapy Explained: Principles and Practice. 4th ed. Butterworth-Heinemann; 2006.
  5. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2018.
  6. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. Elsevier; 2021.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Discuss the application of electric currents for tissue healing.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Electrotherapy — Tissue Healing

★ Memory hook — The body makes its own current of injury — we just copy it.

1Introduction

Electrical stimulation (ES) for tissue healing uses externally applied current to imitate the endogenous bioelectric currents that the body generates around an injury. By mimicking the natural "current of injury", ES accelerates and supports the healing of chronic wounds and injured musculoskeletal tissues. It is an evidence-supported adjunct in wound care and is applied to tendon, ligament and bone healing.

2Physiology

Every wound generates an endogenous electric field — the skin battery — that guides cells to migrate into the wound (galvanotaxis) and drives repair. Electrical current influences cell migration, proliferation, cytokine and growth-factor secretion (for example VEGF, FGF), angiogenesis, bacterial control and keratinocyte and fibroblast activity. These cellular effects map onto the inflammatory, proliferative and remodelling phases of healing.

3Pathophysiology

In chronic wounds and some musculoskeletal injuries, healing stalls — often in the inflammatory phase — because of poor perfusion, infection, diabetes or impaired fibroblast function. Without the normal bioelectric signal, cells migrate poorly, angiogenesis is reduced and the wound does not close. Exogenous ES restores the missing electrical cue.

4Answer

Current types and their application.

  • Direct current (DC): continuous unidirectional flow, useful for galvanotaxis and iontophoresis; polarity matters, and continuous DC can irritate skin.
  • High-voltage pulsed current (HVPC): monophasic twin-peak pulses, the most studied for wound healing; often used with the cathode over the wound in the inflammatory phase and the anode later.
  • Low-intensity/microcurrent: very low amplitude, mimics endogenous currents.
  • Pulsed and interferential current: used for tendon, ligament and soft-tissue healing and pain.
  • Pulsed electromagnetic fields / capacitive coupling: used for bone and fracture healing.

Wound-healing protocol (typical). HVPC at approximately 100–150 pulses per second, amplitude 100–500 microamps to a few milliamps (enough to produce a comfortable sensation), for 45–60 minutes, three to seven times a week, with the active electrode placed over or near the wound. For DC, amplitude is typically in the hundreds of microamps.

Musculoskeletal tissue healing. Pulsed or interferential currents are applied around injured tendon or ligament to support proliferation and reduce pain; PEMF is used for delayed union and fracture healing.

Current typeKey effectTypical use
DCGalvanotaxis, polarityWound, iontophoresis
HVPCCellular migration, antibacterialChronic wounds, oedema
MicrocurrentMimics endogenous currentWounds, tissue repair
Pulsed/interferentialProliferation, pain reliefTendon, ligament
PEMFOsteogenesisBone, fracture healing

Precautions and contraindications: avoid over the pregnant uterus, over the heart in patients with pacemakers, over malignant tissue, over thrombophlebitis and in areas of impaired sensation; ensure correct polarity and check skin regularly.

5Recent advances

  • Rajendran et al. (2021) — a review of 30 studies concluded electrical stimulation improves chronic wound healing by limiting inflammation, increasing perfusion, controlling bacteria, and promoting fibroblast migration, angiogenesis and keratinocyte activity, with pulsed current most used.
  • Arora et al. (2020) — the Cochrane review of electrical stimulation for treating pressure ulcers found adding it to standard care probably increases the proportion of ulcers healed within 12 weeks.
  • Koel & Houghton (2014) — a meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials found adding electrical stimulation to standard wound care increased the four-week percentage area reduction by about 27%, supporting it as an evidence-based adjunct to wound care.
  • Avendaño-Coy et al. (2022) — a meta-analysis of randomised trials found electrical microcurrent therapy reduced wound surface area, shortened healing time and reduced pain, with no increase in adverse effects.

6References

  1. Watson T, ed. Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice. 12th ed. Elsevier; 2008.
  2. Robertson V, Ward A, Low J, Reed A. Electrotherapy Explained: Principles and Practice. 4th ed. Butterworth-Heinemann; 2006.
  3. Kloth LC. Electrical stimulation technologies for wound healing. Adv Wound Care. 2014;3(2):81–90.
  4. Arora M, Harvey LA, Glinsky JV, et al. Electrical stimulation for treating pressure ulcers. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020;(1):CD012196.
  5. Khouri C, Kotzki S, Roustit M, et al. Hierarchical evaluation of electrical stimulation protocols for chronic wound healing: an effect size meta-analysis. Wound Repair Regen. 2017;25(5):883–891.
  6. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2018.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the current designs in assistive technology for work related musculoskeletal disorders.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper IV, Unit on Ergonomics and Assistive Technology

★ Memory hook — Change the task first, the tool second, the worker last.

1Introduction

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are the leading occupational health problem, driven by repetitive movement, sustained posture, high force, vibration and psychosocial stress. Assistive technology for WMSDs spans ergonomic redesign, wearable devices and, most recently, industrial exoskeletons and smart sensing. Current designs aim to reduce the biomechanical load on the back, shoulders, knees and upper limbs while preserving function and safety.

2Physiology

WMSDs arise from cumulative load on muscles, tendons, nerves and joints. Reducing the external moment at a joint (for example the lumbar spine during lifting), lowering muscle activation and sharing load between the device and the body are the physiological goals. Devices work best when they reduce peak and cumulative tissue stress without introducing new stresses elsewhere.

3Pathophysiology

Repetitive strain and sustained awkward postures cause tendon overload (tendinopathy), muscle fatigue, nerve compression and joint degeneration. The mismatch between task demands and human strength or endurance produces injury. Assistive technology addresses this mismatch directly.

4Answer

Current designs.

  • Passive exoskeletons: use springs, dampers or counterbalance mechanisms (no power) to support posture; common for the back, shoulder and knee in construction, assembly and logistics.
  • Active exoskeletons: use electric motors, pneumatics or hydraulics to provide powered assistance; some are adaptive, sensing load in real time.
  • Soft exosuits: textile-based devices that assist movement with less bulk.
  • Wearable sensors and smart PPE: inertial sensors and EMG biofeedback that monitor posture and load and warn the worker.
  • Adaptive control: force-myography and machine-learning controllers adjust support to the lifted mass in real time.
  • Ergonomic aids and adaptive tools: height-adjustable workstations, lift assists, powered tools and ergonomic seating.

Assessment and prescription. Risk is assessed with tools such as REBA, RULA, the NIOSH lifting equation and the Key Indicator Method. Devices are selected by body region and task (overhead work, stooping, kneeling, lifting) and evaluated with objective measures (EMG, kinematics, forces) and subjective measures (discomfort, usability).

FeaturePassive exoskeletonActive exoskeleton
Power sourceNone (springs)Motors/pneumatics
WeightLighterHeavier
AdaptabilityFixed supportAdaptive/real-time
Typical useStooping, overhead, kneelingLifting, dynamic tasks

Principles. Follow the hierarchy of controls: engineering and administrative controls first, with exoskeletons as a supplement (like PPE), not the only measure. Ensure correct fit and training, monitor for new hazards (pressure, hyperextension, instability) and guard against over-reliance and workload creep. Combine devices with job rotation and ergonomic redesign.

5Recent advances

  • NIOSH (2022) — its science bulletin on exoskeletons in construction summarises research showing passive back-support exoskeletons reduce lumbar muscle activity and discomfort, and knee-assistive exoskeletons reduce knee muscle activation during kneeling.
  • de Looze et al. (2016) — a review of 26 industrial exoskeletons found passive low-back devices reduce back muscle activity by 10–40% and active devices by up to 80%, while discomfort, device weight and poor anatomical fit still limit real-world use.
  • Golabchi et al. (2022) — proposed a three-dimensional framework for evaluating industrial exoskeletons based on efficacy metrics, target tasks and supported body postures.
  • Sierotowicz et al. (2022) — demonstrated adaptive control of a shoulder exoskeleton using force myography and machine learning, adjusting support to the lifted mass in real time and reducing muscle activity.
  • Cardoso et al. (2024) — a systematic review of 49 studies (2014–2024) found passive and active devices reduce WMSD risk factors but highlighted ergonomic limitations, user discomfort and the need for real-world evaluation, stressing the hierarchy of controls, correct fit and training.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA, Borstad J. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2018.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention. 5th ed. McGraw Hill; 2020.
  3. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). Exoskeletons: potential for preventing work-related musculoskeletal injuries and disorders in construction workplaces. NIOSH Science Blog; 2022.
  4. De Bock S, Ghillebert J, Govaerts R, et al. Benchmarking occupational exoskeletons: an evidence mapping systematic review. Appl Ergon. 2022;98:103582.
  5. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. FA Davis; 2019.
