Q2. Describe the screening of neck following C3-C4 disc prolapse.

Full answer →

Anchor every neurological line to C3/C4 — the high-collar dermatome, the shrug myotome, and 'no C4 reflex, test C5/C6'.

  • What earns marks: Anchor every neurological finding to C3/C4 — a generic neck exam loses marks · Draw the C3-C4 'high-collar' dermatome map with the myotome, reflex and special tests beside it · Name the red flags and finish with a clear conclusion.
  • Core idea: A C3-C4 prolapse usually compresses the C4 nerve root.
  • Pain pattern: pain in the suboccipital/neck region radiating to the shoulder cap and clavicular area (C4 dermatome — a 'high-collar' distribution).
  • C3 referral: C3 gives occipital/sub-occipital referral.
  • History: ask about onset, trauma, posture/occupation (e.g. prolonged laptop flexion), and night pain.
  • Red flags: myelopathy signs (gait change, hand clumsiness, bowel/bladder), fever, weight loss, trauma.
  • Observation: forward head posture, loss of cervical lordosis, antalgic tilt.
  • Palpation: paraspinal muscle spasm/guarding, segmental tenderness at the C3-C4 level, upper trapezius trigger points.
  • ROM: flexion/extension, side-flexion, rotation — look for painful arcs and a capsular vs non-capsular pattern.
  • Provocation: extension combined with ipsilateral rotation reproduces radicular symptoms in the affected dermatome.
  • Segmental mobility: central and unilateral posterior-anterior glides (PAIVMs) at C3-C4 for stiffness vs pain; intersegmental movement testing (PPIVMs).
  • Myotome C4: scapular elevation (shoulder shrug) and diaphragm (C3-C5) — 'C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive'; test the resisted shrug.
  • Reflex: there is no pure C4 DTR — test the biceps jerk (C5) and brachioradialis (C6) to exclude adjacent-root involvement.
  • Sensation: pinprick/light touch over the neck, clavicle and upper shoulder cap.
  • Also: complete the upper-limb screen for a broader deficit pattern.
  • Special tests: Spurling's test (extension + ipsilateral rotation + axial compression — radicular reproduction).
  • Special tests: cervical distraction (relief is confirmatory), shoulder-abduction (bakery) relief sign, and ULNT/neurodynamic testing for mechanosensitivity.
  • Special tests: Hoffman's test for myelopathy; quadriceps/Babinski if cord signs are suspected.
  • Close: integrate findings into a working PT diagnosis and baseline (NDI — Neck Disability Index).
  • Close: refer urgently for MRI if myelopathy or red flags appear.

Myotome ladder: C5 abduct, C6 wrist extend, C7 elbow extend, C8 finger flex, T1 finger abduct; Spurling (compression) pairs with distraction (relief).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2a.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (reference 4) — cervical spine chapter.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1)

Q3. Describe the screening of upper back for fibromyalgia.

Full answer →

State both criteria sets (ACR 1990 tender-point count and ACR 2010 WPI + SSS) and quote the 4 kg thumb pressure.

  • What earns marks: Quote BOTH criteria sets — the ACR 1990 tender-point count AND the ACR 2010/2016 WPI + SSS · Give the exact numbers — 18 sites, about 4 kg thumb pressure, 11 or more positive · Contrast a myofascial trigger point with a fibromyalgia tender point.
  • Definition: Fibromyalgia is chronic widespread pain (axial + bilateral, above and below the waist) for more than 3 months, with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms.
  • ACR 1990: 11 or more of 18 tender points on about 4 kg thumb pressure.
  • ACR 2010/2016 revision: Widespread Pain Index (0-19) + Symptom Severity Scale — usable without a tender-point count.
  • History: female predominance (7:1), ages 30-50.
  • History: pain 'all over' and migrating; sleep disturbance, morning stiffness over 30 min, irritable bowel/bladder, mood symptoms; and no mechanical relieving postures.
  • Observation: often normal posture but 'hurting everywhere' on light touch; guarded, protective posturing.
  • Palpation — 9 paired sites (4 in/around the upper trunk): suboccipital muscle insertions, low-cervical (C5-C7) interspinous ligaments, mid-upper trapezius, and supraspinatus at the medial scapular border.
  • Complete the set with: 2nd rib costochondral junctions, lateral epicondyles, gluteal and greater-trochanteric sites — 18 sites in total.
  • Technique: thumb pressure of about 4 kg; positive when the patient winces (the 'jump sign').
  • ROM & chest: thoracic mobility, chest expansion (normal 5 cm or more — markedly restricted suggests ankylosing spondylitis, not fibromyalgia), and scapulothoracic rhythm.
  • Differential: myofascial trigger points are local, with a taut band and reproducible referral — fibromyalgia points are systemic tender points with no taut band.
  • Differential: also rule out hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica (age over 50, raised ESR), inflammatory arthritis, and cervical/thoracic spondylosis.
  • Central sensitisation: screen for allodynia to light touch.
  • Quantify: use the FIQR (Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire) and a pain diagram.
  • Conclusion: document a body map of positive sites and score the FIQR for baseline.
  • Conclusion: coordinate a multidisciplinary plan — education, graded aerobic exercise, and sleep and stress management; physiotherapy is a cornerstone of fibromyalgia management.

Fibromyalgia numbers: ACR 1990 — 18 sites, 4 kg pressure, 11 or more needed; ACR 2016 — WPI + SSS, no palpation. Trigger point = taut band (local); tender point = systemic (central sensitisation).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4).
  • Wolfe F et al. The American College of Rheumatology 1990 / 2010/2016 criteria for fibromyalgia. Arthritis Rheum / Semin Arthritis Rheum. (primary)
  • McCarty DJ, Koopman WJ. Arthritis and Allied Conditions. (syllabus reference 11).
410 marks

Q4. Describe the importance of direct access in Physiotherapy.

Full answer →

Balance importance across patient, profession and system, then add the safeguards — never celebrate autonomy without red-flag screening.

  • What earns marks: Cover three angles — importance for the patient, the profession and the health system · Always add the safeguard paragraph (red-flag screening and referral criteria) — autonomy alone reads as naive · Mention both the global and the Indian scenario.
  • Definition: Direct access means patients may seek physiotherapy assessment and treatment without a physician's referral.
  • Role: the physiotherapist acts as a first-contact, autonomous practitioner in a primary-care musculoskeletal service.
  • Self-referral: patient self-referral is the operational form of direct access.
  • Importance — earlier treatment: no waiting for referral; early intervention in acute LBP/ankle sprain improves outcomes and prevents chronicity.
  • Importance — cost-effectiveness: studies (US military, UK NHS self-referral pilots) show fewer physician visits, imaging and medication without worse outcomes.
  • Importance — professional autonomy: recognises the physiotherapist's competence to diagnose within scope, screen for red flags and refer appropriately.
  • Autonomy detail: it is the foundation of the 'doctor of physiotherapy' and primary-spine-care models.
  • Importance — patient choice & satisfaction: shorter care pathways, fewer consultations, and better access in underserved areas.
  • Importance — system decongestion: frees physician time for complex disease; in India, it addresses the specialist-burden crisis.
  • Global scenario: direct access is legal in 50+ US states, the UK, Australia, the Netherlands and much of the EU.
  • Indian scenario: it remains partial — some states' practice and the IAP support autonomous practice, but referral culture, insurance rules and Clinical Establishments Act implementation vary.
  • Indian view: it is an evolving frontier for the profession.
  • Responsibility — competence: first-contact practitioners must be competent in differential diagnosis and red-flag screening (cancer, fracture, infection, visceral referral).
  • Responsibility — safeguards: maintain strict referral criteria, indemnity insurance, meticulous documentation and continuing competency.
  • Key line: autonomy is earned by clinical rigour, not demanded.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 3 (a-d).
  • World Physiotherapy (2011/2019) policy statement — Description of physiotherapy / direct access and patient self-referral.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).

Q5. A 30-year-old female comes with a history of ankle injury. Describe the various special tests for the ankle.

Full answer →

Cluster the tests by structure (lateral ligaments, syndesmosis, medial, tendon/fracture) and keep the exact angles and translation values.

  • What earns marks: Cluster the tests by structure — lateral ligaments, then syndesmosis, then medial, then tendon/fracture screen · Give the exact positions — drawer in 10-15 degrees plantarflexion for ATFL, and 90 degrees for CFL in talar tilt · Say that acute-day testing is unreliable; tests are more reliable at day 4-5.
  • Background: a 30-year-old woman with an inversion injury most likely sprains the lateral ligament complex.
  • Order of injury: anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) first, then calcaneofibular (CFL), rarely posterior talofibular (PTFL).
  • Grades: Grade I (stretch), II (partial), III (complete).
  • Timing: acutely, effusion and pain limit testing — examinations are more reliable at day 4-5.
  • Anterior drawer (ATFL): patient prone/supine, foot relaxed in about 10-15 degrees plantarflexion.
  • Anterior drawer technique: one hand stabilises the tibia while the other draws the talus forward on the fibula.
  • Anterior drawer positive: more than 4-5 mm anterior translation (or a clunk/soft end-feel) suggests ATFL rupture.
  • Talar-tilt (inversion stress) for CFL: foot at 90 degrees, invert the talus in the mortise; compare sides.
  • Talar-tilt positive: more than 5-10 degrees asymmetry or a soft end-feel indicates CFL injury.
  • Squeeze test: squeeze at the mid-calf; cross-over pain helps localise ligament territory.
  • Syndesmosis — calf/squeeze test: compress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calf; distal syndesmotic pain is positive.
  • Syndesmosis — external rotation (Kleiger) test: stabilise the leg, dorsiflex + externally rotate the foot — gives syndesmotic and deltoid pain.
  • Syndesmosis — Cotton (fibular translation) test: anteroposterior fibular glide; plus the point-toe (plantarflex-external rotation) test.
  • Deltoid ligament (eversion stress): medial pain/valgus laxity; implies possible syndesmosis/fracture.
  • Ottawa ankle rules (fracture triage, not laxity): X-ray if pain over the malleolar zone plus bone tenderness over the posterior edge/tip, or inability to bear weight 4 steps.
  • Also: Thompson/Simmonds test for an intact Achilles, anterior impingement test, and a peroneal-tendon subluxation screen.
  • Conclusion: grade the sprain and baseline the patient with the FAAM/Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool.

Ankle ligament tests: plantarflexion, then ATFL (drawer); 90 degrees, then CFL (talar tilt); syndesmosis trio = Squeeze, Kleiger, Cotton.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4b.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — ankle & foot chapter.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1) — ankle biomechanics.
  • Stiell IG et al. Ottawa ankle rules. JAMA. 1993 (primary, for triage).
610 marks

Q6. Write in detail about the various investigations used for osteoporosis.

Full answer →

Cover DEXA (with sites L1-L4 + hip), FRAX, other imaging and labs — and keep the -1 / -2.5 cutoffs exact.

  • What earns marks: Name the DEXA sites — lumbar spine L1-L4 plus proximal femur (hip) · Quote the WHO T-score cutoffs exactly: -1 or above normal; -1 to -2.4 osteopenia; -2.5 or below osteoporosis; a fragility fracture upgrades to severe · Explain that BMD is only a risk factor — FRAX converts it into a 10-year fracture probability.
  • Gold standard: DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) measures areal bone mineral density (g/cm2) at the lumbar spine (L1-L4) and proximal femur.
  • DEXA radiation: minimal — about 1/10 of a chest X-ray.
  • T-score: compares with the young-adult mean; WHO cutoffs in postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or more: -1 or above normal; -1 to -2.4 osteopenia; -2.5 or below osteoporosis; with a fragility fracture = severe osteoporosis.
  • Z-score: age-matched; -2 or below = 'below expected for age' (used in premenopausal women and younger men).
  • FRAX: computes the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic and hip fracture from BMD plus clinical risk factors.
  • FRAX risk factors: age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parent hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis, alcohol, and secondary causes.
  • FRAX thresholds: treatment is FRAX-based, not BMD alone (e.g. hip-probability 3% or more in Indian guidelines, adapting WHO/NOF cut-points).
  • Plain radiographs: show complications (vertebral compression, cortical thinning, trabecular rarefaction) only after 30-40% bone loss; also used for vertebral fracture assessment morphometry.
  • Quantitative CT: true volumetric BMD, sensitive but a higher dose; pQCT for peripheral sites.
  • Quantitative ultrasound (heel): radiation-free screening (SOS/BUA) — not for diagnosis.
  • MRI/bone scan: for occult fracture and malignancy differentiation.
  • Labs (to exclude secondary causes): serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH, TSH, renal/liver profile; in men, testosterone.
  • Turnover markers: resorption (serum/urine CTx) and formation (P1NP) — mainly used to monitor therapy.

T-score ladder: above -1 normal, -1 to -2.4 osteopenia, -2.5 or below osteoporosis; a fragility fracture upgrades to severe. DEXA sites: L1-L4 + hip.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4d.
  • McKinnis LN. Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging. FA Davis (reference 8).
  • Greenspan A, Beltran J. Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach. (reference 9).
  • WHO Technical Report / Kanis JA. FRAX — Assessment of osteoporotic fracture risk (primary).

Q7. Write in detail about the postoperative assessment following supracondylar fracture of elbow.

Full answer →

Put neurovascular and compartment screening first, then ROM and radiology, and always warn: never force passive extension.

  • What earns marks: Put the neurovascular and compartment check FIRST — it is the safety half of the answer · State clearly — NEVER force passive extension in a post-supracondylar elbow (myositis ossificans risk) · Keep the exact angles — carrying angle about 11 degrees valgus in men, Baumann's angle about 75-80 degrees.
  • Context: supracondylar humerus fracture (Gartland I-III) is the commonest elbow fracture of children (fall on an outstretched hand).
  • Treatment: displaced types are treated by closed/open reduction and K-wire fixation, with a cast for 3-4 weeks.
  • Timing: post-op assessment begins the day after surgery.
  • Vascular: check radial pulse, capillary refill, and colour/temperature of the hand — brachial-artery injury/kinking threatens the limb.
  • Watch for Volkmann's ischaemic contracture — the 5 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis), especially pain on passive finger extension.
  • Neural: test anterior interosseous (median — OK sign), main median, radial (wrist/thumb extension) and ulnar nerves — all are at risk from both injury and K-wires.
  • Compartment syndrome screen: tense forearm, pain out of proportion.
  • Local: wound/pin sites — check for discharge and infection; check the cast/splint condition.
  • ROM: elbow flexion-extension and pronation-supination once the cast is off (expect stiffness; grade objectively by goniometer).
  • Carrying angle: normal valgus about 11 degrees in men, about 13 degrees in women (Dutton: 11-14 / 13-16 degrees); loss = cubitus varus ('gunstock', the classic malunion).
  • Radiology: Baumann's angle (humeral capitellar angle, about 75-80 degrees; a falling value warns of varus) plus callus formation define union progression.
  • Strength: MMT of elbow/forearm/wrist musculature once pain allows; circumference for atrophy.
  • Function: functional tasks (writing, feeding); outcome instruments (QuickDASH, pediatric PROMIS).
  • Complications to hunt for: pin-tract infection, myositis ossificans (calcification anteriorly — avoid forceful passive stretching), stiffness, malunion (varus), nerve palsy, growth disturbance.
  • Conclusion: findings set the rehabilitation stage — early gentle active motion, no forced passive stretching, progressive strengthening — re-assessed every visit against a documented baseline.

Supracondylar alarm: the 5 Ps + pain on passive finger extension = compartment syndrome — the earliest sign. NEVER force extension (myositis ossificans); Baumann angle about 75-80 degrees.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 5a.

  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — elbow chapter.
  • Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13).

Q8. Describe in detail the assessment following below-knee amputation.

Full answer →

Follow the structure — residual limb, proximal joints, prosthesis, gait, scales, psychosocial — and name AMP/LCI-5 with their purpose.

  • What earns marks: Follow the structure — residual limb, then proximal joints, then prosthesis, then gait, then functional scales, then psychosocial · Name at least one standardised scale (AMP or LCI-5) with its one-line purpose · Differentiate phantom-limb pain from residual-limb pain — the viva's pet question.
  • Residual-limb shape: ideal is firm — cylindrical for total-surface-bearing sockets, conical for traditional patellar-tendon-bearing; matured by 3-6 months post-op.
  • Residual-limb skin: scars, grafts, moisture, breakdown over bony points; check wound healing and whether the scar is adherent or mobile.
  • Sensation: check for hyper-sensitivity and neuroma (Tinel's sign).
  • Volume: oedema/volume fluctuation (circumferential measurements; test socks); limb length and soft-tissue padding over the bone end.
  • Musculoskeletal: hip and knee ROM — a knee flexion contracture is the enemy of prosthetic gait (even 10 degrees matters).
  • Strength: hip flexors/extensors, abductors, quadriceps and hamstrings (MMT); knee stability.
  • Also: upper-limb strength (crutch/transfer readiness) and trunk control/balance.
  • Pain: differentiate phantom-limb pain (painful sensations in the absent foot) from residual-limb pain (neuroma, bone spur, socket pressure) and back pain.
  • Prosthesis: socket fit (pistoning, pressure marks, redness that doesn't fade in 10-15 min), suspension, and alignment in standing and walking; component condition (foot category, SACH etc.).
  • Gait: observe for vaulting, circumduction, lateral trunk bending, knee instability and unequal step length — each names a fitting or weakness problem.
  • Functional instruments: Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) (with/without prosthesis), Locomotor Capabilities Index-5, and Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire.
  • Also: 2-minute/6-minute walk test, TUG, and the SIGAM mobility grades; K-levels (0-4) classify mobility potential.
  • Energy: the O2 cost of amputee gait is higher — relevant to rehab planning.
  • Psychosocial: body image, depression screening, motivation, family support, occupation and financial access to prosthetic services — decisive in the Indian setting for prosthetic success.

Ideal stump: gently cylindrical, firm, healed, volume-stable by 3-6 months, scar mobile, soft-tissue pad over bone. Assess with AMP / LCI-5 for mobility prediction.

Q9. Describe various outcome measures used for shoulder pain.

Full answer →

Give each scale's item count and best use, pair one measure per ICF level, and never call VAS a function measure.

  • What earns marks: Pair one measure per ICF level — body function plus activity/participation · Give each scale's item count and best use — one line each beats a paragraph on any one scale · Never write 'VAS is the gold standard for shoulder function' — VAS measures pain intensity, not function.
  • Selection principles: choose by ICF level (impairment / activity / participation), region vs condition specificity, psychometric quality in the target population, and responsiveness with a known MCID.
  • Body function — ROM: goniometry of flexion, abduction and rotations (pain arc 60-120 degrees); inclinometer/smartphone apps.
  • Body function — strength: handheld dynamometry / MMT of rotator cuff and scapular muscles.
  • Body function — pain: VAS/NRS at rest and with provocation; a pain diary.
  • SPADI: 13 items (5 pain, 8 disability), 0-100 — best for general shoulder pathology; sensitive in frozen shoulder.
  • DASH / QuickDASH: 30 / 11 items, 0-100 — upper-limb-wide disability; good for multiple joints.
  • ASES: 13 items, 0-100 — rotator-cuff pathology; physician- plus self-rated.
  • Constant-Murley: 100 points (35 subjective + 65 objective) — European standard including ROM and strength.
  • UCLA: best for arthritis & arthroplasty.
  • SST: 12 yes-no single-answer questions.
  • Penn: general shoulder pathology.
  • WORC: rotator-cuff disease.
  • WOSI: instability.
  • PSFS: 3 patient-chosen activities (0-10) — individualised and very responsive.
  • Interpretation: report baseline to discharge change against the MCID of the chosen scale (SPADI about 8-10 points; DASH about 10-15 points).
  • Interpretation: use two complementary levels (an impairment measure plus a self-report scale) for a defensible ICF-rounded evaluation.

Q10. Explain the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults following total hip replacement.

Full answer →

Answer as a decision chain — impairments, gait/balance, functional tests, fit or continue — and keep the exact numbers (TUG 12 s or less, gait speed 1 m/s or more).

  • What earns marks: Answer as a chain — impairments, then gait/balance, then functional tests, then fit or continue rehab · Keep the numbers exact — TUG 12 s or less, gait speed 1.0 m/s or more, abductors 4/5 or more, single-leg stance 10 s or more · Name one patient-reported scale (Harris/Oxford/HOOS) to complete the ICF triangle.
  • Surgical & safety screening: confirm radiological implant position and stability, a healed wound, and absence of infection/heterotopic ossification (HO).
  • Note the surgical approach — posterior precautions vs direct-anterior (fewer restrictions).
  • Pain level: 3/10 or less on activity; medical clearance if there is cardiac comorbidity.
  • ROM criteria: hip flexion 110 degrees or more, abduction 30 degrees or more, ER in abduction; documented risk-relevant limits per approach.
  • Strength criteria: abductors grade 4/5 or more (no Trendelenburg sign in single-leg stance for 10-30 s), extensors and flexors 4/5 or more; no pain on resisted tests.
  • Leg-length equality within 1-1.5 cm; no fixed contracture.
  • Gait: independent gait without an assistive device, symmetrical cadence and step length, no limp/Trendelenburg lurch.
  • Balance: single-limb balance 10 s or more (eyes open), Stork/functional reach within norms.
  • Stairs: ascending and descending reciprocally with a rail.
  • Timed Up-and-Go: community ambulation benchmark 12-14 s or less; 8-10 s or less for near-normal.
  • Six-minute walk test: compare with age norms (roughly 400-600 m for healthy adults; a post-THR patient should exceed about 70% predicted).
  • 10-metre walk: gait speed 1.0 m/s or more = community standard; also the stair test and sit-to-stand x5.
  • Fitness verdict: the adult is declared fit for independent community ambulation/work when — painless independent gait, abductor strength 4/5 or more, negative Trendelenburg, functional ROM, TUG 12 s or less, safe stairs, and stable 6MWT performance.
  • Reassessment: the criteria are graded on reassessment at 3, 6 and 12 months.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 4f & 6.
  • Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13) — THR criteria.
  • Wilk KE et al. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. (reference 14).
  • ACSM. Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. (reference 12).

List the methods of training to improve muscle performance in post-traumatic fracture at the wrist joint.

Full answer →

Show the exercises in the order the fracture heals, not just a random list of methods.

  • What earns marks: show phase logic — training must follow fracture healing (immobilisation, then after the cast, then remodelling), not a random list · name one method from each family — isometric, isotonic, CKC, isokinetic, PNF — plus grip and function · give the grip-strength target (within 10-15% of the uninjured side) and use PRWE as an outcome.
  • Principle first: after a distal-radius / Colles' wrist fracture, muscle performance is rebuilt in a healing-driven order — immobilisation, then post-immobilisation, then remodelling.
  • Treatment moves from isometric (no joint motion, protects the fracture site) to active/isotonic, to resisted, to functional training.
  • Progression is decided by callus maturity, pain and effusion.
  • Isometric (during the cast / early healing): work the muscles that cross the immobilised joint.
  • Use tendon-gliding isometrics for the wrist flexors and extensors.
  • Cast-squeezing routine: gentle graded holds of 6-10 s x10, kept within pain limits.
  • These prevent muscle wasting and help pump out oedema.
  • Also work the shoulder, elbow and full hand outside the cast to keep the whole chain active.
  • Teach active finger movement (AROM) of the free fingers every hour.
  • Isotonic and isoinertial progression: once X-ray union and pain allow, start active, then active-assisted, then dynamic (isotonic) contractions against gravity.
  • Then add graduated resistance — wrist curls, reverse wrist curls, pronation/supination with a small dumbbell or elastic band.
  • Add eccentric emphasis later for tendon tolerance.
  • Progressive-resistance rule (DeLorme/Zinovieff or daily adjustable): 2-3 sets of 8-12 at 60-75% of estimated 1RM.
  • Progress the load by about 5-10% when 12 repetitions become easy.
  • CKC: closed-kinetic-chain weight-bearing — palm-down table pressing, quadruped rocking, wall push-ups — loads the wrist with co-contraction and less shear.
  • Isokinetic dynamometry at 6-12 weeks: constant-speed training gives objective, accommodated resistance and documented torque curves.
  • PNF: rhythmic stabilisation around the wrist for endurance of the stabilisers; contract-relax for wrist-flexion range restriction.
  • Functional and grip progression: grip — putty progression (soft to firm), pinch boards, towel wringing.
  • Dexterity — pegboards, coins, writing; then task-specific loading (carrying a bucket, turning a jar).
  • Outcome tracking: dynamometric grip strength (target within 10-15% of the uninjured side) and PRWE score.

The staircase: each step = one healing phase; progress when pain-free and callus mature; track grip within 10-15% of sound side (PRWE).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 1a.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — resistance exercise chapters.
  • Hislop H et al. Daniels & Worthingham's Muscle Testing. (reference 7).
  • Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. (reference 16).
210 marks

Explain the mechanism of pain relief using electrotherapy modalities.

Full answer →

Explain HOW each modality relieves pain — the mechanism with its settings, not just "TENS closes the gate".

  • What earns marks: give the mechanism AND the parameters for each modality — the exam trap is writing only "TENS closes the gate" · the opioid mechanism (2-4 Hz, naloxone-reversible) carries the second half of the marks · finish with a one-line conclusion.
  • Segmental gate control — the workhorse: TENS floods the large-diameter Aβ afferent fibres.
  • These excite the substantia gelatinosa interneurons of the dorsal horn.
  • This closes the gate on pain transmission to the T cells (Melzack and Wall).
  • Conventional TENS: high frequency 80-100 Hz, short pulse duration 50-100 μs, amplitude strong but comfortable.
  • It gives rapid onset and short carry-over, and is best for acute pain.
  • Endogenous opioid (descending) system: low-frequency acupuncture-like TENS — 2-4 Hz, 200-300 μs, high intensity enough to produce rhythmic muscle contraction.
  • This drives C-afferent / muscle-afferent input to hypothalamic-PAG activation.
  • The raphe magnus and locus coeruleus then descend via the dorsolateral funiculus.
  • They release serotonin/noradrenaline to inhibit dorsal-horn cells.
  • β-endorphin, met-enkephalin and dynorphin are released — this is naloxone-reversible.
  • It has a slower onset but hours of carry-over, best for chronic pain.
  • Other mechanisms — counter-irritation / hyperstimulation analgesia: intense input suppresses pain at spinal and supraspinal levels (brief-intense TENS).
  • Vasomotor and anti-oedema effects: muscle pumping and IFT improve circulation and clear pain-causing metabolites; HVPG reduces oedema-dependent pain.
  • Placebo/expectation: a genuine neurobiological component through descending pathways — honestly explaining the modality makes it work better.
  • Modality settings — conventional TENS: 80-100 Hz, 50-100 μs, 20-30 min (gate control).
  • Acupuncture-like TENS: 2-4 Hz, 200-300 μs, muscle twitch (opioid/descending).
  • IFT: beat 20-80 Hz (DeLisa); 90-130 Hz analgesia common in practice (2-10 Hz also); vector and quadripolar (gate + circulation).
  • HVPG: high voltage, twin-peaked pulses (deep comfort + oedema).
  • Ultrasound: 3 MHz superficial, 1 MHz deep (thermal + non-thermal tissue repair).

TENS pair: conventional 40-80 Hz (DeLisa; 80-100 Hz in Indian texts) vs 2-4 Hz (up to 8 Hz) acupuncture-like (with contraction, naloxone-reversible).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 2b; Paper II Unit 10.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. — pain-suppression systems.
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Science. 1965 (primary).
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
310 marks

Methods used to improve balance after an ankle sprain.

Full answer →

Give the causal chain (torn mechanoreceptors to poor balance to re-sprain) FIRST, then the training methods.

  • What earns marks: state the rationale first — torn mechanoreceptors lead to poor balance and re-sprain risk · give the progression (floor to foam to wobble board to BOSU to perturbation) and a discharge criterion · quote the recurrence-reduction figure only if you attribute it correctly (Verhagen et al.); otherwise say "substantially reduces".
  • Why balance training at all: ligament injury damages the mechanoreceptors of the ATFL/CFL.
  • This causes an arthrogenic proprioceptive deficit — delayed peroneal reaction time and impaired single-leg stance.
  • This is the strongest predictor of chronic ankle instability and re-sprain.
  • Balance retraining cuts recurrence roughly by half in trials — this is the rationale the examiner wants in line one.
  • Static balance progression: single-leg stance on the floor — eyes open, then eyes closed, then head turns.
  • Progress to foam/air-disc surfaces and a stork stance with reach tasks.
  • Bilateral to unilateral stance on a tilt board fixed to one plane.
  • Target 30-45 s of stable single-leg stance as a milestone before using dynamic tools.
  • Dynamic balance training: wobble/rocker boards and BOSU — two-leg, then single-leg, then with ball-catch; 3-5 min sets daily.
  • Star Excursion / Y-Balance Test as both training and retest (target: within about 90%+ of the uninjured limb and no pain).
  • Multi-directional stepping/lunges onto discs and resisted band walks with single-leg control.
  • Reactive and sport-specific: perturbation training — the therapist nudges the tilt board while the patient stabilises; sudden ball drops for reaction training.
  • Hopping/jumping progressions — sagittal, frontal, rotational; single-leg hop-and-stick landings.
  • Agility: shuttle runs, ladder drills, cutting and turning on the previously injured ankle; taping/bracing as an adjunct during early return.
  • Progression and discharge: progress by surface (stable to unstable), stance (bilateral to unilateral), sensory (eyes open to closed to distracted) and task (static to dynamic to reactive).
  • Discharge: symmetric SEBT reach, at least 95% hop-test limb symmetry, and confident single-leg balance — before return to sport.

Balance progression ladder: floor, foam, disc, wobble board, BOSU, perturbation.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 3c.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — balance training chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  • Verhagen E et al. Balance-board training & ankle-sprain recurrence. Am J Sports Med. (primary evidence)
410 marks

Functional training in individuals who have undergone TKR.

Full answer →

Follow the post-op timeline, give criteria for each stage, and add Indian daily-life tasks with the flexion-limit caveat.

  • What earns marks: follow the post-op timeline (day 0-3 to 6-12 weeks) and make it criteria-based, not calendar-based · quote the stair rule "up with the good, down with the bad" · add Indian-context tasks (low toilet, cross-legged sitting, temple kneeling) with the flexion-limit caveat.
  • Principles: functional training practises the task itself — transferring, walking, climbing — in the real environments the patient returns to (home, fields, factory floors).
  • It is built on a foundation of range of motion (ROM), strength and endurance.
  • After TKR the sequence follows post-op days and is criteria-based, not calendar-based.
  • Day 0-3: ankle pumps, quad sets, SLR (if active extension allows), CPM as per protocol, cryotherapy.
  • Sit on the bed edge and stand within the frame — think hallux-to-hip activation, not just the knee.
  • Day 1-5: transfer training — log-roll to sit, sit-to-stand from a raised chair pushing the armrests.
  • Gait in a walker/rollator (frame, then crutches, then stick, as quad control returns).
  • Short ward-walk distances building up to 100 m.
  • Stair training in late week 1-2: "up with the good, down with the bad."
  • Week 2-6: functional strengthening — mini-squats (0-45°), step-ups on a 10-15 cm block, sit-to-stand from lowering chair heights, leg press in safe ROM.
  • Stationary cycle starting with a high seat, gradually lowered; outdoor uneven-terrain walking.
  • Week 6-12: advanced function — reciprocal stairs, single-leg balance, tai-chi-style weight-shifts, cycling outdoors, swimming (avoid breast-stroke whip-kick with prosthetic stress).
  • Return to light work and driving usually at 6 weeks or more, once quad control and reflexes are sound.
  • ADL integration: practise the actual tasks — squatting to a low Indian toilet (start with a commode chair).
  • Floor-level activities with caution for high-flexion prostheses; carrying weights while walking.
  • Temple kneeling/lotus positions graded per implant flexion limits (most standard implants 110-125° flexion — deep squat/sitting cross-legged needs caution and prosthetic design advice).
  • Progress criteria: independent painless gait, stair-descent control and TUG.

TKR timeline skeleton: day 0-2 bed exercises + first ambulation; about 2 wk ~90° flexion, wounds healed; about 6 wk normal gait pattern; about 3 months full function.

Sources

  • Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13) — TKR protocol.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — functional training chapters.
510 marks

Describe the neurodynamic management of the peripheral nervous system.

Full answer →

Define slider vs tensioner in one crisp line each, and name a technique with its nerve bias.

  • What earns marks: define slider vs tensioner in ONE crisp sentence each · name a technique with its nerve bias (e.g. ULNT1 = median nerve) · state the dosage and precautions — vague talk of "nerve stretching" loses the whole technique section.
  • Concept: neurodynamics (Butler, Shacklock) examines and treats the mechanical interface of the nervous system.
  • Nerves must glide, slide (a few mm) and elongate (about 2-15% strain tolerance) within their containers.
  • These containers include the intervertebral foramina, muscle tunnels (carpal tunnel, pronator) and fascial beds.
  • When interfaces narrow (disc bulge, oedema, fibrosis) or the nerve becomes mechanically sensitive, movement reproduces symptoms — this is "adverse neural tension".
  • Neurodynamic tests — ULNT1 (median nerve): shoulder abduction-external rotation, forearm supination, wrist-finger extension, elbow extension; neck side-flexion sensitises.
  • ULNT2 (median, anterior): shoulder girdle depression + elbow extension + wrist supination/extension.
  • ULNT3 radial bias; ULNT4 ulnar bias.
  • Lower limb: straight-leg-raise + ankle dorsiflexion/eversion; slump long-sit — to tell neural from hamstring.
  • Interpret by the symptom response across the sensitising additions, side-to-side differences, and whether structural differentiation changes the symptoms.
  • Treatment — sliders (gliding): move the joint proximal to the nerve one way while the distal joint moves the opposite way.
  • This gives maximal nerve glide with minimal tension; painless, used in irritable conditions (e.g. during ULNT1, abduct the shoulder while flexing the neck).
  • Tensioners: lengthen both ends of the nervous system at the same time (e.g. knee extension with cervical flexion).
  • Tensioners give a stronger stretch — used only when irritability is low, always short of symptom reproduction.
  • Progression and precautions: dosage is low amplitude, low velocity, frequent (10-15 oscillations, several sets daily), progressed by range and load.
  • Contraindicated/cautioned over acute inflammation, spinal cord signs, unresolved central sensitisation and recent nerve repair.
  • Evidence: neural mobilisation adds small-to-moderate benefit over exercise alone for carpal tunnel syndrome and cervicobrachial pain — combine it with interface treatment, never as an isolated ritual.

Neurodynamics rule: tensioners lengthen both ends (strong); sliders move one end while the other releases (gentle) — slide for irritable, tension for stable.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 4b.
  • Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System. (reference 26).
  • Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics. (reference 27).
610 marks

What are the therapeutic effects of orthotics? What are the various orthotics used in the upper limb?

Full answer →

Match each orthosis to ONE indication and ONE joint position, starting from the three-point pressure system.

  • What earns marks: start from the three-point pressure system — one corrective force, two counter-forces · match each orthosis to ONE indication and ONE joint position · add joint-position specifics (e.g. MCPs at 60-70° flexion in the resting splint).
  • Therapeutic effects: an orthosis (an externally applied device) supports and stabilises — it rests painful joints.
  • It immobilises/protects (fracture, tendon repair).
  • It corrects or prevents deformity (serial casting principles; prevents contracture).
  • It assists or substitutes for weak muscles (dynamic splints).
  • It gives controlled motion (hinged joints permitting a safe arc).
  • It controls oedema and scar, and reduces pain through rest and alignment.
  • It enhances function (positioning the hand for use).
  • Classification: static (no moving parts) vs dynamic (with springs/rubber-band outriggers).
  • Also prophylactic vs corrective vs functional; serial vs wearable.
  • Materials: low-temperature thermoplastics, plaster, prefabricated vs custom.
  • Hand and wrist-hand orthoses: cock-up/resting wrist splint (median nerve palsy, wrist tendonitis, carpal tunnel).
  • Static resting hand splint (spastic hand, burns).
  • Thumb spica (de Quervain's, CMC OA, scaphoid).
  • Gutter/MCP-ulnar drift splint (RA); opponents splint; finger gutter and mallet-finger splints.
  • Knuckle-bender and dorsal block (after flexor-tendon repair); swan-neck/zig-zag correction rings.
  • Dynamic splints: spring-wire outriggers for radial nerve palsy (wrist drop); low-profile dynamic MCP flexion assist; reverse knuckle benders.
  • Elbow: static posterior splint / hinged-locked brace (ligament injury, post-op limits); turnbuckle splint for elbow flexion contracture.
  • Shoulder: sling/abduction pillow (post-op repair, humeral fracture — 30-45° for rotator cuff repair); airplane splint (burn axilla); clavicle strap, figure-of-eight; hemi-sling for subluxation after neurological injury.
  • Prescription principles: match the orthosis to the pathology phase and the goal.
  • Check the fit (no pressure over bony prominences — ulnar head, radial styloid); check skin at each removal and daily.
  • Use the 3-point pressure system for correction; review at every visit.
  • Combine with therapeutic exercise — the splint positions, but the muscle still has to be retrained.

Every orthosis answer starts at the three-point pressure system: one corrective force, two counter-forces.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 5b & Paper IV Unit 6c.
  • Chui KC et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. (reference 18).
  • Saunders R et al. Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation. (reference 20).
  • Cooper C. Fundamentals of Hand Therapy. (reference 21).
710 marks

Describe the evidence-based electrotherapy management in soft tissue injury.

Full answer →

Match the modality and dose to the healing phase, and quote one negative trial to prove you are evidence-based.

  • What earns marks: match the modality and dose to the healing phase — dose logic first · quote at least ONE negative trial finding (e.g. Cochrane: ultrasound vs sham — no significant difference) · end with the message that exercise is the driver and modalities only buy the pain-free window.
  • Phase logic first: soft-tissue healing passes through haemostasis/inflammation (days 0-5), proliferation (day 5 to 3 wk) and remodelling (3 wk to 12+ mo).
  • "Evidence-based" means the modality and dose must match the phase's cell population.
  • Exercise — not machines — remains the primary driver of repair.
  • Acute/inflammatory phase: give analgesia without adding swelling — conventional TENS (80-100 Hz) or IFT (beat 20-80 Hz per DeLisa; 90-130 Hz for pain in Indian practice) for the pain gate.
  • Cryotherapy in the first 48 h for vasoconstriction and analgesia.
  • Pulsed shortwave (non-thermal, low intensity) and low-dose therapeutic ultrasound (pulsed 1:4, 0.1-0.3 W/cm²) to support membrane repair and oedema resolution — evidence modest; use where pain/effusion blocks active movement.
  • HVPG for oedema control (muscle pumping).
  • Microcurrent (µAT) claims to boost ATP for epithelial repair — weak clinical evidence.
  • Proliferative and remodelling phase: continuous therapeutic ultrasound (3 MHz, 0.5-1.0 W/cm² for superficial structures like the lateral epicondyle; 1 MHz for deep).
  • Its thermal effect increases collagen extensibility (before stretch) and perfusion.
  • Low-level laser (820-904 nm) for tendon injuries — evidence debated: DeLisa finds no benefit in lateral epicondylitis, while newer trials report short-term pain relief.
  • Extracorporeal shockwave therapy for insertional tendinopathies (plantar fasciitis, calcific supraspinatus) — the strongest modern evidence in this family.
  • Progressive loading exercise is the proven remodelling driver — modalities buy the pain-free window that allows it (e.g. eccentric Alfredson protocol for Achilles tendinopathy).
  • Evidence caveats: Cochrane reviews find ultrasound no better than placebo for most soft-tissue injuries.
  • Shockwave and eccentric loading carry the strongest support; TENS has short-term analgesic benefit.
  • So justify every modality with a goal (pain window, tissue extensibility, oedema), set measurable reassessment endpoints, and stop what isn't working.
  • That — not brand loyalty to machines — is the evidence-based behaviour.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 5 (b-e).
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  • Robertson VJ, Baker KG et al. Electrotherapy evidence reviews. Phys Ther / Aust J Physiother.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — tissue-healing & loading chapters.

Plan an ergonomic table for a software professional who has a condition of Trapezitis.

Full answer →

Give a real table (element/specification/reason) and link every element to trapezius overload.

  • What earns marks: give a real table with element / specification / reason columns · the "reason" column linking each element to trapezius overload is where the higher marks live · include the break and micro-pause schedule and a follow-up/outcome plan.
  • The problem: trapezitis in a software professional is a classic work-related upper-limb disorder.
  • Static upper-trapezius elevation + forward head posture during 8-10 h of screen work causes ischaemic overload and trigger points.
  • The ergonomic plan removes the sustained postural demand.
  • A RULA/rapid exposure assessment documents the risk before redesign.
  • Monitor: top at/slightly below eye level, 50-70 cm away, perpendicular to windows — kills forward-head and sustained flexion.
  • Chair: lumbar support, seat height letting feet rest flat, hips 90-110° — unloads the cervico-scapular chain.
  • Armrests: height so elbows rest at 90-100° with shoulders relaxed — prevents chronic trap elevation, the direct culprit.
  • Keyboard/mouse: close to the body, elbows at sides, wrists neutral; document holder beside the screen — avoids reaching and trap activation.
  • Desk: at elbow height; keyboard tray/standing-desk option — position variation and neutral limbs.
  • Laptop: never on the lap for long work — use a riser + separate keyboard/mouse; otherwise neck flexion is forced.
  • Lighting: ambient + task light, anti-glare, contrast set — prevents leaning-in postures.
  • Phone: use a headset — never shoulder-crunching; that is classic acute trap overload.
  • Breaks and movement: rest breaks of 2-5 min every 30-60 min.
  • True micro-pauses of 20-30 s every 20-30 min of typing; the 20-20-20 rule for the eyes.
  • Trap-specific routine every hour: shoulder shrug-rolls x10, chin tucks x10, doorway pectoral stretch 30 s, scapular retractions x10; plus hydration.
  • Follow-up: reassess the RULA score at 2 and 6 weeks; track pain (VAS/NPS) and NDI.
  • Combine with physiotherapy (postural re-education, trigger-point release, scapular strengthening — lower/middle trap and serratus).
  • Educate about early-warning symptoms so the patient self-corrects.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Unit 6 (a, c).
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — posture & work-related disorder chapters.
  • OSHA Computer Workstations eTool / McAtamney & Corlett RULA (ergonomic standards).

Physiotherapeutic strategies for Osteosarcoma.

Full answer →

Show that therapy is phased around the CHEMOTHERAPY cycle, not just the surgery, and name an outcome measure.

  • What earns marks: state that physiotherapy is phased around the CHEMOTHERAPY cycle, not just the surgery · say that high-impact sport is contraindicated after a megaprosthesis · name an outcome measure (TESS or MSTS) in the conclusion.
  • Overview that matters: osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour of adolescents/young adults.
  • It arises typically at the distal femur/proximal tibia metaphysis (about 60% of cases are near the knee).
  • Management: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then wide resection by limb-salvage surgery with a megaprosthesis/endoprosthesis (or rotationplasty/amputation), then adjuvant chemo.
  • Physiotherapy is needed across ALL phases, always inside the oncology team.
  • Pre-operative and peri-operative: baseline assessment (ROM, strength, function — MSTS score, TESS) and patient education.
  • Pre-hab: maintain knee/hip ROM and quadriceps strength between chemo cycles.
  • Aerobic conditioning to counter chemo deconditioning; respiratory preparation; gait training on the planned assistive device; psychological preparation.
  • Post-operative (limb salvage), Phase 1 (0-2 wk): pain management (TENS as adjunct, cryotherapy), oedema control, isometrics within the surgeon's protocol.
  • Protected weight-bearing (touch-down to partial, per prosthesis fixation); chest physiotherapy during chemo-induced immunosuppression.
  • Phase 2 (2-6 wk): progressive active knee ROM, patellar mobilisation, scar/soft-tissue mobilisation.
  • Gradual weight-bearing progression, gait re-education, isotonic quadriceps/hamstring work.
  • Phase 3 (6 wk to months): strengthening in functional patterns, proprioceptive and balance training, endurance walk programme.
  • Return to low-impact function — usually NOT high-impact sport with a megaprosthesis; home-programme compliance training.
  • Precautions and complications: protect against pathological/periprosthetic fracture (fall prevention, controlled loading).
  • Guard against infection (pin/wound), extensor-mechanism insufficiency after distal-femoral resection, and prosthetic loosening.
  • Adjust for chemo side effects (fatigue, neuropathy, cardiotoxicity); avoid forceful passive stretching; monitor for recurrence symptoms in follow-up.
  • Holistic care: energy-conservation pacing during chemo, nutritional counselling referral, psychosocial support (body image, school/work re-entry for adolescents).
  • Palliative and end-of-life physiotherapy when disease progresses — comfort, positioning, chest care.
  • Outcome tracking with TESS/MSTS and quality-of-life scales; in amputees, prosthetic rehabilitation.

  • Wilk KE et al. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. (reference 14).

Types of meniscal tear. What are the causes and mechanism of injury to the meniscus? Plan PT intervention.

Full answer →

Cover the tear types with a sketch, the mechanism sentence, and the conservative-vs-surgery evidence reversal.

  • What earns marks: give the mechanism sentence — flexed, loaded knee + rotation · link a locked knee to a bucket-handle tear · state the conservative-vs-surgery evidence reversal for degenerative tears (FIDELITY/METEOR).
  • Types of tears: bucket-handle — a longitudinal vertical tear with the central fragment displaced into the intercondylar notch; the classic "locked knee".
  • Longitudinal (vertical) — runs along the circumference; common in young athletes.
  • Radial — from the free edge toward the periphery (parrot-beak when oblique).
  • Oblique/flap — diagonal, with symptomatic catching.
  • Horizontal cleavage — splits the meniscus into upper/lower laminae; common in older, degenerative menisci (often with cysts).
  • Complex/degenerative — multi-pattern tears in the aged meniscus.
  • Causes and mechanism: traumatic (young athletes) — the foot is planted, the knee is flexed and loaded while the femur rotates on the fixed tibia.
  • The meniscus is crushed and sheared between the condyle and plateau, tearing like a washer twisting under a bolt.
  • Seen in squatting-and-twisting in cricket, football cutting and kabaddi.
  • The medial meniscus tears more often — it is firmly attached to the medial capsule and less mobile.
  • Degenerative (40+): age-related chondrocalcinosis and mucoid degeneration tear from trivial activities (rising from a cross-legged squat) — horizontal/complex patterns.
  • Risk factors: discoid meniscus, ACL insufficiency (an unstable knee shears the menisci), repetitive deep-squatting occupations.
  • Vascular zones: the red-red peripheral third is vascular (heals).
  • The red-white middle has partial healing potential; the inner white-white two-thirds is avascular.
  • This decides repair vs partial meniscectomy vs conservative care.
  • PT intervention — conservative (small, stable, degenerative tears; now the evidence default): phase-wise — control effusion/pain (cryotherapy, TENS), restore ROM.
  • Then quadriceps/hamstring strengthening (isometrics to closed-chain), proprioception, gait normalisation, return-to-sport criteria.
  • Evidence (FIDELITY and METEOR trials) shows structured exercise matches arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for degenerative tears.
  • Post partial meniscectomy: rapid progression — day 1-3 quadriceps activation, full weight bearing as tolerated, ROM, closed-chain strengthening from week 1, running at about 4-6 wk, sport at about 6-8 wk.
  • Post meniscal repair: protected — brace limiting flexion (0-90° for about 4-6 wk), toe-touch to partial weight bearing 4-6 wk, no deep squats/deep flexion for 12-16 wk.
  • Progressive strength and proprioception — healing is the priority, speed comes later.
  • Outcome tracking: Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), Tegner activity scale, effusion and thigh-circumference measures.

Meniscus: outer third = red-red zone (vascular, heals best), inner two-thirds avascular; bucket-handle tears lock the knee.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper IV Units 1-3.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1) — knee menisci.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — McMurray/Apley tests.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. — post-meniscal surgery protocols.

Q1. Discuss the role of history taking in physiotherapy assessment.

Full answer →

Show that history taking is the first and highest-yield part of assessment: what it is for, how it is structured, what red flags it hunts, and how it drives everything that follows.

  • What earns marks: define history taking and its objectives (2 marks) · list the components of a structured physiotherapy history (2.5 marks) · name the special questions — red flags, yellow flags, co-morbidities, drugs (2 marks) · show ICF-based recording and goal setting (1.5 marks), then application — hypothesis generation, EBP pretest probability and conclusion (2 marks).
  • What it is: history taking (the subjective examination) is the structured clinical interview that opens every physiotherapy encounter.
  • Mechanism first: the history generates the hypotheses and the objective examination tests them. No assessment battery is chosen until listening has told us what to test.
  • It is the cheapest, safest and most informative investigation we own — no machine, gauge or scale tells you the pain started after lifting a filled water drum, the hand goes numb at night, or the patient fears returning to farm work.
  • Its roles: build rapport and consent; screen for pathology that must be referred; direct the physical examination; select outcome measures; form the baseline record; and create a medico-legal document of the therapist's clinical reasoning.
  • Demographics and occupation matter (a construction worker and a software engineer get different shoulders); take the chief complaint in the patient's own words; map the history of present illness by OPQRST — Onset, Provocation and palliation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, Timing.
  • Also cover: past history of the same problem; past medical history (diabetes, cardiac and thyroid disease modify healing and exercise tolerance); current medication (steroids, anticoagulants, analgesics mask symptoms); previous physiotherapy and its result; investigations and imaging already done; and family history.
  • Social history — sleep, stress, domestic situation, work demands.
  • Indian practice: ask for old prescriptions and reports (patients rarely carry them), and confirm the timeline against a festival or harvest calendar rather than exact dates.
  • Red flags to hunt in every history: night pain unrelated to position, unexplained weight loss, fever, history of carcinoma, trauma in the elderly, progressive neurological deficit, and loss of bladder or bowel control (a cauda equina emergency).
  • Yellow flags to screen: fear-avoidance beliefs, low mood, poor outcome expectations — they predict chronicity better than any imaging finding. This screening decides whether we treat or refer.
  • ICMR ethical guidance: what a patient tells us is confidential information held in trust, not gossip for the OPD corridor.
  • Record findings under the WHO ICF: body functions and structures (restricted shoulder abduction, weak quadriceps), activity (cannot comb hair, cannot squat), participation (unable to attend office, cannot lift the child), environmental factors (lives on second floor without lift) and personal factors (age 62, retired teacher).
  • An ICF-written problem list converts directly into SMART goals that can be retested at discharge.
  • Evidence-based practice: the history sets the pretest probability. Sackett's model says a test result means something only when it moves probability away from what the history already told us — a positive test in a low-probability patient is often a false positive.
  • Conclusion: history taking is the first and highest-yield assessment, not paperwork before assessment — a physiotherapist who listens well needs fewer machines, not more.
  • Four-step flow: 1. LISTEN (chief complaint + OPQRST) → 2. SCREEN (red flags / yellow flags) → 3. HYPOTHESISE (2 to 3 working diagnoses, written down before touching the patient) → 4. TEST (focused objective assessment + outcome measures, then set ICF goals).

Examiner's tip: open with "the subjective examination generates hypotheses; the objective examination tests them" — that sentence plus a named red-flag list separates a 6/10 script from a 9/10 script.

Sources
  • Sackett DL, Straus SE, Richardson WS, et al. Evidence-Based Medicine: How to Practice and Teach EBM.
  • Herbert RD, Jamtvedt G, Mead J, Hagen KB. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
  • World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice and Ethical Principles.
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
