  • Assess with the swimming history (stroke, weekly distance, hand-entry pattern), painful arc, Neer or Hawkins tests, labral provocation tests, scapular observation in repeated elevation, and a measured glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) using the side-lying comparison against total arc rotation.
  • Acute phase: relative rest from the aggravating volume, not total rest — swimmers decondition fast and can kick-train with a pull-buoy between the ankles.
  • Modalities are optional adjuncts; the real work is pain-free range, isometric cuff loading, and posture correction.
  • Address posterior capsule tightness early with sleeper and cross-body stretches.
  • Definitive phase — rebuild the power chain from inside out: rotator cuff strength with external rotation at 0 and 90 degrees abduction using elastic resistance.
  • Then scapular control — retraction, low-row, prone Y-T-W and serratus wall slides.
  • Then closed-chain work and plyometric catching.
  • Then dry-land swim-specific strength — pull-ups and cable internal rotation mimicking the pull-through.
  • Correct GIRD to bring the total rotation arc back to symmetry (sleeper stretch, cross-body adduction stretch and joint mobilisations in external rotation).
  • Restore thoracic extension-rotation for the breathing pattern and core strength to anchor the kinetic chain.
  • Technique and load: correct thumb-entry to fingertip-first entry, avoid midline crossover, balance bilateral breathing, and increase body roll.
  • Coordinate with the coach on training-load change — cut only the painful sets and keep the aerobic base.
  • Return to full training when the shoulder is pain-free through the full arc, external-rotation strength is within 10 percent of the sound side, and the scapula stays controlled after a fatigue set.
  • Prevention: a season-long programme of cuff and scapular strengthening, GIRD surveillance, and a gradual (not sudden) rise in weekly distance.

GIRD rule — internal rotation deficit more than 20 degrees with total-arc asymmetry = stretch programme.

Sources
  • Wilk KE, Brotzman SB. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. Shoulder chapters.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Shoulder chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Shoulder section.
610 marks

Explain the role of assistive devices in the workplace.

Full answer →

Define and classify assistive devices, show the ergonomic assessment and matching, and give named low-tech and high-tech examples with benefits and barriers.

  • Structure the answer as classify → assess → match → train → follow up.
  • Give at least six named devices, each with one condition it helps.
  • Generic phrases like 'helps the worker' carry no marks.
  • An assistive device is any tool, product or technology that lets a person with an impairment do a task they otherwise could not do, or do it more safely.
  • They run along a spectrum: low-tech ergonomic aids, mid-tech, and high-tech assistive technology.
  • Low-tech examples: reachers, splints, adapted cutlery.
  • Mid-tech examples: ergonomic keyboards, voice-amplifiers, sit-stand desks, powered wheelchairs.
  • High-tech examples: screen readers, voice-recognition software, environmental control units.
  • Orthoses, prostheses and mobility aids used on the job belong to the same family.
  • Prescribe only after an ergonomic job analysis: the physical demands of the post (lift, reach, keyboard hours, standing time), the environment, the impairment profile, and the worker's own goals.
  • Match the device to the task, not to the diagnosis.
  • Involve the worker in selection — a device the worker rejects is a device that will sit in a cupboard.
  • Check safety, training time, maintenance and cost before finalising the recommendation.
  • Low-tech devices (cheap and immediate): reachers and long-handled tools for limited mobility after back injury.
  • Adjustable chair with lumbar support and footrest for the desk worker with chronic low back pain.
  • Angled or split keyboards and vertical mice for carpal-tunnel and work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSD).
  • Standing desks and anti-fatigue mats.
  • Lifting aids such as hoists and transfer boards in hospitals.
  • Jar openers, one-handed boards and splints in food or assembly work.
  • Amplified phones and visual alarms for hearing impairment.
  • High-tech: voice-recognition software for severe hand WRMSD or high spinal involvement; screen readers, magnification and Braille displays for visual impairment.
  • Eye-gaze systems and environmental controls for severe motor loss; powered mobility with work-specific modifications; myoelectric hands for amputees returning to office or technical work.
  • Indian context: the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 obliges employers to provide reasonable accommodation.
  • Benefits: earlier and safer return to work, retention of employment and income, reduced re-injury and compensation cost, improved productivity and morale.
  • Barriers: cost, employer attitudes, lack of trial and training, poor follow-up.
  • Evidence: providing ergonomic devices with workplace assessment reduces WRMSD symptom progression and lost workdays versus advice alone; work-hardening programmes that use the actual devices and tasks return more workers to sustained employment.
  • Conclusion: the device is the visible half — the assessment, training and follow-up are what make it work.

Sequence — Classify → Assess → Match → Train → Follow up.

Sources
  • Maxey L, Magnusson P. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. Work and ADL chapters.
  • Chui L et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Work conditioning section.
710 marks

What are the tendon transfer techniques for median nerve injury? Add a note on physiotherapy management.

Full answer →

Give the principles of tendon transfer, the specific transfers for low and high median nerve lesions, and the pre- and post-operative physiotherapy including re-education.

  • Name the donor AND the insertion for each transfer (FDS of ring finger TO abductor pollicis brevis) — a transfer without its insertion is half a mark.
  • Do not forget the physiotherapy half of the question: splint, donor-contraction re-education, then strengthening.
  • A tendon transfer re-routes the muscle-tendon unit of a working muscle to the insertion of a paralysed one.
  • Donor requirements: the muscle must be expendable, of adequate strength (grade 4 plus) and similar amplitude.
  • Joints must be mobile and supple, the transfer should run straight in a single direction, and it should be synergistic with the movement it replaces.
  • Fix correctable contractures and get adequate soft-tissue cover first — no transfer survives a stiff, scarred bed.
  • Low median lesion paralyses the thenar intrinsic muscles, so thumb opposition and abduction are lost, and sensation over the radial three and a half digits is absent.
  • Low-lesion transfer: the FDS of the ring finger (Royle-Thompson) routed subcutaneously to the abductor pollicis brevis insertion.
  • Camitz transfer: palmaris longus with a strip of palmar aponeurosis passed to the APB — quick, single-incision, and best in carpal-tunnel thenar wasting.
  • Extensor indicis proprius split and transferred to the first dorsal interosseous and APB for opposition plus pinch.
  • A slip of abductor digiti minimi (Huber) for thenar bulk in visible thumb-position deficit.
  • The goal is a thumb that can abduct, rotate and reach the fingers — the opponensplasty.
  • High median lesion (above the elbow) also loses FPL and FDP to the index, so thumb interphalangeal and index distal joint flexion go as well as opposition and sensation.
  • High-lesion reconstruction: brachioradialis or extensor carpi radialis longus to FPL for thumb flexion.
  • Side-to-side tenodesis of the index FDP to the middle-finger FDP for index flexion.
  • The same opposition transfers as above, plus an FCR or ECRL addition when a strong donor is needed.
  • Sensation can be improved by neurovascular island flaps in selected cases.
  • Pre-operatively: keep full passive joint range, mobilise scar and oedema, strengthen the donor muscles consciously (the patient must fire FDS or palmaris longus on command), and desensitise and protect the anaesthetic zones.
  • Post-operatively: the transferred tendon is protected in a thumb-spica splint for 3 to 4 weeks, then controlled mobilisation begins.
  • Re-education is the heart of physiotherapy: the transferred muscle still fires in its old pattern, so train the new action — the patient flexes the ring finger (donor action) while watching and feeling the thumb abduct.
  • Use biofeedback, mirror work and repeated attempted opposition until it becomes a single unconscious synergy.
  • Then progress through graded resistance to functional pinch, precision grip and ADLs, with sensory re-education for the median territory in parallel.
  • Outcomes: well-selected opposition transfers achieve functional pinch in most hands, though power and fine sensory discrimination never equal the original.
  • Conclusion: surgery re-routes the tendon; physiotherapy rewires the movement.

Re-education rule — think donor action, get thumb opposition; thumb-spica 3–4 weeks.

Sources
  • Saunders RJ. Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation. Nerve injury chapters.
  • Cooper C. Fundamentals of Hand Therapy. Tendon transfer sections.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Peripheral nerve injuries.
810 marks

Describe the role of myofascial release in trapezitis.

Full answer →

Explain the mechanism of trapezitis and trigger points, how to assess them, the MFR techniques for the upper trapezius, and the release-lengthen-strengthen progression.

  • The sequence 'release — lengthen — strengthen' is the spine of this answer.
  • Write the referral pattern of the upper trapezius (temple, angle of jaw, ipsilateral neck) — examiners ask it in vivas more often than the techniques themselves.
  • Trapezitis is overload of the upper trapezius: sustained low-grade contraction from desk posture, phone-on-shoulder habits, emotional stress and poor workstation ergonomics keeps the muscle continuously active and exhausts its local circulation.
  • The resulting myofascial trigger point is a hyperirritable spot in a taut band.
  • Integrated hypothesis: an energy crisis — ischaemia releases sensitising substances that lower the local pain threshold and sustain abnormal acetylcholine release, producing the taut band, which further compresses the local vessels.
  • The patient feels aching at the point plus the classic referral to the temple, angle of jaw or between the scapulae.
  • Diagnose on palpation: a taut band in the upper trapezius, an exquisite spot, reproduction of the patient's recognised pain, a local twitch response to snapping palpation, and restricted painful cervical rotation or side-flexion.
  • Screen for perpetuating factors — sleep, workstation, spectacles, stress — because a trigger point with perpetuating factors never stays released.
  • MFR works on the fascia-muscle complex with sustained, low-load, gentle pressure and elongation rather than forceful kneading.
  • Direct release: gentle thumb or knuckle pressure at 90 degrees to the taut band, held until the tissue softens (typically 60 to 90 seconds).
  • Skin rolling over the cervicothoracic fascia to restore fascial mobility.
  • Positional release: find the tender point, move the neck into the position of ease and hold, letting the point quieten.
  • Sustained stretch with the head side-flexed away and gently rotated toward, held for the full release time.
  • Follow every release with active use of the range gained — the muscle must learn its new length.
  • Progression order: release the trigger point, lengthen the muscle, then retrain.
  • Dosage: 2 to 3 sessions per week over 3 to 4 weeks, with a home programme of heat, self-pressure with a ball, and stretching.
  • Adjuncts: spray-and-stretch with ethyl chloride or ice, post-isometric relaxation, dry needling for stubborn points, ergonomic correction of the workstation, breathing retraining for stress-related elevation, and strengthening of the mid and lower trapezius.
  • Evidence: MFR and sustained-pressure techniques give short-term reductions in pain and improved neck range and disability versus placebo in neck-pain trials, strongest when combined with exercise; dry needling adds short-term benefit.
  • Conclusion: MFR releases the taut band, but only posture correction and lower-trapezius retraining keep it released — treat the fire, then remove the fuel.

Release — Lengthen — Strengthen.

Sources
  • Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System / myofascial approaches.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Soft-tissue intervention chapter.
  • Shacklock M. Clinical Neurodynamics. Mechanosensitivity chapters.
910 marks

How do you manage pain in fracture cases based on educational and behavioral strategies?

Full answer →

Show how education and behaviour change control fracture pain — gate control, pain neuroscience education, pacing, operant methods and graded exposure by healing phase.

  • The question is set under educational and behavioural strategies — do NOT spend half the answer on TENS and cryotherapy; one sentence on adjuncts is enough.
  • Build the marks on gate control, pain education, pacing, operant reinforcement and graded exposure.
  • Fracture pain is acute nociceptive pain with an inflammatory phase, then movement-related pain during healing, and — if mishandled — a shift to chronic pain with fear of movement, guarded patterns and disuse.
  • Gate control theory explains it: descending anxiety and attention open the gate; confidence and understanding close it.
  • Educational and behavioural strategies change what the patient does and expects, which changes what the nervous system transmits.
  • Education first — pain neuroscience: explain in the patient's language that pain is an alarm produced by the brain on the basis of danger, not a meter of tissue damage; a healing fracture protected by a cast is safe to move.
  • Show the healing timeline (inflammation days 1 to 5, soft callus to about 3 weeks, hard callus to about 3 months) so the patient reads twinges correctly.
  • Give clear rules: weight-bearing status, dos and don'ts, red flags.
  • Set expectations for mobilisation pain and control pathways, and teach relaxation breathing to use before and during painful procedures such as cast removal and pin-site care.
  • Give a written home plan — knowledge that is not written down does not travel home.
  • Behavioural techniques: relaxation and breathing retraining, progressive muscle relaxation of uninvolved segments, guided imagery and distraction for procedural pain.
  • Cognitive restructuring to catch catastrophising thoughts (for example, 'the bone is breaking again').
  • Pacing to break the boom-bust cycle of overdoing on good days.
  • Operant strategies: teach the family to reinforce function ('well done for walking to the gate') and not to reinforce pain behaviour.
  • Goal-setting and self-monitoring with a simple diary, and positive reinforcement tied to achievement, not to suffering.
  • After immobilisation, many patients show fear-avoidance: they equate pain with damage and stop moving.
  • Assess with the Tampa Scale and map their fear hierarchy, then expose them in graded steps — pain-free isometrics, assisted range, weight-bearing, stairs and return to work — each step mastered before the next.
  • Use time-contingent rather than pain-contingent scheduling ('walk ten minutes at 8 am daily') so the patient is not ruled by the pain meter.
  • Combine with goal-setting for functional milestones and progress visible to the patient.
  • Evidence: pain neuroscience education reduces pain, disability and fear in musculoskeletal cohorts; behavioural graded activity matches or beats standard physiotherapy for return-to-function after injury.
  • Conclusion: the physiotherapist controls the psychology and behaviour of pain — education that the patient can repeat back is the cheapest analgesic on the ward.

Melzack and Wall 1965 — fear opens the gate, education and movement close it.

Sources
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology. Pain chapters.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. Pain management chapter.
1010 marks

Explain the physiotherapy intervention for improving endurance in individuals with a sedentary lifestyle.

Full answer →

Explain why endurance fails in the sedentary, how to screen and test, and how to design and progress an aerobic programme using the FITT principle.

  • Quote two number-sets: 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week plus strengthening on two days (WHO 2020), and the 10-percent-per-week progression rule.
  • Write FITT as four separate labelled boxes, not one paragraph.
  • A sedentary lifestyle produces deconditioning through central and peripheral mechanisms.
  • Central: a lower stroke volume and cardiac output reserve.
  • Peripheral: reduced capillary and mitochondrial density in muscle, and a shift toward glycolytic fatigability.
  • Insulin sensitivity falls, visceral fat accumulates, and the patient gets breathless on one flight of stairs.
  • The good news is the trainability — even modest volumes of activity reverse much of this, and the WHO position is that some activity is always better than none.
  • Screen with a physical-activity readiness questionnaire (PAR-Q+) and risk-factor profile; flag the sedentary middle-aged desk worker with hypertension or diabetes for medical clearance before vigorous training.
  • Baseline tests that need no lab: resting and exercise heart rate, the six-minute walk test, a submaximal step or cycle test (Astrand or Chester), a sit-to-stand test for strength endurance, and simple anthropometry.
  • Always record the baseline — the whole motivational architecture of the programme depends on being able to show change.
  • Prescribe by the FITT framework — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.
  • Frequency: five days per week of moderate, or three of vigorous, aerobic activity.
  • Intensity: begin at 40 to 50 percent of heart-rate reserve or a Borg RPE of 10 to 12, progressing to 60 to 70 percent; use the talk test as the field check.
  • Time: start at 20 to 30 minutes of accumulated moderate activity — three 10-minute walks count — progressing to 150 to 300 minutes per week (WHO 2020), plus muscle-strengthening on two or more days.
  • Type: walking is the Indian default — cheap, safe and sociable — with cycling, swimming, or home-based step-ups and dance as alternatives.
  • Add circuit training with body-weight resistance (sit-to-stand, step-ups, wall push-ups, resistance band rows) at 12 to 20 repetitions, two days per week.
  • Progress by roughly 10 percent per week in duration first, then intensity.
  • Monitor with RPE, morning resting heart rate, session adherence and symptom review, plus step counters or phone apps.
  • Include warm-up, cool-down and safety education.
  • Adherence decides the outcome: match the intervention to the patient's stage of change, use motivational interviewing, goal-setting and self-monitoring, embed activity into daily routine (stairs, walking to the market, cycle commutes), and use social supports and follow-up.
  • Conclusion: the WHO 2020 message — some activity is better than none, more is better still.

FITT — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

Sources
  • WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour, 2020.
  • ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise. Aerobic endurance chapters.
110 marks

Describe the documentation procedure adopted in terms of assessment, management in rehabilitation based on International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF).

Full answer →

Explain the ICF model, then show how you document assessment findings and rehabilitation plans using ICF codes and qualifiers.

  • What earns marks: cover all four rows of the marking scheme — define ICF and its purpose (WHO 2001), draw the components, show assessment codes, then show management planning.
  • Never call ICF a "classification of disability" — the C stands for functioning AND disability, and forgetting environmental factors is the commonest way to lose the full two marks of the components row.
  • What ICF is: the World Health Organization's working form of the biopsychosocial model. Instead of documenting only the disease (ICD), we document what the disease does to the person.
  • Functioning and disability are the health condition interacting with body functions, body structures, activities, participation, and the surrounding environmental and personal factors.
  • The shift examiners look for: from "what is wrong with the knee" to "what the stiff knee does to the farmer who has to squat to work."
  • ICF has two parts. Part 1 covers functioning and disability with three components: body functions (code b), body structures (code s), and activities and participation (code d).
  • Part 2 covers contextual factors: environmental factors (code e) and personal factors, which are described but not classified.
  • Every code carries a qualifier from 0 to 4 — no impairment to complete impairment. So d450.2 means moderate difficulty walking.
  • Fig to draw: health condition on top, the three functioning boxes in the middle, contextual factors at the bottom; every arrow is two-way — each box can help or harm the others.
  • Assessment procedure (post-stroke patient, district hospital OPD): organise history and examination findings by level.
  • Body function and structure: b730 muscle power impairment 2, spasticity b735.1, shoulder subluxation s73016.
  • Activity: d450 walking with quadripod, moderate limitation.
  • Participation: d920 recreation and d850 remunerative employment, severely restricted.
  • Contextual factors: e310 immediate family is supportive (facilitator, +3); e140 work products absent; e115 assistive products unavailable in the village (barrier).
  • Each finding gets a code plus a qualifier — that pairing is what turns a case sheet into ICF documentation.
  • Management documentation: write SMART goals at each level.
  • Body level goal: improve shoulder abduction power by one MRC grade in six weeks.
  • Activity goal: independent walking for 200 metres with a stick by week eight.
  • Participation goal: return to light farm work by twelve weeks.
  • Every intervention column must cite the level it targets, and every re-assessment must use the same qualifiers so the change is measurable.
  • Link standard scales to codes: the SPADI documents shoulder pain and disability; a 10-metre walk test documents d450.
  • Why examiners award this: ICF prevents impairment-only physiotherapy, gives the whole rehabilitation team a common language, and justifies goal setting the family understands.
  • Indian context: it forces you to document environmental barriers — a house with a squat toilet, a workplace with no seating, a bus with a high step — which decides whether your exercise programme translates to real life.
Sources
  • World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice.
  • WHO. International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), 2001.
  • Roach KE et al. The Shoulder Pain and Disability Index. Arthritis Care & Research, 1991.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
210 marks

Define Competency. Add a note on Competency-Based Physiotherapy Education.

Full answer →

Define competency with all three domains, then explain how competency-based physiotherapy education designs teaching and assessment around outcomes.

  • What earns marks: the definition must contain all three domains AND the word "habitual".
  • Link CBPE to assessment at the apex of Miller's pyramid ("does").
  • Use Bloom's taxonomy verbs (assess, evaluate, create) instead of "understand" to pick up easy extra marks.
  • Definition: competency is the habitual and judicious integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes displayed in real clinical practice.
  • Three domains, never two — knowledge, skills, attitudes. A therapist who passes a written test on gait training but cannot communicate the plan to an anxious grandfather is knowledgeable, not competent.
  • "Habitual" matters: one lucky performance on exam day is not competency; it must be reproducible over time and across situations.
  • CBPE turns the curriculum inside-out: instead of "we taught ten lectures on electrotherapy, therefore the student is ready," it declares the desired graduate outcome first (the competent entry-level clinician) and designs teaching, learning and assessment backwards from it. This is constructive alignment.
  • Content is organised into competencies with milestones that state observable behaviours, mapped to Bloom's revised taxonomy verbs — a student must be able to assess, plan, apply and evaluate, not merely describe.
  • Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) convert competencies into real clinical units of work, such as "assess and manage a patient with mechanical low back pain under supervision."
  • Assessment — George Miller's pyramid: base "knows" (MCQs), "knows how" (case discussions and vivas), "shows how" (OSCE stations on simulated patients), apex "does" (workplace-based assessment and direct observation at the patient's side).
  • In CBPE the dominant assessment becomes the apex; feedback is continuous and formative rather than a single summative verdict; progression is by demonstrated achievement, not time served.
  • Advantages: transparency of outcomes, learner-centred flexibility (a student may take twelve weeks or sixteen to master a skill), early clinical exposure, and assessment that mirrors actual practice.
  • Challenges in India: batch sizes of sixty-plus make individualised feedback expensive; faculty need training in direct observation; workplace assessment demands clinical infrastructure that colleges attached to small hospitals struggle to provide; and a national competency framework for physiotherapy is still maturing, though the CBME model adopted for MBBS gives a ready template.
Sources
  • Miller GE. The assessment of clinical skills/competence/performance. Academic Medicine, 1990.
  • Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing (Bloom revised).
  • World Physiotherapy. Physiotherapist education framework and Standards of Practice.
310 marks

Describe various methods of sampling and sample size determination.

Full answer →

List the sampling methods with examples, then give the sample-size formula and the worked figure.

  • What earns marks: define population, sample and sampling frame first; then list probability and non-probability methods with examples; then give the sample-size formula with the worked figure of 384.
  • Always write "sample size was calculated for the primary outcome" — a study powered for one outcome is not powered for all of them.
  • Why we sample: studying the entire population of Indian knee-osteoarthritis patients is impossible, but the sample must behave like the population it came from.
  • Three terms: target population (everyone we want to study), accessible population (those we can reach), and sampling frame — the complete, reachable list of population members from which you actually draw.
  • In India the frame is the honest weak link: electoral rolls miss migrants, hospital registers miss those who never reach hospital — every such gap is selection bias before your study begins.
  • Probability sampling: every subject has a known, non-zero chance — this allows estimation and inference.
  • Simple random sampling: every member has an equal chance; use random number tables or software; unbiased but needs a complete frame and spreads travel over wide geography.
  • Systematic sampling: pick every k-th person from a list after a random start — convenient for OPD registration queues.
  • Stratified sampling: split the frame into layers (sex, age band, urban or rural) and sample within each — guarantees a minority group is not wiped out by chance.
  • Cluster sampling: randomly select whole clusters (villages, schools, anganwadi centres) then study everyone inside — cheapest for community surveys in dispersed rural populations, at the price of design effect and lower precision.
  • Multistage sampling stacks these: random districts, then random PHCs, then households.
  • Non-probability sampling is practical, but generalisation dies — it is hypothesis-generating only.
  • Convenience sampling: whoever walks into your OPD that month — the default of most Indian student dissertations, acceptable for pilot studies only.
  • Purposive sampling: you deliberately select information-rich cases — the backbone of qualitative work.
  • Snowball sampling: each enrolled subject recruits peers from the same hidden network — essential when studying stigmatised groups such as drug users.
  • Quota sampling: fill fixed numbers in each category for speed.
  • Consecutive sampling: every eligible patient during a defined window — the least-biased clinical option and always worth naming.
  • Sample size is not a tradition of thirty per group; it is calculated from four inputs: the expected effect size or prevalence, the acceptable margin of error d, the confidence level (usually 95%, Z = 1.96), and the power (usually 80%, Z = 0.84) against the assumed type II error.
  • Formula for a proportion or prevalence: n = Z squared times p times q, divided by d squared. With no prior estimate take p = 0.5, d = 0.05, giving 384 — the number behind most Indian prevalence surveys.
  • Formula for comparing two means: n = 2 times Z-squared times s-squared divided by effect-size squared, where the standardised difference is Cohen's d.
  • Add 10 to 20 percent for attrition, and for cluster designs multiply by the design effect.
  • Too small a study misses a true effect; too large wastes scarce resources and exposes more subjects than needed to risk — both are ethical failures, which links this question to Unit 2.
  • Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis (false alarm), guarded by the significance level alpha; type II error is missing a real effect, guarded by power — one minus beta.
  • Report that you calculated sample size before, not after, data collection — a post-hoc power justification reads as an excuse. In ICMR-funded multicentric trials the statistician finalises this calculation in the protocol stage.
Sources
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics.
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
410 marks

Explain the ethical principles in practice of physiotherapy in a hospital and community.

Full answer →

Give the four ethical principles with a physiotherapy example each, then contrast hospital and community practice.

  • What earns marks: the four principles with a physiotherapy example each — plus the hospital-versus-community contrast, which is where the distinction marks come from.
  • Ethics rests on two legs: the four prima facie principles of Beauchamp and Childress, and the professional codes that convert them into rules of conduct — the World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice and, for research and community programmes in India, the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines 2017.
  • Principles give the philosophy; codes give the enforceable behaviour. Quoting both lifts the answer from a philosophy essay to a professional one.
  • Autonomy: the patient's right to decide — exercised through informed consent, truth-telling about the diagnosis, and respect for refusal. An OPD patient may decline a passive-mobilisation technique, and we document and respect it.
  • Beneficence: act for the patient's benefit — choose the exercise programme with the best evidence for that person, not the most profitable for the clinic.
  • Non-maleficence: do no harm — screen for red flags, avoid over-pressure on osteoporotic spines, and apply a risk-benefit justification for every modality.
  • Justice: fairness in distribution — equal quality of care for a ward patient and a private cubicle patient, transparent fees, and no discrimination by caste, religion, gender, HIV status or ability to pay.
  • Hospital — consent: obtain it before the first assessment and again for any change of plan, in the patient's language. Remember a signature without understanding is not consent.
  • Hospital — confidentiality: no case discussions in hospital corridors, no patient photos on personal phones, and digital records protected as the ICMR data-protection expectations require.
  • Hospital — boundaries: maintain professional boundaries — no personal relationships with patients under care.
  • Hospital — documentation: record every session honestly; the case sheet is the ethical record that protects the patient and you.
  • Hospital — scope: practise within your scope and refer onwards to an orthopaedician or a physician when red flags exceed physiotherapy.
  • Hospital — honesty: follow infection control, be truthful about fees and likely outcomes, and do not promise cures — "guaranteed pain relief in three sittings" is an ethical breach, not marketing.
  • Community — voluntariness must be real: a free camp attended by the whole village because the employer sanctioned leave is not entirely voluntary.
  • Community — cultural and religious sensitivity decides whether an exercise programme is followed: prescribing knee flexion postures where squatting is required for daily life is poor rehabilitation.
  • Community — justice dominates: reach patients who cannot reach us.
  • Community — data ethics: use ICMR 2017 standards when the programme involves data collection — ethical committee approval, anonymised records, and benefit flowing back to the community studied, not only to the researchers.
Sources
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
  • World Physiotherapy. Standards of Practice.
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
510 marks

Explain the instrumentation for neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES).

Full answer →

Trace the signal from mains to patient and give the parameter settings — instrumentation needs physics, not just a parameter list.

  • What earns marks: say the words transformer, rectifier, oscillator, coupling transformer and patient isolation — the physics, not just the parameter list.
  • Add the key sentence: phase duration, not the machine's frequency label, decides which tissue depolarises. That single sentence separates the 7-mark script from the 10-mark one.
  • Principle: NMES does not excite the muscle fibre directly — it depolarises the motor axon under the cathode, and the action potential travelling to the neuromuscular junction produces contraction exactly as voluntary effort does.
  • Because it bypasses the voluntary motor drive, even a patient with upper motor neuron weakness contracts.
  • Recruitment order is reversed: electrical stimulation recruits large, fast type II axons before small type I axons — the opposite of the Henneman size principle. This is why NMES fatigues muscle faster than voluntary work.
  • Block diagram, step 1 — power supply: the mains at 230 volts AC enters a step-down transformer, is rectified to DC and smoothed by a filter to give a safe, stable low-voltage supply.
  • Step 2 — oscillator: the timing circuit, classically a 555-type timer, generates the pulse train and sets frequency, phase duration and on-off timing.
  • Step 3 — output stage: a transistorised amplifier raises current to the therapeutic level, usually through a coupling transformer that isolates the patient from the mains — the safety heart of the instrument.
  • Step 4 — patient: the current reaches the skin through electrodes placed over the motor point of the target muscle.
  • Controls to memorise: frequency 20–50 Hz; phase duration 200–400 µs; duty cycle 1:1 to 1:5; ramp-up 100–300 ms; amplitude = maximum tolerated.
  • Waveform: the waveform of choice is a symmetrical or asymmetric biphasic pulsed current — balanced charge leaves no net DC component and prevents iontophoresis-like skin irritation and burns under the electrode.
  • Frequency use: low rates 2 to 10 Hz twitch the muscle for drainage and the muscle pump; 20 to 50 Hz produce tetanic contraction for strengthening; up to 80 to 100 Hz are used for spasm inhibition, at the cost of fast fatigue.
  • Phase duration: 200 to 400 microseconds sits over the strength-duration curve's comfortable motor threshold for innervated muscle.
  • Duty cycle (the on:off ratio): 1:5 in early reconditioning and about 1:1 for strengthening; more off-time means less fatigue.
  • Ramp-up and ramp-down of 100 to 300 milliseconds let the patient tolerate higher amplitude, and amplitude is turned to the maximum tolerated, aiming for a strong, comfortable tetanic contraction.
  • Electrodes: match size to muscle bulk — larger electrodes lower current density and improve comfort; placement over the motor point lowers the threshold; prep the skin and check impedance, because broken current paths cause burns.
  • Contraindications and precautions: cardiac pacemakers and implanted devices, the carotid sinus, the pregnant uterus, active deep vein thrombosis, areas of active malignancy, and sensory loss where the patient cannot report excessive current.
  • Instrument types: Russian current (medium frequency 2500 Hz, burst-modulated at 50 bursts per second, for strengthening); functional electrical stimulation (stimulation synchronised to a task such as foot-drop walking); TENS (sensory-level sibling for pain); and stimulators for denervated muscle, which must deliver long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds — often triangular or exponential — because denervated fibre has no axon to depolarise.
Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
610 marks

Explain the various study designs in research.

Full answer →

Classify designs as observational or experimental, then describe each with its statistic and its bias controls.

  • What earns marks: for every design give one physiotherapy example and one statistic it produces — odds ratio for case-control, relative risk for cohort — and for the RCT use the phrase "randomisation plus concealment plus blinding plus intention-to-treat".
  • Designs described without their bias controls read like a menu, not an answer.
  • Classification axis one: does the investigator allocate the exposure? If not, the design is observational; if yes, it is experimental.
  • Observational splits into descriptive (case report, case series, cross-sectional survey) and analytical (case-control, cohort).
  • Experimental includes the randomised controlled trial, quasi-experiment, pre-experimental pre-post designs, and the single-case (n-of-1) experiment.
  • Axis two — timing: retrospective looks backwards from outcome; prospective looks forward from exposure.
  • Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time point; they give prevalence, not incidence, and cannot prove sequence — useful for a survey of low back pain prevalence among Bengaluru autorickshaw drivers.
  • Case-control studies start from the outcome and compare past exposure between cases and controls, yielding an odds ratio; efficient for rare outcomes like transient brachial plexopathy, but memory bias is the toll.
  • Cohort studies start from exposure and follow forward for the outcome — relative risk, temporal sequence established; the ethical design when withholding treatment is impossible, at the price of time, expense and loss to follow-up.
  • Case reports and series generate hypotheses, one patient at a time.
  • RCT is the reference standard: randomisation distributes known and unknown confounders equally between groups, concealed allocation prevents selection bias, blinding of patient, therapist and assessor prevents expectation bias, and an intention-to-treat analysis preserves the randomisation.
  • State the PICO question explicitly — population, intervention, comparison, outcome — and the design becomes obvious rather than memorised.
  • Below the RCT: quasi-experimental designs (allocation by ward or by week, when randomising individuals is impossible); pre-post single-group designs (no control, only a hypothesis); the single-case experimental design with repeated baseline phases (a clinician's method for one patient); and crossover trials, where each patient is their own control and a washout period separates phases.
  • Evidence pyramid, bottom to top: expert opinion and bench research, case reports and series, case-control studies, cohort studies, RCTs, systematic reviews. Higher means better protection against bias, not automatic truth.
  • Qualitative designs answer meaning questions: phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography — analysed by the Braun and Clarke six-phase thematic analysis (for example, why patients abandon home programmes).
  • Match the design to the question: a therapy question wants an RCT or systematic review; a prognosis question wants a cohort; a diagnostic accuracy question wants a cross-sectional comparison against a gold standard; a meaning question wants qualitative work.
Sources
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
  • Herbert R et al. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
  • Braun V, Clarke V. Using thematic analysis in psychology, 2006.
710 marks

Discuss in brief parametric and non-parametric tests.

Full answer →

Pair each parametric test with its non-parametric twin, and say how to choose between them.

  • What earns marks: write the answer as a paired table — parametric test on the left, its non-parametric twin on the right — and add one line on why you chose each, e.g. "VAS pain is ordinal, so Wilcoxon signed-rank."
  • Always state the design first, then the test — a paired test on unpaired data is a more serious error than choosing the wrong family.
  • Parametric tests assume the data follow a specific distribution — the normal (Gaussian) curve — and estimate its parameters, mean and standard deviation.
  • Four assumptions of parametric tests: normality; data measured on interval or ratio scale; homogeneity of variance across compared groups; and independence of observations.
  • Non-parametric tests make no distributional assumption — hence "distribution-free" — and work on ranks, so they tolerate ordinal scales like pain scores and skewed data like hospital stay or income.
  • Check normality with the Shapiro-Wilk test, or by eyeballing the histogram and Q-Q plot — naming an actual check is worth more than reciting the assumption.
  • One group versus a known value: one-sample t-test.
  • Two paired measurements (pain before and after ten sittings of interferential therapy): paired t-test.
  • Two independent groups (conventional exercise versus physiotherapist-supervised exercise in two OPD cohorts): unpaired (independent) t-test.
  • Three or more independent groups: one-way ANOVA, with a post-hoc test such as Tukey to find which pair differs.
  • Repeated measurements across time: repeated-measures ANOVA.
  • Relationship between two continuous variables: Pearson's correlation coefficient r.
  • Each test outputs a p-value and, in modern reporting, a confidence interval. Say: p less than 0.05 means evidence against the null, not proof of a large effect.
  • Non-parametric twins — paired setting: the sign test (direction only) and the more powerful Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
  • Two independent groups: Mann-Whitney U test.
  • Three or more groups: Kruskal-Wallis H test.
  • Repeated measures: Friedman test.
  • Correlation: Spearman's rho.
  • Categorical data: the chi-square test — goodness of fit and independence in a contingency table — with Fisher's exact test when expected cell counts fall below five.
  • Choosing: normal, interval data with comparable variances choose parametric; ordinal, ranked, skewed or outlier-heavy data choose non-parametric. Both paths must still respect independence and the pairing structure of the design.
  • If the data look nearly normal, prefer the parametric test — it is more powerful, and on mildly non-normal data the rank tests retain roughly 95 percent of that efficiency, so little is lost either way.
Sources
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra RK. Medical Biostatistics.
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
810 marks

Considerations for exercise prescription in obesity.

Full answer →

Write a real prescription — pre-participation screening, then FITT-VP with numbers, using the Asian Indian cutoffs.

  • What earns marks: the answer must read as a prescription, not an essay on obesity — four FITT letters with numbers, the Asian Indian cutoffs (BMI 25, waist 90/80), and the hypoglycaemia-with-insulin warning.
  • Candidates who write "advise exercise" without numbers cap at half marks; you are prescribing a drug called movement.
  • Define your patient: obesity is excess body fat with health risk, and for Asian Indians the thresholds arrive early.
  • Asian Indian cutoffs (Misra et al. JAPI 2009): obesity is a body mass index of 25 or more (overweight 23 to 24.9) — not the Western cutoff of 30; central obesity is a waist circumference of 90 cm or more in men and 80 cm or more in women.
  • Indians develop the "thin-fat" phenotype — metabolic risk at lower BMI — which is why we screen and treat earlier.
  • Before the first session, review comorbidities: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, and painful knees or low back from the mechanical load.
  • Diabetes caution: exercise after an insulin or sulfonylurea dose risks hypoglycaemia — advise carrying glucose and adjusting the dose with the physician.
  • Blood pressure: record resting blood pressure; defer if 180/110 or above until controlled.
  • Stratify cardiovascular risk: the apparently healthy obese adult can begin moderate activity without testing, while symptomatic patients or those planning vigorous exercise need medical clearance.
  • Baseline measures to document: waist circumference, resting heart rate and blood pressure, a six-minute walk test, and functional joint status.
  • Frequency: aerobic exercise on five days a week (or every day if lighter); resistance training on two to three non-consecutive days.
  • Intensity: moderate — 40 to 60 percent of heart-rate reserve, or a talk-test pace where the patient can still converse, rating of perceived exertion 11 to 13 on the Borg 6-to-20 scale.
  • Time: 30 to 60 minutes daily, accumulated in bouts of at least ten minutes, building to the guideline volume of 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity weekly.
  • Type: load-friendly aerobic choices first — brisk walking, stationary cycling, swimming or aqua exercise (buoyancy unloads the knees) — later progressing to jogging; plus large-muscle resistance training, because each kilogram of added muscle raises resting metabolic rate and preserves lean mass during weight loss.
  • Quantify energy cost in METs — brisk walking is about 4, cycling about 8 — so the patient can see that walking thirty minutes burns roughly the calories of one chapati. Diet must change in parallel: exercise alone rarely outpaces a calorie surplus.
  • Progress volume first, intensity later — add roughly five to ten minutes per fortnight of tolerated walking before touching speed or incline.
  • Protect joints: aquatic exercise, cycles and graded walking paths for the painful knee; cushioned footwear on hard Indian roads; avoid deep squats early.
  • Safety: time outdoor sessions for early morning or evening in Indian heat and humidity, and enforce hydration.
  • Behaviour and adherence: written goals, step counters, exercise logs, walking groups for company, and family involvement — in Indian households the kitchen decides the calorie side of the equation, so involve whoever cooks.
  • Reassess monthly with waist circumference and walk time, not the weighing scale alone, and coordinate with a dietitian and physician: exercise preserves lean mass during weight loss, which dieting alone squanders.
Sources
  • Misra A et al. Consensus statement for diagnosis of obesity, abdominal obesity and the metabolic syndrome for Asian Indians. JAPI, 2009.
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
910 marks

Differentiate aerobic and anaerobic exercise in terms of energy expenditure.

Full answer →

Contrast the two in terms of energy expenditure — which substrate, how much ATP, how fast it arrives, and the oxygen and lactate cost.

  • What earns marks: the mark is for "in terms of energy expenditure", so anchor every difference in ATP — which substrate, how much ATP per glucose molecule (2 versus about 32), how fast it arrives, and what it costs in oxygen and lactate.
  • A pure list of "aerobic means jogging" scores half; the mechanism scores full.
  • All exercise is powered by ATP, regenerated by three systems on a time-and-intensity clock.
  • Phosphagen system (stored ATP and creatine phosphate): fuels the first eight to ten seconds of all-out effort anaerobically, without oxygen, without lactate.
  • Anaerobic glycolysis: breaks glucose to pyruvate and, when oxygen supply lags demand, ferments it to lactate, regenerating ATP rapidly for roughly ten seconds to two minutes of heavy work — at the cost of hydrogen-ion accumulation and early fatigue.
  • Oxidative (aerobic) system: burns carbohydrate and fat in the mitochondria with oxygen, yielding far more ATP per glucose molecule but only at a slower rate; it dominates from about two minutes onward and supports hours of submaximal work.
  • The systems never switch on and off; they share the load, and the intensity of the exercise decides the share.
  • Intensity: aerobic work is moderate, sustainable and below the lactate threshold (roughly 55 to 70 percent of maximal oxygen uptake); anaerobic work is near-maximal, above the lactate threshold, where blood lactate climbs past about 4 mmol per litre.
  • Oxygen demand: aerobic exercise is steady state — uptake meets demand; anaerobic exercise creates an oxygen deficit that must be repaid.
  • Fuel: aerobic uses both carbohydrate and fat (fat burns only in a carbohydrate flame, and only aerobically); anaerobic burns carbohydrate alone.
  • Duration and power: anaerobic delivers high power for seconds to about two minutes; aerobic delivers lower power for minutes to hours.
  • By-products: anaerobic accumulates lactate and hydrogen ions; aerobic yields carbon dioxide and water.
  • ATP yield: anaerobic gives 2 ATP per glucose molecule versus roughly 32 aerobically.
  • Physiotherapy examples a therapist meets daily: a patient rising from a chair once (phosphagen), a stair-climbing test (glycolytic), a six-minute walk test (aerobic).
  • Oxygen deficit: at exercise onset, oxidative phosphorylation lags behind demand — covered meanwhile by the phosphagen system and glycolysis.
  • EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, the modern name for oxygen debt): after stopping, oxygen uptake remains raised — it repays the phosphagen stores, clears lactate by gluconeogenesis in the liver (the Cori cycle), restores myoglobin, and funds the raised temperature and catecholamine-driven metabolism.
  • Anaerobic exercise produces a large, fast-rising EPOC; aerobic exercise, when severe and prolonged, produces a slower but longer-lasting one — the physiological basis of interval-training prescriptions for cardiometabolic patients.
  • Aerobic training adaptations: more mitochondria and aerobic enzymes, higher capillary density and haemoglobin mass, lower resting heart rate and higher maximal oxygen uptake — tested by graded exercise tests with gas analysis or field tests like the six-minute walk or 20-m shuttle.
  • Anaerobic training adaptations: larger phosphagen stores and glycolytic enzymes, and better hydrogen-ion buffering — tested by the 30-second Wingate anaerobic test or vertical jumps.
  • For our patients, most rehabilitation is aerobic; anaerobic dosing belongs to return-to-sport phases, and the physiotherapist's skill is prescribing on the correct side of the lactate threshold.

Aerobic vs anaerobic in three numbers: 10 seconds : 2 minutes : unlimited — then name the fuel each system burns.

Sources
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
1010 marks

Describe electrical stimulation and its effect on various systems.

Full answer →

Describe the current, then its effects system by system with a mechanism for each.

  • What earns marks: the question says "various systems", so an answer that only discusses muscle caps itself at five marks — give one heading each for muscle, nerve, circulation and at least two other systems, each with a mechanism, not just a claim.
  • The type-II recruitment reversal and the pain-gate mechanism are the two most-tested mechanisms in this unit.
  • Definition: therapeutic electrical stimulation is the application of controlled electrical current through surface electrodes to excite nerve or muscle and produce a physiological or therapeutic effect.
  • Classification by pulse shape: rectangular, triangular, exponential, sinusoidal.
  • Classification by continuity: direct versus pulsed.
  • Classification by clinical intent: NMES for muscle activation, functional electrical stimulation synchronised to a task, TENS for sensory analgesia, and Russian current for strengthening.
  • Unifying mechanism: depolarisation of the excitable membrane under the cathode when the stimulus crosses the threshold defined by the strength-duration curve.
  • Muscle — contraction follows frequency: twitches below about 10 to 15 Hz, tetanic contraction from 20 to 50 Hz, and rapid fatigue above that.
  • Muscle — recruitment is reversed compared with voluntary effort: large type II motor axons fire first, which makes NMES a useful fast-twitch trainer but an early fatiguer.
  • Muscle — used repeatedly, it maintains muscle mass in disuse and immobilisation, retards atrophy after injury or surgery, strengthens weak quadriceps and pelvic floor, re-educates a muscle the patient has "forgotten" to recruit, and pumps venous and lymphatic return through the muscle pump.
  • Denervated muscle needs a different instrument entirely: long pulse durations of tens of milliseconds and triangular or exponential waveforms, because there is no axon to depolarise and the fibre itself must be excited.
  • Nervous system — sensory: low-intensity high-rate stimulation recruits large-diameter afferents and closes the pain gate in the dorsal horn (the mechanism of conventional TENS); low-rate (2 to 4 Hz) stimulation recruits descending opioid pathways for diffuse analgesia.
  • Nervous system — sensory: stimulated sensory input also improves proprioceptive awareness of a joint.
  • Nervous system — motor: stimulation preserves axonal excitability and conduction in disuse, and cyclic stimulation of the common peroneal nerve in foot drop is the classic functional application of motor-nerve stimulation.
  • Circulation: rhythmically stimulated skeletal muscle acts as a peripheral heart — the pumping action drives venous and lymphatic return, reduces oedema after injury and encourages arterial inflow.
  • Circulation: large-muscle stimulation raises heart rate and blood pressure because the metabolic demand of contracting muscle triggers sympathetic cardiovascular responses — a consideration in cardiac patients.
  • Metabolism: local metabolism rises in the stimulated muscle with increased substrate use, and stimulation-induced movement aids nutrition of cartilage and soft tissue in immobilised joints.
  • Bone: mechanical strain generates piezoelectric currents, and clinically applied electrical stimulation is used to support delayed-union fracture healing.
  • Skin and viscera: long-standing sensory stimulation can produce trophic changes; smooth muscle and viscera respond poorly to brief pulses, though some bladder and pelvic-floor applications exist.
  • Precautions and contraindications: cardiac pacemakers and implanted electronic devices, stimulation over the carotid sinus, the pregnant uterus, active deep vein thrombosis, malignant tissue and infected areas, and sensory loss where the patient cannot report excess current.
  • Indian context: remember the practical system factors — cost, machine availability and adherence — that decide whether a stimulation programme survives beyond the OPD.
  • Conclusion: electrical stimulation is an adjunct that activates the tissue; the retraining still comes from exercise and function.
Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017.
110 marks

Explain the components of the skeletal system.

Full answer →

Name the parts of the skeleton, give the bone counts, then finish with a clinical point on bone remodelling.

  • Marks first: start with a definition, then the axial and appendicular bone counts, then classification — that is where the easy marks sit.
  • Marks first: name the five functions — support, protection, movement, haemopoiesis, mineral storage.
  • Marks first: the last 2 marks are clinical — write Wolff's law plus one Indian-context line (vitamin D deficiency, osteoporotic kyphosis).
  • Definition: the skeletal system is the body's living framework — 206 bones in the adult, plus the cartilage, ligaments and joints that bind them.
  • Key idea: bone is living, active tissue that keeps remodelling in response to the loads it feels.
  • Function — support: rigid levers that hold posture.
  • Function — protection: the skull protects the brain, the rib cage protects the heart and lungs.
  • Function — movement: bones act as levers for muscles to pull.
  • Function — haemopoiesis: red marrow makes blood cells.
  • Function — mineral storage: about 99% of body calcium and most phosphorus are stored in bone; yellow marrow stores fat.
  • Axial skeleton: the upright axis of the body — 80 bones in all.
  • Axial — skull: 22 bones, plus 6 ear ossicles and the hyoid.
  • Axial — vertebral column: 26 bones — 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx.
  • Axial — thoracic cage: 24 ribs and the sternum.
  • Mechanism: the axial column carries all the body weight downwards and protects the spinal cord, so axial loading injuries (like a fall from a scaffold) hurt it most at the thoracolumbar junction.
  • Appendicular skeleton: the limbs and their girdles — 126 bones in all.
  • Appendicular — pectoral girdles: clavicle and scapula, 4 bones, anchoring the upper limbs of 60 bones.
  • Appendicular — pelvic girdles: 2 hip bones, anchoring the lower limbs of 60 bones.
  • Mechanism: the pectoral girdle gives up stability for mobility (shallow glenoid); the pelvic girdle gives up mobility for stability (deep socket, strong ligaments) to bear weight.
  • Classification by shape: long (femur), short (carpals), flat (ilium), irregular (vertebra), sesamoid (patella).
  • Patella note: the largest sesamoid, sitting in the quadriceps tendon to improve leverage and shield the knee.
  • Classification by structure: compact bone (dense outer shell, resists bending) and cancellous bone (spongy inner mesh with trabeculae along stress lines, resists compression).
  • Development: bones form by intramembranous or endochondral ossification.
  • Associated structures: articular hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces — low friction, no blood supply, so it heals poorly.
  • Associated structures: fibrocartilage forms menisci and discs and resists compression.
  • Associated structures: ligaments passively limit joint range.
  • Joints: classified as fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial.
  • Synovial joint: capsule, synovial membrane, cartilage and reinforcing ligaments — the unit we treat every day.
  • Clinical: Wolff's law — bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress, thickening where loaded and resorbing where unloaded.
  • Clinical: prolonged immobilisation causes disuse osteoporosis; graduated weight bearing rebuilds bone.
  • Indian context: widespread vitamin D deficiency and postmenopausal osteoporosis make axial bone loss show up as thoracic kyphosis and fragility fractures.
  • Prevention: early weight-bearing exercise and DEXA screening are our tools.

206 bones = axial 80 + appendicular 126

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — skeletal tissue structure.
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — axial and appendicular divisions.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — bone remodelling and calcium homeostasis.
210 marks

Enumerate the tools for measurement of body fat analysis.

Full answer →

List the tools from cheap field methods to laboratory methods, and end with the Indian cutoffs.

  • Marks first: the question says "enumerate" — the marks are for the complete list, so name seven or more tools with one mechanism line each.
  • Marks first: finish with the Asian-Indian cutoffs — that is your last mark.
  • Why measure: body mass splits into fat mass and fat-free mass (water, protein, bone mineral).
  • Why measure: total body weight alone hides the difference between a muscular athlete and a sarcopenic obese patient — both can share a BMI of 28.
  • Why measure: fat measurement quantifies obesity, tracks rehabilitation progress and stratifies cardiometabolic risk.
  • Structure: arrange your answer as a ladder — from cheap field tools to criterion laboratory methods.
  • Measuring tape: waist circumference and waist–hip ratio estimate central (visceral) fat.
  • Indian cutoffs for waist: 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women — lower than the western 102/88 — because Indians develop diabetes at lower BMI.
  • BMI: weight in kg divided by height in metres squared — an obesity screen.
  • Indian BMI action point: 23 kg/m², not 25.
  • Skinfold caliper: pinches subcutaneous fat at standard sites to estimate total body fat using regression equations.
  • Standard skinfold sites: Durnin–Womersley four sites (biceps, triceps, subscapular, suprailiac) or Jackson–Pollock three or seven sites.
  • BIA (bioelectrical impedance analysis): a painless, portable 50 kHz current is passed through the body.
  • BIA mechanism: fat-free mass is water- and electrolyte-rich and conducts better, while fat resists, so impedance predicts total body water and hence fat-free mass.
  • BIA caution: it assumes constant tissue hydration, so dehydration or post-exercise readings distort it.
  • Hydrostatic (underwater) weighing: the patient is submerged and fully exhales; body density is found from underwater weight by Archimedes' principle.
  • Hydrostatic: the two-compartment Siri equation then converts density to fat percentage — accurate but laborious and unpleasant.
  • Air-displacement plethysmography (Bod Pod): replaces water with air displacement in a sealed chamber — same principle, far better tolerated.
  • DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry): today's practical gold standard — splits the body into fat, lean soft tissue and bone mineral at a low radiation dose, with regional (trunk vs limb) output.
  • Isotope dilution (deuterated water): measures total body water.
  • Others to name for the enumeration mark: near-infrared interactance, ultrasound of subcutaneous fat, and, for research, CT and MRI volumetry.
  • If you remember it: potassium-40 whole-body counting.
  • Choosing: match the tool to the purpose — tape and BMI for every clinic screening, calipers for percentage fat on a budget, DEXA when you need regional fat and bone together.
  • Comparison line: field tools are cheap and repeatable but population-specific; criterion methods are accurate but costly and immobile.

Ladder: tape/BMI → skinfold caliper (4 Durnin–Womersley sites) → BIA → tank/Bod Pod → DEXA (criterion)

Sources
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — body composition assessment.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — anthropometry in clinical practice.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — body fluid compartments underlying BIA.
310 marks

Describe the applications of Newton's second law in the human body.

Full answer →

State the law in both linear and angular form, then give named body examples in each domain.

  • Marks first: write BOTH the linear equation and the angular (torque) equation — giving only force = mass × acceleration caps you at 4 of 10.
  • Marks first: give one named example per domain — gait, throwing, fall injury, and one treatment application.
  • The law: the net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration (net force = mass × acceleration).
  • Direction: acceleration is in the direction of the net force.
  • Angular form: net torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration.
  • Mechanism: the law is the bridge between muscle (which creates force) and motion (which is acceleration); almost every therapeutic exercise is an application of it.
  • Walking: the ground reaction force is roughly 1.1 to 1.5 times body weight at loading response.
  • Running: this rises to 2 to 3 times body weight — every step is your mass being decelerated and re-accelerated.
  • Vertical jump: the athlete must generate force well above body weight to leave the ground.
  • Sit-to-stand: quadriceps force must exceed body weight enough to produce upward acceleration of the trunk — which is why elderly patients rock forward first, building acceleration over a longer path.
  • Indian context: head-load carriers and porters walk with shorter, smoother steps — minimising the acceleration component lowers peak force on the spine.
  • Angular: muscles create torque about joints, and a segment's angular acceleration depends on its moment of inertia (how mass is distributed about the axis).
  • Example: a figure skater pulling the arms in reduces moment of inertia and spins faster with unchanged angular momentum.
  • Example: a cricket bowler or badminton-smash player sequences proximal-to-distal so each segment accelerates off the previous one — the kinetic chain.
  • Example: a long lever arm (outstretched arm holding a dumbbell) multiplies the torque demand on the shoulder compared with the elbow-bent position.
  • Injury: injury happens when net force produces an acceleration the tissue cannot survive.
  • Fall on the outstretched hand: the body's momentum is dissipated through the wrist in milliseconds — large deceleration, large force, hence Colles' fracture.
  • Whiplash: the head accelerates forward on a fixed trunk, loading cervical soft tissue beyond its tolerance.
  • Non-contact ACL rupture: a strong quadriceps contraction decelerates an extending tibia rapidly — the same force that protects also tears.
  • Helmets: helmets and crash helmets work by extending the deceleration time, which by the impulse relationship lowers the peak force.
  • Treatment: progressive resistance training works because strength adapts to the force demand.
  • Treatment: in osteoarthritis we teach slow, controlled movement — small accelerations mean small peak joint forces.
  • Treatment: plyometrics deliberately train rate of force development.
  • Treatment: a walker with a heavy patient needs a controlled, gradual rise from a chair rather than a quick push, because the force needed falls when acceleration falls.

F = ma · torque = I × angular acceleration

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — kinetics chapters.
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — torque and levers.
  • Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — determinants of gait and force in locomotion.
410 marks

Write basic concepts of exercise metabolism during core muscle strengthening.

Full answer →

Explain which energy system fuels core holds and how a sustained hold changes muscle metabolism — not a list of exercises.

  • Marks first: the question asks for metabolism, not a list of core exercises — anchor every paragraph to ATP.
  • Marks first: end with one line on avoiding Valsalva — that shows theory turned into safe practice.
  • Core anatomy: the core is a cylinder with two systems.
  • Local stabilisers: transversus abdominis, multifidus, diaphragm and pelvic floor — working at low intensity, continuously, anticipating limb movement.
  • Global movers: rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, erector spinae — producing force and trunk motion.
  • Mechanism: the deep system gives segmental stiffness (spinal stability at low energetic cost); the superficial system produces torque.
  • Energy systems: three systems supply ATP.
  • Phosphagen system: immediate, about 10 seconds of all-out work.
  • Anaerobic glycolysis: up to roughly 2 minutes, lactate-forming.
  • Aerobic metabolism: unlimited in duration at low intensity, yielding about 36 ATP per glucose molecule in the mitochondria.
  • Core work fits aerobic: core strengthening is classically low-load, high-duration — sustained submaximal isometric holds of 10 to 30 seconds, repeated many times.
  • So it runs predominantly on the aerobic system, with anaerobic glycolysis contributing as hold time and fatigue build up.
  • Inside a hold — recruitment: follows the size principle — small, fatigue-resistant type I motor units fire first; type II units join only as force demand rises.
  • Inside a hold — blood flow: a sustained isometric hold above about 15 to 20% of maximal voluntary contraction compresses intramuscular vessels, occluding local blood flow.
  • Inside a hold — oxygen: oxygen delivery falls while the muscle keeps consuming ATP, so stored phosphocreatine depletes, glycolysis accelerates, and hydrogen ions and inorganic phosphate accumulate.
  • Burning feeling: that accumulation — not lactate itself — is what the student feels as burning, trembling and the breath-holding urge.
  • Recovery: releasing the hold restores reperfusion and clears metabolites.
  • Adaptations — neural first: better anticipatory activation timing of transversus abdominis and multifidus.
  • Adaptations — then peripheral: increased mitochondrial density and capillarisation of the deep stabilisers, higher oxidative enzyme activity, and greater fatigue resistance.
  • Why: stabiliser training emphasises endurance — more repetitions, longer holds, brief rests — rather than heavy loading, which would merely recruit the global movers.
  • Prescription: begin with 5 to 10 second holds with rest, progress to 20 to 30 seconds, because brief rests allow reperfusion and metabolite clearance.
  • Breathing: teach diaphragmatic breathing during holds — a core exercise is also a breathing exercise.
  • Valsalva: breath-holding (a Valsalva manoeuvre) spikes blood pressure, which matters in the many hypertensive Indian patients in our OPDs.
  • Diabetes: in type 2 diabetes, regular aerobic-dominant core and endurance work improves glucose uptake.
  • Clinical sign: if a patient trembles or burns early, that is metabolic fatigue telling you the load — not the willpower — is wrong.

Low-load long holds = aerobic (~36 ATP/glucose) · isometric hold over 15–20% MVC occludes blood flow → metabolite burn · progress 5 s to 30 s holds

Sources
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — energy systems and muscle metabolism.
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — metabolic responses to resistance training.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — core stabilisation progression.
510 marks

Explain mechanics and pathomechanics of the knee joint.

Full answer →

Describe normal knee mechanics first, then the abnormal (pathomechanics) — keep the two halves balanced.

  • Marks first: "mechanics and pathomechanics" means normal first, abnormal second — keep the symmetry.
  • Marks first: the easy anchors are screw-home (with popliteus unlocking), meniscal hoop stress, the Q angle with 3×–7× body weight patellofemoral reaction, and one named malalignment with its compartment consequence.
  • Osteokinematics: the knee moves mainly in the sagittal plane — flexion about 0 to 135 or 150 degrees, extension to 0, with hyperextension up to about 5 to 10 degrees in some.
  • Rotation: rotation is only possible when the knee is unlocked — about 45 degrees total when flexed — and it is coupled.
  • Screw-home mechanism: as the knee approaches terminal extension the tibia rotates laterally about 10 to 15 degrees, locking the knee into a close-packed, energy-efficient standing position.
  • Reference note: the femur rotates medially on the tibia if you describe it from the femur's side — state your reference.
  • Unlocking: popliteus unlocks the knee by laterally rotating the femur.
  • Arthrokinematics: the femoral condyles both roll and glide posteriorly on the tibia during flexion, and the menisci travel with the femur — moving posteriorly in flexion, anteriorly in extension.
  • Menisci structure: fibrocartilage, mostly circumferentially arranged type I collagen, carrying roughly half the joint load.
  • Menisci mechanism: their wedge shape converts vertical compression into hoop stress along their circumference, spreading load onto the tibial rim.
  • Consequence: after total meniscectomy, contact stress in that compartment rises several-fold — which is why degenerative changes follow, and why we now preserve, repair or transplant menisci.
  • Patella: the patella acts as a pulley, increasing the quadriceps extensor moment arm by roughly 30% in early flexion.
  • Q angle: anterior superior iliac spine to patella centre to tibial tuberosity, about 13 to 18 degrees.
  • Q angle effect: it directs the quadriceps pull laterally on the patella, resisted by the vastus medialis obliquus and the medial retinaculum.
  • Patellofemoral reaction force: rises with knee flexion — near 3 times body weight climbing stairs, up to about 7 times body weight in a deep squat.
  • Why it matters: that single number explains anterior knee pain in deep-squatting activities.
  • Pathomechanics — coronal malalignment: genu varum (bow legs, not uncommon in India from nutritional rickets) shifts load medially and accelerates medial compartment osteoarthritis; genu valgum shifts it laterally.
  • Pathomechanics — ligament failure: ACL insufficiency removes the check to anterior tibial translation and rotational laxity — the pivot-shift give-way on pivoting.
  • Pathomechanics — PCL: posterior cruciate injury reverses the translation, worse on downhill steps.
  • Pathomechanics — extensor mechanism: excessive Q angle, weak vastus medialis obliquus or tight lateral retinaculum cause lateral patellar tracking, retropatellar compression and eventual chondromalacia.
  • Pathomechanics — meniscal derangement: a locked bucket-handle tear blocks terminal extension — a knee that will not fully straighten is a mechanical sign, not pain behaviour.
  • Assessment: varus and valgus stress tests for the collateral ligaments; Lachman (most sensitive) and the anterior drawer for the ACL; posterior sag and drawer for the PCL; McMurray for meniscal tears; patellar apprehension for instability.
  • Treatment: strengthen quadriceps (especially vastus medialis) and hamstrings, correct dynamic valgus in landing and squatting, restore full extension after a locked knee.
  • Cultural note: respect the deep squat and cross-legged sitting central to Indian daily life — after meniscal repair or arthroplasty, graded return to floor sitting is a realistic, culturally relevant goal.

Screw-home: tibia laterally rotates in terminal extension; popliteus unlocks · PF reaction ~3× BW stairs, ~7× deep squat · Q angle 13–18°

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — knee arthrokinematics.
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — joint forces and meniscal load sharing.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — knee special tests.
610 marks

Explain postural abnormalities seen in the thoracic region.

Full answer →

Give the normal thoracic curve first, then each abnormality with its one discriminating feature, and finish with assessment.

  • Marks first: the structure of this answer is the marks — normal parameters first, then each abnormality with its one discriminating feature, and always end with assessment.
  • Marks first: don't write four kyphosis paragraphs and forget flat back and scoliosis — that loses 2 easy marks.
  • Normal: the thoracic spine is a primary (kyphotic) curve, present from birth, measuring roughly 20 to 45 degrees of forward convexity.
  • Purpose: the curve is a shock absorber — it increases column flexibility and raises load-bearing capacity.
  • Purpose: the attached rib cage converts the thorax into a stiff protective cylinder for heart and lungs.
  • Normal posture test: assessed against a plumb line through the ear, shoulder and greater trochanter.
  • Normal posture: the small compensatory interplay of cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis and lumbar lordosis keeps the head over the pelvis at minimal energy cost.
  • Postural (flexible) kyphosis: increased round-back from sustained slouched sitting, weak thoracic extensors and tight anterior structures.
  • Flexible kyphosis test: the deformity corrects on voluntary extension or on lying prone over a bolster.
  • Flexible kyphosis symptoms: fatigue-type ache across the mid-scapular region.
  • Flexible kyphosis treatment: postural re-education, thoracic extension strengthening and ergonomic correction.
  • Indian clinic: in young students, heavy backpacks carried on one shoulder make this a daily OPD presentation.
  • Scheuermann's disease: a structural adolescent kyphosis — at least three adjacent vertebrae each wedged 5 degrees or more, with irregular vertebral end-plates and Schmorl's nodes.
  • Scheuermann's typical patient: classically in the thoracic or thoracolumbar spine of teenage boys.
  • Scheuermann's key test: it is rigid — it does not correct on extension or prone hyperextension over a bolster.
  • Scheuermann's features: pain is variable; cardiopulmonary compromise appears only in severe curves.
  • Diagnostic hinge: differentiating rigid from flexible is the key of the whole answer.
  • Thoracic flat back: loss of the normal kyphosis — a straight, stiff thoracic spine that transmits axial load more like a column, reducing shock absorption.
  • Flat back associations: often a flat scapular posture and posterior ligamentous strain.
  • Thoracic scoliosis: a lateral curvature with vertebral rotation — most often adolescent idiopathic.
  • Scoliosis signs: asymmetric shoulder height, a prominent scapula, and a rib hump on forward bending.
  • Third structural kyphosis: osteoporotic compression fractures in the elderly.
