  • Osteoporotic spine: multiple wedge fractures in the postmenopausal Indian woman present as the dowager's hump, with loss of height and a compensatory cervical extension posture to keep the eyes level.
  • Assessment: inspect from the side and behind with the patient standing — plumb line alignment, shoulder and scapular symmetry, depth of the cervical and lumbar curves.
  • Assessment: the prone extension test distinguishes flexible from rigid kyphosis.
  • Assessment: the Adam's forward bend test with a scoliometer quantifies the rib hump.
  • Assessment: radiographic Cobb angle grades scoliosis (10 degrees defines it; bracing is usually considered above 25 to 40 degrees in a growing child).
  • Always: screen the whole spine — a primary lumbar curve produces a compensatory thoracic one.
  • Treatment — flexible kyphosis: postural re-education, thoracic extensor and scapular retractor strengthening, anterior chest stretching, ergonomic advice.
  • Treatment — structural kyphosis: extension exercises over a roll or bolster; for progressive Scheuermann's in the growing child, a brace plus a structured exercise programme.
  • Treatment — scoliosis: observation for small curves, bracing for moderate progressive curves in the immature, physiotherapeutic scoliosis-specific exercises as an adjunct, and surgery for severe ones.
  • Treatment — osteoporotic spine: medical bone protection, safe weight-bearing and balance training to prevent the next fracture.

Normal kyphosis 20–45° · flexible corrects on extension; Scheuermann's is rigid: 3 vertebrae × 5° wedging + Schmorl's nodes · Cobb 10° defines scoliosis

Sources
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — spinal curves and posture.
  • McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine — postural syndrome and sagittal alignment.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — scoliosis and kyphosis examination.
710 marks

Write the biomechanical analysis of gait in ankle instability.

Full answer →

Analyse gait phase by phase — normal trace first, then stance, swing and the measurable kinetics.

  • Marks first: "biomechanical analysis" demands a phase-by-phase structure — normal first, then stance, then swing, then the measurable kinetics.
  • Marks first: spend the first paragraph on the normal trace — deviations only earn marks when the reader can see what they deviate from.
  • Normal — initial contact: the ankle is neutral.
  • Normal — loading response: it plantarflexes, then dorsiflexes progressively to about 10 degrees by terminal stance as the tibia advances over the foot.
  • Normal — push-off: it finally plantarflexes sharply to about 20 degrees at push-off.
  • Normal — subtalar: the subtalar joint pronates at loading response (mobile adapter, shock absorption), then supinates into a rigid lever through push-off.
  • Normal — muscles: the ankle plantarflexors deliver the burst for push-off, and the triceps surae works eccentrically through mid-stance to control tibial advancement.
  • Two halves of instability: chronic instability follows the typical inversion sprain.
  • Mechanical instability: ligament laxity (anterior talofibular ligament, calcaneofibular ligament) on stress testing.
  • Functional ankle instability: recurrent giving way without measurable laxity — a sensorimotor failure.
  • Mechanism: damaged mechanoreceptors in the torn ligaments and capsule feed inaccurate proprioception to the central nervous system, so reflex correction of sudden inversion arrives late.
  • Stance deviations: excessive or prolonged pronation or sudden inversion episodes at loading response.
  • Stance deviations: early heel rise from a shortened, guarded push-off.
  • Stance deviations: reduced single-limb support time on the affected limb.
  • Stance deviations: decreased stride and step length, slower comfortable speed, and a wider base of support.
  • Stance mechanism: the ground reaction force vector passes lateral to the ankle precisely when the peroneals are least ready.
  • Swing deviations: the unstable foot is carried in slight plantarflexion and inversion to protect the lateral structures, so toe clearance suffers.
  • Swing compensations: increased hip and knee flexion (an exaggerated steppage-like strategy), hip hiking of the swing-side pelvis, and sometimes circumduction.
  • Swing result: an energy-costly swing with poor foot placement accuracy at the next initial contact — and the cycle of self-distrust continues.
  • Kinetics: reduced peak plantarflexion moment and power burst at push-off (a weak push).
  • Kinetics: altered vertical ground reaction force shape with a flattened second peak, and increased ankle inversion moments in some patients.
  • EMG: delayed peroneal reaction time, reduced peroneus longus strength, and co-contraction of the pretibial group with the triceps surae to splint the joint.
  • Clinic test: the Star Excursion Balance Test anterior reach — an anterior reach deficit greater than about 4 cm between limbs predicts future sprain.
  • Clinic test: single-leg hop tests also objectify it.
  • Rehabilitation: because the mechanism is sensorimotor, rehabilitation is more than strengthening — proprioceptive and balance training (single-leg stance progressions, wobble board, eyes closed).
  • Rehabilitation: peroneal strength and reaction training, perturbation and hopping/landing control, agility before return to sport, and taping or bracing during the vulnerable early weeks.
  • Indian setting: barefoot balance work on uneven surfaces is practical where much daily life occurs unshod — a culturally native form of proprioceptive training.

Mechanical = laxity (ATFL); functional = give-way without laxity · SEBT anterior reach deficit over 4 cm predicts sprain

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — ankle complex mechanics.
  • Saunders, Inman & Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — determinants of gait framework.
  • Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — ankle rehabilitation.
810 marks

Explain the theories and models of pain.

Full answer →

Show the progression of pain theories, name each with date/journal, and give one clinical application each.

  • Marks first: name, date, journal — Melzack and Wall, Science, 1965; Melzack, Pain, 1999.
  • Marks first: give one clinical application per theory — theories with no application read like history.
  • Why theories exist: pain is the commonest reason a patient reaches a physiotherapist, yet it correlates poorly with tissue damage.
  • Example: phantom limb pain hurts in a limb that no longer exists; imaging-identical disc bulges incapacitate one patient and not another.
  • Structure: show the progression — each model fixes the failure of the one before it, not four unrelated paragraphs.
  • Specificity theory (Descartes' pathway concept, refined by von Frey): pain is a dedicated modality with its own receptors, dedicated A-delta and C afferents, and a specific line to a pain centre in the brain.
  • Specificity — strong point: it predicted nociceptors, which were later found.
  • Specificity — weak point: it cannot explain why gentle touch relieves pain or why pain persists after healing.
  • Pattern (intensity) theory (Goldscheider): there are no dedicated pain fibres; pain results from intense stimulation producing a specific spatio-temporal pattern of firing.
  • Pattern — strong point: it recognised central summation.
  • Pattern — weak point: intense stimuli do not always cause pain.
  • Study tip: keep each theory to a strong-point, weak-point pair — that is the analytical style that scores.
  • Gate control theory (Melzack and Wall, published in Science in 1965): modulation sits in the dorsal horn.
  • Gate mechanism: large-diameter A-beta (touch) fibres and small-diameter A-delta and C (nociceptive) fibres both end on transmission cells in the substantia gelatinosa.
  • Gate mechanism: large-fibre activity closes the gate (inhibits transmission); small-fibre activity opens it.
  • Gate control: descending fibres from the brain can set the gate too — the first theory to put the brain inside the pain loop.
  • Gate explains: why rubbing an injury helps, why TENS at high frequency relieves pain, and why distraction and mood matter.
  • Gate limitation: it stops at the spinal cord, so it still cannot fully explain chronic pain or phantom phenomena.
  • Neuromatrix theory (Melzack, Pain, 1999): pain is the output of a widely distributed neural network — the body-self neuromatrix.
  • Neuromatrix inputs: it integrates somatosensory, limbic, thalamic and cortical inputs with genetic and experiential determinants.
  • Neuromatrix idea: pain is a multidimensional percept produced by the brain's "neurosignature" of the body, not a direct readout of tissue signals.
  • Neuromatrix explains: phantom limb pain (the neurosignature persists after the input is gone), chronic pain without ongoing damage, and why stress, sleep and beliefs modulate pain.
  • Neuromatrix role: the conceptual foundation of modern pain neuroscience education.
  • Biopsychosocial model: the current working model treats pain as the product of interacting biological (tissue state, sensitisation), psychological (fear, catastrophising, expectations) and social (family, work, culture) factors.
  • Translation: TENS, massage, thermal agents and movement all act by closing the gate with large-fibre input.
  • Translation: graded exposure and pain education target fear-avoidance; exercise remodels the neurosignature.
  • Indian clinic: pain beliefs shaped by family opinion and the cultural meaning of rest versus activity are genuinely part of the biology you are treating — address them or your exercise programme fails.

Specificity → pattern → gate control (Melzack & Wall, Science 1965) → neuromatrix (Melzack, Pain 1999) → biopsychosocial · TENS and rubbing = closing the gate

Sources
  • Melzack R, Wall PD. Pain mechanisms: a new theory. Science 1965;150:971–979.
  • Melzack R. From the gate to the neuromatrix. Pain 1999;Suppl 6:S121–S126.
  • Butler DS, Jones MA. Mobilisation of the Nervous System — pain physiology and clinical translation.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — pain management principles.
910 marks

Describe soft tissue repair and healing in meniscal injury.

Full answer →

Link meniscal structure and blood supply to the three healing phases and explain why the meniscus heals poorly.

  • Marks first: this is two answers braided into one — soft tissue healing phases AND meniscal specifics.
  • Marks first: the braiding sentence is "the blood supply decides whether the general healing script even begins."
  • Structure: the menisci are C-shaped fibrocartilaginous wedges built of densely packed type I collagen, predominantly circumferential with a few radial tie fibres.
  • Structure mechanism: that architecture converts compressive load into hoop tension.
  • Cells: their cells are fibrochondrocytes — hybrids that behave part-fibroblast, part-chondrocyte — sitting sparse and avascular in the deep matrix.
  • Blood supply: the peripheral third receives blood from the genicular arterial network; the inner two-thirds are nourished only by diffusion from synovial fluid.
  • Surgical zones: red-red (outer, vascular), red-white (middle, transitional), and white-white (inner, avascular).
  • Key idea: every prediction about healing follows from this one anatomical fact — build the answer on it.
  • Inflammatory (bleeding) phase, roughly days 0 to 7: only a red-zone tear forms a fibrin clot scaffold, releasing platelet-derived growth factor and attracting inflammatory cells.
  • Critical point: a white-zone tear does not even bleed — the healing cascade never starts.
  • Proliferative (fibroblastic) phase, roughly 2 to 6 weeks: fibrochondrocytes and invading vascular buds migrate into the clot and lay down disorganised type I and III collagen.
  • Proliferative: a fibrovascular scar bridges the tear, weakest at about 1 to 2 weeks.
  • Remodelling phase, months: scar collagen reorients to withstand shear and compression, cellularity falls, and the tissue approaches — but never equals — native organisation and strength.
  • Poor healing reason 1: the avascular inner two-thirds cannot mount the inflammatory first phase without a clot.
  • Poor healing reason 2: fibrochondrocyte density is low and their proliferative capacity is modest.
  • Poor healing reason 3: constant loading and motion in synovial fluid dilutes and washes out the fibrin scaffold and growth factors.
  • Poor healing reason 4: the complex load environment — hoop tension plus shear — repeatedly tests the immature scar.
  • Summary: this is why a peripheral vertical tear can heal while a complex degenerative white-zone tear cannot.
  • Factors — zone: red-red heals, white-white does not.
  • Factors — tear pattern: peripheral vertical-longitudinal heals best; complex, horizontal and degenerative tears poorly.
  • Factors — rim width: tears within about 3 mm of the synovial attachment heal best.
  • Factors — patient: age and vascularity.
  • Factors — knee stability: an unstable ACL-deficient knee repeatedly displaces the meniscus and impairs healing.
  • Factors — rehabilitation quality: protected weight bearing and controlled motion stimulate; premature deep flexion under load disrupts.
  • Treatment: repairable red-zone tears in the young (peripheral vertical tears) are sutured (inside-out, all-inside techniques) because they can heal.
  • Treatment: irreparable white-zone degenerative tears in the older patient undergo partial meniscectomy, sacrificing the least tissue possible.
  • Rehabilitation: a phased progression of range and weight bearing over about 4 to 6 weeks, avoiding deep loaded flexion in the early scar phase.
  • Rehabilitation: then a graded return to the squats and cross-legged sitting of daily Indian life, and back to sport with landing-control training.

Zones: red-red (vascular, heals) / red-white / white-white (avascular, no clot, no healing) · inflammation 0–7 d → proliferation 2–6 wk (weakest scar) → remodelling months

Sources
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — meniscal structure and load sharing.
  • Donatelli & Wooden, Orthopaedic Physical Therapy — meniscal injury management.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — soft tissue healing and rehabilitation timelines.
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — meniscal testing and surgical decision context.

Describe mechanics and pathomechanics of the hip joint.

Full answer →

Give the hip's structure and lever mechanics with the key numbers, then the pathomechanics and gait changes.

  • Marks first: the lever arm diagram is the highest-yielding single drawing of this paper.
  • Marks first: numbers that must appear — 3× body weight joint reaction in single-leg stance, the roughly 2:1 moment arm ratio, and cane in the opposite hand.
  • Marks first: then one line each on OA, Trendelenburg, impingement and childhood hip — breadth plus one mechanism drawn deep.
  • Structure: the hip is a synovial ball-and-socket joint — the femoral head (about two-thirds of a sphere) seated in the deep acetabulum.
  • Structure: the socket is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous labrum and secured by the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments — the strongest ligament in the body among them.
  • Ranges: flexion about 0 to 120 degrees (more with knee flexion), extension 0 to 10 or 15 degrees, abduction 0 to 45, adduction 0 to 30, and medial and lateral rotation about 0 to 45 each.
  • Mechanism: the socket trades the shoulder's mobility for near-dislocation-proof stability, because this joint must transmit the largest loads in the body.
  • Load mechanics: in single-leg stance, body weight acts through a vertical line roughly two-thirds of the way between the hip and the midline, at a moment arm about twice that of the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus).
  • Equilibrium: abductor force must therefore be roughly two times body weight.
  • Joint reaction: the femoral head compresses under a joint reaction force of about two to three times body weight in single-leg stance.
  • Higher loads: rising toward about four times body weight in fast walking or stairs (Levangie & Norkin, 6th ed.).
  • Practical: add 10 kg of shopping and the arithmetic punishes the head.
  • Master key: this lever model is the key to the pathomechanics below.
  • Pathomechanics — osteoarthritis: cartilage loss and superolateral femoral head migration shorten the abductor moment arm, raise the required abductor force, and increase joint stress.
  • OA pattern: pain, effusion and capsular contracture produce the classic pattern of flexion, abduction and lateral rotation deformity, with apparent (not true) shortening.
  • Pathomechanics — abductor failure: weakness of gluteus medius or superior gluteal nerve palsy produces a positive Trendelenburg sign — the pelvis drops on the unsupported side.
  • Pathomechanics — femoroacetabular impingement: a cam deformity (aspherical head) or pincer over-coverage jams the head against the labrum in deep flexion and adduction.
  • FAI sign: the sitting-induced anterior groin pain of the younger patient.
  • Pathomechanics — childhood hip: developmental dysplasia (shallow socket, unstable head) and Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the capital epiphysis) deform the growing head and cause secondary osteoarthritis decades later.
  • Childhood screening: Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres at birth matter in Indian screening programmes.
  • Gait — Trendelenburg: in gluteus medius weakness, an uncompensated Trendelenburg gait shows lateral trunk lurch toward the weak side during its stance phase.
  • Gait compensation: most patients lean over the stance hip to shorten the body-weight moment arm and reduce the required abductor force.
  • Gait — flexion contracture: produces an anterior pelvic tilt and compensatory lumbar hyperlordosis in stance, and a shorter step on the affected side.
  • Gait — hip OA: antalgic shortening of stance phase, and a coxalgic limp with the trunk lurching toward the painful side to reduce joint reaction force.
  • Treatment: strengthen gluteus medius (side-lying abduction, supported single-leg stance), stretch the hip flexors and adductors that contracture shortens.
  • Treatment: teach trunk-lean economy when weakness is fixed.
  • Cane biomechanics: a cane held in the hand opposite the affected hip lengthens the counter-lever of the body-weight moment arm and reduces the joint reaction force by up to half or so.
  • Post-arthroplasty: the same lever logic underlies gait re-education and abductor protection.
  • Cultural goal: in floor-sitting Indian habits, a graded return to cross-legged posture after arthroplasty is a culturally real functional goal.

Single-leg stance: abductors ~2× BW, joint reaction ~3× BW, body-weight arm ≈ 2× abductor arm · cane in OPPOSITE hand

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — hip joint forces and lever arms.
  • Lehmkuhl & Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — hip mechanics and Trendelenburg analysis.
  • Levangie & Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — hip joint structure and pathomechanics.
  • Hislop, Avers & Brown, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — gluteus medius testing.

Q1. Enumerate basic assessment methods for joint play movements.

Full answer →

List the assessment methods for joint play as a numbered list, after explaining what joint play is.

  • What earns marks: Answer as a numbered list of the methods — the word "enumerate" means list them, not write long paragraphs · First explain the two layers of joint movement, then the methods · Include the five accessory words — roll, spin, glide, traction, compression · Finish with one short clinical example.
  • Every joint moves in two layers.
  • The layer the patient controls is osteokinematics — flexion, abduction, rotation.
  • Underneath is joint play (arthrokinematics) — the accessory roll, spin and glide of the surfaces, plus traction and compression between them.
  • If the voluntary range looks normal but the joint hurts or feels tight, the problem usually sits in the accessory layer.
  • Convex-concave rule: a convex surface moving on a fixed concave one glides opposite to its roll; a concave surface moving on a fixed convex one glides in the same direction as the movement.
  • This rule tells you the direction in which your glide must be tested and treated.
  • The methods: (1) Passive accessory intervertebral and peripheral joint movements (PAIVMs) — central and unilateral glides for the spine, translatoric glides for peripheral joints.
  • (2) Passive physiological movements (PPIVMs) — the therapist moves the joint through its voluntary arc and grades the feel.
  • (3) Assessment of roll, spin and glide in the loose-packed position; (4) long-axis traction and distraction.
  • (5) Compression and joint-springing to reproduce the patient's symptom; (6) end-feel at the physiological limit — bony, capsular or soft-tissue approximation.
  • (7) Maitland's grading of the oscillation — grades I to IV, small-to-large amplitude within or up to the limit; (8) ligamentous stress tests for stability of the accessory restraint system.
  • (9) Hypermobility screening on the other side of the spectrum — the Beighton score.
  • How to test: put the joint near its loose-packed position so the capsule is slack; steady the proximal segment with one hand, glide with the other, take up the slack, then grade the oscillation.
  • Compare with the contralateral side — the patient is their own control; ask two questions of every glide: how far does it travel, and does it reproduce the familiar pain?
  • Interpretation: a firm or hard end-feel with reduced glide = hypomobility (wants mobilisation); a soft, spongy end-feel with excessive travel = hypermobility (wants control, not stretching).
  • Note whether the symptom comes at grade I (pain-dominant, irritable) or only near the limit (stiffness-dominant).
  • Example: knee osteoarthritis that lacks the last 15 degrees of extension — the missing movement is a restricted anterior tibial glide, and graded anterior glides become the treatment.

The five words: roll, spin, glide, traction, compression. "Enumerate" means a numbered list — nine one-line items score better than three paragraphs.

Sources
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — principles chapter and regional chapters.
  • Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function — arthrokinematics chapters.
  • Maitland GD. Peripheral Manipulation — grades of movement.

Q2. Explain screening the head and neck in upper cross syndrome.

Full answer →

Describe the upper cross muscle pattern, the screening sequence, the key neck tests, and what the findings lead to.

  • What earns marks: Draw the crossed X — name the tight muscles on top and pair each with its weak opponent below · Give the screening sequence — look first, then test · Name the key tests — craniocervical flexion test, endurance test, length tests · Close with the treatment direction.
  • Upper cross syndrome is Janda's classical muscle-imbalance pattern of the head, neck and shoulder girdle.
  • Two lines cross like an X on the trunk.
  • Tight line (top): upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals, pectoralis major and minor.
  • Weak (inhibited) line (bottom): deep neck flexors, lower and middle trapezius, serratus anterior.
  • Result: forward head, loss of the cervico-thoracic angle, rounded shoulders with protracted and elevated scapulae, and a chin that pokes forward.
  • For the eyes to stay level, the upper cervical spine extends and the lower cervical spine flexes; the suboccipitals shorten while the deep flexors are held long and weak.
  • Step 1 — Observation: stand the patient in profile; the ear should sit over the acromion, but in the syndrome it falls forward.
  • Look at the cervico-thoracic angle, the prominence of the C7 spinous process, scapular position (protracted, elevated, winged), and pectoral prominence.
  • Palpate upper trapezius and levator scapulae for tone and tenderness; take the cervical spine through active range with overpressure to clear the joints.
  • Step 2 — Craniocervical flexion test (the heart of the answer): supine, an inflatable pressure sensor under the neck at a 20 mmHg baseline; the patient nods the head in five graded stages of 2 mmHg; watch for superficial flexor substitution.
  • Step 3 — Deep neck flexor endurance test: chin tuck, lift the head about 2-3 cm off the couch and hold while the quality of the position is timed.
  • Step 4 — Length tests for the tight side: pectoralis minor length in supine (distance of the acromion from the couch); pectoralis major and suboccipital length; upper trapezius and levator length in side-lying.
  • Step 5 — Janda's shoulder abduction test: scapular hitching before 60 degrees of humeral elevation confirms that upper trapezius and levator dominate over the weak lower stabilisers.
  • Interpretation: findings cluster — the chin juts and the sternocleidomastoid tightens during the test; endurance holds fall far short; pectoralis minor measures more than the normal few centimetres; the scapula hikes early in abduction.
  • That cluster — not any single test — is the screen.
  • Where it leads: deep neck flexor retraining with the biofeedback cuff, lengthening the pectorals and suboccipitals, strengthening lower trapezius and serratus anterior, and ergonomic correction of desk and phone posture.

The four words that score: tight, weak, forward, rounded. Pair every tight muscle with its weak opponent.

Sources
  • Janda V. Evaluation of muscular imbalance, in Liebenson C. Rehabilitation of the Spine.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — cervical spine chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — posture chapters.

Q3. Illustrate primary care of intervertebral disc prolapse.

Full answer →

Show the primary-care pathway as a flow: red-flag triage first, then conservative care, then when to refer.

  • What earns marks: Structure it as a clinical pathway — triage first, treat second, refer third · Start with red flags before any treatment line · Explain the mechanism (posterolateral prolapse at L4-L5/L5-S1) and the key idea of centralisation · Give the referral criteria.
  • The nucleus pulposus sits within the annulus fibrosus; the posterior longitudinal ligament is strong in the midline but weak at its lateral edges.
  • So under repeated flexion-and-load the disc fails posterolaterally — most often at L4-L5 and L5-S1, irritating the L5 and S1 roots and producing dermatomal sciatica.
  • In primary care the physiotherapist is often the first clinician to see this patient, so the answer must read like a pathway, not a list of modalities.
  • Red flags come first: cauda equina features — saddle anaesthesia, retention or incontinence of bladder or bowel, bilateral or rapidly progressive leg weakness — are an emergency needing immediate referral.
  • Also screen: fever with spinal pain, night pain unrelated to position, unexplained weight loss, history of cancer, recent significant trauma, and progressive neurological deficit.
  • Neurological screen: myotomes (ankle dorsiflexion, big-toe extension, plantarflexion), dermatomes, ankle reflexes, and the straight leg raise.
  • Document all of it — in direct-access practice the red-flag screen protects both the patient and you.
  • The pathway: acute low back pain with sciatica → screen red flags now; positive → refer immediately, negative → McKenzie (MDT) assessment.
  • If pain centralises → directional preference exercise; if it peripheralises or does not change → reassess and refer at 4-6 weeks.
  • Throughout: stay active, no bed rest, review every 1-2 weeks.
  • Conservative care: educate first (the disc heals; most radicular pain settles within six to twelve weeks; strict bed rest is harmful), then McKenzie mechanical diagnosis and therapy — repeated movements in the direction of preference.
  • Centralisation: distal leg pain retreating toward the low back with the correct repeated movement predicts a good response to that exercise programme.
  • Add graded activity, neural mobilisation once acuity settles, trunk (core) stabilisation, ergonomic advice for sitting and lifting, and a short course of traction only where it clearly centralises symptoms.
  • Analgesia sits with the referring physician; the physiotherapist's prescription is movement.
  • Escalate: routine imaging is not needed in the first four to six weeks if red flags are absent; refer urgently for cauda equina features or progressive motor weakness.
  • Refer for surgical opinion when disabling radicular pain persists despite a competent six-to-twelve-week conservative programme, or when the neurological deficit fails to improve.

Ten-mark structure for any "primary care" question: triage first, treat second, refer third.

  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — lumbar spine.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — lumbar spine chapter.
  • McKenzie R, May S. The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy.

Q4. Describe physiotherapy diagnosis in lower cross syndrome.

Full answer →

Give the lower cross mechanism and tests, then write an actual physiotherapy diagnosis statement as a cluster, not just positive signs.

  • What earns marks: Give the mechanism and the tight/weak muscle pairs first · Name the confirming tests — Thomas, prone hip extension, leg lowering, Trendelenburg · Write a physiotherapy diagnosis statement (a cluster of findings), not a shopping list of signs · Frame it in ICF terms.
  • Lower cross syndrome is the pelvic mirror of the upper cross.
  • Tight line: iliopsoas and rectus femoris (often tensor fasciae latae and adductors) and the thoracolumbar erector spinae.
  • Weak line: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius and the deep abdominals.
  • Result: anterior pelvic tilt with lumbar hyperlordosis — the tight hip flexors pull the pelvis forward, the erectors reinforce the lordosis, and the gluteals are held long and inhibited.
  • The protruding, splayed abdomen gives the classic silhouette; facet-joint compression and ligamentous strain in the lordotic segment explain the ache.
  • Screening — observation: pelvic tilt from the ASIS-PSIS relationship, depth of the lumbar curve, gluteal bulk, splayed lower abdomen, and genu recurvatum.
  • Gait: a lurching trunk lean toward the stance leg suggests gluteus medius weakness; the hip often extends poorly with compensatory lumbar extension.
  • Single-leg stance (Trendelenburg test) and squatting — the lumbar spine is recruited for hip extension when the gluteals fail.
  • Modified Thomas test (supine, one knee held to chest): the thigh lifts off the plinth = hip flexor tightness; the knee extends = rectus femoris; the thigh drifts into abduction = TFL tightness.
  • Prone hip extension test: a strong patient extends the hip with gluteus maximus first; the crossed patient fires the hamstrings and erector spinae with an anterior pelvic tilt.
  • Leg-lowering test and double straight-leg raise grade the deep abdominals, which fail to control the pelvis long before the legs reach low angles.
  • Link each test to the muscle it confirms — that is what makes this a physiotherapy diagnosis rather than a collection of positive signs.
  • Writing the diagnosis: a physiotherapy diagnosis is a syndrome-level, movement-system statement, distinct from the medical label of "mechanical low back pain".
  • Write it as a cluster, e.g. "Anterior pelvic tilt with lumbar hyperlordosis, shortened hip flexors (positive modified Thomas), gluteal weakness with substitution in prone hip extension, and poor deep abdominal control on leg lowering — consistent with lower crossed syndrome."
  • ICF framing: impairment = muscle imbalance and restricted hip extension; activity limitation = pain-limited standing, walking and lifting; participation follows from there.
  • Where it leads: lengthen the iliopsoas, rectus femoris and TFL; strengthen the gluteals and deep abdominals; retrain the hip-hinge pattern; and address the sitting postures that maintain the syndrome.

The marks hide in one sentence: "a physiotherapy diagnosis describes the movement dysfunction, not the pathology." Then give the cluster of findings and name it.

  • Sahrmann S. Diagnosis and Treatment of Movement System Impairment Syndromes.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — hip and posture chapters.

Q5. Write exercise testing in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

Full answer →

Describe the post-ACLR test battery — strength, hop tests, balance and psychological readiness — and the criteria for return to sport.

  • What earns marks: Open with the three key numbers — 90% symmetry, four hop tests, 9-12 months · Give the strength testing (isokinetic 60 and 180 degrees per second, limb symmetry index) · List the four hop tests · Include balance, landing mechanics and psychological readiness for return to sport.
  • After reconstruction — bone-patellar tendon-bone or hamstring autograft — the graft passes through biological maturation and is weakest to re-injury in the middle months.
  • Return to pivoting sport is criteria-based, not calendar-based: earliest at six months, safer at nine to twelve, and only if the test battery is passed.
  • Strength testing: isokinetic dynamometry at 60 and 180 degrees per second gives quadriceps and hamstring peak torque of the operated limb against the uninvolved limb.
  • The key index is the limb symmetry index (LSI) — the ratio expressed as a percentage — with 90 per cent or better in both quadriceps and hamstrings as the accepted threshold.
  • Also report the hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio, because a strong hamstring set protects the graft.
  • Where no isokinetic machine exists, a handheld dynamometer with a fixed belt and the same symmetry calculation is an acceptable substitute.
  • Baseline laxity testing with the Lachman test or an arthrometer completes the objective record of the graft.
  • The functional hop battery: the single hop for distance, the triple hop for distance, the crossover hop, and the six-metre timed hop.
  • Each hop is scored as a limb symmetry index, again 90 per cent or better.
  • Add the side-hop endurance test and a drop-jump landing screen — watch for the valgus collapse and stiff-knee strategy that preceded the original injury.
  • The hop battery matters because strength measured lying down does not guarantee control under landing forces.
  • Balance and proprioception: single-leg stance errors on firm and foam surfaces, the Star Excursion or Y-balance test (compared between limbs), and agility drills in the final phase.
  • Psychosocial domain: readiness scales such as the ACL-RSI, fear measures, and a patient-reported outcome such as the IKDC.
  • Young athletes who pass every physical test but still distrust the knee re-injure at higher rates.
  • Interpreting the battery: the decision is all-or-nothing per criterion — symmetrical strength, all hop indices at or above 90 per cent, clean landing mechanics, restored balance, and psychological readiness.
  • Failing even one index means continuing rehabilitation.
  • Athletes under 25 returning to pivoting sport carry the highest re-injury risk.

Three numbers open the answer and three close it: 90 per cent symmetry, four hop tests, nine to twelve months.

  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — knee chapter.

Q6. Explain pre-operative and post-operative assessment of fracture neck of femur.

Full answer →

Show that the assessment depends on the operation performed, and separate pre-operative from post-operative assessment.

  • What earns marks: Say "assessment depends on the operation performed" in your first paragraph · Give the Garden classification and how it decides the operation · Separate pre-operative from post-operative assessment · Screen for complications and name the outcome measures.
  • The typical patient is elderly with osteoporotic bone — a trivial fall, groin pain, inability to stand, and a shortened and externally rotated limb.
  • Because the fracture is intracapsular, the retinacular blood supply to the head is at risk, making avascular necrosis and non-union the defining complications of displaced fractures.
  • The Garden classification grades the injury in four stages and predicts the operation: stages I and II → internal fixation; stages III and IV → arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty in the low-demand elderly, total replacement in the fit and active).
  • Garden I = incomplete, valgus impacted; II = complete, undisplaced; III = complete, partly displaced; IV = fully displaced with translation.
  • Pre-operative — history: mechanism of injury, comorbidities (cardiac disease, diabetes, osteoporosis, anticoagulant use), and the pre-injury mobility level (the single best predictor of outcome).
  • Physical: pain, deformity, limb shortening and external rotation, skin integrity over the trochanter, a full neurovascular examination, and an abbreviated chest, heart and hydration screen.
  • Review the radiograph and the Garden stage with the team.
  • Physiotherapy pre-op work: teach ankle pumps, static quadriceps, breathing exercises and effective coughing; practise bed-to-chair transfer and gait with a frame on the unaffected side; counsel the family on stairs and toilet arrangements at home.
  • Post-operative — structure it day by day and procedure by procedure.
  • Early: vital state, wound and drain, pain, oedema, and quadriceps sets.
  • Fixation cases carry the surgeon's weight-bearing orders and need protection of the construct.
  • Hemiarthroplasty by a lateral approach allows freer flexion but still needs gluteal retraining.
  • Total hip replacement through a posterior approach needs the standard dislocation precautions — no adduction, internal rotation beyond neutral, or flexion past 90 degrees in the first six weeks.
  • Then assess hip range of motion, manual muscle testing of the abductors and quadriceps, sitting and standing balance, gait (frame to crutches to stick), and stair training; measure limb length and gait deviations each visit.
  • Complication screening: deep vein thrombosis (calf swelling, tenderness), pulmonary infection in the bed-bound patient, wound infection, dislocation (sudden shortening and pain with rotation), and in fixation cases the late failures of non-union and avascular necrosis presenting as persistent groin pain. Any of these is a referral.
  • Outcome measures: Harris Hip Score, Timed Up and Go, walking distance achieved, and independence in transfers and toileting.
  • Discharge planning: floor-level versus western toilet, stair access, and a family member trained in safe assistance; follow up at six weeks and three months.

Say "assessment depends on the operation performed" in your first paragraph — half the marks are for distinguishing fixation from arthroplasty.

Q7. Describe assessment methods in poliomyelitis.

Full answer →

Describe polio assessment — muscle testing with MRC grading, atrophy and deformity checks, and functional/gait/spinal/respiratory screening.

  • What earns marks: State early that sensation is intact — this separates polio from other lower motor neuron lesions · Make manual muscle testing with MRC grading the heart of the answer · Include atrophy, deformity and joint range measurement · Add functional, gait, spinal and respiratory assessment, then how the grades lead to orthotic or surgical plans.
  • The poliovirus destroys anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, producing lower motor neuron flaccid paralysis.
  • It is characteristically asymmetrical and patchy — a whole limb is rarely equally weak.
  • Sensation is intact — this separates it from every compressive radiculopathy and from leprosy neuropathy.
  • Stages: acute febrile stage, recovery phase over months, and the long residual stage with atrophy, imbalance and deformity (where most physiotherapy assessment happens).
  • Motor assessment: manual muscle testing of every major muscle group of the limbs and trunk using Daniels and Worthingham's positions, graded on the MRC scale from 0 to 5.
  • Polio-specific habits: test in the gravity-eliminated plane first for muscles below grade 3; chart a detailed segmental map muscle by muscle, not one summary grade per limb.
  • Grade each muscle at its strongest joint position, watch for trick movements, and note fatigue — a muscle that holds grade 4 for five repetitions may collapse by the tenth.
  • MRC reminder: grade 3 = full range against gravity; below 3 needs gravity-eliminated testing.
  • Atrophy: limb circumference at fixed bony landmarks (10, 15, 20 centimetres from the joint line), compared between sides.
  • Joint range charting picks up the contractures of the residual stage — hip flexion-abduction, knee flexion, and equinus at the ankle.
  • Record leg-length discrepancy (ASIS to medial malleolus) and check for joint laxity in the flail limb.
  • Gait reading: gluteus medius lurch; hand-on-thigh or hand-on-knee push-off for quadriceps weakness; high stepping if the dorsiflexors are gone; calcaneal gait if triceps surae is lost.
  • Assess transfers, floor sitting and rising, and independence in activities of daily living.
  • Examine the spine in forward bending for paralytic scoliosis and measure the rib hump.
  • In severe involvement, record respiratory muscle function (vital capacity, breath-hold, accessory muscle use).
  • Screen for post-polio syndrome: new weakness, fatigue and pain decades after the original illness.
  • Interpretation: grade 3 quadriceps with weak hip flexors → knee-ankle-foot orthosis with a knee lock; unbalanced feet → tendon-transfer referral; progressive scoliosis → bracing or surgery.
  • Each grade on the chart should be traceable to one recommendation.

Write "sensation is intact" early — that single phrase separates lower motor neuron disease from peripheral nerve lesions.

Sources

Q8. Enumerate ergonomic risk assessment in musculoskeletal disorders.

Full answer →

List the risk factors, give the stepwise assessment process, and enumerate the tools — pairing each tool with its task.

  • What earns marks: List the risk factors first — that is what the tools measure · Give the stepwise process (job analysis → hazard identification → quantification → interpretation → intervention → re-assessment) · Enumerate the tools and pair each with its task · End with action levels and the hierarchy of controls.
  • Ergonomic risk assessment quantifies the mismatch between job demands and worker capacity.
  • Risk factors to enumerate: forceful exertion; repetition and pace; awkward and static postures; whole-body and hand-arm vibration; contact stress; prolonged sitting or standing; cold environment and poor lighting; and psychosocial factors such as low control over work.
  • Together these drive the work-related musculoskeletal disorders seen in clinics — low back pain, neck and shoulder complaints of computer users, and hand-wrist conditions of repetitive workers.
  • Stepwise process: (1) Job analysis — observe the actual task, tools, cycle times and workstation layout.
  • (2) Hazard identification — match observed exposure to the risk-factor list.
  • (3) Risk quantification with a validated instrument.
  • (4) Interpretation of scores against action levels.
  • (5) Intervention by the hierarchy of controls — engineering change before administrative change before worker training.
  • (6) Re-assessment after the change.
  • Tools — lifting: the NIOSH lifting equation computes a recommended weight limit from load, horizontal distance, vertical height, travel distance, asymmetry and frequency; the actual load becomes a lifting index, where values above 1 indicate increased risk.
  • Whole-body posture: RULA scores the upper limb (used at computer and assembly workstations); REBA scores the entire body including force and activity, giving action levels 0 to 4 from negligible to immediate change.
  • Repetitive upper-limb work: OCRA counts technical actions against a recommended frequency; the Strain Index rates distal upper-limb exposure (e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome in hand-intensive trades).
  • The Quick Exposure Check lets the worker co-rate exposure — fast, participative, useful on a live shop floor.
  • OWAS classifies whole-body postures from observation and video.
  • Alongside the instruments sit job-demand analysis and worker symptom surveys, which complete the picture with the worker's own report.
  • Interpretation: each tool ends in an action level that dictates the response — engineering redesign (raise the workbench, add a hoist), administrative limits (rotate jobs, micro-breaks), and worker training.
  • Indian application: garment and electronics assembly lines for RULA and OCRA; hospital patient handling and agricultural lifting for REBA and NIOSH; small workshops where the physiotherapist's assessment is the only one the worker will ever get.

Marks live in the pairing of tool with task: RULA for seated assembly work, REBA for whole-body, NIOSH for lifting, Strain Index for the wrist.

Sources
  • Kroemer KHE, Grandjean E. Fitting the Task to the Human — ergonomics text.
  • Waters TR, Putz-Anderson V, Garg A. NIOSH Revised Lifting Equation (primary).
  • Hignett S, McAtamney L. REBA (primary paper); McAtamney L, Corlett EN. RULA (primary paper).
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice — occupational context.
910 marks

Q9. Explain evaluation of work capacity and return to work.

Full answer →

Explain the concepts, the functional capacity evaluation, job demand matching, and the graded return-to-work plan.

  • What earns marks: Define the three concepts — impairment, capacity, disability · Describe the functional capacity evaluation (FCE) — its structure and its validity checks · Explain job demand analysis and matching capacity to the job · Give the graded return-to-work ladder and the psychosocial flags.
  • Three words students blur: impairment is what the body has lost (a weak back after disc surgery); work capacity is what the person can actually sustain in a real task; disability is the gap between capacity and the job's demands.
  • Work capacity evaluation measures the middle term and judges it against the third.
  • Frame it in ICF language — impairment, activity, participation.
  • Psychosocial flags that predict slower return: yellow flags (fear-avoidance and catastrophising in the worker), blue flags (the worker's perception of the workplace), and black flags (actual system barriers — no light duty available, pending compensation).
  • Capacity is behavioural as much as physical.
  • The FCE is a standardised, two-day battery performed over four to five hours each day to capture fatigue.
  • It tests the real demands of work: lifting floor-to-waist and waist-to-shoulder, carrying, pushing and pulling, overhead reach, crouching and kneeling, hand grip and endurance, standing and sitting tolerance, and repeated trunk bending.
  • Scores are recorded as safe maximum weights and tolerances.
  • Validity matters: consistency of effort across dissimilar tests, physiological plausibility (does the heart rate rise with the load?), and behaviour during testing.
  • A full FCE with inconsistency documented is a defensible report; a gym session is not.
  • Job demand analysis breaks the worker's job into physical requirements: weights and frequencies of lifting, distances carried, postures held, walking and climbing hours, and grip demands.
  • Physical demand levels then classify work from sedentary through light, medium and heavy to very heavy.
  • Return-to-work decisions compare FCE results against these demands — a worker with a 15-kilogram safe lift returning to a 25-kilogram heavy job is not ready for full duty, whatever the MRI says.
  • Building the plan: early, graded return beats prolonged rest — the strongest evidence in this field.
  • Work conditioning (physical reconditioning, two to four hours a day) progresses to work hardening (simulated job tasks, real tools, real pace, half to full day).
  • On the job, the plan uses modified duties — reduced hours, restricted lifting, alternate tasks — reviewed every one to two weeks with the employer and communicated in writing.
  • Address yellow flags with graded exposure and reassurance, not more passive treatment.
  • The report must state safe limits in plain numbers (kilograms, minutes, postures), the gap to job demands, and the next review date.

One line carries the concept: "return to work is decided by matching capacity to job demands, not by the medical diagnosis."

Sources
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — work evaluation chapters.
  • King PM. Sourcebook of Occupational Rehabilitation (functional capacity evaluation).
  • World Health Organization. ICF framework.
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice.
1010 marks

Q10. Describe screening the sacroiliac and pelvic joint.

Full answer →

Explain SI stability, the history and observation clues, the motion tests, and the Laslett pain-provocation cluster with the 3-of-5 rule.

  • What earns marks: Explain form closure and force closure first · Give the history clue (Fortin finger sign) and the observation landmarks · Present the Laslett pain-provocation cluster and the 3-of-5 rule · Note that provocation tests beat motion tests, and give the treatment direction.
  • The sacroiliac joint is a genuine pain generator in a meaningful share of low back complaints.
  • It refers pain over the posterior superior iliac spine and buttock, rarely below the knee.
  • Form closure: the tight bony and ligamentous fit of the sacrum between the ilia.
  • Force closure: the compression generated by muscles (gluteus maximus, biceps femoris through the sacrotuberous ligament, latissimus via the thoracolumbar fascia) coordinated by motor control.
  • Screening asks two questions in order: is the SI joint the pain source, and is the instability a form or a force problem (because the treatment differs).
  • History: the Fortin finger sign — the patient points to the SI area with a thumb, unhesitatingly — is the classical clue.
  • Ask about pregnancy or recent delivery, a fall on the buttock, asymmetric loading, and pain rolling in bed or on single-leg stance.
  • Observation: compare iliac crest heights, ASIS and PSIS levels, pelvic obliquity, leg-length appearance, lumbar curvature, and any lateral shift.
  • Gluteal bulk asymmetry and overactive erector spinae tell the force-closure story on visual inspection alone.
  • Motion screening: the stork or Gillet test (standing flexion — does the PSIS move down and lateral on the tested side), the sitting flexion test, the long-sitting test, and the supine-to-sit test for pelvic rotation asymmetry.
  • Present these as screening of movement symmetry, not diagnostic proof — their reliability is poor and the examiner knows it.
  • The Laslett pain-provocation cluster: distraction (gapping) with the patient supine; compression across the iliac crests in side-lying; the thigh thrust (posterior shear through the flexed hip); the sacral thrust (prone spring); and Gaenslen's test (couch edge, one hip flexed and the other extended).
  • Three or more positives identify the SI joint as the pain source.
  • Palpation completes the screen — tenderness over the sacral sulcus and long dorsal ligament, and springing of the sacrum.
  • Interpretation: three or more positives → treat with a trial of a pelvic belt (which also supports the force-closure mechanism), gluteal and deep-abdominal retraining, and correction of asymmetric loading habits.
  • A negative cluster with a positive lumbar screen redirects the search to the lumbar spine or hip, which are far more common culprits.

Two sentences that lift the answer: "provocation tests are more reliable than motion tests" and "the cluster is diagnostic, the single test is not."

Sources
  • Laslett M, et al. Diagnostic validity of a cluster of sacroiliac joint provocation tests (primary paper).
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — sacroiliac joint chapter.
  • Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders — pelvis.
  • Pool-Goudzwaard A, et al. The sacroiliac part of the iliolumbar ligament (form and force closure).
110 marks

Describe the impaired mobility seen in ankle injuries.

Full answer →

A two-sided answer: show BOTH stiffness (hypomobility) and ligamentous instability (hypermobility) in the ankle, with the mechanism, assessment and treatment.

  • What earns marks: give a two-sided answer — name BOTH stiffness (hypomobility) and instability (ligamentous hypermobility). Most students write only about stiffness · name the ankle capsular pattern — more restriction of dorsiflexion than plantarflexion · give the one-line mechanism — no posterior talar glide means no dorsiflexion.
  • What it means: ankle injuries (usually inversion sprains of the anterior talofibular ligament, but also fractures, syndesmotic injuries and chronic instability) disturb mobility in two opposite directions.
  • Acute stage: fluid (effusion) in the tight talocrural joint plus pain inhibition of the anterior tibial muscles splints the joint in a comfortable plantarflexed-inverted position, so active movement is lost all over.
  • Subacute stage: scar adhesion and shortening of the anterior capsule and the anterior talofibular ligament give a true capsular pattern.
  • Arthrokinematic problem: dorsiflexion needs the wide front of the talus to roll and glide backwards between the malleoli; if posterior talar glide is lost, movement is blocked even when the capsule looks normal.
  • Opposite direction: a torn ligament leaves the joint too roomy, giving instability rather than stiffness.
  • Talocrural joint: loss of dorsiflexion dominates — often 10–20 degrees short of the normal 20 degrees; at least 10 degrees of dorsiflexion is needed for normal terminal stance.
  • Because of that loss the patient walks with a compensated abducted gait, early heel lift or a functional equinus.
  • Subtalar joint: restriction of inversion and eversion follows sinus tarsi involvement or cast immobilisation, disturbing shock absorption on uneven ground.
  • Syndesmosis injury: end-range dorsiflexion is painful because the widened mortise jams the wider anterior talus; the squeeze test and loss of external rotation mark it.
  • Accessory movements lost: posterior glide of the talus on the tibia, and glide of the fibula on the tibia at the distal tibiofibular joint.
  • Hypermobile side: a torn anterior talofibular ligament gives a positive anterior drawer; a torn calcaneofibular ligament gives a positive talar tilt — this laxity drives recurrent sprains when proprioception is not retrained.
  • Assessment: measure active then passive range with a goniometer (align along the fibula and fifth metatarsal) and compare sides — the uninjured ankle is the best control.
  • Weight-bearing dorsiflexion by the knee-to-wall (lunge) test is more functional than table goniometry; assess accessory glides and end-feel (talus gliding posteriorly, fibula gliding anteriorly).
  • Grade ligament laxity with the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests; confirm functional instability with single-leg stance, the star excursion balance test or a wobble-board balance timer; palpate the joint line for effusion and the sinus tarsi for tenderness.
  • Treatment: protect and settle first (relative rest, ice, compression, elevation), then restore arthrokinematics.
  • Mobilisation: grade I–II oscillatory posterior talar glides for pain, progressing to grade III–IV sustained glides with the joint at the end of available dorsiflexion.
  • Convert to self-treatment quickly: knee-to-wall lunges, self-mobilisation with a strap, towel stretches, and eccentric calf work in the functional range.
  • Rebuild proprioception progressively: double-leg to single-leg, stable to unstable surfaces, eyes open to closed, adding hopping and cutting when control returns; tape or brace during the risky late phase.
  • Progression order: settle, glide, stretch, load, retrain balance.
  • Evidence: Verhagen and colleagues showed a proprioceptive and balance training programme roughly halves the recurrence of ankle sprains.
  • Conclusion: ankle injuries cause stiffness (effusion, capsular shortening, lost accessory glide) and instability (ligament laxity plus proprioceptive deficit) in the same joint; treatment of one without the other fails.

No posterior talar glide, no dorsiflexion — draw the talocrural joint with one arrow.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — ankle hypomobility and ligamentous instability sections.
  • Verhagen et al., ankle-sprain recurrence, American Journal of Sports Medicine.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — ankle and foot interventions.
210 marks

Write in detail about the role of various educational strategies in managing low back pain.

Full answer →

Show education as active treatment — list at least five delivery modes, link content to behaviour change, and end with the evidence that advice alone is weak but education plus graded exercise works.

  • What earns marks: the marks sit in the MENU — list and classify at least five modes, with one content line each · close with the evidence line — advice alone is weak; education plus graded exercise is strong.
  • Most low back pain is non-specific: no fracture, no nerve root compression, no sinister pathology.
  • What decides the outcome is not the imaging but the patient's beliefs and behaviour — whether they fear the pain, rest too much, or keep moving.
  • Education is a real treatment tool in the biopsychosocial model: it targets the psychosocial flags (fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophising, low self-efficacy) that turn an ordinary sprain into chronic disability.
  • In the Indian clinic, 'complete bed rest for 15 days' is still commonly advised — correcting beliefs early is high-yield treatment.
  • Individual advice in the consultation: stay active, avoid prolonged bed rest, keep working, and understand that 'hurt does not equal harm'.
  • Back schools: structured group programmes of anatomy, posture, lifting technique and exercise, first formalised in Sweden; effective mainly in occupational settings when combined with exercise.
  • Printed and audio-visual media: pamphlets, videos, mobile-phone messages; cheap and scalable but passive.
  • Pain neurosciences education: explaining pain processing so the patient understands pain reflects sensitivity of the nervous system, not ongoing damage; best delivered before or alongside exercise.
  • Group exercise classes with embedded education, and cognitive-behavioural informed classes (the UK Back Pain Exercise And Manipulation trial model), have the best evidence for reducing disability.
  • Yoga-based programmes suit our context — movement, breathing and relaxation in a culturally familiar package.
  • Content must change behaviour: reduce fear-avoidance, teach graded activity and pacing rather than boom-and-bust cycling, and set self-management goals.
  • Correct faulty beliefs about imaging ('disc degeneration is normal ageing, like grey hair') and give clear flare-up plans so a bad day does not become a catastrophe.
  • Education should always be paired with an active component — advice alone changes little; advice plus exercise changes function.
  • Evidence: systematic reviews find education alone (especially pamphlets) gives small short-term effects; structured programmes combining education with exercise reduce pain and disability more meaningfully.
  • Back schools show modest benefit in occupational cohorts; bed-rest advice is actively harmful.
  • Conclusion: education is the frame on which every other low back pain intervention hangs; delivered early, matched to the patient's beliefs and paired with graded activity, it is among the most cost-effective treatments.

Education alone = small effect; education + exercise = real effect.

Sources
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — education and back school content.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — functional activity education sections.
  • McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine (24) — patient self-management and education principle.
310 marks

Describe the role of anti-gravity muscles in maintaining postural stability.

Full answer →

Name the anti-gravity muscles and give the mechanism first (postural tone and the gamma system), then the balance strategies, then assessment and training.

  • What earns marks: the three names that lift this answer are the gamma motor system, the anticipatory postural adjustment, and the ankle strategy · give the mechanism (spindle bias) first, then the strategies, then assessment and training.
  • Anti-gravity muscles are the tonic extensors that hold the skeleton upright against gravity: soleus (the workhorse of standing), quadriceps, gluteus maximus, the lumbar erector spinae, and the neck extensors for the head.
  • They are the slow, fatigue-resistant, type-I fibre-rich muscles of the extensor thrust system.
  • In decerebrate rigidity their tone is exaggerated — classical proof that the nervous system is biased to keep the extensor chain ready.
  • In quadrupeds the anti-gravity muscles are the limb extensors; in upright humans the same system must fight gravity at every joint above the ground.
  • Standing is not a statue's pose: the body continuously sways over the base of support, and the anti-gravity muscles turn that sway into controlled sway.
  • Low-level tonic activity in soleus and erector spinae holds resting posture, driven by the gamma motor system, which keeps muscle spindles sensitive so the tonic stretch reflex can respond within milliseconds.
  • Postural tone is a reflex background, continuously recalibrated by the cerebellum and vestibular nuclei against visual, vestibular and proprioceptive input.
  • The result is a stable but adjustable column — like a stick balanced on a moving hand, where the 'hand' is the ankle strategy.
  • When balance is threatened, the muscles act in coordinated muscle synergy patterns, not one by one.
  • Small sway on a firm surface: the ankle strategy — gastrocnemius-soleus and hamstrings on posterior sway, tibialis anterior and quadriceps on anterior sway.
  • Faster or compliant-surface perturbation: the hip strategy — rapid trunk and thigh motion using the same extensor chain; large displacements: the stepping strategy.
  • These muscles also fire BEFORE movement: anticipatory postural adjustments — transversus abdominis and multifidus with the diaphragm pre-tension the trunk, and the soleus stiffens the ankle before the arm lifts.
  • Fatigue of the anti-gravity muscles shifts control to the hip strategy, increases sway velocity, and is a documented risk factor for falls in the elderly.
  • Assessment — static: Romberg test, sharpened Romberg, single-leg stance time (less than 10 seconds with eyes open flags falling risk in older adults), functional reach test, and limits-of-stability platform measures.
  • Assessment — dynamic: timed up-and-go, Berg Balance Scale, or computerised posturography which quantifies sway path and strategy use.
  • Test eyes open versus closed to separate the sensory contributions, and fatigue the muscles (repeated heel raises) to expose the reserve.
  • Training: progressive balance work (stable to unstable, double to single leg, eyes open to closed), perturbation training, eccentric and endurance work for soleus and quadriceps, and core stability training that restores the anticipatory postural adjustments.
  • Conclusion: postural stability is a reflex-managed equilibrium where the tonic extensor chain supplies the force against gravity, the spindle-gamma system supplies the sensitivity, and the CNS supplies the strategy; treat instability by training all three layers.

Soleus, erector spinae, gluteus maximus, quadriceps, neck extensors — the tonic extensor chain vs gravity.

Sources
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — postural reflexes and muscle spindle-gamma system.
  • Hislop, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing (7) — anti-gravity muscle testing positions.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — balance and postural stability training progression.
410 marks

Describe McKenzie's principles of mobilization.

Full answer →

Avoid 'McKenzie means extension exercises' — show response-guided loading, where centralisation decides the direction and the syndrome decides the technique; name all three syndromes.

  • What earns marks: do not write 'McKenzie means extension exercises' — the principle is RESPONSE-GUIDED loading · name all three syndromes with one treatment line each.
  • MDT (Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy), the McKenzie method, rests on one idea: the patient's symptomatic response to repeated end-range loading is the most reliable guide to classification and treatment.
  • Assessment begins with a full history and baseline symptom mapping (where the pain is now, how far it spreads, what makes it better and worse).
  • The examiner performs repeated movement testing — sagittal first (flexion, extension in lying and standing), then frontal plane if needed — five to ten repetitions at end range, watching the DISTAL extent of symptoms.
  • McKenzie deliberately says little about pathology; the behaviour of the pain under load is the diagnosis.
  • Centralisation: referred or radicular pain retreats proximally towards the midline spine in response to a specific repeated movement — the single best prognostic sign in MDT.
  • Peripheralisation is the opposite: the pain marches distally, and that movement is immediately withdrawn and avoided.
  • Directional preference is the movement direction that produces centralisation or lasting relief — most commonly extension in the lumbar spine; a patient with a directional preference is treated in that direction.
  • Derangement syndrome (most common): internal displacement of nuclear material causing mechanically changeable, intermittent pain that centralises or peripheralises.
  • Derangement treatment: repeated end-range movements in the directional preference (classically prone press-ups or standing extension); force is progressed only as far as needed to achieve centralisation.
  • Postural syndrome: pain only on sustained end-range static loading (slumped sitting in a young, normal spine), relieved instantly by position change; treatment is postural correction plus education, with no hands-on needed.
  • Dysfunction syndrome: shortening or scarring of tissue producing consistent end-range pain in a fixed direction that does not change with repetition (for example, flexion dysfunction after a healed disc episode).
  • Dysfunction treatment: static end-range stretching in the restricted — and painful — direction, remodelling the adapted tissue over weeks.
  • Always mention the 'other' category (non-mechanical presentations, red flags, chronic pain states) for red-flag safety.
  • Force progression ladder (only if the response is incomplete): patient-generated movement, then clinician overpressure, then sagittal mobilisation, then (rarely) manipulation — always re-testing centralisation after each step.
  • Second pillar: the patient treats the patient — exercises are home exercises performed ten times a day; the clinician finds, teaches and progresses them.
  • Maintenance: posture correction (lumbar roll, standing extension after prolonged sitting), regular self-mobilisation, and recurrence management.
  • Evidence: systematic reviews support directional preference as a real, clinically useful phenomenon, centralisation as a strong prognostic marker, and MDT as at least as effective as other conservative care for acute and subacute low back pain.
  • Conclusion: MDT is a classification-driven, assessment-led system where repeated end-range loading identifies a directional preference, defines one of three syndromes, and hands the treatment to the patient.

Repeated movements → centralisation / peripheralisation / no change → three syndromes.

Sources
  • McKenzie R & May S, The Lumbar Spine: Mechanical Diagnosis and Therapy (24).
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — spine mobilisation progression context.
  • Butler & Jones, Mobilisation of the Nervous System (26) — contrast with neurodynamic schools.
510 marks

Describe the role of various external appliances used for rehabilitation in patients following L2-L3 disc prolapse.

Full answer →

Say that L2-L3 is upper lumbar, so a plain belt will not do — the orthosis must extend thoracically; and state the weaning principle (orthosis plus exercise, never instead).

  • What earns marks: avoid a generic 'lumbar belt' essay — L2-L3 is upper lumbar, so the orthosis must extend thoracically (TLSO logic) · state weaning — orthosis plus exercise, never orthosis instead of exercise.
  • An L2-L3 prolapse is an UPPER lumbar lesion: the segment moves mainly in the sagittal plane, and the extension-biased loading taught for L4-S1 must be applied with more caution this high.
  • The appliance has four jobs: limit painful flexion, raise intra-abdominal pressure so the abdominal cylinder shares spinal load, give proprioceptive feedback ('posture reminder'), and in the acute phase allow movement while protecting the healing annulus.
  • A well-fitted corset can reduce the load on the lumbar column by roughly a third during lifting.
  • An lumbosacral orthosis is a prescribed spinal support whose rigid panels and closure system control segmental motion — the umbrella term for most of what follows.
  • Soft canvas corset with abdominal binder: commonest in Indian practice — inexpensive, off the shelf, gives abdominal compression and posture cueing with little true motion control; suits the comfort phase.
  • Semi-rigid lumbosacral orthosis: corset with posterior moulded plastic or metal stays and paraspinal steels; controls flexion-extension partially — the workhorse for the four-to-six-week protected phase.
  • Rigid three-point lumbosacral orthosis (chairback or Williams-type): anterior and posterior panels with a three-point system (sternal/sacral and abdominal pads) that genuinely blocks lumbar flexion.
  • Rigid thoraco-lumbo-sacral orthosis: for an L2-L3 lesion, control must extend above the lesion, so the orthosis must include a thoracic band (Boston-type overlap or custom-moulded TLSO) — the key level-specific point.
  • Hyperextension orthosis (Jewett type): blocks flexion while allowing some extension, mainly post-fracture but worth naming.
  • Each of these works WITH the physiotherapy programme, never instead of it.
  • Ancillary appliances in the acute phase: an adjustable walking aid (rollator or cane on the opposite side) to reduce axial load and improve confidence; a firm mattress or bed board under a lumbar roll for sleeping; and log-rolling technique taught.
  • For daily activities: raised toilet seat and commode chair, long-handled reacher and shoe horn (dressing without trunk flexion), elevated chair with armrests, and a lumbar cushion for unavoidable sitting.
  • Prescription principles: fit at the level of the lesion with the pelvic band anchored on the sacrum, worn during activity and weaned at rest, and checked for pressure areas in our hot climate.
  • Pair from day one with an isometric abdominal and back programme — because every orthosis unloads the very muscles that must eventually take over.
  • Wearing schedule typically tapers over four to six weeks; prolonged bracing produces trunk muscle atrophy and dependence — the classic complication to warn about.
  • Evidence: randomised evidence suggests orthoses add only modest benefit over exercise-plus-advice alone for uncomplicated disc prolapse, so the modern role is a short, well-defined protective and confidence-building phase.
  • Conclusion: at L2-L3 the appliance must reach higher (TLSO logic), buy time for the annulus, use the abdominal cylinder to unload the segment, cue posture, and be withdrawn before dependency develops.

Three-point system blocks flexion; control must extend ABOVE L2.

Sources
  • Chui et al., Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation (18) — spinal orthosis designs and control levels.
  • Maxey & Magnusson (13) — orthotic prescription and wearing schedules.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — spinal intervention progression.
  • McKenzie & May, The Lumbar Spine (24) — loading considerations at upper lumbar levels.
610 marks

Describe the evidence-based electrotherapy management of fibromyalgia.

Full answer →

Frame electrotherapy as an adjunct to exercise and education, never a substitute, and grade each modality honestly as strong, moderate or weak evidence.

  • What earns marks: the scoring phrase is 'adjunct to exercise and education — never a substitute' · grade each modality as strong / moderate / weak evidence instead of listing every machine.
  • Fibromyalgia, by the Wolfe et al. American College of Rheumatology criteria, is chronic widespread pain lasting at least three months with somatic and cognitive symptoms — classified by the widespread pain index and symptom severity scale (the older 1990 criteria counted tender points out of 18).
  • It is a disorder of central pain processing: diffuse hyperexcitability with reduced descending inhibition, fatigue and non-restorative sleep.
  • Electrotherapy never treats the disease; it treats pain and sleep symptoms as an ADJUNCT to the cornerstones — graded aerobic exercise, education and cognitive-behavioural therapy.
  • Mechanism: by the gate control theory of Melzack and Wall, stimulating large-diameter A-beta afferents in the dorsal horn closes the gate on nociceptive transmission — high-frequency, sensory-intensity TENS exploits this.
  • Low-frequency, acupuncture-like TENS at motor intensity recruits endogenous opioid release.
  • Any modality must be judged by whether it increases activity and sleep, not by immediate pain relief alone, because the problem is central sensitisation.
  • TENS: the most studied; best used high-frequency (40–80 Hz per DeLisa; 70–100 Hz in practice), strong but comfortable, over the most symptomatic regions for 30 minutes, several times daily, self-applied for flares; trials show modest short-term pain reduction.
  • Interferential therapy (four-pole; beat 20–80 Hz per DeLisa, commonly 90–100 Hz for pain in Indian clinics): widely used with a similar gate-control rationale; comfort-oriented evidence, less trial support than TENS.
  • Microcurrent therapy (microamperage currents): small trials suggest pain and sleep benefit; evidence remains weak.
  • Electroacupuncture: systematic reviews find it better than sham for pain and stiffness in the short term — one of the better-supported electrical options.
  • Frequency-specific magnetic stimulation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation target the central component directly; promising but not yet routine physiotherapy practice — mention them as emerging evidence.
  • Superficial heat (hot packs, warm showers before exercise) and warm-water balneotherapy or hydrotherapy are the strongest physical-agent options: randomised trials show durable improvements in pain, function and quality of life; cryotherapy has a role for local flares.
  • Evidence grading: strongest — warm-water exercise and graded land-based aerobic exercise (core, not adjunct); moderate — electroacupuncture, some TENS benefit for short-term pain; weak — interferential, microcurrent, static magnets.
  • Conclusion: an evidence-based electrotherapy plan uses TENS or electroacupuncture for symptomatic relief and heat or hydrotherapy to enable activity, always subordinate to graded exercise, sleep and education — and is reviewed against function, not pain scores alone.

Large fibres in, gate closes, pain falls (Melzack & Wall).

Sources
  • Wolfe F et al., American College of Rheumatology fibromyalgia criteria.
  • Melzack R & Wall PD, Pain mechanisms: a new theory, Science 1965.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — pain physiology and descending inhibition.
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation (10) — chronic pain rehabilitation.
710 marks

Describe adjuvant therapies in managing pain.

Full answer →

Give the definition first, then classify adjuvants into four shelves (physical, hands-on, psychosocial, pharmacological), and close with the evidence that they multiply the engine.

  • What earns marks: definition marks are free — 'administered alongside primary treatment to enhance effect or reduce drug burden' — write it in the first line · classify into four shelves instead of a random list; structure turns a list into a 10-mark answer.
  • Definition: an adjuvant therapy is one administered ALONGSIDE the primary treatment to enhance its effect, address a component the primary therapy does not reach, or reduce overall drug burden.
  • In pain management the primary tools are exercise, manual therapy, education and analgesics; adjuvants are the supporting cast.
  • Mechanism: most adjuvants work through segmental gate control, descending inhibitory pathways, altered tissue fluid dynamics, or psychological (attention and expectancy) mechanisms — which is why they relieve pain without changing the disease.
  • Classify them as physical, hands-on and movement-based, psychosocial, and pharmacological — a four-shelf answer.
  • Physical — superficial heat (hot packs, paraffin wax baths for hand pain) reduces muscle spindle excitability and stiffness before exercise.
  • Physical — deep heat (ultrasound, 1 MHz) targets deeper fascia and tendon; cryotherapy reduces conduction velocity and acute inflammation after trauma.
  • Physical — topical counterirritation (menthol, methyl salicylate, capsaicin balms) stimulates superficial receptors to compete with nociceptive input; capsaicin also depletes substance P over days of use.
  • Physical — TENS and interferential therapy act as electrical adjuvants through the gate mechanism; time them around the active programme (heat before stretching, cold after loading).
  • Hands-on — massage (effleurage and petrissage) reduces perceived pain and muscle guarding via mechanoreceptor stimulation and improved local circulation; myofascial release and soft-tissue mobilisation address trigger points.
  • Hands-on — dry needling and acupuncture de-nociceptise trigger points and stir endogenous opioid release — moderate evidence in myofascial pain.
  • Hands-on — kinesio taping provides continuous cutaneous afferent input and tactile cueing of posture.
  • Movement and mind-body — relaxation techniques (progressive muscle relaxation, diaphragmatic breathing), yoga and meditation modulate sympathetic arousal and improve pain coping.
  • Pharmacological (know what the physician adds): adjuvant analgesics — tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline at low dose for neuropathic and fibromyalgia pain), serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin), and topical lidocaine and capsaicin patches.
  • Psychosocial — cognitive-behavioural therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, and guided imagery target catastrophising and fear-avoidance, the strongest drivers of chronicity.
  • Evidence: adjuvants reliably deliver short-term symptomatic relief and rarely change long-term outcomes alone; their value appears when combined with exercise, education and graded exposure.
