  • Conclusion: adjuvant therapies are the multiplier, not the engine, of pain management — selected to remove the barriers (pain, stiffness, fear, arousal) that block the primary active treatment, timed around it, and reviewed by whether the patient can do more.

Adjuvants feed the engine (exercise + education), never replace it.

Sources
  • Melzack R & Wall PD, Science 1965 — gate control mechanism of most adjuvants.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — soft-tissue and physical agent adjuncts.
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — pain modulation pathways.
  • Wolfe F et al., ACR fibromyalgia criteria — context for adjuvant use in widespread pain.
810 marks

Describe wrist ergonomics for a computer operator.

Full answer →

Give the neutral-wrist principle with the key numbers (extension beyond about 15 degrees, elbow near 90 degrees, RULA above 5), the workstation layout, and the breaks/education.

  • What earns marks: numbers buy marks — wrist extension beyond about 15 degrees is the danger zone; elbows near 90 degrees; RULA grand score above 5 needs prompt change · mention that palm rests are for pauses, not typing — a favourite examiner discriminating detail.
  • Mechanism: carpal tunnel pressure rises steeply when the wrist leaves neutral — wrist extension beyond about 15 degrees, plus sustained ulnar deviation and forearm pronation, increase pressure inside the tunnel.
  • Repetition matters: fast keyboard work can reach 8,000 to 12,000 keystrokes per hour — the exposure the NUDATA study linked to arm and elbow pain.
  • Add static loading, contact stress at the wrist rest, and cold or vibration, and you have the recipe for carpal tunnel syndrome, De Quervain's tenosynovitis and non-specific forearm pain.
  • Goal: keep the hand working on a neutral wrist posture — forearm supported, wrist straight, no lean — while the bigger joints (elbow at about 90 degrees, shoulders relaxed) absorb the posture.
  • Keyboard: flat or negatively tilted (back feet folded DOWN, not up), directly in front, at elbow height, and close to the body so the wrists need not extend to reach.
  • Mouse: beside the keyboard at the same height, size matched to the hand, operated with the whole arm; a keyboard tray with a mouse platform prevents reaching.
  • Wrist or palm rests: used during PAUSES, not while typing — leaning on them while typing creates contact stress.
  • Chair: height so the forearms are parallel to the floor, feet flat, lumbar support; forearms lightly supported on the chair arms or desk edge.
  • Monitor: top at or just below eye level, an arm's length away, so a flexed neck does not drag the whole kinetic chain down.
  • Desk: adequate depth so the monitor is not pushed back into extension-heavy reaching; document holder inline with the screen.
  • Indian setting: the commonest faults are laptop use at a low table (forced wrist and neck flexion) and shared workstations never adjusted for the individual.
  • Assessment: screen with the OSHA Computer Workstations eTool checklist, and quantify posture with RULA (the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment of McAtamney and Corlett) — a grand score above 5 demands prompt change.
  • Symptom survey (discomfort charts), keystroke rates and overtime patterns complete the picture; risk factors to hunt are deviation, extension, repetition, static hold, contact stress, cold and psychosocial pressure.
  • Work organisation: micropauses of 30-60 seconds every 20-30 minutes; stretch the wrist flexors and extensors; alternate tasks; keep typing load realistic with software break reminders.
  • Encourage early symptom reporting with a no-blame culture; educate the operator in self-checking neutral posture — the 'handshake' position is the memory hook.
  • Evidence: ergonomic interventions (adjusted workstation plus education plus breaks) reduce discomfort and symptoms in office workers more consistently than exercise alone, and combined ergonomic-plus-exercise programmes are most effective.
  • Conclusion: wrist ergonomics is the marriage of a neutral-wrist workstation (keyboard and mouse at elbow height, flat keyboard, palm rests for pauses only) with regular breaks and posture education — engineering first, behaviour second, both audited by RULA.

Neutral = the 'handshake' position for the wrist.

Sources
  • OSHA Computer Workstations eTool — workstation checklist.
  • McAtamney L & Corlett EN, RULA: a survey method, Applied Ergonomics 1993.
  • Cooper C, Fundamentals of Hand Therapy (21) — wrist pathology and activity modification.
  • Saunders, Hand and Upper Extremity Rehabilitation (20) — tendinopathy management context.
910 marks

Describe the role of assistive devices in industrial setups which work with heavy loads.

Full answer →

Open with the hierarchy of controls, give the NIOSH numbers (23 kg constant; lifting index above 1 = risk), list the device categories, and dismiss the back belt.

  • What earns marks: open with the hierarchy of controls — eliminate, engineer, redesign, administrate, protect · give the NIOSH numbers (23 kg constant for an ideal lift; lifting index above 1 flags risk) and dismiss the back belt explicitly.
  • Mechanism: during a freestyle stoop lift the lumbar disc compression can exceed the 3.4 kN action limit for repeated loading — approaching the NIOSH maximum permissible limit of about 6.4 kN — because the spine acts as a long lever with a short, poor-efficiency erector spinae moment arm.
  • The disc, not the muscle, is the weak link.
  • Manual handling is the single largest source of occupational injury in Indian industry — construction sites, godowns, warehouses and small-scale assembly units.
  • The professional answer does not begin with 'teach safe lifting'; it begins with the hierarchy of controls: eliminate the lift, engineer it away, redesign the task, change the work organisation, and only lastly rely on training and personal protective equipment.
  • Assistive devices are the engineering tier — the most effective one.
  • Category 1 — load movement instead of load lifting: trolleys, hand trucks, pallet trucks, conveyor belts, roller tracks and chutes (the cheapest, highest-yield tier).
  • Category 2 — position the load at waist height: lift tables, scissor lifts, tilt tables, turntables and self-levelling dispensers, so the worker never bends below knuckle height or reaches above shoulder height.
  • Category 3 — vertical handling: hoists, jib cranes, gantry cranes, vacuum tube lifters for sacks and sheet material, and powered stackers — removing the spine from the chain altogether.
  • Category 4 — tool-integrated supports: balancers and torque arms that absorb the weight and reaction of heavy power tools.
  • Emerging — passive industrial exoskeletons that support the shoulders or trunk during sustained overhead or stooped work; promising for fatigue, still accumulating safety evidence.
  • The back belt is NOT a reliable assistive device: evidence shows it does not prevent injury in untrained workers and may promote over-reliance — mention it to dismiss it correctly.
  • Assessment: the NIOSH lifting equation computes a recommended weight limit from horizontal distance, vertical height, travel distance, asymmetry, frequency and coupling quality (a constant of 23 kg for an ideal lift under it), giving a lifting index — a value above 1 means the task exceeds the recommended limit.
  • Supplement with postural screens (RULA or REBA) for the upper limb and whole body, and a walkthrough of the actual task in the actual shift pattern; the assessment drives the purchase, not the catalogue.
  • Human tier: manual-handling training (load close to the body, neutral spine with hip hinge, pivot not twist, team lifts above about 25 kg per person) and job rotation across loading tiers.
  • For the injured worker returning to heavy industry, a structured work hardening and work conditioning programme — simulated job tasks at real loads with cardiovascular conditioning and ergonomic education — has good evidence for return-to-work outcomes.
  • Evidence: engineering controls (mechanical aids, adjustable workstations) show consistent reductions in manual-handling injury rates, whereas lifting-training-only interventions have small and short-lived effects; back belts do not prevent low back injury.
  • Conclusion: assess with the NIOSH equation and RULA, then push the fix up the hierarchy — eliminate, then mechanise (trolleys, conveyors, hoists, lift tables), then position (waist-height zones), then prepare the worker with training and work hardening.

Zones make the risk visible; devices move every lift into green.

Sources
  • Maxey L & Magnusson (13) — industrial rehabilitation and work hardening.
  • McAtamney L & Corlett EN, RULA, Applied Ergonomics 1993 — postural risk assessment.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — work conditioning and functional progression.
  • OSHA Computer Workstations eTool — assessment checklist principles (adapted to manual handling walkthrough).
1010 marks

Describe the role of evidence-based rehabilitation following arthroscopic meniscus repair.

Full answer →

Say repair is not meniscectomy — protect the suture line for six weeks, then closed-chain loading, then criteria-based return — and close with the FIDELITY trial.

  • What earns marks: the examiner's discriminator is that repair is NOT meniscectomy — say 'protect the suture line six weeks, delay twisting and deep flexion' · close with FIDELITY — for degenerate tears, rehab first, the scope adds nothing.
  • Mechanism: the meniscus is vascular only in its outer third; a repair (inside-out, all-inside or outside-in sutures) succeeds only where the tear sits in the red-red or red-white zone with blood supply to heal.
  • A white-white tear is usually excised, not repaired — that single fact drives the whole programme.
  • After meniscectomy you protect nothing but the effusion; after repair you protect the suture line for about six weeks while fibrocartilaginous healing proceeds.
  • Complex or bucket-handle repairs, and repairs done with ACL reconstruction (common in the young Indian athlete with a twisting football or kabaddi injury), demand even more caution with rotation and deep flexion.
  • Phase I (weeks 0-6): brace locked in extension for ambulation, partial weight-bearing on crutches (toe-touch to 30-50 percent, surgeon-dependent), avoiding twisting, squatting and deep flexion.
  • Phase I goals: full knee extension (matching the other side), control of effusion with ice and compression, patellar mobilisations to prevent retinacular adhesions, quadriceps re-education with isometrics, straight-leg raises, ankle pumps, and gentle 0-90 degree flexion per protocol.
  • Phase I is about PREVENTING stiffness and arthrogenic muscle inhibition without loading the repair.
  • Phase II (weeks 6-12): weight-bearing progresses to full, the brace is weaned, gait normalises, and range moves beyond 120 degrees.
  • Phase II strengthening becomes closed kinetic chain dominant — mini-squats to 45 degrees, leg press in protected arcs, step-ups, calf raises, stationary cycling with a raised seat — because closed-chain loading compresses and stabilises the joint while protecting the repair from shear.
  • Open-chain knee extension stays in the protected arc, avoiding the terminal 30-45 degrees of extension where shear is highest.
  • Phase II adds proprioceptive retraining: single-leg balance, wobble board, perturbation work; aquatic therapy is invaluable where available.
  • Phase III (months 3-6): progress to running from month three (for isolated repair) on level surfaces, then agility, plyometrics and sport-specific drills — cutting, pivoting and change of direction — around months four to five.
  • Return is guided by limb-symmetry criteria, not the calendar: quadriceps and hamstring strength within about 90 percent of the other limb, single-leg hop tests symmetric, no effusion, and full painless range.
  • Heavy-labour workers follow the same strength criteria with simulated task training.
  • Maintenance education: a repaired meniscus is a long-term investment — quadriceps strength, load management and avoiding deep squats under load in the first year protect it.
  • Evidence: Sihvonen and colleagues' FIDELITY trial (New England Journal of Medicine) showed that for DEGENERATIVE meniscal tears, arthroscopic partial meniscectomy was no better than sham surgery — rehabilitation, not surgery, is first-line there.
  • That is precisely why repair of repairable traumatic tears is protected so carefully (Wilk and Brotzman's protocols supply the criteria-based progression).
  • Conclusion: evidence-based rehab after meniscus repair is a protection-then-progression story — six weeks guarding the sutured zone while regaining extension, then closed-chain loading and neuromuscular control, then criteria-based return to sport.

Criteria decide return, not the calendar.

Sources
  • Wilk KE, Brotzman SB et al., Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation (14) — meniscus repair protocols.
  • Sihvonen R et al., Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy versus sham surgery (FIDELITY), New England Journal of Medicine 2018.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — closed-chain progression and criteria-based return.
110 marks

Q1. Explain ICF in documentation of rehabilitation assessment and management.

Full answer →

Show that you know what the ICF is, its two lists and three levels, and that you can really use it to write a patient's assessment and set goals.

  • What earns marks: define the ICF (WHO 2001) and say it records functioning, not just disease — 2 marks · name the two lists and three levels, and give the coding qualifier scale 0–4 — 3 marks · show one real patient written up at all three levels and use the ICF to set goals — 4.5 marks.
  • ICF = International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, made by WHO in 2001 — a common language for what a patient can and cannot do, not only the diagnosis they carry.
  • The old ICD-10 only named the disease ('hemiplegia following cerebral infarction'); the ICF moves documentation from 'disease' to 'functioning'.
  • The ICF adds the real clinical problem: because of the stroke, the patient cannot hold a glass of water, walk to the bus stop, or work as a tailor.
  • Part 1 — Functioning and Disability — has three levels: body functions and structures, activity, and participation.
  • Body functions and structures = impairment level (what we find on examination, e.g. reduced knee flexion, weak quadriceps grade 3).
  • Activity = limitation (what the person cannot do, e.g. sit-to-stand, gait).
  • Participation = restriction (the lost social role, e.g. cannot return to farming).
  • Part 2 — Contextual factors — has environmental factors (family support, terrain of the village, wheelchair availability, stigma) and personal factors (age, motivation, occupation, education).
  • Every component is coded with a letter and a number qualifier from 0 (no problem) to 4 (complete problem); example 'b7300.2' = power of muscles, moderate impairment.
  • Assessment example — a 58-year-old diabetic tailor with a below-knee amputation: impairment (stump oedema, hip flexion contracture 15 degrees, grade 3 hip abductors), activity limitation (transfers need moderate assistance, 40 m ambulation on axillary crutches), participation restriction (cannot sit cross-legged at the shop, cannot cycle to work).
  • Environmental factors are written as facilitators or barriers — 'kaya clinic on ground floor (facilitator), employer unwilling to modify the workbench (barrier)'.
  • So documentation becomes measurable, coded and comparable across therapists and follow-up visits; the qualifier number at week 1 versus week 6 is your outcome evidence.
  • Management flows down the same framework: impairment goals (increase hip abductor strength to grade 4, reduce contracture to 5 degrees) feed activity goals (independent transfer, 200 m community ambulation on prosthesis) which feed participation goals (return to tailoring with modified seating, driving to work).
  • Write functional goals ('walk 200 m') rather than machine-based ones ('gave IFT and SWD'); when the barrier is environmental, the answer is counselling, assistive devices or workplace modification, not exercise.
  • Advantages: it is WHO-standard, goal-directed, measurable, and it stops the therapist documenting only impairments.
  • Indian angle: participation questions (return to field labour, sitting on the floor for meals, using an Indian-style toilet) expose cultural barriers no foreign scale captures; ICMR-funded community rehabilitation programmes report outcomes in ICF terms.
  • Caution: personal factors are never coded, only noted — a favourite one-mark trap.

Five-box ICF map — health condition, body functions and structures, activity, participation, contextual factors — reproduce it and the whole framework follows.

Sources
  • WHO. International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health. Geneva: WHO; 2001.
  • World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
210 marks

Q2. Describe the ICMR ethical guidelines.

Full answer →

Name the twelve ICMR principles, describe the ethics committee, and cover vulnerable groups — not one vague blob.

  • What earns marks: list the twelve principles as a numbered list, naming at least eight with one line each — 4 marks · describe the ethics committee's composition and powers (2 marks) and cover the special situations and vulnerable groups (1.5 marks) · quote 'ICMR 2017, updates 2006' and link the guidelines to physiotherapy research in India — 2.5 marks.
  • ICMR = Indian Council of Medical Research; its National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (2017) update the 2006 and 1980 versions.
  • They answer a global lineage: the Nuremberg Code (1947), the Declaration of Helsinki (1964, revised repeatedly), CIOMS, and the Belmont Report's three pillars — respect, beneficence and justice.
  • When a drug is involved they are registered with the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules (CDSCO); this is the document every Indian institutional ethics committee (EC) applies when your MPT dissertation is screened.
  • The 2017 revision now also covers public health research, social media data, biobanking and cluster trials.
  • Principle 1 — Essentiality: the research must be necessary for human welfare.
  • Principle 2 — Voluntariness, informed consent and community agreement: participants may withdraw without penalty.
  • Principle 3 — Non-exploitation: especially of poor, illiterate or captive populations.
  • Principle 4 — Privacy and confidentiality.
  • Principle 5 — Risk minimisation and non-maleficence.
  • Principle 6 — Adequacy of benefit versus risk; Principle 7 — Equity in distribution of burdens and benefits.
  • Principle 8 — Professional competence and medical research quality: you must be qualified and supervised.
  • Principle 9 — Accountability and transparency in all transactions; Principle 10 — Maximisation of public interest (findings should benefit the population studied).
  • Principle 11 — Institutional arrangements: research must pass through a registered ethics committee; Principle 12 — Totality of responsibility: everyone in the chain, from investigator to funding agency, remains answerable.
  • The EC is the operational arm: minimum 7 members — a chairperson from outside the institution, a basic medical scientist, a clinician, a legal expert, a social scientist or NGO representative, a layperson from the community, and a member secretary.
  • The EC can approve, modify, defer or reject a protocol, and keeps post-review powers — annual reports, on-site monitoring, and re-examination of any serious adverse event (SAE reported within 24 h).
  • Vulnerable groups: children (assent plus parental consent, minimal risk only), pregnant and lactating women, prisoners, employees and students (no coercion — a caution for MPT colleges recruiting their own undergraduates), the economically and socially disadvantaged, the cognitively impaired, and emergency settings where deferred consent is permitted; special guidance covers genetic research, stem cells, organ transplantation, vaccine trials, and digital health data and herd-immunity cluster designs.
  • Every MPT dissertation — even a low-risk exercise protocol on post-operative knees — needs EC clearance before the first patient is recruited; informed consent (purpose, procedures, risks, benefits and the right to withdraw, in the participant's own language, before any data collection) is the single most testable principle.

Lineage chain: Nuremberg 1947 → Helsinki 1964 → Belmont; then ICMR 2017 (updates 2006, 1980).

Sources
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants. New Delhi: ICMR; 2017.
  • World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice.
  • Declaration of Helsinki, World Medical Association.
310 marks

Q3. Explain in detail the important experimental designs.

Full answer →

Explain what makes a design experimental, go deep on the RCT, and give one physiotherapy example for every design you name.

  • What earns marks: state what makes a design experimental and explain internal and external validity — 2 marks · go deep on the RCT and its crossover and factorial variants, giving one physiotherapy example for each design — 3 marks · cover quasi-experimental and pre-experimental designs with their weaknesses — 3 marks · include single-subject designs and how to choose a design in an Indian setting — 2 marks.
  • An experimental design is one in which the investigator assigns the intervention — that act of allocation, ideally by chance, is what separates an experiment from an observational study.
  • Quality is judged by internal validity (does the change truly reflect the treatment?) and external validity (does it hold outside the study?).
  • Threats to internal validity: history, maturation, regression to the mean, selection bias and attrition.
  • The hierarchy runs true experimental → quasi-experimental → pre-experimental; every design buys validity at a price a clinician can pay.
  • The randomised controlled trial (RCT) is the gold standard: eligible patients are allocated by randomisation to experimental and control conditions, and outcomes are compared.
  • Randomisation is chance assignment that balances known and unknown prognostic factors between arms.
  • Allocation concealment stops the enroller predicting the next slot; blinding keeps participants, therapists or outcome assessors unaware of group membership, killing expectation and observer bias — the assessor is the minimum you must blind in physiotherapy trials.
  • RCT example (CONSORT-style): eligibility → randomisation → Group A (mobilisation + exercise, n = 30) and Group B (sham US + exercise, n = 30) → blinded outcome comparison.
  • Crossover design: every subject receives both treatments in random order, separated by a washout, so each patient is his own control — powerful for stable chronic conditions like chronic low back pain, but invalid where carry-over exists (manual therapy).
  • Factorial design: tests two interventions at once — exercise (yes/no) crossed with education (yes/no) gives four cells and answers whether the combination is additive, all from one sample; efficient when interactions are plausible.
  • Quasi-experimental — non-equivalent control group design: compares a naturally occurring treatment group (your OPD) with a matched comparison group (a nearby clinic); vulnerable to selection bias but realistic for hospital-based Indian dissertations.
  • Quasi-experimental — time-series design: repeated measurements before and after intervention (A-B-A or multiple baselines); the run of pre-intervention points controls for maturation and regression.
  • Quasi-experimental — regression-discontinuity design: allocates by a cutoff score on a continuous variable; heavily used in health-policy evaluation.
  • Pre-experimental designs (mention to dismiss them): the one-shot case study (X then O — no internal validity at all), the one-group pretest–posttest (O X O), and the static group comparison.
  • Single-subject (N-of-1) designs repeat a baseline (A) and intervention (B) phase within one patient — A-B, A-B-A, A-B-A-B or multiple-baseline across behaviours — with the patient as his own control and the graph as the analysis.
  • Choosing a design: ask three questions — can I randomise? is the condition stable enough to crossover? can I repeat measurements? In India most MPT dissertations end up quasi-experimental or single-subject because 60 fresh ACL reconstructions cannot be randomised in one centre in one year.

RCT = randomise, conceal, blind — the assessor at minimum.

Sources
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
  • Herbert R, Jamtvedt G, Mead J, Hagen KB. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
410 marks

Q4. What does a measure of central tendency indicate? Describe the important measures of central tendency.

Full answer →

Say what central tendency means, describe mean, median and mode with their merits and uses, and end with which measure suits which data.

  • What earns marks: explain what central tendency means and why it is used — 2 marks · give the mean's merits, demerits and uses (2.5) and the median's calculation and uses (2) — with the formula · cover the mode and the relation among the three measures (1.5) and finish with which measure suits which data (2).
  • A measure of central tendency is a single summary value that locates the centre of a distribution — the typical or most representative value of the data set.
  • It does two jobs: it condenses a column of 30 VAS scores into one communicable number, and it is the anchor from which dispersion (how far data scatter around that centre) is measured.
  • Used alone it hides spread — 'mean 4.2, SD 1.1' is a sentence, 'mean 4.2' is half a sentence.
  • The arithmetic mean is the sum of all observations divided by their number: x-bar = ΣX / n.
  • Merits: it uses every data point, is amenable to algebra, and is the foundation of parametric testing — the default in physiology and laboratory research.
  • Demerit: it is sensitive to outliers — five patients with pain 4, 4, 5, 5, 5 give mean 4.6; add one patient with 10 and it jumps to 5.5.
  • Grouped data are handled by the midpoint method; the geometric mean (log-then-average) tames skewed distributions like antibody titres.
  • The median is the middlemost observation after ranking the data — half the values lie below it and half above.
  • Calculation: for odd n take the (n + 1)/2th value; for even n take the mean of the two central values.
  • The median is unaffected by extremes, so it is the correct summary for ordinal data (a 6-point functional scale) and skewed data (hospital stay, income, pain scores with a long right tail); it is reported with the interquartile range.
  • For heavily skewed Indian hospital cost data, the median is what the health economist reports.
  • The mode is the most frequently occurring value — the only measure definable for nominal data (most common referral diagnosis in an OPD: 'low back pain').
  • A distribution may be unimodal, bimodal (two humps) or uniform; the mode's instability in small samples is its weakness, but for categorical reporting (most common affected side, most common age band) it is the only option.
  • Relation under skew: in a right (positive) skewed curve the order is always mode, then median, then mean; in a symmetric curve all three coincide.
  • A neat rule: the mean follows the tail, the median resists it, the mode ignores it.
  • Choice: symmetric roughly normal data (height, some strength scores in large samples) → mean with standard deviation; ordinal or skewed data (MRC grades, Berg Balance Scale, pain duration, cost of surgery) → median with interquartile range; nominal data (diagnosis, blood group, affected side) → only the mode.
  • Compute one tiny median live — 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 gives median 5 — and always end with the pairing rule; misreporting a skewed variable as mean plus SD, then running a t-test on it, is the commonest statistical sin in physiotherapy theses.

Right skew: mode, then median, then mean — the mean follows the tail, the median resists it, the mode ignores it.

Sources
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra K. Medical Biostatistics.
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
510 marks

Q5. What are the guiding considerations in the construction of a questionnaire? Explain the difference between collection of data through questionnaires and schedules.

Full answer →

Half 'how to build a questionnaire' and half 'compare questionnaire with schedule' — give the comparison as a table.

  • What earns marks: say what a questionnaire is, fix purpose and target population (1.5 marks) and give the construction steps (4 marks) · cover validity, reliability and pilot testing with numbers — Cronbach's alpha 0.7 or above (2 marks) · make the questionnaire-versus-schedule comparison a clear table (2 marks).
  • A questionnaire is a standardised, self-administered instrument that converts a construct (pain, function, quality of life) into answerable items.
  • Before writing a single question, fix three things: the purpose (screening? outcome measure? survey?), the target population (literate urban post-graduates differ from rural labourers), and the domains the construct contains.
  • For knee OA, decide in advance that you will capture pain, stiffness and physical function, so items map onto a framework rather than appearing ad hoc.
  • Each item should be short, single-barrelled and concrete.
  • Ban the classic faults: double-barrelled questions ('can you walk and climb stairs without pain?'), leading questions, technical jargon, negatives, and vague quantifiers ('often', 'sometimes').
  • Use closed questions with balanced response options; a Likert scale (ordered graded responses from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', sometimes with a neutral midpoint) is the workhorse for attitudes, and graded frequency scales (0 = never to 4 = always) for symptoms.
  • Sequence questions from easy to sensitive (demographics last), open questions early to warm up the respondent, and sensitive items (income, sexual function) late.
  • Add a title, a purpose statement, an instruction block, a thank-you, and keep the respondent's burden under about 15 minutes.
  • The construction staircase: 1. purpose and target population → 2. domains + item writing → 3. expert content validity check → 4. pilot (30) + reliability testing → 5. final version.
  • Content validity comes first: experts in knee OA review each item for relevance and clarity, deleting or rewording.
  • Then pilot on 30 or so respondents drawn from — but not identical with — the study population, checking that every item is understood as intended, that completion time is realistic, and that there are no floor or ceiling effects.
  • Reliability is quantified: internal consistency by Cronbach's alpha (a 0-to-1 index, conventionally acceptable at 0.7 or above) and test–retest stability by intraclass correlation or weighted kappa.
  • Translation into a regional language must follow the forward–back translation cycle, not a friend with a dictionary; a validated Tamil or Marathi version is itself publishable work.
  • Questionnaire — filled in by the respondent himself, in his own time: cheap to mass-administer, postal or online reach across districts, complete anonymity (so more honest answers on stigmatised topics); but literacy-dependent, prone to misinterpretation of items, and response rates often below half with nobody to clarify.
  • Schedule — the same proforma administered face-to-face by a trained interviewer who reads each question aloud and records the answer: it demands literacy of nobody, allows clarification, probing and observation, and achieves far higher response rates and completeness; it costs more, takes interviewer time, risks interviewer bias, and loses anonymity.
  • In an Indian OPD where literacy varies, the schedule is often the realistic option; the questionnaire suits educated, dispersed populations and large surveys.
  • Plan for mixed literacy: bilingual forms, interviewer-assisted mode in rural community surveys, and data-quality spot back-checks; preserve anonymity on sensitive topics, apply ICMR consent and confidentiality principles to survey data, and use an already validated Indian-language instrument rather than inventing one.

Construction staircase: purpose → domains → item writing → validity → pilot (n about 30) → final.

Sources
  • Hulley SB et al. Designing Clinical Research.
  • Indrayan A, Malhotra K. Medical Biostatistics.
  • WHO. International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (for domain frameworks).
610 marks

Q6. Describe in detail the influence of different types of exercises on various systems.

Full answer →

Open with the four exercise families, then say which family drives which change in each body system.

  • What earns marks: open with the four-family classification of exercise — 2 marks · give the cardiovascular and respiratory effects with their numbers — 2.5 marks · cover muscular and skeletal effects (2) and neural, endocrine and metabolic effects (2.5) · finish with application to prescription and safety (FITT) — 1 mark.
  • Four families cover almost everything we prescribe: aerobic (endurance), resistance (strength), flexibility, and neuromotor/balance.
  • Aerobic = rhythmic large-muscle work at moderate intensity (walking, cycling); resistance = muscle loading against high tension (weights, bands); flexibility = stretching to restore or maintain range; neuromotor/balance = coordination and proprioceptive retraining, agility, tai-chi.
  • Aerobic training remodels the heart at both ends: stroke volume rises (greater end-diastolic filling and eccentric hypertrophy) and resting heart rate falls (increased vagal tone), so cardiac output at any submaximal load drops — the trained man climbs the same stairs on a smaller heart rate.
  • Blood volume expands, capillary and mitochondrial density in muscle increase, and the trained muscle extracts more oxygen, so VO2 max (the maximum oxygen the body can consume per minute during exhaustive whole-body exercise) rises typically 15 to 25 percent over months.
  • Blood pressure falls about 5 to 10 mmHg in hypertensives, HDL rises, triglycerides fall, and insulin sensitivity improves — exercise is genuine pharmacology.
  • Resistance training produces smaller VO2 max gains but healthy eccentric cardiac adaptation and pressure-related strengthening; during a heavy lift the Valsalva response spikes systolic pressure transiently — a safety point worth a sentence.
  • In the lungs, chronic training spares resting lung volumes but improves endurance of the respiratory muscles and ventilatory efficiency; in COPD, specific inspiratory muscle training delays the ventilatory limit of exercise.
  • Muscular effects — resistance training works through neural then structural adaptation: improved motor unit recruitment, rate coding and synchronisation first (the early weeks of strength gain are largely neural), then myofibrillar hypertrophy with strengthening of fast-twitch fibres and increased tendon stiffness.
  • Aerobic training drives angiogenesis and mitochondrial biogenesis in slow-twitch fibres — fatigue resistance more than force; stretching produces viscoelastic and, over weeks, sarcomere-number changes with improved stretch tolerance.
  • Skeletal effects — bone follows Wolff's law: weight-bearing and impact loading raise osteoblastic activity, which is why walking, stair-climbing and progressive resistance are frontline management for osteoporosis, and why prolonged bed rest causes roughly 1 to 1.5 percent of bone mineral lost per month.
  • Collagen structures (tendon, ligament, cartilage) respond to cyclic loading with better alignment and glycosaminoglycan content — moderate compression feeds articular cartilage, so immobilisation, not movement, is the OA joint's enemy.
  • Neural effects — acute exercise increases sympathetic drive, and chronic training raises vagal tone while improving motor control, proprioception and reaction time; neuromotor training cuts falls in the elderly by about a quarter.
  • Exercise acutely raises brain-derived neurotrophic factor, serotonin and endorphins — the basis of exercise as an adjuvant in depression and anxiety.
  • Endocrine/metabolic effects — cortisol and growth hormone respond to intensity, catecholamines rise acutely, and repeated sessions raise insulin sensitivity for up to 48 hours via GLUT4 translocation; the Indian phenotype carries high metabolic risk at lower waist cutoffs (Misra et al. 2009).
  • Moderate aerobic work is predominantly fat-fuelled; high-intensity work switches to carbohydrate with lactate accumulation — substrate choice is intensity-dependent, not exercise-family-dependent.
  • Prescription payoff (ACSM/WHO framing): 150 minutes per week of moderate aerobic activity plus resistance exercise on two or more days plus flexibility and balance work in older adults; the FITT principle tailors these families to the pathology, and every system benefit named is also a monitoring point — safety is part of the mark.

Four families — aerobic, resistance, flexibility, neuromotor — then map each one onto the body systems.

Sources
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
  • Misra A et al. JAPI 2009 (Indian metabolic cutoffs).
710 marks

Q7. Explain the consideration of age and sex in exercise and training.

Full answer →

Answer in two parallel halves — age and sex — and anchor each half with one memorable number.

  • What earns marks: state the governing principle that age and sex modify reserve and risk — 1 mark · give children and adolescents (2.5) and older adults with sarcopenia, falls and safety (2.5) · cover sex differences — hormonal, morphological and female-athlete considerations (3) — and end with practical Indian prescription (1).
  • Governing principle: age and sex are not contraindications — they are modifiers of physiological reserve, response speed and risk profile.
  • Children are not small adults, older adults are not 'deconditioned young adults', and women are not 'smaller men' with a different hormonal calendar; the same principles (overload, specificity, progression) apply with different doses, expectations and safeguards.
  • Children have immature thermoregulation (large surface area, poor sweating economy) — hydrate and watch heat.
  • Anaerobic capacity is limited before puberty because glycolytic enzymes and muscle mass are undeveloped, so intensity should be play-based and submaximal.
  • Strength-training gains pre-puberty are real but predominantly neural — supervised, low-load, high-repetition programmes are safe, whereas maximal lifts and explosive power are discouraged until skeletal maturity because growth plates are vulnerable to shear.
  • Bone is most responsive in the pre- and early-pubertal years — this window is the bank account for lifelong bone health; games beat sets-and-reps for adherence.
  • Older adults: after roughly 30, muscle mass declines about 3 to 8 percent per decade (about 5 percent on average), accelerating after 60 — this is sarcopenia (the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and power driven by denervation, anabolic hormone decline, inactivity and inflammation).
  • Sarcopenia alone predicts falls, disability and hospitalisation; type II fibres are lost preferentially, so power fades before endurance; tendons stiffen, cartilage thins, balance reactions slow, and VO2 max falls 5 to 10 percent per decade.
  • The clinical translation: resistance training remains highly effective in the very old (strength gains even at 90 years), power and balance work must be built in deliberately to combat falls, and aerobic work targets function (walking to the market, stair-climbing).
  • Safety screens for older adults: cardiac risk, BP response (avoid breath-holding in hypertensives — exhale on effort), arthritic joints need warm-up and load progression, and polypharmacy — beta-blockers blunt the heart-rate response, so use RPE, not pulse, to dose intensity.
  • Sex differences — women have a smaller heart and stroke volume, so they reach a given submaximal oxygen uptake at a higher heart rate; haemoglobin is lower by about 12 percent, capping absolute VO2 max at roughly 70 percent of male values, yet the percentage training gains are identical.
  • Morphology: wider pelvis, greater Q-angle and genu valgum, more joint laxity — a biomechanical association with patellofemoral pain and ACL injury in cutting sports.
  • The female athlete triad — low energy availability (with or without disordered eating), menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density — must be screened in any athletic girl with a stress fracture or amenorrhoea; a missed triad can end a career in a hip fracture at 25.
  • Hormonal cycle: relaxin in pregnancy loosens pelvic ligaments (care in the third trimester with supine positioning and heavy loading), and post-menopausal oestrogen loss accelerates bone loss, making resistance and impact work non-negotiable then.
  • Men show larger absolute strength from greater muscle mass; both sexes gain strength at similar relative rates, and women hypertrophy without 'bulking' because of lower androgen levels — the commonest counselling point in an Indian gym or post-mastectomy fitness class.
  • Practical translation: screen before you load (cardiac risk with age, bone health and triad with sex), progress conservatively in the extremes of age, and prefer functional modes (walking, stairs, sit-to-stand) for older Indians.
  • Indian realities: women in many households need female trainers or home programmes, older adults may be vegetarian with lower protein intake (which worsens sarcopenia and merits dietitian referral), and school PE for children is often the only structured activity they will ever get.

Age 30 onward: 3 to 8 percent muscle lost per decade; female athlete triad = energy, menses, bone.

Sources
  • McArdle WD, Katch FI, Katch VL. Exercise Physiology: Nutrition, Energy, and Human Performance.
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques.
810 marks

Q8. Explain the electrical properties of muscle and nerve.

Full answer →

Give the electrical facts with exact numbers: resting potential, threshold, action potential, chronaxie and conduction speeds.

  • What earns marks: give the resting membrane potential and its ionic basis with the −70 mV value — 2.5 marks · describe the action potential and conduction in nerve and muscle — 2.5 marks · give the excitability parameters — rheobase, chronaxie and accommodation — with their exact values — 2.5 marks · contrast nerve and muscle and give the clinical application — 2.5 marks.
  • Both nerve and muscle are excitable tissues — they can turn a stimulus into an all-or-none electrical event; at rest the membrane keeps a resting membrane potential of roughly −70 mV (inside negative).
  • It is generated by the sodium–potassium pump exporting 3 sodium ions for every 2 potassium ions imported, and by the membrane being far more permeable to potassium, whose slow leak outward leaves fixed intracellular anions behind.
  • So the resting cell is a charged battery with an uneven ion distribution: potassium rich inside, sodium rich outside — the precondition for excitation.
  • When a stimulus depolarises the membrane to its threshold (about −55 mV), voltage-gated sodium channels snap open, sodium floods in and the inside spikes to roughly +30 mV (depolarisation); then sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels open, restoring and briefly overshooting the resting level (repolarisation with after-hyperpolarisation).
  • This spike is the action potential, all-or-none: sub-threshold stimuli produce nothing; threshold and above produce the full spike.
  • Conduction along the nerve is a regenerating wave — the depolarised patch opens adjacent channels; in myelinated fibres the event leaps node to node (saltatory conduction).
  • That is why a large myelinated A-alpha fibre conducts at up to about 100 m/s while a thin unmyelinated C fibre manages about 1 m/s — a difference that decides which fibre your electrical stimulation will reach first.
  • Muscle fibres similarly conduct along the sarcolemma to the T-tubules, where excitation–contraction coupling links the electrical event to calcium release and mechanical work.
  • In muscle, electrical activity also carries diagnostic meaning: needle EMG records motor unit potentials at rest (fibrillations and positive sharp waves in denervation), on minimal effort (fasciculations, recruitment pattern) and on maximal effort (complete versus reduced interference pattern).
  • Rheobase is the minimum current that excites the tissue with an infinitely long pulse.
  • Chronaxie is the minimum pulse duration required at twice rheobase strength — about 0.05 to 1 ms for nerve (which is why short-pulse currents like Russian or TENS waveform durations excite nerve so readily) and about 20 to 100 ms for chronically denervated muscle (demanding the long-duration triangular or exponential pulses of faradism).
  • Accommodation is the tissue's habituation to a slowly rising stimulus — nerve accommodates to slow ramps and may not fire at all, which is why exponentially rising currents selectively recruit denervated muscle while the intact nerve beside it accommodates and stays silent.
  • Refractory periods limit firing frequency (absolute roughly 0.5 to 2 ms), and the strength-duration curve built from threshold measurements across durations is the classical graph of these properties.
  • Nerve versus muscle: nerve is more excitable and fatigues at the synapse, while skeletal muscle is less excitable but virtually unfatigable electrically; nerve has a shorter chronaxie, higher conduction velocity, and all-or-none conduction over distance, while muscle's electrical event is coupled to mechanical output via calcium.
  • Clinical application: sensory-level TENS works because large-diameter A-beta fibres have the lowest threshold; NMES drives muscle through its intact nerve (short pulse) or directly in denervation (long pulse); nerve conduction studies time an action potential over a known distance to compute velocity and localise entrapment such as carpal tunnel.
  • The motor unit — one anterior horn cell, its axon, and all the muscle fibres it supplies — is the unit whose electrical signature the needle EMG records and whose loss defines denervation and reinnervation; safety follows the same physics: current frequency above roughly 10 kHz produces little stimulation, and alternating mains-frequency current is dangerous precisely because it is close to the most excitable frequency range of the heart.

Numbers to quote: −70 mV resting, −55 mV threshold, +30 mV peak; chronaxie 0.05 to 1 ms nerve vs 20 to 100 ms denervated.

Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques (electrotherapy sections).
  • WHO. International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (for functional framing of denervation).
910 marks

Q9. Evaluate the components of electrophysiological assessment devices.

Full answer →

The verb is 'evaluate' — for each block of the signal chain give a quality criterion and a number, then close with safety, calibration and validity.

  • What earns marks: say what electrophysiological assessment means and name the device families — 2 marks · evaluate the stimulator and electrodes with parameters and quality criteria — 3 marks · cover the amplifier, filters and signal processing with their numbers (CMRR 90+ dB, 50 Hz notch, bands) — 2.5 marks · cover display, recording and analysis and close with the safety-calibration-validity trio — 2.5 marks.
  • 'Electrophysiological assessment devices' are instruments that measure the electrical activity of excitable tissues — nerve conduction studies (NCS), needle electromyography (EMG), evoked potentials, and surface EMG systems used in physiotherapy for biofeedback and gait analysis.
  • To evaluate any such device, ask a fixed set of questions about each block in its signal chain: can it deliver a defined stimulus, can it pick up microvolt signals cleanly, can it separate signal from noise, and can it display, store and quantify the result — all without harming patient or operator.
  • The universal signal chain: stimulus → electrodes → amplifier → filters → display; evaluate each block against its purpose in turn.
  • The stimulator must deliver a controlled pulse with adjustable intensity, duration (typically 0.05 to 1 ms for nerve stimulation) and frequency.
  • Constant-current output is generally preferred because current is what excites tissue; its output must remain stable across skin impedance changes, and it needs an isolated output so no leakage current reaches the patient.
  • Electrodes translate electronics to biology: stimulating electrodes are usually surface discs or a hand-held bipolar stimulator, and the cathode is the active depolarising pole.
  • Recording electrodes for surface EMG are silver–silver chloride (Ag/AgCl), chosen for low polarisation and low noise, with impedance minimised by skin preparation (abrasion and alcohol swabbing — sweat and talc are the enemy in an Indian summer clinic).
  • The electrode–skin interface, gel quality and inter-electrode distance determine most of the artefact in a surface recording; electrode placement standardisation decides whether two therapists measure the same muscle.
  • The raw biological signal is tiny — sensory nerve action potentials are microvolts, needle EMG up to a few millivolts — riding on mains interference thousands of times larger.
  • The differential amplifier subtracts the signal common to both inputs (the noise) and amplifies the difference (the wanted signal); its quality is the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR), which should exceed about 90 dB in a good instrument.
  • The 50 Hz notch filter in India suppresses the mains hum that plagues every Indian EMG lab.
  • Band-pass filtering shapes the analysis window — roughly 10 Hz to 10 kHz for needle EMG and 20 to 500 Hz for surface EMG; too low a high-pass cut lets movement artefact through, too high removes meaningful low-frequency content.
  • Averaging — repeating the stimulus and averaging the sweeps — pulls a sensory potential out of noise, trading time for signal-to-noise ratio; modern devices add digital sampling, sweep controls and automated measures (latency, amplitude, area, conduction velocity).
  • The display must show latency markers adjustable to the take-off point, amplitude calibrations, and a gain and sweep range suited to the study — a sensory study at 10 µV per division, a motor study at 5 mV per division.
  • For a physiotherapy surface EMG unit, evaluate instead its biofeedback display (audio-visual), its ability to quantify activation as a percentage of a maximum voluntary contraction, its inter-session reliability and its simplicity of operation in a busy OPD.
  • Evaluation criteria to close with: electrical safety standards (isolation, leakage current within IEC limits, patient-applied parts type CF for cardiac-adjacent use), calibration with a signal simulator before use, measurement validity and reliability, usability (set-up time, portability), service support and cost — a device is only 'good' relative to the clinical question it must answer.

Signal chain: stimulator → electrodes → differential amplifier → filters → display; CMRR 90+ dB with a 50 Hz notch.

Sources
  • Guyton AC, Hall JE. Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine (for evaluation criteria framing).
  • ICMR. National Ethical Guidelines 2017 (device safety and human participant protection).
1010 marks

Q10. Why is entrepreneurship important in physiotherapy? Write in detail the challenges faced in physiotherapy practice.

Full answer →

Two halves: why entrepreneurship matters, then the challenges grouped under four headings with Indian examples and strategies.

  • What earns marks: explain the concept and relevance of entrepreneurship in physiotherapy — 3.5 marks · list the opportunities — clinic, services, products, education, digital — 2 marks · group the challenges under clean headings (professional, financial, operational, legal-ethical) with an Indian example each — 3 marks · close with strategies and the way forward for Indian practice — 1.5 marks.
  • Entrepreneurship is the capacity to identify a health need, organise resources, and take a measured risk to build a service that meets it.
  • In physiotherapy that means a physiotherapist who owns and runs a clinical practice or service, rather than only being employed in one.
  • Why it matters — employment supply: India produces far more MPT graduates each year than hospital and teaching posts can absorb, so private practice is not an alternative career but the default one.
  • Access: most physiotherapy need in India is chronic and community-based (low back pain, stroke rehabilitation, ageing-related disability), and only locally owned clinics and home-care services reach into tier-2 and tier-3 towns and villages.
  • Professional autonomy and quality: the person who owns the practice sets the standards; entrepreneurship is also how services evolve (specialisation, home care, corporate ergonomics, community programmes) — it multiplies employment and anchors evidence-based practice in the market, because a practice that delivers outcomes is the practice that survives.
  • Opportunities — the classic route is the independent OPD clinic, around which grows a full ecosystem: home-visit physiotherapy for post-stroke and post-operative elderly patients, on-site industrial physiotherapy and ergonomics consultancies for IT parks and factories, sports coverage for academies and district-level teams, fitness and fall-prevention programmes for old-age homes, corporate wellness contracts, and education ventures (CEU courses, clinical internships and skill training for assistants).
  • Product and digital opportunities — low-cost assistive devices, telerehabilitation follow-up, regional-language exercise apps — are expanding under initiatives such as Start-up India and Digital India, and health-insurance coverage of physiotherapy, though still partial, is widening the paying market.
  • SWOT of the practice itself: Strengths — clinical skill, low entry cost, direct patient trust, recurring chronic caseload.
  • Weaknesses — no business training, limited capital, one-person dependency; Opportunities — ageing population, NCDs, home care and telerehab, insurance slowly widening; Threats — quack practice, price undercutting, regulatory ambiguity.
  • Professional/market challenges: low public awareness of what physiotherapy is (patients arrive expecting 'massage' or a machine session) and direct, unqualified competition from informal 'maalis' and untrained operators in many states.
  • This is made worse by the absence of a robust central regulatory act and enforcement for the profession, and referral dependence on physicians limits autonomy in some settings.
  • Financial challenges: limited start-up capital for equipment and premises, banks hesitant to lend against a service business, delayed or absent insurance reimbursement (which keeps physiotherapy an out-of-pocket expense), and thin margins in smaller towns where patients cannot pay sustained package prices.
  • Operational challenges: the clinician must also be manager, marketer, accountant and HR department — skills nowhere in the MPT curriculum — and burnout in a one-person practice is real; staffing with trained assistants is hard when there is no formal cadre of physiotherapy assistants.
  • Legal and ethical challenges: consumer-protection litigation, taxation and clinical-establishment registrations, and the ethical line between marketing and solicitation; knowledge-related: keeping pace with updating clinical evidence while running a business demands deliberate CPD discipline.
  • Strategies and way forward: treat the practice as a business by design — a written business plan with SWOT analysis, costing and break-even; a narrow initial service focus (e.g. neuro-rehab or sports) to build a referral reputation; simple systems for billing, records and follow-up; and reinvestment in equipment and staff before lifestyle.
  • Collaborative models (associations with hospitals, orthopaedic chains and community health centres) reduce marketing cost; professional bodies and state councils should lobby for regulatory clarity; group practices share overheads; mentorship through IAP chapters and formal training in practice management convert entrepreneurs from accidental to deliberate.

SWOT — strengths and opportunities answer 'why important'; weaknesses and threats are the challenges.

Sources
  • World Physiotherapy Standards of Practice.
  • Herbert R et al. Practical Evidence-Based Physiotherapy.
  • Sackett DL et al. Evidence-Based Medicine.
  • Anderson LW, Krathwohl DR (eds). A Taxonomy for Learning, Teaching, and Assessing.
110 marks

Explain the structure and functions of the neuro-muscular system.

Full answer →

Describe how the nervous system and muscle are wired together, then link every structure to a function and to physiotherapy practice.

  • What earns marks: put structure first, then map each structure onto a function. Do not write pages on fibre chemistry and forget the loop back to movement · draw the labelled motor-unit diagram before you write. Make sure the phrases "size principle", "alpha–gamma co-activation" and "final common pathway" each appear once · end with clinical application — muscle testing, the Ashworth scale and resistance training.
  • Big idea: the neuro-muscular system is the nervous system joined to skeletal muscle. Sherrington called it the "final common pathway" — the one route through which every intention to move becomes force on bone.
  • Structural unit = the motor unit: one anterior horn cell, its axon, and every muscle fibre that axon supplies.
  • Motor unit size varies: fine-control muscles such as the extraocular muscles have a few fibres per unit; postural giants such as gastrocnemius may have over a thousand. The CNS trades precision for power by choosing unit size.
  • Muscle fibre types: type I (slow, oxidative, fatigue-resistant, postural), type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic) and type IIx (fast glycolytic, fatiguable).
  • Sensory receptors: the muscle spindle senses length and the rate of length change (intrafusal fibres; Ia and II afferents).
  • The Golgi tendon organ senses tension (Ib afferent).
  • Joint, skin and vestibular receptors feed the same loop.
  • The wiring is a closed loop: command travels down, information about length and tension travels back.
  • Function — force production and grading: force is raised by recruitment obeying Henneman's size principle (small units first) and by rate coding of discharge.
  • Function — posture and tone: alpha–gamma co-activation keeps the spindle sensitive while the muscle shortens, so the antigravity muscles hold a steady background tone.
  • Function — protection: the myotatic stretch reflex, the withdrawal (flexor) reflex and the crossed extensor reflex guard the limb within milliseconds.
  • Function — proprioception: the same afferents give the cortex its map of joint position — the raw material for movement re-education.
  • Clinical use: manual muscle testing interrogates the motor output; the Ashworth scale interrogates tone.
  • Progressive resistance training works because recruitment and rate coding respond to load within weeks, while fibre transformation takes months.
  • Lower motor neuron lesions waste the muscle and abolish reflexes; upper motor neuron lesions do the opposite — knowing the wiring tells them apart at the bedside.
  • One-line summary: the neuro-muscular system converts electrical intention into graded mechanical force and reports back; every assessment and treatment we give is read or written through that loop.

One command wire — many force generators.

Sources
  • Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — motor unit and reflex physiology.
  • Lehmkuhl and Smith, Brunnstrom's Clinical Kinesiology — muscle structure and fibre types.
  • Hislop, Montgomery, Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing — clinical application of motor output.
210 marks

How would you analyze, using the various anthropometry methods, to differentiate normal and abnormal curvature of the spine?

Full answer →

Show, step by step, how you measure spinal curvature with anthropometric tools and where you draw the line between normal and abnormal.

  • What earns marks: the question says "how would you analyse", so phrase everything as what YOU do next, in order: observe, plumb, flexicurve, scoliometer, refer. Method marks live in the sequence · quote the scoliometer threshold of about 5–7 degrees and the Cobb criterion of 10 degrees — this shows you know where field anthropology ends and radiology begins · state the reference values — examiners award the definition marks for numbers, not for adjectives.
  • Anchor the answer in "normal" first. In the coronal plane the spine is straight; a plumb line dropped from the external auditory meatus should pass through the shoulder, the greater trochanter, just behind the knee and the lateral malleolus.
  • Sagittal reference values: cervical lordosis about 20–40 degrees, thoracic kyphosis about 20–45 degrees and lumbar lordosis about 40–60 degrees.
  • Method 1 — observation with a plumb line and a marked grid: check shoulder level, scapular and iliac crest levels, skin folds at the waist and head tilt. Free, repeatable, and the backbone of any school-screening camp in India.
  • Method 2 — the flexible ruler (flexicurve): mould it along the spinous processes from C7 to the sacrum, trace it on paper, and measure the kyphosis angle or the lateral deviation index on the tracing.
  • Method 3 — the inclinometer and scoliometer: with the patient in Adam's forward-bend position, read the angle of trunk rotation at the apex. An angle of about 5–7 degrees or more is the accepted referral threshold.
  • Method 4 — goniometric inclinometry in standing for sagittal curves: two inclinometers over T12–L1 and the sacrum give a lumbar lordosis angle.
  • Method 5 — stature anthropometry: standing height, sitting height and arm span, which expose growth-related changes and track progression in adolescent deformity. A rib hump can be quantified with callipers or a level and ruler in centimetres.
  • Coronal plane interpretation: any measurable lateral curvature is suspicious. Scoliosis as a diagnosis is reserved radiologically for a Cobb angle of 10 degrees or more.
  • So the anthropometric job is to find the asymmetry that predicts it: trunk rotation above about 5–7 degrees, a positive plumb deviation, or unequal shoulder or iliac crest levels by more than about 1 cm.
  • Sagittal plane interpretation: kyphosis beyond about 45–50 degrees, a lumbar lordosis outside roughly 40–60 degrees, or a C7 plumb line falling well ahead of the sacrum signals abnormal curvature — for example postural kyphosis versus Scheuermann or a flat-back.
  • In a growing child, progressive loss of sitting-height gain flags a worsening curve.
  • Clinical algorithm: observe with plumb line and levels; if asymmetry is found, flexicurve and scoliometer quantify it.
  • If the scoliometer reads above the threshold or the curve progresses on serial measurement, refer for radiographic Cobb measurement, which remains the gold standard.
  • Conclusion: anthropometry gives you a cheap, radiation-free way to screen, document and follow up.

Observe, plumb, flexicurve, scoliometer, refer — method marks live in the sequence.

Sources
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment — posture and spinal alignment assessment.
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — spinal curvatures and loads.
  • Levangie and Norkin, Joint Structure and Function — vertebral column mechanics.
310 marks

Explain the concepts of energetics in chronic osteoarthritis of knee.

Full answer →

Define work, energy, efficiency and oxygen cost first, then apply them to why a chronic knee OA patient spends more energy to walk.

  • What earns marks: the phrase "concepts of energetics" signals that definitions of work, efficiency and oxygen cost must come before the disease talk. Write the four definitions, then apply them to OA in the same order · name the deconditioning spiral — it earns the analysis mark · state it as one chain — OA raises the cost of walking, and our job is to lower the cost, raise the capacity, or both.
  • Movement costs fuel. Mechanical work is the product of force moving through displacement.
  • Mechanical work divides into internal work (moving limb segments against each other) and external work (moving the body against gravity and ground).
  • Metabolic energy is the fuel bill, paid in oxygen — roughly five kilocalories per litre of oxygen consumed.
  • Efficiency links the two: mechanical work divided by metabolic cost. For level walking the body manages only about 25–30 percent.
  • The oxygen cost of walking is expressed per kilogram per metre walked.
  • What OA does — pain and effusion drive co-contraction: simultaneous quadriceps and hamstring activation that splints the joint.
  • Protection has a price: a stiff, co-contracted knee does not swing freely, so internal work rises.
  • Cartilage loss and varus alignment shift the ground reaction force medially, enlarging the knee adduction moment — so the same step demands more muscle force at the knee.
  • The patient responds with a slower, shorter-stride, more flexed-knee gait — comfortable per second, but costlier per metre.
  • The energetic optimum for walking is near the self-selected speed that OA now forces them to abandon.
  • Quadriceps weakness — partly arthrogenic inhibition — means each newton of support costs a larger fraction of the available muscle, so higher relative intensity for the same stroll to the bus stop.
  • The deconditioning spiral: walking feels expensive, so the patient walks less; walking less lowers cardiovascular fitness; lower fitness makes the same walk a higher percentage of maximum capacity — breathlessness, fatigue, then still less activity.
  • Measuring energetics: indirect calorimetry from expired gases gives oxygen cost per metre.
  • When a metabolic cart is unavailable — the usual Indian OPD reality — the physiological cost index approximates it: heart rate while walking minus resting heart rate, divided by walking speed.
  • Always document speed too, because cost per metre without speed is half a story.
  • Treatment read energetically: aerobic and strengthening training raise the efficiency of the engine; weight loss shrinks the load — every kilogram of body weight transmits roughly three to four kilograms of force through the knee during stairs and squats.
  • A cane in the opposite hand unloads the medial compartment and trims the adduction moment; pacing and energy conservation spread the budget across the day.

OA raises the cost of walking — lower the cost, raise the capacity, or both.

Sources
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — work, energy and efficiency of gait.
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — oxygen cost and training implications.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — functional training and energy conservation in chronic disease.
410 marks

Discuss the changes in gait in older adults.

Full answer →

Set the baseline mature gait, then list the spatiotemporal and joint-level changes in older adults and separate normal ageing from pathology.

  • What earns marks: quote double support 18 to 26 percent and speed 1.3 to 1.0 metres per second — the numbers that separate a pass from a distinction · say "shorter stride, not slower steps" — most candidates write the reverse · give the baseline mature gait first, then measure every change against it.
  • Baseline mature gait is free, reciprocal and economical: self-selected speed near 1.3 metres per second in healthy younger adults.
  • Stride length is about one and a half times leg length; stance phase is 60 percent and swing 40 percent of the cycle; smooth arm swing is opposite the legs.
  • Saunders' classic determinants of gait — pelvic rotation, pelvic tilt, knee flexion in stance, foot and ankle mechanisms, and lateral pelvic displacement — flatten the path of the centre of gravity and minimise the metabolic cost of transport.
  • Spatiotemporal change — older adults walk slower, nearer 1.0 metre per second by the seventies.
  • The slowing is driven mainly by shorter stride length rather than slower steps; cadence changes little or even rises slightly.
  • Stance phase lengthens, and double support time grows from about 18 percent of the cycle in youth toward 26 percent and beyond.
  • Both feet on the ground longer means the body spends less time balancing on one leg — the biomechanical signature of trading speed for safety.
  • Base of support widens slightly, and step-to-step variability increases — a better falls predictor than slow speed alone.
  • Joint-level change: the consistent finding is a reduced ankle plantarflexor burst at push-off (the A2 power peak), with compensation at the hip — a hip strategy gait.
  • Ankle range falls, knee flexion in stance may be slightly reduced, and arm swing diminishes.
  • The head-and-trunk path oscillates a little more, so the determinants that once smoothed the ride work less efficiently and oxygen cost per metre rises.
  • Fear of falling adds co-contraction of the shank muscles — the older person carries a stiffer, more guarded leg.
  • Sarcopenia of the plantarflexors removes the engine.
  • Normal ageing versus pathology: slowing alone is an adaptation, not a disease.
  • What should alarm the clinician: a speed below about 0.8 metres per second (the rough threshold for independent community ambulation), marked variability, a Parkinsonian or hemiplegic pattern, or a new widening of the base.
  • Assessment combines observation, the timed up-and-go, and 10-metre walk timing.
  • Treatment is strength and balance training, supervised challenge to the balance systems, and management of vision, vestibular function and foot-wear.
  • Message for the exam: the older gait is a negotiated compromise between mobility and stability, and our job is to keep it from tipping into falls.

More time on two feet = trading speed for safety.

Sources
  • Saunders, Inman and Eberhart, JBJS 1953 — the major determinants of gait.
  • Nordin and Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System — gait kinetics and kinematics.
  • O'Sullivan and Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation — gait assessment and balance training in older adults.

Explain the adaptation of different systems during an exercise program.

Full answer →

Go system by system — cardiovascular, respiratory, neuromuscular, metabolic, tissue — giving a time-scale or number for each, and separate acute response from chronic adaptation.

  • What earns marks: organise strictly system by system — cardiovascular, respiratory, neuromuscular, metabolic, tissue — with one number or time-scale in each. General essays about "exercise is good" score nothing · say overload, specificity and reversibility in your first paragraph · distinguish acute responses (one bout) from chronic adaptations (a program).
  • Frame it: every single session produces acute responses — heart rate climbs, ventilation rises, muscle burns substrate — which subside within hours.
  • A program is repeated, progressive doses; chronic adaptation is the body rebuilding itself between sessions in the direction of the imposed demand.
  • The overload principle decides the direction, specificity decides the system, and reversibility decides the fate of anyone who stops.
  • Cardiovascular: resting heart rate falls because stroke volume rises — a larger, more compliant ventricle filling better through an expanded plasma volume.
  • Submaximal heart rate for a given workload drops, and cardiac output at max rises.
  • Capillary density and mitochondrial density in trained muscle increase, and endothelial function improves with a modest fall in resting blood pressure.
  • Clinical link: the post-MI or post-arthroplasty patient who could barely walk the ward corridor ends up comfortably walking to the market within months.
  • Respiratory: the lungs change little structurally in healthy adults, but ventilation becomes more efficient — lower breathing frequency at a given workload, better coordination, and improved lactate buffering through adaptations in muscle.
  • Neuromuscular: this is the early superstar. In the first two to four weeks, strength rises out of proportion to any visible muscle growth because the nervous system learns — better recruitment, higher discharge rates, less antagonist co-activation, refined motor unit synchrony.
  • Clinical link: the frail elderly patient on the ward doubles her sit-to-stand score in week two, long before hypertrophy could account for it.
  • Metabolic: insulin sensitivity improves within days of a single session's effect on GLUT4 translocation and persists with training; oxidative enzymes multiply; fat oxidation becomes a larger share of the fuel mix.
  • Bone follows Wolff's law — it thickens where the load is imposed, which is why weight-bearing and resistance exercise, not just tablets, are part of osteoporosis management.
  • Tendon and ligament gain tensile strength slowly, weeks behind muscle — a timing mismatch the prescribing therapist must respect.
  • Sleep quality, mood and pain thresholds also shift — worth one line, because our musculoskeletal patients notice these first.
  • Conclusion as a prescription: adaptation is predictable and time-sequenced — neural in the first month, cardiovascular and metabolic across the first two months, structural tissue over months to a year.
  • A program that ignores this sequence — maximal loads to a tendon in week one — invites injury; a program that respects it turns a deconditioned MSK patient into a functioning one.

Neural first, cardiovascular and metabolic next, structural last.

Sources
  • ACSM's Resource Manual for Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription — systemic adaptations to training.
  • Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — cardiovascular and metabolic responses.
  • Kisner and Colby, Therapeutic Exercise — progression and tissue-healing timelines.
