Q6. Write in detail about extra corporeal shock wave therapy used for tissue healing.

Full answer →

What shockwave therapy is, how it heals tissue, and the practical dose and uses.

  • ESWT sends high-energy sound (pressure) waves into a tissue from outside the body.
  • It was first used to break kidney stones, then adapted for tendons and other musculoskeletal problems.
  • It works by controlled micro-trauma that restarts the body's own healing.
  • Mechanisms: it stimulates tendon cells, grows new blood vessels, boosts growth factors and collagen, and reduces harmful enzymes.
  • It also breaks up calcium deposits in calcific tendinitis and reduces pain.
  • Two types: focused (energy concentrated at a point) and radial (energy spread over an area).
  • Typical dose: 1,500-3,000 pulses per session, 0.1-0.5 mJ/mm2, 4-15 Hz, three to five weekly sessions.
  • Best evidence is for plantar fasciitis and mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy.
  • Weaker evidence for insertional Achilles and patellar tendinopathy.
  • It works best combined with exercise and load management, not alone.
  • Avoid over tumours, infection, open wounds, lungs, major nerves/vessels, and in pregnancy or children's growth plates.
  • Side-effects are usually minor: redness, bruising and short-term soreness.

Shock waves are controlled micro-trauma: they wake a sleeping tendon and make it heal itself.

Q7. Describe work related musculoskeletal disorders seen in rock drillers.

What problems rock drillers get from vibrating tools and how to prevent and manage them.

  • Rock drillers use heavy vibrating drills - the main risk is hand-arm vibration syndrome (HAVS).
  • HAVS has three parts: vascular, nerve (sensorineural) and musculoskeletal.
  • Vascular: 'white finger' - fingers go white and numb after cold, from spasm of blood vessels.
  • Nerve: numbness, tingling, poor feeling and clumsy hands.
  • Musculoskeletal: weak grip, carpal tunnel, tennis elbow, shoulder and back problems.
  • It is dose-related - more years of vibration means more severe disease.
  • Classic studies found white finger in about half of rock drillers, appearing after about 7-8 years.
  • Prevention first: use low-vibration tools, maintain them, limit and rotate exposure, wear anti-vibration and warm gloves.
  • Keep hands warm and stop smoking (smoking narrows blood vessels).
  • Health surveillance picks up early signs so workers can be redeployed.
  • Physiotherapy: strengthen forearm and shoulder muscles, nerve gliding, and sensory re-education.
  • Advise on grip technique, rest breaks and ergonomic redesign of the job.
  • Treat secondary problems (carpal tunnel, epicondylalgia, shoulder tendinopathy).
  • Once the blood-vessel damage is established it is largely permanent, so early reporting matters.

The drill shakes the hand, the hand shakes the nerve, and the nerve shakes the whole arm.

  • Work conditioning is a structured, work-oriented programme that rebuilds strength, endurance and task tolerance.
  • First assess pain, movement, strength and function, and analyse the actual job tasks (weights, heights, repetition).
  • Control pain and symptoms, then restore shoulder and thoracic movement.
  • Strengthen the cuff and scapular muscles, then progress to larger pushing, pulling and overhead patterns.
  • Add cardiovascular and endurance training (arm ergometry, circuits) to build shift tolerance.

  • Programme runs 3-5 days a week, 2-4 hours a day, for 4-8 weeks.
  • Include ergonomics, lifting technique and pacing education.
  • Address fear of movement with CBT or psychologically informed practice.
  • Return to work when strength is about 80% of the other side and simulated tasks are tolerated.
  • Use modified duties or graded hours as a bridge back to full work.

Q9. Describe the management and rehabilitation following total Patellectomy.

Full answer →

How to manage and rehabilitate a knee after the patella has been removed.

  • Total patellectomy means removing the whole kneecap - done only as a last resort.
  • The kneecap is the fulcrum of the thigh muscle, so removing it makes the leg weaker and slower to straighten.
  • The quadriceps loses up to 45-60% of its power and full straightening against gravity becomes hard.
  • Rehabilitation is phase-based and protects the repaired tendon while rebuilding strength.
  • Weeks 0-2: protect, control swelling with ice and compression, isometric quads and hamstrings, gentle knee bending.
  • Weeks 2-6: active movement, straight-leg raises, terminal knee extension, mini-squats, gait re-education.
  • Weeks 6-12: progressive strengthening of quadriceps and hamstrings, balance, cycling, stairs.
  • 3-6 months: advanced and job/sport-specific training.
  • Strengthen the hamstrings as well as the quadriceps - weak hamstrings predict a poor result.
  • Train eccentric control and full extension against gravity.
  • Restore a normal walking pattern to reduce effort and compensations.
  • Active bending often reaches only about 110 degrees - set realistic goals.
  • Measure progress with range of motion, isokinetic strength, extensor lag, LEFS and Knee Society Score.

No patella, no lever - so rebuild the brake and the spring with muscle.

Q10. Write in detail about management of complex regional pain syndrome following Colles fracture.

Full answer →

How CRPS develops after a wrist fracture and the full movement-based management plan.

  • CRPS is severe, persistent pain that is out of proportion to a wrist (Colles) fracture.
  • Type 1 has no nerve injury; type 2 does.
  • It causes pain, swelling, colour and temperature changes, sweating, stiffness and weakness in the hand.
  • It happens because the nervous system becomes over-protective and the brain's map of the hand is disrupted.
  • Diagnosis uses the Budapest criteria - symptoms and signs across several categories.
  • Treat early: explain the condition, keep the hand moving, treat the whole person.
  • Pain neuroscience education helps patients understand the pain is real but over-protective.
  • Graded motor imagery in order: left/right recognition, then imagined movement, then mirror therapy.
  • Mirror therapy uses the reflection of the good hand to retrain the brain.
  • Desensitisation and sensory re-education reduce sensitivity to touch.
  • Control swelling with elevation, compression and gentle movement.
  • Do graded wrist and hand movement, tendon gliding and functional tasks - avoid prolonged immobilisation.
  • Add aerobic exercise (also acts as pain-exposure therapy) and TENS for pain.
  • Add CBT for fear and distress, plus medical treatment (neuropathic drugs, blocks) and vitamin C after wrist fracture to prevent CRPS.

Keep the hand moving and the brain connected - or CRPS moves in.

Q1. Explain the scales of measurements with Physiotherapeutic examples for each scale.

Full answer →

Examiners want a clear definition of each of the four scales with a physiotherapy example and the statistic each allows.

  • Measurement means giving numbers or labels to a property using a fixed rule.
  • Stevens described four levels of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio.
  • Nominal = names only, no order. Example: diagnosis group, sex, gait-aid type. Use mode and chi-square.
  • Ordinal = ranked but gaps are unequal. Example: MMT grade 0–5, pain 0–10, Modified Ashworth Scale. Use median and non-parametric tests.
  • Interval = equal gaps but zero is arbitrary. Example: temperature in °C. Use mean and t-tests.
  • Ratio = equal gaps and a true zero. Example: grip strength in kg, gait speed, range of motion, body weight. All maths and tests allowed.
  • Higher scale = more information and more statistics allowed.
  • You must not average nominal data or run parametric tests on ordinal data — that is a common error.
  • Reliability (test–retest, inter-rater) decides whether a scale can be trusted.
  • MDC is the smallest change beyond measurement error; MCID is the smallest change that matters to the patient.
  • Rasch analysis can convert ordinal scores into interval measures.
  • Naming the right scale protects the validity of your statistics.

NOIR: Nominal names, Ordinal orders, Interval equal intervals, Ratio has a Real zero.

  • Related statements cover standards of practice, evidence-based practice and records management.

Q3. What is Research design and explain its different types, also explain the need and features of a good research design.

Full answer →

Examiners want a definition of research design, a classification of its types, and separate sections on why a design is needed and what makes one good.

  • Research design is the overall plan or blueprint for a study.
  • It links the research question to data collection and analysis.
  • Descriptive designs describe what exists; analytical designs test hypotheses.
  • Observational designs: cross-sectional, case–control, cohort, case series.
  • Experimental designs: randomised controlled trial, crossover, quasi-experimental, factorial, pragmatic.
  • Other designs: qualitative, mixed-methods, systematic review and meta-analysis.
  • Cross-sectional gives prevalence; cohort gives incidence; case–control is good for rare outcomes; RCT is best for testing treatment.
  • Need: turns the question into a testable plan, controls bias, saves resources, fixes sample size and analysis in advance, and supports ethics and reproducibility.
  • Features of a good design: clear objective, suitable design, representative sample with enough power, valid and reliable measures, control of confounders, ethical procedures, pre-planned analysis.
  • Common biases to control are selection bias, information bias, confounding and attrition bias.
  • Randomisation, blinding and matching are the main tools against bias.
  • A strong design makes the conclusions credible before any statistics are done.

Research design is the blueprint that answers the who, what, when, where and how of a study.

Q4. Explain objective of research. Describe various steps in testing of hypothesis.

Full answer →

Examiners want the objectives of research explained and the steps of hypothesis testing given in the correct sequence with the errors named.

  • An objective states what the study aims to achieve, in measurable terms.
  • Objectives may be exploratory, descriptive, explanatory or predictive.
  • Broader purposes of research: verify knowledge, build theory, solve practical problems, support evidence-based practice.
  • A hypothesis is a tentative, testable statement about the relationship between variables.
  • The null hypothesis says there is no difference or association; the alternative says there is.
  • Steps in hypothesis testing: state the hypotheses; set the significance level (usually alpha = 0.05); choose the correct statistical test; determine the critical region; compute the test statistic and p-value; compare and decide; interpret clinically.
  • If p is less than or equal to alpha, reject the null hypothesis; if not, fail to reject it.
  • A Type I error is a false positive (probability alpha); a Type II error is a false negative (probability beta).
  • Power is 1 minus beta and is usually set at 80% or more.
  • The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
  • Always report effect size and confidence intervals, not just p-values.
  • Choose the test by data type and design — t-test, ANOVA, chi-square or non-parametric equivalents.

Hypothesis testing in six steps: state the hypotheses, set alpha, choose the test, compute, compare, conclude.

Q5. Explain in detail Chi-Square test. Add a note on its significance in statistics.

Full answer →

Examiners want the formula, the steps, the assumptions and a worked example, plus a note on why the chi-square test matters in statistics.

  • Chi-square tests whether observed counts differ from expected counts.
  • It is used for categorical (nominal) data.
  • Formula: chi-square = sum of (Observed minus Expected) squared, divided by Expected.
  • Expected cell value = (row total times column total) divided by grand total.
  • Degrees of freedom = (rows minus 1) times (columns minus 1); a 2x2 table has df = 1.
  • Critical value at df = 1 and alpha = 0.05 is 3.84.
  • Steps: state hypotheses, set alpha, build the table, find expected values, compute chi-square, find df and critical value, compare and conclude.
  • If the calculated chi-square is greater than the critical value, reject the null hypothesis.
  • Assumptions: frequency data, independent observations, mutually exclusive categories, adequate expected counts.
  • Use Fisher's exact test for small samples and Yates' correction for 2x2 tables.
  • It shows whether an association exists but not its strength or direction — report Cramer's V or odds ratio too.
  • Significance: it is the foundation of categorical data analysis, used in genetics, surveys and epidemiology.

Chi-square compares Observed with Expected counts — the bigger the gap, the bigger the chi-square.

Q6. Compare and contrast the factors influencing the exercises for a 15 year old male and 50 year old male.

Full answer →

Examiners want a clear side-by-side comparison of the physiological, anatomical, psychological and social factors at the two ages, with the exercise implications for each.

  • Age strongly changes how the body responds to exercise.
  • At 15 the male is still growing; growth plates are open and hormones are rising.
  • At 50 growth is complete, muscle mass is slowly declining (sarcopenia) and bones are beginning to lose density.
  • The 15-year-old adapts fast and recovers quickly but is prone to growth-plate overuse injuries like Osgood–Schlatter.
  • The 50-year-old recovers more slowly and has higher risks of tendinopathy, osteoarthritis and cardiac events.
  • The 15-year-old needs supervised technique, bodyweight and light resistance training, plus weight-bearing activity to build peak bone mass.
  • The 50-year-old needs progressive resistance training to preserve muscle, aerobic work for the heart and balance work to prevent falls.
  • Both follow the FITT–VP framework and individualisation.
  • WHO 2020: adolescents need about 60 minutes a day of activity; adults need 150–300 minutes a week plus strengthening twice a week.
  • Screen the 50-year-old for cardiovascular and metabolic risk before vigorous exercise.
  • The adolescent must be protected from growth-plate overuse; the adult from degenerative and cardiac risk.
  • Supervision, progression and adherence support matter at both ages.

At 15 the body is still building (growth plates open); at 50 it is defending (sarcopenia, stiffness, slower recovery).

Q7. Discuss in detail Anaerobic and Aerobic energy metabolism.

Full answer →

Examiners want the three energy systems described clearly, a comparison table, and how they integrate with exercise intensity, plus a modern note on lactate.

  • All muscle work uses ATP as the energy currency.
  • Muscle stores very little ATP, so it must be remade constantly.
  • Three systems remake ATP: the phosphagen (ATP–PCr) system, anaerobic glycolysis, and aerobic oxidation.
  • Phosphagen system: no oxygen, fastest, lasts about 0–10 seconds, used for sprint starts and maximal lifts.
  • Anaerobic glycolysis: no oxygen, fast, lasts about 10 seconds to 2 minutes, makes little ATP (2–3 per glucose) and produces lactate.
  • Aerobic metabolism: needs oxygen, slow to start but makes about 30–32 ATP per glucose and lasts minutes to hours.
  • All three work together; which one dominates depends on exercise intensity and duration.
  • The lactate threshold marks the shift from aerobic to greater anaerobic reliance.
  • Lactate is now known to be a fuel and signalling molecule, not just a waste product — the lactate shuttle.
  • Aerobic training improves mitochondria, capillaries and VO2max; anaerobic training improves power and buffering.
  • Exercise prescription should match the energy system the patient needs to improve.
  • Crossover concept: as intensity rises, the body shifts from fat to carbohydrate use.

Three systems, one currency: ATP-PCr for seconds, glycolysis for a minute, oxidative phosphorylation for the long haul.

  • McArdle WD, et al. Exercise Physiology. 9th ed. 2019.
  • Hargreaves M, Spriet LL. Skeletal muscle energy metabolism during exercise. Nat Metab. 2020;2:817–828.

Q8. Describe electrical stimulation and its effect on various systems.

Full answer →

Examiners want a definition, the common types, the parameters, and a clear account of the effects on each body system, plus cautions.

  • Electrical stimulation uses controlled current to produce therapeutic effects.
  • It works because nerve and muscle membranes are electrically excitable.
  • A pulse depolarises the membrane; reaching threshold fires an action potential.
  • Types include NMES, FES, TENS, interferential therapy, high-voltage pulsed galvanic stimulation and iontophoresis.
  • Key parameters: waveform, pulse duration, frequency, intensity, duty cycle and treatment time.
  • Neuromuscular effect: produces contraction, strengthens muscle and helps re-educate movement.
  • Pain effect: activates large afferents to close the pain gate and releases natural opioids.
  • Circulatory effect: improves blood flow, venous return and reduces oedema.
  • Musculoskeletal effect: preserves muscle mass and supports tendon and bone healing.
  • Skin and wound effect: promotes healing and reduces oedema.
  • Central effect: afferent input can promote cortical plasticity after stroke or spinal cord injury.
  • Cautions: avoid over the heart, pacemakers, pregnancy, bleeding areas and where sensation is impaired.

Electrical stimulation drives nerves with current — depolarising motor axons to contract muscle and sensory axons to gate pain.

Q9. Write note on Muscle Plasticity in response to electrical stimulation.

Full answer →

Examiners want a definition of muscle plasticity, the neural, muscular, metabolic and functional adaptations to electrical stimulation, and a comparison with voluntary training.

  • Muscle plasticity is the muscle's ability to adapt its structure and function to activity, load or neural input.
  • Electrical stimulation provides an artificial, non-voluntary activation of muscle.
  • Electrically evoked contractions recruit motor units non-selectively and synchronously, causing rapid fatigue.
  • Neural adaptations: increased cortical and spinal excitability, BDNF upregulation and axonal sprouting.
  • Muscular adaptations: increased protein synthesis, hypertrophy, greater cross-sectional area and changes in muscle architecture.
  • Fibre-type changes occur, with increased type II fibre size in ageing muscle.
  • Metabolic adaptations: more oxidative enzymes, more mitochondria and better capillarisation.
  • Functional adaptations: gains in strength, power, endurance and preserved muscle mass.
  • It is useful when voluntary contraction is limited by pain, immobilisation or nerve injury.
  • Its effect depends on stimulation parameters, duration and the state of the nerve and muscle.
  • Effects are enhanced when combined with voluntary effort, imagery or blood-flow restriction.
  • Used after surgery, in stroke and spinal cord injury, and to counter sarcopenia.

Plasticity means the muscle rebuilds itself to match the demand — ES is an artificial demand that still remodels muscle and nerve.

  • A competency combines knowledge, skills and attitudes needed for real practice.
  • CBE is built on domains of competence, competencies, milestones and Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs).
  • It uses constructive alignment — outcomes, teaching and assessment matched together.
  • Teaching is learner-centred and assessment is continuous, formative and workplace-based.
  • Progression is by competence, not by time served.
  • Domains include practice, professionalism, communication, learning and development, management and research.
  • Traditional education is teacher-centred, content-driven and assessed by summative exams.
  • Traditional education often has a theory-practice gap; CBE is built around real practice tasks.
  • In India, the NCAHP Act, 2021 and the National Physiotherapy Curriculum Handbook have adopted a competency-based approach.
  • Challenges include faculty training, valid assessment tools, clinical placement quality and resource intensity.
  • Benefits include better alignment to practice, clearer expectations, accountability and patient safety.

Traditional education asks what was taught; competency-based education asks what the learner can actually do — and only then advances them.

Sources
  • WHO. Rehabilitation Competency Framework. 2020.
  • NCAHP. National Physiotherapy Curriculum Handbook. 2023.
  • Fitzpatrick JA, et al. Fundamentals of competency-based education in physical therapy. J Phys Ther Educ. 2024;38(2):1.
  • Frank JR, et al. Competency-based medical education: theory to practice. Med Teach. 2010;32:638–645.

Q1. Describe the effects of strength training on the neuromuscular system.

Full answer →

Name the neural and muscular changes that strength training produces, and separate early neural gains from later muscle growth.

  • Strength training makes the nervous system work better first, then the muscle gets bigger.
  • The brain sends stronger signals to the muscle (more voluntary drive).
  • More motor units switch on, and they switch on at a lower threshold.
  • Each motor unit fires faster (higher discharge rate).
  • Firing of motor units becomes better synchronised.
  • Inhibition in the motor cortex decreases, so output increases.
  • Muscles co-contract less, so movement is more efficient.
  • Later, muscle fibres thicken (hypertrophy) and cross-sectional area grows.
  • Fast fibres shift from type IIx to type IIa.
  • Pennation angle and fascicle length increase.
  • Tendons get stiffer and store more elastic energy.
  • Result: more strength and power, better balance and joint stability.
  • Bone also gets stronger, reducing injury risk.

Train the nerve first, the muscle later — early strength is a learned skill.

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.
  • Folland & Williams, Sports Med 2007 (adaptations to strength training).
  • Siddique et al., Sports Med 2020 (sites of neural adaptation).

Q2. Describe the changes seen in the neuromuscular system following prolonged bed rest due to spinal fracture.

Full answer →

List the muscle, motor-unit, neuromuscular-junction and sensorimotor changes after prolonged bed rest, and note the rehabilitation implication.

  • Bed rest after a spinal fracture unloads the body and switches off muscle activity.
  • Muscles shrink (atrophy), especially antigravity and back muscles.
  • Strength falls even faster than muscle size.
  • Type II (fast) fibres are lost most, so power drops.
  • Motor units fire more slowly and their potentials change.
  • Voluntary activation falls — the brain cannot fully switch the muscle on.
  • The neuromuscular junction becomes unstable (jitter, agrin fragment rises).
  • Proprioception and balance are impaired.
  • Joints can stiffen into contracture.
  • Bone density falls and the heart and circulation decondition.
  • Gait becomes slow and unsteady, with high fall risk.
  • Recovery needs early loading, electrical stimulation and task practice.

Disuse costs strength faster than it costs muscle — the nervous system switches off first.

Sources
  • Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology.
  • Sarto et al., J Physiol 2025 (21 days bed rest and motor units).
  • Kortebein et al., JAMA 2007 (10 days bed rest in older adults).

Q3. Elaborate the Kinetics & Kinematics of the wrist joint following carpal tunnel syndrome.

Full answer →

Give the kinematic (motion) and kinetic (pressure/force) changes in the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome.

  • The carpal tunnel is a narrow space holding the median nerve and tendons.
  • Kinematics = how things move; kinetics = forces and pressure.
  • Normally the nerve and tendons glide smoothly.
  • In CTS the nerve glides less (reduced longitudinal mobility).
  • The tendon sheath becomes stiff, so tendons glide poorly.
  • Friction between tendon and sheath (shear strain) increases.
  • Pressure inside the tunnel is raised, worst at wrist flexion and extension.
  • The nerve becomes flattened and enlarged on ultrasound.
  • High pressure reduces blood flow to the nerve.
  • Symptoms are worst with gripping and end-range postures.
  • Keeping the wrist neutral and doing gliding exercises helps.
  • Radioulnar compression can open the tunnel and restore glide.

The carpal tunnel is a crowded room — bend the wrist and the door gets tighter.

Sources
  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.
  • Festen-Schrier & Amadio, J Biomech 2023 (carpal tunnel mechanics).

Q4. Describe various methods to improve efficiency of movement following soft tissue injury.

Full answer →

List practical methods that restore efficient movement after soft tissue injury, across mobility, strength, control, balance and function.

  • Soft tissue injury makes movement inefficient and tiring.
  • First restore range of motion: stretching and mobilisation.
  • Reduce scar stiffness with soft-tissue and scar mobilisation.
  • Rebuild strength, especially with eccentric (lengthening) exercise.
  • Use blood-flow-restriction training if heavy loads are not tolerated.
  • Re-train motor control so the right muscles work at the right time.
  • Use biofeedback and mirror therapy to correct movement.
  • Retrain muscle synergies and reduce compensatory patterns.
  • Restore proprioception and balance (static to dynamic).
  • Re-educate gait and then sport- or work-specific tasks.
  • Manage load and progress activity gradually to avoid re-injury.
  • Use pain education and taping to allow pain-free practice.

Get the tissue moving, get it strong, get the brain coordinating it again.

  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise.

Q5. Describe the biomechanical changes seen in mobility of lower limbs in people with tendo-Achilles tightness.

Full answer →

Describe how reduced ankle dorsiflexion from a tight Achilles changes mechanics at the ankle, knee, hip and pelvis during walking.

  • A tight Achilles means the ankle cannot bend up (reduced dorsiflexion).
  • The foot compensates by rolling in (pronation).
  • The heel lifts early during walking.
  • Push-off power at the ankle is reduced.
  • The knee does not straighten fully at midstance.
  • Knee and ankle forces (moments) increase.
  • The hip flexes more and extends less.
  • The pelvis tilts forward (anterior tilt).
  • The lower back arches more (increased lordosis).
  • Step and stride length get shorter and walking slows.
  • Shock absorption is poorer and energy cost rises.
  • Stretching the calf can improve both ankle and upper mechanics.

A tight Achilles pulls the whole chain — the ankle pays, the knee, hip and back borrow.

  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.

Q6. Describe how soft tissue injuries affect movements.

Full answer →

Explain the chain from tissue injury to altered movement: pain and inhibition, loss of range and force, changed control and compensation.

  • Soft tissue injury changes movement in several linked ways.
  • Pain and swelling limit movement straight away.
  • Pain inhibits muscles, so they cannot switch on fully (weakness).
  • Scar tissue makes the injured tissue stiffer and less stretchy.
  • This reduces range of motion and can cause contracture.
  • Proprioception (position sense) is impaired.
  • Muscle activation timing and order change.
  • The person co-contracts muscles protectively.
  • They compensate by shifting load to other joints.
  • This changes joint angles and forces elsewhere.
  • Movement becomes less efficient and costs more energy.
  • Treatment: control pain, restore range, rebuild strength, retrain control.

Injury hurts, hurts inhibit, inhibition changes how you move — and that change outlasts the pain.

Q7. Describe the mechanics of the shoulder following Deltoid injury.

Full answer →

Explain the deltoid's role, the force couples, and what happens mechanically when the deltoid is injured.

  • The deltoid is the shoulder's main lifting (abduction) muscle.
  • It works with the rotator cuff in force couples.
  • Deltoid plus supraspinatus push the ball into the socket during abduction.
  • The cuff also stops the ball sliding upwards.
  • Scapular rhythm keeps the socket moving with the arm.
  • If the deltoid is torn or paralysed, abduction becomes weak.
  • The force couple is lost, so the ball drifts upward.
  • Joint reaction forces change, stressing the socket.
  • The shoulder blade compensates with a shrug.
  • If the nerve is damaged, there is also numbness.
  • Treatment re-trains deltoid and cuff together.
  • The mover and the stabiliser must work as a team.

Deltoid moves the arm, cuff steers the head — injure the mover and the head drifts up.

  • Nordin & Frankel, Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System.

Q8. Describe various changes in lower cross syndrome.

Full answer →

State the tight and weak muscles in lower cross syndrome and the postural and lumbopelvic changes they cause.

  • Lower cross syndrome is a pattern of tight and weak muscles around the hips and lower back.
  • Tight: hip flexors (front of hip).
  • Tight: lower-back (lumbar extensor) muscles.
  • Weak: tummy (abdominal) muscles.
  • Weak: buttock (gluteal) muscles.
  • This tilts the pelvis forward (anterior pelvic tilt).
  • The lower back arches more (hyperlordosis).
  • The chest and upper back may round to compensate.
  • Lumbopelvic rhythm changes, loading the discs and facets.
  • Gluteal activation is delayed; hamstrings may substitute.
  • Core stability and endurance are reduced.
  • Treatment: stretch tight muscles, strengthen weak ones, then integrate.

Crossed at the hips: front hip flexors tight with weak tummy, back extensors tight with weak bottom.

Q9. A 30 year old man comes with a history of pelvic fracture following which he is unable to stabilize his right knee. Describe the pathological gait.

Full answer →

Give a systematic analysis of the gait: mechanisms, spatiotemporal, kinematic, kinetic findings and management.

  • A pelvic fracture can weaken the hip abductors and the quadriceps.
  • Weak hip abductors cause the opposite hip to drop (Trendelenburg).
  • The trunk may lurch over the standing leg (Duchenne limp).
  • Weak quadriceps make the knee give way or over-flex.
  • Walking speed, step length and cadence all reduce.
  • Support time on the affected leg is shorter.
  • The hip abducts and extends less on that side.
  • Hip abduction and extension forces (moments) are lower.
  • Pelvic drop increases loading on the inner (medial) knee.
  • Shock absorption is poor and energy cost is high.
  • Treatment: strengthen abductors and quadriceps, retrain gait and balance.
  • A cane in the opposite hand reduces the load on the hip.

Weak abductors drop the opposite hip; weak quads make the knee give way — two faults, one limp.

Q10. Write in detail about the various methods of assessing subjects.

Full answer →

Outline the main categories of assessment methods and the measurement properties a good method must have.

  • Assessment identifies the problem, guides treatment and measures progress.
  • Start with the history and pain scales.
  • Observe posture, gait, swelling and alignment.
  • Palpate for tenderness, warmth and tone.
  • Measure range of motion with a goniometer or inclinometer.
  • Test muscle strength with manual testing or a dynamometer.
  • Test nerves: sensation, power, reflexes, and EMG if needed.
  • Test proprioception and joint position sense.
  • Analyse gait and balance (observation, sensors, Timed Up and Go).
  • Use outcome questionnaires (DASH, LEFS, ODI).
  • Use special tests and imaging when indicated.
  • A good method must be reliable, valid and responsive.

Assess the person, not just the joint — impairment, activity and participation.

Q1. Describe the role of investigations in assessment.

Full answer →

Examiners want you to say what investigations are, the main types, and exactly what they add to physiotherapy assessment — and the caution that they never replace clinical examination.

  • Investigations = lab tests, imaging and electrical tests ordered to support a diagnosis.
  • They are the third pillar of assessment, after history and physical examination.
  • Main job: confirm or rule out the working diagnosis.
  • Screen for red flags: fracture, infection, cancer, inflammatory disease, cauda equina.
  • Grade or stage severity (e.g. fracture type, sacroiliitis grade).
  • Guide and monitor treatment (e.g. weight-bearing after fracture).
  • Help prognosis and provide medico-legal documentation.
  • Types: blood tests; X-ray; CT; MRI; ultrasound; bone scan; EMG/nerve conduction; biopsy/arthroscopy.
  • Many abnormal findings occur in people with no pain, so the report must fit the clinical picture.
  • Order a test only if the result will change your management (appropriateness).
  • Normal tissue has a known appearance and normal blood ranges, which makes abnormality recognisable.
  • Physiotherapists must know when to request imaging, how to read reports, and when to refer.

Memory hook: History tells the story, examination writes the chapter, investigations only confirm the plot.

Q2. Describe screening of the wrist following Colles fracture.

Full answer →

Examiners want a step-by-step screening sequence that hunts for the classic complications after a Colles fracture, with named special tests and outcome measures.

  • A Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture with the fragment displaced backwards (dorsal).
  • Common after a fall on the outstretched hand in older, osteoporotic patients.
  • Screening looks for the complications, not just the healed bone.
  • Key complications: median nerve compression (carpal tunnel), thumb extensor tendon rupture, complex regional pain syndrome, malunion, wrist instability.
  • Step 1 – History: mechanism, hand dominance, numbness, night pain, stiffness.
  • Step 2 – Observation: swelling, deformity, scar, colour/temperature changes.
  • Step 3 – Palpation: distal radius, carpal tunnel, snuffbox, fovea.
  • Step 4 – ROM: wrist flexion/extension, deviation, pronation/supination vs other side.
  • Step 5 – Strength: grip and pinch; resisted thumb extension.
  • Step 6 – Nerve screen: Tinel and Phalen tests for median nerve.
  • Step 7 – Special tests: Watson (scapholunate), fovea (TFCC), piano-key (DRUJ).
  • Step 8 – Function and outcome measures: PRWE, QuickDASH, grip fraction.
  • Step 9 – X-ray: radial inclination, radial height, volar tilt, ulnar variance.

Memory hook: After a Colles check the Nerve, Tendon, Deformity and Function — N-T-D-F.

Q3. Describe screening of the lower back following lumbar canal stenosis at L2-L3 level.

Full answer →

Examiners want the neurogenic claudication story, the L2-L3 neurological findings, the tests that separate it from vascular claudication, and the red flags.

  • Lumbar canal stenosis = narrowing of the spinal canal that squashes the cauda equina and nerve roots.
  • Classic symptom: neurogenic claudication — leg pain on walking/standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward.
  • L2-L3 affects the L2 and L3 roots.
  • L2/L3 findings: anterior and medial thigh pain/numbness, weak hip flexion and knee extension, reduced knee jerk.
  • History clues: age over 60, shopping-cart sign, relief on sitting, normal foot pulses.
  • Provocation: sustained lumbar extension brings on symptoms; flexion relieves them.
  • Walking test upright vs stooped, or walking vs cycling, separates neurogenic from vascular causes.
  • Exclude vascular claudication: check pedal pulses and ankle-brachial index.
  • Neurological exam: dermatomes, myotomes (hip flexion L2, knee extension L3/L4), knee reflex, femoral nerve stretch test.
  • Outcome measures: Oswestry Disability Index, Zurich Claudication Questionnaire, walking tests.
  • Imaging: MRI is the investigation of choice.
  • Red flags: saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel problems, rapidly worsening weakness — refer urgently (cauda equina).

Memory hook: Stenosis loves to walk and stand, hates to sit and stoop — extension provokes, flexion relieves.

Q4. Challenges faced by Physiotherapists in autonomous practice.

Full answer →

Examiners want you to define autonomous/direct-access practice and then list the legal, financial, clinical, educational and interprofessional challenges clearly.

  • Autonomous practice = examining, diagnosing, treating and discharging without needing a doctor's approval each step.
  • Direct access/self-referral is its fullest form.
  • Benefits: better access, faster care, lower cost, higher professional standing.
  • Challenge 1 – Legal: in many places (including much of India) direct access is not permitted and scope laws still tie physiotherapy to medicine.
  • Challenge 2 – Reimbursement: insurers may not pay, or pay less, for self-referred care.
  • Challenge 3 – Liability: missed diagnoses (fracture, infection, cancer) become the physiotherapist's responsibility.
  • Challenge 4 – Competency: older graduates may lack diagnostic and red-flag skills.
  • Challenge 5 – Gatekeeping: deciding what is in scope and when to refer.
  • Challenge 6 – Interprofessional resistance from some doctors.
  • Challenge 7 – Public awareness: patients may not know they can come directly.
  • Challenge 8 – Evidence-based practice and avoiding over-treatment.
  • Challenge 9 – Documentation, audit and lifelong learning.
  • Solutions: clear laws, uniform insurance rules, postgraduate training, teamwork and public education.

Memory hook: Autonomy means you own the decision — and the L-E-G-A-L load: Legal, Ethical, Gatekeeping, Accountability, Liability.

Q5. Describe the various special tests for screening the neck.

Full answer →

Examiners want the special tests grouped by what they screen for, each with position, force and the positive sign.

  • Nerve-root (radiculopathy) tests: Spurling (compression), distraction, shoulder abduction relief, Valsalva.
  • Spurling: neck bent sideways and back toward the painful side with downward pressure; positive if arm pain is reproduced.
  • Distraction: gentle pull upward; positive if arm pain eases.
  • Upper limb neurodynamic tests (ULNT 1, 2a, 2b, 3): arm positions that load the nerve; positive if familiar symptoms return and change with neck position.
  • Myelopathy tests: Hoffmann, Babinski, clonus, Lhermitte sign.
  • Vascular tests: Hautant, De Kleyn, sustained rotation-extension — positive if dizziness, nystagmus or nausea.
  • Instability tests: Sharp-Purser and alar ligament tests for upper-cervical instability.
  • Facet/joint tests: cervical flexion-rotation test, rotation-lateral flexion test, quadrant test.
  • Muscle control: craniocervical flexion test.
  • No single test is perfect — use clusters (e.g. 3 or more positive ULNTs suggest radiculopathy).
  • Myelopathy or vascular signs = urgent medical referral; always screen the vertebral artery before manipulation.

Memory hook: Screen the neck for the 4 M-V-F-I — Myelopathy, Vascular, Facet and nerve-root (plus Instability).

Q6. Write in detail about the various investigations used for ankylosing spondylitis.

Full answer →

Examiners want blood tests, imaging and clinical scoring grouped clearly, with MRI highlighted as the key early test.

  • Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease starting at the sacroiliac joints and entheses.
  • Blood tests: HLA-B27 (positive in ~90%), ESR and CRP (may be raised), RF and anti-CCP usually negative.
  • Plain X-ray of the sacroiliac joints: first-line; graded 0–4 (modified New York criteria).
  • X-ray of the spine: squaring of vertebrae, syndesmophytes, bamboo spine.
  • MRI of the sacroiliac joints: best for early disease; shows bone-marrow oedema (ASAS-positive MRI).
  • CT: for detailed structural change; ultrasound: for peripheral enthesitis.
  • Clinical measures: BASDAI (activity), BASFI (function), BASMI (mobility), ASDAS (combined score).
  • ASAS criteria combine inflammatory back pain with an imaging arm or a clinical (HLA-B27) arm.
  • MRI oedema can occur in healthy people, so criteria are for classification, not diagnosis.
  • Rule out mechanical back pain and other spondyloarthritides.

Memory hook: Ankylosing spondylitis — Blood, X-ray, MRI, Measures (B-X-M-M).

Q7. Write in detail about the postoperative management following fracture of the tibial plateau.

Full answer →

Examiners want staged rehabilitation — protection, early motion, weight-bearing progression, strengthening — with the weight-bearing timetable and complications.

  • Tibial plateau fracture is an intra-articular break of the top of the shin bone, usually fixed with plates and screws.
  • Goal: protect the fixation while preventing stiffness, wasting and clots.
  • Phase 1 (weeks 0–2): pain and swelling control, ankle pumps, isometric quadriceps/hamstrings, brace, non- or toe-touch weight-bearing.
  • Phase 2 (weeks 2–6): regain knee range of motion, continue strengthening; immobilisation gives no benefit.
  • Phase 3 (weeks 6–12): progress weight-bearing — partial around 6–8 weeks, full around 9–12 weeks (later for complex fractures); gait and balance training.
  • Phase 4 (week 12+): progressive strengthening, proprioception, functional and sport training.
  • Monitor pain, swelling, range, power, gait and function (KOOS/Oxford Knee Score).
  • Complications: stiffness, loss of reduction, infection, DVT, delayed/non-union, osteoarthritis.
  • Early motion and early weight-bearing are now favoured over prolonged immobilisation.

Memory hook: Protect the plateau, then Move, Load, Strengthen, Function.

  • Residual limb: length, shape, scars, skin, oedema, volume, neuromas.
  • Range of motion: watch for hip flexion and abduction contracture.
  • Strength: hip abductors and extensors (main muscles for walking with a prosthesis).
  • Sensation and pain: phantom sensation and phantom limb pain.
  • Balance and mobility: transfers, static/dynamic balance, gait.
  • Functional level: assign the K-level (0–4) for prosthetic prescription.
  • Prosthetic fit: socket comfort score, suspension, alignment, skin response.
  • Outcome measures: Amputee Mobility Predictor, Timed Up and Go, 2-minute and 6-minute walk tests, Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire, PLUS-M.
  • Also assess mood, motivation and cardiopulmonary fitness.
  • Reassess before and after prosthetic fitting to track change.

Q9. Describe various outcome measures used for low back pain.

Examiners want outcome measures grouped into pain, disability, psychosocial, quality of life and global change, with the ODI vs RMDQ comparison.

  • Low back pain is multidimensional, so one measure is never enough.
  • Pain: Visual Analogue Scale or Numerical Rating Scale.
  • Disability: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ).
  • ODI = 10 sections, 0–100%; RMDQ = 24 yes/no items, 0–24. They are not interchangeable.
  • Psychosocial: STarT Back Tool, Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire, Pain Catastrophising Scale, Orebro, PHQ-9.
  • Quality of life: SF-36, EQ-5D.
  • Global change: Patient Global Impression of Change.
  • Performance tests: lumbar range of motion, trunk endurance, walking tests.
  • STarT Back stratifies patients into low/medium/high risk and matches treatment.
  • Use the minimal clinically important difference (~30% improvement) to judge real change.
  • Standardise on one disability measure per service for consistency.

Memory hook: Measure low back pain across P-D-P-Q-G — Pain, Disability, Psychosocial, Quality of life, Global change.

Q10. Explain the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults following total knee replacement.

Full answer →

Examiners want both the preoperative fitness/risk criteria and the postoperative fitness-for-progression criteria, using validated tools.

  • Fitness evaluation has two parts: before surgery (is the patient fit for the operation?) and after surgery (is the patient fit to progress and go home?).
  • Pre-op: assess cardiovascular and clot risk (DVT, PE, heart attack, stroke) within 30 days of surgery.
  • Screen functional capacity with a validated tool like the Duke Activity Status Index.
  • If reduced, do an objective test — cardiopulmonary exercise testing (gold standard) or 6-minute walk / sit-to-stand / Timed Up and Go.
  • Optimise comorbidities: diabetes, blood pressure, anaemia, heart and lung disease, obesity, smoking.
  • Check thrombosis and infection risk; review pain medicines.
  • Screen mood and provide education and prehabilitation.
  • Post-op: stable vital signs, controlled pain, no infection/DVT, healing wound.
  • Post-op function: safe transfers, safe walking with the aid, enough knee movement and quadriceps control, good balance.
  • Use outcome measures: Oxford Knee Score or KOOS, range of motion, Timed Up and Go, 6-minute walk test.
  • Improving fitness before surgery (prehabilitation) shortens hospital stay and reduces complications.

Memory hook: Fitness for TKR is H-E-A-R-T-S — History, Exercise capacity, Anaemia, Risk (cardiac), Thrombosis risk, Screening & function.

Sources

  • 2022 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular assessment for non-cardiac surgery. Eur Heart J. 2022.
  • Pre-operative TKR education and prehabilitation: UK modified Delphi study. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2021.
  • Canadian Cardiovascular Society perioperative cardiac risk guidelines. Can J Cardiol. 2017.

Q1. Discuss the interventions to improve muscle performance following flexor tendon repair of the hand.

Full answer →

The examiner wants the phase-wise rehabilitation plan and the reasoning behind early controlled movement.

  • Flexor tendons bend the fingers; a cut tendon is repaired by the surgeon, but it only works well if it slides freely after surgery.
  • The therapist's job: stop the tendon sticking (adhesions), stop it snapping (rupture), and rebuild grip strength.
  • Zone II is the tight tunnel in the finger where tendons stick most easily.
  • Phase 1 (first 3–4 weeks): wear a protective splint; therapist moves the fingers gently; patient does small active holds; exercises every hour, 4–6 sessions a day.
  • Phase 2 (3–6 weeks): start gentle active bending, but only part of the way at first; build to a full fist by about 4–6 weeks.
  • Phase 3 (6–12 weeks): full movement plus light resistance, finger-blocking exercises, and grip strengthening.
  • Phase 4 (after 12 weeks): harder strengthening and practice of real work and daily tasks.
  • Key rule: movement must be early but controlled — the repair is weakest in the first week.
  • Stronger repairs (4–6 stitches) allow more active movement; weak repairs need gentler passive movement.
  • Measure progress with total active motion, grip strength (Jamar) and the DASH score.
  • Newer splints (relative motion flexion, Manchester short splint) let the wrist move earlier and reduce stiffness.
  • Always work with the surgeon on how much load is safe.

Repair the tendon, then make it glide before you make it strong.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • Tang JB, Flexor tendon injuries, Clin Plast Surg, 2019
  • Higgins & Lalonde, Saint John protocol, Plast Reconstr Surg Glob Open, 2016
  • Neiduski & Powell, Flexor tendon rehabilitation in the 21st century, J Hand Ther, 2019

Q2. Explain the educational and behavioural strategies in managing osteoarthritis of knee pain.

Full answer →

The examiner wants the education and behaviour-change strategies that support knee OA management, with their evidence base.

  • Knee OA is not just worn-out cartilage; pain is affected by beliefs, fear and coping.
  • OARSI 2019 says education and exercise are the core treatments — they come first.
  • Teach the patient that pain is a warning signal, not proof of damage.
  • Explain that gentle, regular movement feeds the cartilage and strengthens the muscles.
  • Use self-management programmes: pacing, flare-up plans, problem solving.
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy helps change unhelpful thoughts and fear of movement.
  • Set specific goals and review them; use diaries or apps to track activity.
  • Motivational interviewing and shared decision-making improve sticking to exercise.
  • Weight loss plus exercise is a core treatment for knee OA.
  • Aquatic exercise, Tai Chi and yoga are safe options.
  • Behaviour-change tools: self-monitoring, feedback, prompts, relapse planning.
  • Measure with WOMAC/KOOS, pain score, kinesiophobia and adherence scales.

OA is not wear-and-tear; it is load-and-learn.

Sources
  • OARSI 2019 guidelines, Osteoarthritis and Cartilage
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation, 7th ed., 2019
  • Hurley et al., Arthritis Rheum, 2007

Q3. How do you apply the functional concepts in rehabilitation of adhesive capsulitis of shoulder.

Full answer →

The examiner wants stage-matched, function-oriented rehabilitation of frozen shoulder.

  • Frozen shoulder has three phases: freezing (painful), frozen (stiff), thawing (recovering).
  • Treat each phase differently — match the dose of movement to the pain.
  • Freezing phase: calm the pain first; gentle pendular and assisted exercises, grade I–II mobilisation.
  • Frozen phase: now push range gently — grade III–IV mobilisation, stretching, PNF patterns.
  • Thawing phase: build strength and practise real tasks.
  • Always train the movements the patient actually needs: dressing, hair care, reaching a shelf, hand behind back.
  • Home exercises 3–4 times a day for 10–15 minutes.
  • Use cane/wand, wall slides and pulleys for self-stretching.
  • Stretch the posterior capsule (cross-body, sleeper stretch) and the anterior capsule.
  • Strengthen the rotator cuff and scapular stabilisers.
  • Measure with SPADI/DASH and goniometry.
  • Diabetics do worse and need longer, gentler treatment.

Freezing means calm it, frozen means stretch it, thawing means use it.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, 7th ed., 2021
  • Rangan et al., UK FROST trial, Lancet, 2020
  • Zhang et al., network meta-analysis, Am J Sports Med, 2021

Q4. How would you analyze the selection of exercises to improve postural stability and balance in chronic ankle instability.

Full answer →

The examiner wants a reasoned, deficit-based approach to choosing and progressing balance exercises in CAI.

  • Chronic ankle instability means the ankle keeps giving way after a sprain.
  • It has two parts: loose ligaments (mechanical) and poor control (functional).
  • First assess: Y-Balance/Star Excursion test, single-leg stance, CAIT and FAAM scores, and evertor strength.
  • Choose exercises based on the deficit you find, not one fixed routine.
  • Static balance problem: single-leg stance work.
  • Dynamic balance problem: reaches and wobble board.
  • Reactive problem: hopping, landing, perturbation work.
  • Weakness: train the peroneal and dorsiflexor muscles.
  • Progress: two legs to one, eyes open to closed, firm to soft, easy to hard, single to dual task.
  • Typical dose: 4–6 weeks, three times a week, three to four sets.
  • Gains fade after about six months, so keep a home programme and add strength work.
  • Finish with sport-specific and landing drills before return to play.

Find the deficit, then train that deficit — stable to unstable, eyes open to closed.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, 7th ed., 2021
  • Mollà-Casanova et al., Clin Rehabil, 2021
  • J Foot Ankle Res, supervised balance training one-year study, 2022

Q5. Describe the functional training methods in treatment of musculoskeletal conditions.

Full answer →

The examiner wants the definition, principles and methods of functional (task-oriented) training in MSK conditions.

  • Functional training means practising the real tasks the patient needs, not just single muscles.
  • It works because the nervous system learns skills through repeated, meaningful practice.
  • Training is specific: the closer the exercise to the real task, the better the transfer.
  • Use a continuum: isolated exercise → combined movement → real tasks → work/sport.
  • Task-oriented training: practise reaching, lifting, dressing, stairs, work.
  • Motor skill training: change how the patient performs a painful activity (good for back pain).
  • Work simulation and work conditioning prepare the patient to return to the job.
  • Graded activity/graded exposure helps overcome fear of movement.
  • Key principles: specificity, overload, progression, feedback, variability, individualisation.
  • Measure with the Patient-Specific Functional Scale, DASH, WOMAC and work measures.
  • Evidence supports task-oriented exercise after shoulder fracture and hip replacement.
  • Person-specific motor skill training beats plain strengthening for chronic low back pain.

Train the task, not just the tissue.

Sources
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation, 7th ed., 2019
  • Monticone et al., BMC Musculoskelet Disord, 2021
  • van Dillen et al., JAMA Neurology, 2021

Q6. How do you distinguish and prioritize the selection of different manual therapy methods for chronic non-specific neck pain.

Full answer →

The examiner wants how to tell the manual therapy methods apart and how to decide which to use first.

  • Chronic non-specific neck pain has no single cause, so treatment is multimodal.
  • Manual therapy is one part of care — it must be combined with exercise and education.
  • Mobilisation = gentle, slow, graded movements. Manipulation = one quick thrust.
  • Other methods: Mulligan SNAGs, muscle energy technique, myofascial release, soft-tissue massage, neural mobilisation.
  • First classify the patient: mobility deficit, coordination problem, headache, or radiating pain.
  • Mobility deficit: use cervical and thoracic manipulation or mobilisation.
  • Coordination problem/whiplash: mobilisation plus graded exercise and CBT principles.
  • Cervicogenic headache: C1–2 SNAG or upper cervical techniques.
  • Radiating pain: intermittent cervical traction plus mobilisation.
  • Match intensity to irritability: very sore = gentle grades; not sore = firmer grades.
  • Screen for red flags and upper cervical instability before any thrust.
  • Never rely on manual therapy alone — it only helps in the short term.

Classify first, then choose the technique — and always pair it with exercise.

Sources
  • JOSPT neck pain guideline, 2017
  • Bussières et al., J Manipulative Physiol Ther, 2016
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, 7th ed., 2021

Q7. Elaborate the neurological concepts and functional methods in rehabilitation of musculoskeletal dysfunctions.

Full answer →

The examiner wants the neurological basis of MSK rehabilitation and the functional methods that follow from it.

  • MSK problems are not just tissue problems — pain and injury change the nervous system too.
  • The brain has a map of the body that can rewire with use or disuse (neuroplasticity).
  • Chronic pain can disrupt that map, causing poor body awareness and learned non-use.
  • Neurological concepts: neuroplasticity, pain neuromatrix, sensorimotor integration, central sensitisation.
  • Method 1 — pain neuroscience education: explain pain as a warning signal, not damage.
  • Method 2 — graded motor imagery: left/right recognition, then imagined movement, then mirror therapy.
  • Method 3 — sensory retraining: two-point discrimination and touch localisation.
  • Method 4 — motor control retraining: re-teach good movement patterns.
  • Method 5 — task-oriented and functional training to embed new habits.
  • GMI usually runs about six weeks, two weeks per stage.
  • Use pain scores, two-point discrimination and function scales to measure progress.
  • These methods help CRPS, chronic shoulder and back pain, and post-surgery patients.

Pain lives in the brain; retrain the brain to retrain the movement.

Sources
  • O'Sullivan & Schmitz, Physical Rehabilitation, 7th ed., 2019
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • Moseley, Neurology, 2006 (graded motor imagery)
  • RESOLVE trial protocol, 2021

Q8. How do you determine the importance of physical agents in rehabilitation of low back pain.

Full answer →

The examiner wants how to judge the place of physical agents within evidence-based LBP care.

  • Physical agents = heat, cold, TENS, interferential, ultrasound, laser, traction.
  • They mostly give short-term symptom relief; they do not cure back pain.
  • Core treatment is exercise, manual therapy and education.
  • Judge an agent by guidelines, the stage and type of LBP, and the evidence.
  • Acute, very sore back: short-term heat or TENS may help comfort.
  • Chronic back pain: active exercise matters far more than any machine.
  • WHO 2023 says do not routinely use TENS, ultrasound or traction for chronic back pain.
  • JOSPT 2021 says do not use mechanical traction for chronic LBP with leg pain.
  • Traction may help a small selected group with nerve-root signs.
  • Always combine agents with active therapy — avoid passive dependence.
  • Use agents just before exercise so movement is easier.
  • Stop any agent that gives no measurable benefit.

Physical agents are helpers, not heroes — active exercise leads.

Sources
  • JOSPT/AOPT LBP guideline, 2021
  • WHO guideline for chronic primary low back pain, 2023
  • Watson, Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice, 12th ed.
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
910 marks

Q9. Discuss the application of electric currents for tissue healing.

Full answer →

The examiner wants how electric currents are used to promote tissue healing, with current types and parameters.

  • The body makes its own tiny electric current around a wound; ES copies it.
  • This natural current guides healing cells to move into the wound.
  • Electrical stimulation boosts cell migration, new blood vessels, growth factors and germ-killing.
  • It helps chronic wounds that are stuck and also tendon, ligament and bone healing.
  • Main current types: direct current (DC), high-voltage pulsed current (HVPC), microcurrent, pulsed/interferential, and PEMF.
  • HVPC is the most studied for wounds.
  • Typical wound protocol: HVPC about 100–150 pulses per second, comfortable amplitude, 45–60 minutes, three to seven times a week.
  • Polarity matters — cathode over the wound early, anode later.
  • Pulsed or interferential current is used for tendon and ligament repair.
  • PEMF is used for bone and fracture healing.
  • Do not use over the heart with a pacemaker, over pregnancy, cancer or numb skin.
  • Check the skin regularly during treatment.

The body makes its own current of injury — we just copy it.

Sources
  • Watson, Electrotherapy: Evidence-Based Practice, 12th ed.
  • Robertson et al., Electrotherapy Explained, 4th ed.
  • Cochrane review, electrical stimulation for pressure ulcers, 2020
  • Khouri et al., Wound Repair Regen, 2017
1010 marks

Q10. Explain the current designs in assistive technology for work related musculoskeletal disorders.

Full answer →

The examiner wants the range of current assistive technology for WMSDs and the principles of using it.

  • WMSDs come from repetitive work, awkward postures, force and vibration.
  • Assistive technology tries to reduce the load on the back, shoulders, knees and arms.
  • Passive exoskeletons use springs and need no power; good for stooping, overhead and kneeling.
  • Active exoskeletons use motors or air pressure to help lifting and dynamic tasks.
  • Newer devices adapt in real time using sensors and machine learning.
  • Soft exosuits are lighter, textile-based versions.
  • Wearable sensors and smart PPE monitor posture and warn the worker.
  • Ergonomic aids: height-adjustable desks, lift assists, powered tools.
  • Assess risk with REBA, RULA, NIOSH lifting equation and KIM.
  • Follow the hierarchy of controls — fix the task first; exoskeletons are a supplement.
  • Ensure correct fit and training, and watch for new hazards.
  • Avoid over-reliance and use devices alongside job rotation.

Change the task first, the tool second, the worker last.

Sources
  • NIOSH science bulletin, exoskeletons in construction, 2022
  • Sensors systematic review, industrial exoskeletons, 2022
  • Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise, 7th ed., 2018
  • Dutton, Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation and Intervention, 5th ed.

Glossary of difficult terms (76)

Dotted-underlined words also show the definition on hover or tap.

  • allodynia — Pain from a stimulus that is not normally painful.
  • arthrogenic muscle inhibition — Reflex weakness of a muscle caused by a problem inside its joint (abbreviated AMI).
  • arthrokinematics — The small gliding, rolling and spinning movements between joint surfaces.
  • atrophy — Wasting or shrinking of muscle or tissue.
  • biomechanics — The study of the mechanical laws relating to the movement of living organisms.
  • biopsychosocial — An approach that considers biological, psychological and social factors together.
  • capsular pattern — The characteristic order in which a joint loses range when the whole capsule is involved.
  • capsule — The fibrous sleeve that surrounds and stabilises a joint.
  • catastrophising — Interpreting pain in an exaggerated, worst-case way.
  • central sensitisation — Increased excitability of the central nervous system that makes normal inputs feel painful.
  • collagen — The main structural protein in tendon, ligament, skin and bone.
  • concentric — Muscle work while it shortens under load (the lifting phase).
  • contracture — A permanent tightening or shortening of tissue that restricts movement.
  • contraindication — A condition that makes a treatment unsafe or inadvisable.
  • creep — Slow progressive lengthening of tissue under a constant sustained load over time.
  • cryotherapy — Treatment using cold.
  • dermatome — The area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • dorsal horn — The rear part of the spinal cord's grey matter where sensory nerves first relay pain signals.
  • dorsiflexion — Bending the ankle or wrist so the angle at the front decreases (e.g. lifting the toes up).
  • eccentric — Muscle work while it lengthens under load (the lowering phase).
  • effleurage — A smooth gliding massage stroke.
  • effusion — Fluid collecting inside a joint.
  • electrotherapy — Treatment using electrical currents or electromagnetic energy.
  • end-feel — The quality of resistance felt at the very end of a joint's movement, used to judge what limits it.
  • eversion — Turning the sole of the foot outward.
  • fear-avoidance — Avoiding activity because of fear of pain, which over time worsens disability.
  • gait — The manner of walking.
  • gate control theory — The idea that non-painful input (rubbing, TENS) can 'close a gate' in the spinal cord and reduce pain.
  • golgi tendon organ — A sensor in tendon that detects tension and helps regulate muscle force.
  • goniometry — Measuring joint angles with a goniometer.
  • hyperalgesia — An increased sensitivity to pain.
  • hypermobility — Excessive movement at a joint, usually from lax or torn ligaments.
  • hypertrophy — An increase in muscle or tissue size.
  • hypomobility — Reduced movement at a joint, usually from tight or stiff tissue.
  • ICF — The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health.
  • inflammation — The body's protective response to injury - heat, redness, swelling and pain.
  • inversion — Turning the sole of the foot inward.
  • isometric — A muscle contraction with no change in length (no joint movement).
  • joint play — The small accessory movement available at a joint beyond voluntary control.
  • kinesiophobia — Fear of movement or of re-injury.
  • laser therapy — Red/near-infrared light therapy that stimulates cell repair (photobiomodulation).
  • ligament — Strong fibrous tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises a joint.
  • manipulation — A quick, small thrust applied to a joint by a clinician.
  • manual muscle testing — Grading a muscle's strength by resisting a voluntary contraction (abbreviated MMT).
  • mechanoreceptors — Sensory receptors that detect mechanical stimuli such as touch, pressure and joint position.
  • mechanotransduction — How cells turn mechanical load into chemical signals that change the tissue.
  • moment arm — The perpendicular distance from a force to the joint axis; a longer moment arm produces more torque.
  • muscle spindle — A stretch sensor inside muscle that helps control posture and movement.
  • myofascial — Relating to muscle and its surrounding fascia.
  • myotome — The group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • neurodynamic — Relating to the mechanical and physiological function of nerves; neural mobilisation treats nerve sensitivity.
  • nociceptive — Relating to the detection of painful stimuli.
  • nociceptor — A sensory nerve ending that detects painful or tissue-damaging stimuli.
  • oedema — Swelling caused by fluid trapped in the tissues.
  • osteokinematics — The visible movements of bones at a joint, such as flexion and extension.
  • outcome measure — A standardised tool used to measure a patient's status or change over time.
  • palpation — Examining the body by touch to feel for tenderness, swelling or tissue change.
  • plantarflexion — Pointing the foot downward, as when standing on tiptoe.
  • posture — The position of the body and its parts relative to gravity.
  • precaution — A situation requiring extra care during treatment.
  • proprioception — The sense of body and joint position and movement.
  • proprioceptive — Relating to the body's sense of position and movement.
  • radiculopathy — A nerve-root problem causing pain, numbness or weakness along a limb.
  • range of motion — How far a joint can move (abbreviated ROM).
  • red flag — A sign or symptom suggesting serious pathology that needs medical referral.
  • ROM — Short for range of motion - how far a joint can move.
  • sensitivity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who have the condition.
  • special test — A clinical test used to confirm or rule out a specific structure or condition.
  • specificity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have the condition.
  • synovial — Relating to the fluid-filled lining of a joint.
  • tendinopathy — A tendon disorder causing pain and reduced function.
  • tendon — Strong fibrous tissue that attaches muscle to bone.
  • TENS — Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation - a mild current passed through the skin to relieve pain.
  • torque — A turning force around an axis - the product of force and its moment arm.
  • traction — A gentle pulling force applied to a joint or the spine to relieve pressure.
  • trigger point — A tender, tight knot in a muscle that can refer pain elsewhere.
